0.title: Proverbs: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Knowledge
0.overview:
The message. Proverbs teaches us how to live well in God’s world, and it begins where all wisdom must begin: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). Wisdom here is not cleverness but the skill of living rightly before God, in work and money, speech and silence, friendship, sex, marriage and the home. The book sets two ways before every reader, the way of wisdom that leads to life and the way of folly that leads to death, and it pleads with us to choose. Because the God who made the world made it to work his way, his wisdom reaches into the smallest corners of an ordinary day.

Background: the writers. The book opens with “The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel” (1:1). Solomon reigned from about 970 to 930 BC; God gave him “wisdom and understanding beyond measure”, and he “spoke 3,000 proverbs” (1 Kings 4:29, 32). But Proverbs is a collection of collections, and its headings say so: more proverbs of Solomon (10:1), “the words of the wise” (22:17; 24:23), proverbs of Solomon “which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied” (25:1), and the words of Agur (30:1) and of King Lemuel, taught him by his mother (31:1). Hezekiah reigned from about 715 to 686 BC, more than two centuries after Solomon, so the book was gathered over a long time and reached its final form in or after his day. Agur and Lemuel are otherwise unknown; they may have come from Massa, an Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14), men from outside Israel who had come to trust the LORD.

Where Christians differ. Many scholars think chapters 1–9 were written long after Solomon, as a preface to the older collections; others note that a father’s long instructions to his son were an old form well before his day. Part of “the words of the wise” (22:17–24:22) also closely resembles an Egyptian book, the Instruction of Amenemope, which is probably older. This commentary takes the heading at its word, that Solomon is the source of much of the book, while granting that how much of chapters 1–9 is his own cannot be settled. God was free to take up true observations from beyond Israel, as Luke used earlier accounts (Luke 1:1–4), reshape them under the fear of the LORD and make them his word. Israel’s version gives its own reason for every saying: “That your trust may be in the LORD” (22:19).

The world of the book. Proverbs grew up among farmers, traders and royal officials, in towns where business, law and news were all done at the city gate; Wisdom herself calls out “at the entrance of the city gates” (1:21). Every nation of the ancient Near East collected sayings to train its young. Israel’s wisdom shares that form, but ties every saying to the LORD, the God of the covenant.

How to read a proverb. Proverbs is poetry. Most sayings have two lines, the second repeating, sharpening or, very often in chapters 10–15, contrasting the first: “A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother” (10:1). A proverb is a compressed truth about how life in God’s world ordinarily works, not a promise attached to every case. “Train up a child in the way he should go” (22:6) describes the usual fruit of faithful teaching; it does not promise that no child will stray, nor condemn every parent whose child does. The book even sets opposite sayings side by side (26:4–5): wisdom is knowing which fits the moment. And it admits that the harvest of the poor can be “swept away through injustice” (13:23). So read a proverb slowly, and let the rest of the book and of Scripture balance it.

How the book makes its case. After the heading, purpose and motto (1:1–7), chapters 1–9 lay the foundation in longer poems. A father pleads with his son to get wisdom above everything, to “Trust in the LORD with all your heart” (3:5), and to keep away from violent men and from the adulteress whose house leads down to death (1:8–7:27). Between his speeches Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman, calls in the streets (1:20–33), tells how she was beside the LORD at creation (8:22–31), and spreads her feast for the simple, while Folly copies her invitation word for word, and her guests “are in the depths of Sheol” (9:18). Then come the short sayings: Solomon’s main collection (10:1–22:16), the words of the wise (22:17–24:34), the proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men (chapters 25–29), and the words of Agur (chapter 30) and Lemuel (31:1–9). They show what the choice between those two houses looks like on an ordinary Monday: honest scales, a soft answer, a faithful friend, an open hand to the poor. The book closes with an A to Z poem of the excellent wife (31:10–31), Wisdom lived out in a real home, and ends where it began: “a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (31:30). In this commentary chapters 1–4, 8, 9 and 31 have more room, because the whole book stands on them.

Who is Wisdom in chapter 8? Wisdom says, “I was beside him, like a master workman” (8:30). Some Christians read this as a direct description of the eternal Son; in the fourth century Arius used the Greek translation of 8:22, “created”, to argue that the Son was a creature, and the Council of Nicaea rightly rejected him. This commentary’s view is that chapter 8 is poetry: Wisdom is a personification of God’s own wisdom, as Folly is in chapter 9, and the passage says nothing about when the Son began, for he had no beginning. Yet what the poem says of God’s wisdom the New Testament says plainly of Christ: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3).

Where it leads: to Christ. Proverbs leads to Christ first by the need it exposes. Its standard is beautiful, and no one keeps it: “Who can say, ‘I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin’?” (20:9). Solomon himself did not; in old age “his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4). Second, by pattern: the book is a father’s plea for a wise son, and only one Son has fully answered it. Jesus “increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52), and said, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Third, by revealing God’s own wisdom, which came in person: Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Wisdom called, “Come, eat of my bread” (9:5); Jesus cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The New Testament quotes the book as God’s word to the church, on the Lord’s discipline (Hebrews 12:5–6, from 3:11–12), on grace to the humble (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5, from 3:34) and on feeding an enemy (Romans 12:20, from 25:21–22).

For us. Christ “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). So Proverbs is neither a ladder for climbing up to God nor a weight for crushing those who have failed. His righteousness covers the believer who has broken its every line, and “the righteous falls seven times and rises again” (24:16). His Spirit makes his wisdom ours, a little more each day. So read Proverbs a few sayings at a time, and let it reach your tongue, your wallet, your friendships and your heart. And when you feel how little wisdom you have: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5).

1.title: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Knowledge

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Why This Book Was Written
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any saying, the book tells us what it is and where wisdom starts. The heading names Solomon, the king God made wise (v. 1). The purpose statement then piles up words for wisdom and sets righteousness, justice and equity in the middle of them, because in this book wisdom is never separated from being good (vv. 2–3). It is written for the simple and the young, who do not yet know which voices to trust, and for the wise, who know they have not arrived (vv. 4–6). Then comes the motto of the whole book: the fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins, and the fool is the one who will not be taught (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom in Proverbs is skill for living in God's world, and it starts not with a technique but with reverence for God.

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
This book comes from the king God made wise, but its authority rests on the God who gave him wisdom.

The proverbs of Solomon. When God offered Solomon anything he asked, he asked for “an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9), and God gave it. The book gathers his sayings and those of others (see the introduction). The Hebrew word for proverbs, mashal, is a saying that often sets two things side by side so that one throws light on the other. Other nations collected such sayings too; Israel’s book roots every one in the fear of the LORD (v. 7).

Where its authority rests. Not on Solomon’s brilliance: he ended badly, his heart turned by the very things this book warns against (1 Kings 11:4). It rests on the God who gave him wisdom and then gave these sayings to his people.

Greater than Solomon. There is one more name behind this one. Jesus said of himself, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). The queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon; the reader of Proverbs has the wiser King close at hand, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).
verseByVerse.note: Solomon is credited with 3,000 proverbs. The book also gathers sayings of “the wise,” proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men, and the words of Agur and Lemuel.

verseByVerse.quote: To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight, to receive instruction in wise dealing, in righteousness, justice, and equity; to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book exists to make people skilled at living rightly, and it is written especially for those who are easily led.

To know wisdom and instruction. Instruction appears twice: wisdom is not only information received but a shaping that sometimes hurts, like the LORD’s discipline of his sons in 3:11, quoted in Hebrews 12:5–6.

Righteousness, justice, and equity. Inside the list sit three moral words. Wisdom in this book is not cleverness; a con man can be clever. It is the skill of living rightly, and it is never separated from being good.

To give prudence to the simple. Two audiences are named. The simple are not the mentally slow but the easily led, like a door that swings with any wind, believing whatever they heard last. The youth stands at the start of life with every road open. Proverbs is for anyone who does not yet know which voices to trust: teenagers, and every adult honest about how easily he is still persuaded.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the wise hear and increase in learning, and the one who understands obtain guidance, to understand a proverb and a saying, the words of the wise and their riddles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book is for the wise too, because wisdom always knows it has more to learn.

Let the wise hear and increase in learning. In case the wise reader thinks the book is for other people, the purpose statement turns to him. The fool in this book is always sure; the wise man is always learning.

To understand a proverb and a saying. Proverbs have to be understood, not merely memorised. Each is a compressed truth about how life usually goes, not a guarantee, which is why 26:4 and 26:5 can sit side by side and say opposite things about answering a fool. Riddles here are not puzzles for fun but sayings whose meaning has to be dug for.

Try it as a test. When did you last change your mind about something important because someone corrected you? If you cannot remember, the verse is aimed at you.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All true knowledge starts with reverent awe before the LORD, and the fool’s problem is not his mind but his refusal to be taught. This is the motto of the whole book.

The fear of the LORD. Not cringing terror, as though God were a tyrant; nor only respect, as though he were a distinguished elder. It is the settled awareness that the LORD, the God of Israel, is really there, is holy, sees everything, and is the one you will answer to. It is the reverence of a child who loves his father and would not for the world grieve him, and who also knows his father is not to be trifled with. Both together.

The beginning of knowledge. The Hebrew word means both the first step and the chief part. You cannot start being wise without it, and you never graduate beyond it. A person can be highly educated and successful and still not have begun.

Fools despise wisdom and instruction. The fool in Proverbs is not stupid. He is someone who will not be told; the problem is not in his head but in his will.

Repeated through Scripture. The motto returns in almost the same words at 9:10, and the book closes on the same note: “a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (31:30). The rest of Scripture repeats it: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 111:10), and Job’s great poem on the search for wisdom ends, “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” (Job 28:28).

Where real knowledge begins. For a Christian the motto points to a person. God has made Christ “wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). To fear the LORD now is to bow before the Son, and that is where real knowledge begins.

Doesn’t education make people good? It is one of the quiet faiths of the modern world: when people behave badly, we assume they lack information and answer with a course or a campaign. Socrates held something like it: no one, he argued, does wrong knowingly. The twentieth century strained that faith to breaking point. Germany in the 1930s had some of the finest universities on earth, and doctors, lawyers and professors put their training at the service of horrors. Proverbs is not surprised. Its fool is rarely ignorant; he simply will not bow, and knowledge without the fear of the LORD only makes a cleverer sinner. So the gospel comes not chiefly as better information but as a new heart, and the wisdom of God arrived not as a lecture but as a person, Christ crucified, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), so that people who knew a great deal and loved the wrong things could be made new from the inside.
verseByVerse.note: The book closes on the same note: a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised (31:30).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A father speaks, and the first danger he names is not a lie about God but an invitation to join a gang. He grounds his plea in the home: a father’s instruction and a mother’s teaching are a crown, not a chain (vv. 8–9). Then he puts the gang’s pitch in their own words, so that his son will recognise it: come with us, belong, get rich quickly, share one purse (vv. 10–14). His answer is to stay off their road altogether (v. 15), and his reason is that their trap is really set for themselves. Greed for unjust gain does not just cost money; it takes the life of the one who has it (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The first temptation in the book is not lust but belonging, and the first lie is that greed can be shared without cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching, for they are a graceful garland for your head and pendants for your neck.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is first learned at home, from a father and a mother, and their teaching is a crown, not a chain.

Hear, my son, your father’s instruction. From here to the end of chapter 9, most of the book is a father speaking to his son. Wisdom is taught first at the kitchen table, and in a world where a mother’s voice could be discounted, the book gives your mother’s teaching the same weight as the father’s.

A graceful garland for your head. Parental instruction is not a weight hung round the neck but jewellery. A young man often feels it as a chain; the father says it is a crown. The picture returns in 4:9.

Lois and Eunice. Timothy knew what this looks like. Paul reminds him of the faith that dwelt “first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5), and that “from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings” (2 Timothy 3:15). A mother reading Scripture to a child is doing the work of Proverbs 1.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, "Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason; like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit; we shall find all precious goods, we shall fill our houses with plunder; throw in your lot among us; we will all have one purse"—
verseByVerse.commentary:
When sinners invite you, say no, and learn to recognise their pitch: belonging first, then easy money.

Do not consent. The first warning in the book is short and plain. Temptation is not sin; the son cannot stop sinners from asking, but he can answer no, and the whole battle comes down to one word.

Come with us. The father quotes the gang’s pitch so that his son will recognise it. Before it is an offer of money, it is an offer of belonging. A lonely young man is offered a crew.

Alive, and whole. They speak of swallowing people “alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit”, as the grave swallows the dead. It sounds exciting said quickly; said slowly, it is the language of murderers. Then the money, and the clinching promise of one purse: shared risk, shared reward, loyalty.

We will all have one purse. The Gospels show how that purse ends. Among the Twelve, Judas was the one “having charge of the moneybag”, and “he used to help himself to what was put into it” (John 12:6). He sold innocent blood for thirty pieces of silver, then came back saying, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” The priests who had paid him answered, “What is that to us? See to it yourself” (Matthew 27:4). That is the loyalty of the one purse: the gang that promises to share everything leaves you alone with the guilt.

Not alone. The son does not say no in his own strength. He speaks as a son, with a father’s love and the LORD’s covenant behind him, and for the Christian the grace that saves also trains us “to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions” (Titus 2:12), by the Spirit who gives the strength to refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: my son, do not walk in the way with them; hold back your foot from their paths, for their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood. For in vain is a net spread in the sight of any bird, but these men lie in wait for their own blood; they set an ambush for their own lives. Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay off the road altogether, because the trap the greedy set for others is really set for themselves.

Hold back your foot from their paths. The counsel is physical. Sin is usually reached by steps, not leaps. Some temptations are resisted by debate; most are resisted by not being there.

In vain is a net spread. These men build a trap for others and walk into it themselves. Their greed does not merely cost them their money; it owns them and then kills them: “it takes away the life of its possessors.” Judas again: he “acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness”, and died in it (Acts 1:18).

Their feet run to evil. Isaiah says nearly the same of a whole nation, “Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed innocent blood” (Isaiah 59:7), and Paul gathers those words into his indictment of the human race: “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Romans 3:15). The gang is not an unusual kind of human being. It is what every heart is capable of when greed and bad company come together. That is why the son needs more than good advice: he needs Christ, who was tempted in every way and did not sin (Hebrews 4:15), who obeyed in his place, and whose mercy meets even the one who has already gone with the gang.

Greedy for unjust gain. Paul says the same of the respectable version of this sin: “those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare” (1 Timothy 6:9). The snare is the same in an alley or an office. Is there any gain in my life that I could only have by someone else’s loss? That is the net, and I can see it.

Uncertain wording. The saying about the bird (v. 17) is compressed. It may mean that a bird which sees the net avoids it, so these men are more foolish than a bird; or that the bird sees only the grain and flies in anyway, as these men see the danger and want the plunder more. Either way verse 18 makes the point: their ambush is set for their own lives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–33 — Wisdom Cries Aloud in the Street
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now a second voice answers the gang, and it calls in the same streets. Wisdom, pictured as a woman, shouts in the markets and at the city gate, where everyone can hear (vv. 20–21). She pleads with the simple, the scoffers and the fools to turn, and promises to pour out her heart to them (vv. 22–23). But she also warns: those who refuse her will one day call and not be answered, and will eat the fruit of their own choices (vv. 24–31). The chapter ends with two destinies set side by side: complacency kills the simple, but whoever listens to Wisdom will live secure, without dread of disaster (vv. 32–33).
verseByVerse.theology: The same voice that pleads also warns that the day of pleading ends. The New Testament hears that voice in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice; at the head of the noisy streets she cries out; at the entrance of the city gates she speaks:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom does not hide; she calls out in the busiest public places, so no one perishes because the truth was kept from him.

Wisdom cries aloud in the street. She speaks not in a temple or a hermit’s cave but in the market and at the city gate, where business and lawsuits were settled. The sinners of verse 11 called the young man in the street; Wisdom shouts in the same street, over the traffic. She goes where the gang goes.

Why is Wisdom a woman? The Hebrew word for wisdom is feminine, and the book sets her against another woman, Folly (9:13–18). She is not a goddess but God’s own wisdom given a voice.

He walked into the same streets. The New Testament hears this voice in Jesus. “On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’” (John 7:37). He spoke of himself in Wisdom’s terms: “wisdom is justified by her deeds” (Matthew 11:19). And where Luke records “the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles’” (Luke 11:49), Matthew records Jesus saying in his own person, “Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes” (Matthew 23:34). Wisdom in this poem is a figure of speech, not a secret name for Jesus (see the introduction and the note on 8:22–31); but the wisdom of God she gives a voice to took flesh in him, “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and walked into the same streets.
verseByVerse.note: Wisdom speaks again, at greater length, in 8:1-36 and 9:1-6.

verseByVerse.quote: "How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge? If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you; I will make my words known to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom pleads with those who drift, mock and refuse: turn, and she will give herself to you.

How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? Three kinds of people, a descending staircase: the simple drift, scoffers mock what they have not considered, fools hate knowledge. The chilling word is love: the simple prefer their ignorance, because never making up your mind means never having to commit yourself. How long? is the impatience of love, like a mother calling a child in from the road.

If you turn at my reproof. Wisdom does not ask the simple to become wise first and then come. She asks them to turn, and then she will give herself: her spirit and her words. The turning is repentance; the gift is grace.

I will pour out my spirit to you. Read with the whole Bible open, the line has a fuller echo. God said through Joel, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28), and Peter declared it fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Jesus’ cry at the feast was about exactly this: “Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:39). What Wisdom offers in the street, Christ, the wisdom of God, has poured out on his people.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for spirit (ruach) can also mean breath or mind, and some translations render the line I will pour out my thoughts to you, matching the parallel “I will make my words known to you.” In its own setting that is probably the sense: Wisdom will open her heart in words. The echo of Joel is a reading with the whole Bible open, not a claim about what the first hearers understood.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I have called and you refused to listen, have stretched out my hand and no one has heeded, because you have ignored all my counsel and would have none of my reproof, I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you, when terror strikes you like a storm and your calamity comes like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who keep refusing Wisdom’s outstretched hand will find that disaster comes, and that their defiance was absurd.

I have called and you refused to listen. Now the tone is frightening. Her outstretched hand reaches to pull a person out of danger. Paul uses the same picture of God with Israel: “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people” (Romans 10:21).

I also will laugh at your calamity. How can Wisdom laugh at anyone’s disaster? Not at the suffering person, but at the folly that thought it could defy God and win. Psalm 2 uses the same figure of the kings who plot against the LORD and his Anointed: “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4). The laughter shows how absurd it is to rebel against God; every warning the fool dismissed as overcautious has come true.

Your calamity comes like a whirlwind. The consequences of folly arrive like weather, suddenly and from every side: a marriage that ends, a career that collapses in a week, after years of warnings ignored.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer; they will seek me diligently but will not find me. Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There comes a time when it is too late, and God’s judgment on those who refused him is to give them what they chose.

They will call upon me, but I will not answer. A hard sentence. Proverbs 8 promises, “those who seek me diligently find me” (8:17); here the same seeking finds nothing. The difference is what they are seeking. Verse 29 explains: “they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD.” They want the consequences removed, not the heart changed. It is the cry of Esau, who “found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears” (Hebrews 12:17). He wanted the blessing back, not the God of the blessing.

Did not choose the fear of the LORD. The verb is choose. The fool was not unlucky; he decided, again and again, until the decisions became who he was. So God gives such people what they chose, in full. They wanted their own way; now they “have their fill of their own devices.” The worst thing God can do to a person who insists on his own way is to let him have it.

Too late. The word then is real: a time comes when it is too late. Jesus told of the master of the house who has “risen and shut the door”, and those outside knocking and calling, “Lord, open to us” (Luke 13:25). The door does not stay open forever. That is why the Bible’s urgency always falls on the present: “Seek the LORD while he may be found” (Isaiah 55:6); “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

A word to the anxious. If you fear that you have sought God too late, your anxiety is itself evidence that you are not the person of verse 29. The people in this verse do not grieve that they hated the fear of the LORD. They only grieve the storm.

verseByVerse.quote: For the simple are killed by their turning away, and the complacency of fools destroys them; but whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Comfortable drifting destroys people, but whoever listens to Wisdom lives secure, without dread of what is coming.

The simple are killed by their turning away. Two killers are named, and neither is dramatic. Turning away: not open rebellion, just walking off when Wisdom is talking. And complacency: the ease of a person who assumes tomorrow will look like today. Jesus told of a rich man who said to his soul, “relax, eat, drink, be merry. But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you’” (Luke 12:19–20). Most people are destroyed not by one great act of defiance but by being comfortable.

Whoever listens to me will dwell secure. The chapter ends with rest. The fool was falsely at ease and destroyed by it; the one who listens to Wisdom is truly at ease, without dread of disaster: not necessarily without disaster, but without dread of it. His security rests on something the storm cannot take.

The same offer of rest. Christ called as Wisdom called, with the same offer: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15). The whole book is an invitation to be the person of verse 33, and it begins by bowing before the Lord who is himself the wisdom of God.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel:<sup>2</sup>To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight,<sup>3</sup>to receive instruction in wise dealing, in righteousness, justice, and equity;<sup>4</sup>to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth—<sup>5</sup>Let the wise hear and increase in learning, and the one who understands obtain guidance,<sup>6</sup>to understand a proverb and a saying, the words of the wise and their riddles.<sup>7</sup>The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.<sup>8</sup>Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching,<sup>9</sup>for they are a graceful garland for your head and pendants for your neck.<sup>10</sup>My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent.<sup>11</sup>If they say, "Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason;<sup>12</sup>like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit;<sup>13</sup>we shall find all precious goods, we shall fill our houses with plunder;<sup>14</sup>throw in your lot among us; we will all have one purse"—<sup>15</sup>my son, do not walk in the way with them; hold back your foot from their paths,<sup>16</sup>for their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood.<sup>17</sup>For in vain is a net spread in the sight of any bird,<sup>18</sup>but these men lie in wait for their own blood; they set an ambush for their own lives.<sup>19</sup>Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors.<sup>20</sup>Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice;<sup>21</sup>at the head of the noisy streets she cries out; at the entrance of the city gates she speaks:<sup>22</sup>"How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge?<sup>23</sup>If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you; I will make my words known to you.<sup>24</sup>Because I have called and you refused to listen, have stretched out my hand and no one has heeded,<sup>25</sup>because you have ignored all my counsel and would have none of my reproof,<sup>26</sup>I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you,<sup>27</sup>when terror strikes you like a storm and your calamity comes like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish come upon you.<sup>28</sup>Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer; they will seek me diligently but will not find me.<sup>29</sup>Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD,<sup>30</sup>would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof,<sup>31</sup>therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices.<sup>32</sup>For the simple are killed by their turning away, and the complacency of fools destroys them;<sup>33</sup>but whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster."
1.overview:
Where we are. This is the front door of the book. Before a single short saying, Proverbs tells us what it is for and where wisdom starts, then opens the long poems of chapters 1–9, where a father pleads with his son and Wisdom calls in the streets.

The message. Wisdom is the skill of living rightly in God’s world, and it begins not with a high IQ but with the fear of the LORD. Two voices compete for every young life: the voice of sinners offering easy money and a place to belong, and the voice of Wisdom calling in the open street. Whoever listens to Wisdom lives secure; whoever turns away is destroyed, not by bad luck but by getting exactly what he chose.

Why it was said. The book was shaped to train Israel’s young in a world full of plausible voices (see the introduction). They were as easily led as we are, and it names their danger plainly: not ignorance, but the will that will not be told.

How the chapter makes its case. The heading names Solomon and states the book’s purpose: prudence for the simple and the young, and more learning for the wise (vv. 1–6). Then comes the motto of the whole book: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (v. 7). A father speaks next, and the first danger he names is a gang whose offer is belonging and plunder, but whose ambush is set for their own lives (vv. 8–19). Finally Wisdom shouts at the city gate, pleading with the simple, the scoffers and the fools to turn, warning that a day comes when calling is too late, and promising rest to all who listen (vv. 20–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by God’s character revealed in him and by the need the chapter exposes. Wisdom’s voice in the street, calling the simple to turn and offering to pour out her spirit, is heard again in Jesus, who “stood up and cried out, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’” (John 7:37), and whom Paul calls “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). And the gang’s violence is not a strange evil: Paul uses its words of us all (Romans 3:15), so the son needs more than advice. He needs the Son who refused every enticement and bore the judgment the foolish deserve.

For us. The first question Proverbs asks is not how clever you are but where you stand before God. Listen for the voices that are quietly recruiting you, and turn now, while Wisdom is still calling: Christ still says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
1.theology:
Wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD, the reverent and loving awareness of the holy God (v. 7; 9:10; Ps 111:10). Folly is a matter of the will, not the intellect: fools despise wisdom. Wisdom is inseparable from righteousness, justice and equity (v. 3).

Temptation offers belonging before it offers gain, and sin is self-destructive: the ambush is set for the ambushers (vv. 10-19; Rom 3:15; 1 Tim 6:9).

Wisdom calls publicly and freely, offers her spirit to those who turn (v. 23; Acts 2:17), and warns that the time of calling ends (vv. 24-31; Luke 13:25). The New Testament presents Christ as the Wisdom of God who cries out and gives rest (Luke 11:49; John 7:37; 1 Cor 1:24, 30; Col 2:3).
1.examples: A teenager invited into a group chat that mocks someone, or a colleague offered a cut of a scheme everyone else is in on, hears the gang's first words, Come with us, and can learn to answer no. A mother reading Scripture to a child at bedtime is doing what Lois and Eunice did. And someone carrying an anxious fear of having left it too late can take heart from verse 33: the promise is not a life without disaster, but a life without dread of it.

keyVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.
keyVerse.note: This is the motto of the whole book, repeated at 9:10 and echoed in its last chapter (31:30). Every saying that follows assumes it: wisdom starts with bowing before the LORD, and folly is not a lack of brains but a refusal to be taught. For the Christian, to fear the LORD is now to bow before Christ, whom God made “our wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

1.reflection:
Verse 7 says knowledge begins with the fear of the LORD. How would you explain that fear to a friend who thinks it means being frightened of God? Where in your life do you most need it?

The gang’s first words are “Come with us” (v. 11): they offer belonging before money. What groups or voices offer young people (or you) a place to belong at the cost of your conscience today?

Verses 17–19 say that greed “takes away the life of its possessors.” Where have you seen someone caught in a net they set for others? Is there any gain in your life that depends on someone else’s loss?

Wisdom calls in the busiest streets, and Jesus cried out in the same way (John 7:37). Why do you think the people of verses 28–32 refused to listen until it was too late? How does Christ’s invitation (Matthew 11:28) answer the fear that we may have left it too late?

2.title: If You Seek It Like Silver

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Search and the Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Search for wisdom with all your heart and you will find God himself, because he is the one who gives it. The father lays down the conditions, each stronger than the last: receive my words, treasure them, lean in to listen, cry out for understanding, dig for it like silver (vv. 1–4). Then comes the result: the son will understand the fear of the LORD and know God, who gives wisdom from his mouth and guards those who walk with him (vv. 5–8). And knowing God, he will understand how to live: wisdom will come into his heart, become a pleasure instead of a duty, and stand guard over him (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The effort is ours and the gift is God's, and neither cancels the other.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you, making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding; yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom comes to those who want it badly enough to treasure it, ask for it aloud and dig for it like buried silver.

If you receive my words. In Hebrew the chapter is one sentence, a chain of if and then, and the conditions grow stronger step by step. A word heard and forgotten has not been received; to treasure up is to store it somewhere safe, within reach. Inclining your heart is leaning toward a speaker so as not to miss a word: hearing that goes inward.

Raise your voice for understanding. In chapter 1 Wisdom raised her voice in the street (1:20). Now the son is to raise his voice for her: she calls; he calls back. The one who wants wisdom must ask out loud, which means admitting he lacks it. “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God” (James 1:5).

Seek it like silver. Now the chapter’s main picture: men tunnelling into rock and spending years on the hope of a seam. Job’s great poem describes exactly that, “Surely there is a mine for silver”, and then asks, “But where shall wisdom be found?” (Job 28:1, 12).

The treasure has a name. Jesus told of a man who found “treasure hidden in a field”: “Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44). The treasure at the bottom of this mine is Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), and the LORD who gives wisdom (v. 6) gives it by his Spirit to those who ask.

What do you search for with that kind of energy? A promotion, a house, a relationship? Those are not wrong, but wisdom deserves at least as much. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

How do I treasure up his words? Keep a time and a place. Miners go back to the same seam: choose a set time, even fifteen minutes before work, and read a passage right through rather than a verse snatched from a feed. Ask as you dig. Begin with the prayer of verse 3, and bring two questions to the text: what does this show me of God, and what does it ask of me? Carry one piece out. Write a verse on a card or in your phone and say it over at the bus stop or the sink. Dig with others. Listen to the sermon expecting to find something, and talk about it over lunch. You will not strike silver every day, but you are not digging blind.

verseByVerse.quote: then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding; he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity, guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The searcher went looking for wisdom and found God, because wisdom is finally his gift, not our wage.

Find the knowledge of God. Here is the then. The fear of the LORD is where wisdom begins (1:7) and where the search ends. The treasure at the bottom of the mine is not a technique for living but the knowledge of God: not facts about him, but knowing him.

The LORD gives wisdom. Verse 6 is the hinge of the chapter. After four verses of digging, the reason anyone finds wisdom is that the LORD gives it; nobody earns it the way a miner earns silver. It comes from his mouth, which means it comes by his word.

He stores up sound wisdom for the upright. The son was to treasure up the father’s words (v. 1); here God stores up wisdom for the upright, laying up a supply before they need it, and he is their shield. The son on this road is not walking it alone.

The way of his saints. His saints are not an elite of especially holy people, but those bound to God in his covenant love. Every believer walking the path of justice has God on watch over that path.

Both halves together. The New Testament holds effort and grace together in the same way: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). The effort does not cancel the grace, nor the grace make the effort pointless. “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7).

Uncertain wording. The word translated sound wisdom (tushiyyah) is rare and hard to pin down. It seems to mean the practical good sense that makes things succeed, so some translations render it “success”. Either way, God holds in store for the upright what they need to live well.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path; for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul; discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing God teaches a person how to live, and what began as hard digging becomes a delight that guards him from within.

Then you will understand righteousness. The second then is about knowing how to live, and the order matters: Proverbs never offers moral skill cut off from God; it comes out of knowing him. Righteousness and justice and equity are the three words of the book’s purpose statement (1:3); this is where the book was heading. And every good path is generous: wisdom does not only tell a person what to avoid; it opens every good road there is.

Wisdom will come into your heart. At first the son searches as a duty, digging because his father told him to. But wisdom will come into his heart, and then it becomes pleasant. This is what God, by his Spirit, does to the desires of those he teaches. The psalmist could say, “The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces” (Psalm 119:72). The search for silver ends with the searcher preferring what he found to silver.

Discretion will watch over you. God watched over the way of his saints (v. 8); now the wisdom he gave watches from inside. Discretion is the ability to see a situation for what it is before you are in the middle of it: to recognise the smooth voice on the first sentence rather than the fifth. That is what the rest of the chapter needs.

If you are still digging. If obedience still feels like a mine shaft to you, keep digging. The promise is that it will not always feel that way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — Delivered from Two Ways of Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wisdom God gives is a rescuer, and the father names two dangers it rescues from, both of them smooth talkers. The first is a kind of man: one whose speech twists right and wrong, who has left the straight road for the dark, and who has come to enjoy evil (vv. 12–15). The second is the forbidden woman, who has broken faith with her husband and with God, and whose house, for all its welcome, is sliding down to the dead (vv. 16–19). Against both, wisdom sets the young man on the road of the good, and the chapter ends with two futures: the upright remain in the land God gives, and the treacherous are rooted out of it (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The two great seductions of a young man, crooked company and illicit sex, both speak smoothly and both lead down.

verseByVerse.quote: delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech, who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness, who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil, men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom rescues you from men who talk evil into sounding reasonable and who have come to enjoy it.

Men of perverted speech. Wisdom’s first rescue is from a kind of man known by his speech: talk that twists things, that makes the wrong sound reasonable and the right sound naive. The gang of chapter 1 was dangerous because of what it said: “Come with us” (1:11). Most young people are not dragged into evil. They are talked into it.

The ways of darkness. These men once knew the paths of uprightness; they walked away, and prefer darkness, where they cannot be seen.

Delight in the perverseness of evil. The last stage of corruption: not doing evil reluctantly, but enjoying it, and enjoying it in others. Paul describes the same end of the road: “they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them” (Romans 1:32). When a group laughs together about wrongdoing, that is what verse 14 describes.

Men whose paths are crooked. On a crooked path you cannot see where it bends next; wisdom lets you see the bend before you take it.

verseByVerse.quote: So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words, who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom rescues you from the flattering voice that invites you to break faith, with a spouse and with God at once.

The forbidden woman. Like the men of verse 12, she works by smooth words. Chapter 5 will say her lips “drip honey” and her speech is “smoother than oil” (5:3). Sexual temptation almost never introduces itself as adultery. It introduces itself as being understood, admired, listened to. The discretion of verse 11 is what hears the flattery for what it is.

With her smooth words. Both dangers in this chapter work through words, so both are defeated by a better word: the father’s commandments treasured up in the heart (v. 1), ready to answer the smooth voice.

The covenant of her God. She has left the companion of her youth, her husband, and forgotten the covenant of her God. Marriage in the Bible is never merely a private arrangement between two people; God is party to it. Malachi says it outright: “the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14).

Breaking faith twice. So adultery is not a sin against one person only. It breaks faith with a spouse and with God at the same time. “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4).

The faithful bridegroom. Against her forgetting stands the God who never forgets his covenant, and who has shown it in Christ, the bridegroom who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). His faithfulness is the pattern for every marriage, and the hope of everyone who has broken faith.

Two ways of reading her. The forbidden woman is a real danger: adultery, plainly warned against. She is also the dark counterpart of Lady Wisdom, and in chapter 9 she reappears as Folly herself. The warning is literal, and it also stands for every voice that lures us away from God’s wisdom.

Uncertain wording. “Forbidden woman” is literally “strange woman”, and “adulteress” literally “foreign woman” (see the note). Some think she was a foreigner; but she has a husband and “the covenant of her God”, so she may well be an Israelite, “strange” because she stands outside the boundary God set around marriage: another man’s wife.
verseByVerse.note: “Forbidden woman” is literally “strange woman,” and “adulteress” is literally “foreign woman” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed; none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The road to her house runs down to death, and few who take it find their own way back, but God’s mercy reaches further than the road.

Her house sinks down to death. Her house looks like a house, with a door, a bed, perfume. The father sees what the young man cannot: the whole building is sinking. The departed are the shades in Sheol, the realm of the dead, roused to greet a fallen king in Isaiah 14:9. Chapter 7 ends with the same picture: “Her house is the way to Sheol” (7:27).

None who go to her come back. The warning is meant to frighten. Adultery rarely stays one act. It rewires a person’s desires, breaks trust that is almost never fully rebuilt, wounds children, and often changes the whole direction of a life. “He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself” (6:32).

For those already on that road. A reader who has already been down that road needs the rest of the Bible too. Proverbs describes the destination of the path, not the limit of God’s mercy. David took another man’s wife. When Nathan confronted him, “David said to Nathan, ‘I have sinned against the LORD.’ And Nathan said to David, ‘The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die’” (2 Samuel 12:13). Paul wrote to Corinthians who had been adulterers, “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). No one regains the paths of life by his own strength. Christ brings back people who could not come back.

Uncertain wording. The departed is in Hebrew “the Rephaim” (ESV note), a word used both for the shades of the dead and for an ancient people (Deuteronomy 2:11); here it plainly means the dead. The first line is awkward in Hebrew, since the verb does not quite agree with “house”, and some render it she sinks down to death, which is her home. Either way, to go to her is to go towards the grave.

verseByVerse.quote: So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous. For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it, but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom puts you on the road with the good, which ends in a lasting home in God’s world.

You will walk in the way of the good. After the two warnings, the positive goal. The best protection against bad company is good company: “Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart” (2 Timothy 2:22).

The upright will inhabit the land. For an Israelite, the land meant the inheritance God had promised Abraham, the place of his blessing and presence. To be cut off from it was to lose everything the covenant offered. Psalm 37 says the same: “The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever” (Psalm 37:29).

The treacherous will be rooted out. Two futures: the treacherous are uprooted like a plant that looked established and had no hold; the upright remain. “The world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17).

Jesus widened the promise. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). The land was always a picture of something larger, the whole creation renewed and given to God’s people, secured for them by Christ, the one truly upright man, who was cut off so that they never will be. The silver the young man was told to dig for turns out to be a place in God’s world for ever.

What it does not mean. Proverbs is not promising that every upright person will keep his house or farm in this life; it describes where the two roads finally end.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you,<sup>2</sup>making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding;<sup>3</sup>yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding,<sup>4</sup>if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,<sup>5</sup>then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding;<sup>7</sup>he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity,<sup>8</sup>guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.<sup>9</sup>Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path;<sup>10</sup>for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul;<sup>11</sup>discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,<sup>12</sup>delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech,<sup>13</sup>who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness,<sup>14</sup>who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil,<sup>15</sup>men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.<sup>16</sup>So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words,<sup>17</sup>who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;<sup>18</sup>for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed;<sup>19</sup>none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.<sup>20</sup>So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous.<sup>21</sup>For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it,<sup>22</sup>but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.
2.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 1 Wisdom called in the street and the gang called the young man to join them. Now the father answers both with one long plea: go after wisdom with everything you have.

The message. Search for wisdom as men dig for silver, and you will find something better than wisdom: you will find God, because the LORD himself gives it. The wisdom he gives then gets inside you, becomes your delight, and keeps you from the two smooth voices that destroy young lives, the man who talks you into evil and the woman who talks you out of faithfulness.

Why it was said. The son is at the age when the world starts speaking to him persuasively (see the introduction). The father knows he cannot stand guard over him for ever; his hope is that wisdom, given by God, will stand guard from the inside.

How the chapter makes its case. In Hebrew the chapter is one long sentence built on “if” and “then”. If the son receives the words, cries out for insight and digs for it like hidden treasure (vv. 1–4), then he will find the knowledge of God, who gives wisdom and guards his saints (vv. 5–8). Then he will understand every good path, and wisdom will become pleasant to him and watch over him (vv. 9–11), delivering him from men of perverted speech who delight in evil (vv. 12–15) and from the forbidden woman whose house sinks down to death (vv. 16–19). So he will walk with the good and remain in the land, while the treacherous are rooted out (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him and by promise. The God who “gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding” (v. 6) has spoken his last and fullest word in his Son, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), so the treasure at the bottom of the mine has a name. The covenant faithfulness the adulteress forgets (v. 17) is perfectly kept by Christ, the bridegroom who never betrays his bride. And the promise that the upright will inhabit the land (v. 21) is widened by Jesus: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).

For us. What do you dig for with real energy? God gives his wisdom to people who want it badly enough to ask and search, chiefly in his word, and he makes it sweet to them. And if you have already gone down the road this chapter warns against, the same God brings back people who could never find the way back themselves.
2.theology:
The search for wisdom requires real effort (vv. 1-4), yet wisdom is God's gift from his mouth (v. 6); human seeking and divine giving work together (Phil 2:12-13; Jas 1:5). Its goal is knowing God himself (v. 5), and moral understanding follows from that (v. 9). God changes desire, so that wisdom becomes pleasant (v. 10).

Evil and sexual sin both work through deceptive speech (vv. 12, 16). Marriage is a covenant before God, so adultery breaks faith with God as well as a spouse (v. 17; Mal 2:14). The road of adultery leads to death (vv. 18-19), but the gospel restores the repentant (2 Sam 12:13; 1 Cor 6:11). The inheritance of the land anticipates the meek inheriting the earth (v. 21; Matt 5:5).
2.examples: A student who gives an hour a day to Scripture with the energy others give to exams is digging in the right mine, and may find that what began as duty becomes a delight. Someone who notices a colleague's flattery beginning to feel like being understood can recognise the smooth voice of verse 16 on the first sentence rather than the fifth. And the person who has already gone down that road can read David's story and Paul's such were some of you: the end of the path is not the limit of mercy.

keyVerse.quote: For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding;
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the chapter. After four verses of digging, the reason anyone finds wisdom is that the LORD gives it, and he gives it by his word. The search is real, but it is not a wage: wisdom is a gift, and its fullest form is Christ, the Word made flesh.

2.reflection:
Verses 1–4 describe the search for wisdom as mining for silver. What do people around you search for with that kind of energy? What would it look like for you to “treasure up” God’s words this week?

Verse 6 says “the LORD gives wisdom”, yet verses 1–4 call for hard searching. How do God’s gift and our effort fit together (Philippians 2:12–13)? Where do you tend to lean too far one way?

Both dangers in this chapter work through words: perverted speech and smooth words (vv. 12, 16). What kinds of persuasive talk most easily lead people into sin today, and how does Scripture stored in the heart help us answer them?

Verse 17 says the adulteress “forgets the covenant of her God.” What changes when we see marriage as a covenant God himself witnesses? How does the faithfulness of Christ to his people bring hope to those who have broken faith?

3.title: Trust in the LORD with All Your Heart

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Trust, Honour and the Father's Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lean your whole weight on the LORD, in every part of life, and receive even his hard dealings as a father’s love. The father begins with memory and character: keep my teaching, and wear steadfast love and faithfulness on your neck and heart (vv. 1–4). At the centre stands the call to trust the LORD with all your heart instead of your own understanding, to acknowledge him in all your ways and to turn from evil (vv. 5–8). That trust reaches the bank account, giving God the first and best (vv. 9–10), and it holds in hardship, because the LORD disciplines the son in whom he delights (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Every line in this section is about the heart's posture toward God: trusting him, honouring him, and not resenting him when he corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments, for length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep the father’s teaching in your heart, because God’s commands are the shape of a whole and peaceful life.

Do not forget my teaching. The father begins with memory and the heart. Most people who abandon what they were taught do not reject it in one decision; they forget it slowly, by not returning to it. So the teaching is to be kept in the heart, where it shapes what a person wants and not just what he knows.

Years of life and peace. The commandments are not a fence to keep good things out; they are the shape of life as God made it to work.

What peace means. We usually think of peace as something missing: no noise, no war, no argument at the dinner table. The Hebrew shalom is something present: everything in its right place, right with God, at ease with your neighbour, the body, the household and the work all well. We chase pieces of it, a calmer week, a better salary, and find that something is still out of joint, because the deepest break is between us and God. That is the break Christ came to mend. Isaiah said of the servant, “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5), and Paul says, “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). So the father’s commandments do not buy shalom; they describe the shape of a life Christ has already begun to make whole. When anxiety tells you that one more thing must go right before you can rest, remember who made your peace, and live from it. See Peace in the Theological Dictionary.

Is this a promise that every godly person lives to old age? The book itself does not read it that way, and neither does the rest of Scripture. Proverbs gives patterns, not promises: a life of honesty, self-control and peace with neighbours tends to be longer and fuller than a life of drunkenness, violence and deceit. Abel was righteous and died young. The deepest fulfilment of length of days lies beyond this life, in the one who promises eternal life to all who trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not steadfast love and faithfulness forsake you; bind them around your neck; write them on the tablet of your heart. So you will find favor and good success in the sight of God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wear God’s own character, steadfast love and faithfulness, on the outside and write it on the inside, and you will be well thought of by God and people.

Steadfast love and faithfulness. Two of the richest words in the Old Testament, hesed and emet. They are the words God used of himself before Moses, “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6): the son is to bear the character of the God who first showed it to him.

Write them on the tablet of your heart. They are worn on the outside, around your neck, and kept on the inside. What God wrote on stone at Sinai, the father wants written on his son’s heart. That is what God promised to do in the new covenant: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). Paul told the Corinthians they were a letter “written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3).

Grace and truth. When the Word became flesh, John saw these two qualities in a human life: Jesus was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), steadfast love and faithfulness in New Testament words. And Luke says the boy Jesus increased “in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52), the clearest picture there is of verse 4 lived.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated good success is uncertain; the ESV notes that it may be rendered “repute”, a good name. Either way, the person marked by steadfast love and faithfulness is well regarded by God and by people.

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put your whole weight on the LORD instead of on your own understanding, bring every part of life under him, and he will clear the road ahead.

Trust in the LORD. To trust is to rely on, to put your whole weight down on something, the way you sit on a chair without testing it first. The question is never whether you trust; everyone leans on something. It is whether you lean on the LORD.

With all your heart. This rules out the divided trust that relies on God for eternity and on itself for Tuesday. The great command asks for the same wholeness: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

Do not lean on your own understanding. It does not say, do not use your understanding; Proverbs is full of commands to think and plan. It says, do not lean on it. Your understanding is a useful tool and a terrible foundation: limited, because you do not know tomorrow, and bent, because your heart tilts it toward what you want.

In all your ways acknowledge him. Acknowledge translates the ordinary Hebrew word for know. To acknowledge someone is to recognise who he is and act accordingly, the way a soldier acknowledges his commanding officer not with a nod but by taking his orders. It is more than mentioning God before doing what you had already decided.

He will make straight your paths. The picture is of a road being levelled, as on Isaiah’s highway where “the uneven ground shall become level” (Isaiah 40:4). It does not promise a map of the whole journey, a road without hills, or an inner voice naming which job to take. It promises that God clears the way ahead of the one who trusts him, and gets him where he is meant to go. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (16:9).

The one who trusted perfectly. Jesus lived every hour like this: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29), and he trusted the Father even on the cross (Luke 23:46). Every believer finds he has not trusted with all his heart; Christ did, in our place, and his Spirit renews trust in those who are his. So this is not a test to pass but a way to walk with a Father who has already accepted us in his Son.

What acknowledging him looks like. In any area of life, from a job offer to a difficult conversation, it means five things. Ask him first. Bring the matter to God before your mind is made up, asking what he wants rather than asking him to bless what you want, and learn to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). Check it by what he has said. Most of God’s will is not hidden; it is written. Is it honest? Is it kind to the people it affects? Does it keep his priorities: worship, family, generosity, rest? Many choices are settled here, and no special sign is needed for the rest. Let him be Lord of that area. A budget acknowledges God when giving is planned first, not fitted in last (v. 9); a career, when you would turn down the promotion that requires dishonesty. Own him openly. “So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32). Receive the outcome from his hand. When it goes well, thank him rather than crediting yourself (Deuteronomy 8:17–18); when it goes badly, accept that it has not slipped out of his hands, and ask what he is teaching you. Try it before your next decision: a short prayer before, one honest question from his word, and thanks or trust after.

Isn’t this blind faith? Many hear this as an order to switch the mind off. But nobody lives by his own understanding alone. You trust the pilot you have never met and the surgeon who operates while you sleep: not blindly, but with reasoned trust in someone whose knowledge is greater than yours and whose record gives you grounds to rely on him. A small child crossing a busy road cannot work out the traffic, but she knows the hand she is holding. So the real question is whether God has a record worth trusting, and the gospel answers it where it cost him most: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). Faith is not a leap in the dark. It is putting your weight on the one who has already shown you his heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil. It will be healing to your flesh and refreshment to your bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not trust your own cleverness; revere the LORD and turn from evil, and you will be healthier for it.

Be not wise in your own eyes. This is what leaning on your own understanding (v. 5) looks like: the man who does not ask advice because he already knows, and does not pray about a decision because it is obvious. Isaiah pronounced a woe on him: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes” (Isaiah 5:21), and Paul told the Romans, “Never be wise in your own sight” (Romans 12:16).

Fear the LORD, and turn away from evil. The cure is the fear of the LORD, the beginning of knowledge (1:7), and it shows itself practically. A person who says he trusts God and keeps walking toward evil is still wise in his own eyes. Yet the way back is open: “he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (28:13).

Healing to your flesh. Humility before God is good for body as well as soul: a person not carrying the burden of being his own god carries less strain. Pride is exhausting.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that flesh is literally “navel”, and that healing may be rendered “medicine”. Why the navel is named is not certain; it probably stands for the body’s centre, or the whole body, as bones does in the next line. The sense is clear: health for the whole person.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce; then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will be bursting with wine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trust shows in what you do with your money: give God the first and best, and he will see that you have enough to keep giving.

Honor the LORD with your wealth. Trust in God shows up in the bank account. Under the law Israel brought the first and best of the harvest to God, the firstfruits: “The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God” (Exodus 23:19). The firstfruits were given before the farmer knew how big the harvest would be, an act of trust; giving God what is left over after the bills requires no faith at all. For a Christian the principle stands: give to God first and gladly, as people who have received everything from him. “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Your barns will be filled with plenty. Paul gives the New Testament form of the promise, and says what the abundance is for: “God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8). The full barn is given so that the giving can continue.

Is this the prosperity gospel, give to get? No. God does reward generosity, but Proverbs describes how his world generally works; it is not a formula for getting money out of him. Job feared God, gave to the poor and lost everything in a day, and said, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). If you have given faithfully and are still struggling, God has not broken his word to you; the richest return on a gift to him is himself, and treasure in heaven that no thief can reach (Matthew 6:20).

Where Christians differ: does this bind Christians to a tithe? Some hold that Christians must give exactly a tenth, as Israel did. This commentary’s view: firstfruits and tithes belonged to Israel’s law, and the New Testament does not set a percentage; it calls for giving that is regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:6–7). A tenth is a helpful benchmark and a good place to begin, and many should give more.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline or be weary of his reproof, for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When life hurts, neither shrug it off nor give up, because the LORD’s discipline is a father’s love for a son he delights in.

Do not despise the LORD’s discipline. What about when life hurts? To despise discipline is to shrug off hardship and learn nothing; to be weary of it is to be crushed and give up. Neither is right, because discipline is love. A father who never corrects his son cares about him less, not more.

Quoted in Hebrews. Hebrews quotes these verses to Christians who were suffering and ready to give up: “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:5–6). Discipline is “for our good, that we may share his holiness”, and “later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness” (Hebrews 12:10–11). The risen Christ says the same to a lukewarm church: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19).

The son in whom he delights. That delight is secure because the punishment that would have crushed us has already fallen on Christ, the Son in whom the Father delighted above all. What reaches us now is the training of sons, not the sentence of a judge.

When suffering comes. Not all suffering is punishment for a specific sin; Job is the Bible’s long proof of that. All of a believer’s suffering is in the hands of a Father who loves him, and it is right to ask what he may be teaching. But lament is also faithful: Psalm 88 ends in darkness, Job poured out his complaint, and both stand in Scripture. Not every sorrow is a lesson you are failing to learn; sometimes the Father’s word in it is simply that he is with you.

How do I receive his discipline? Ask, but do not accuse yourself. When the redundancy, the illness or the rebuke comes, ask God honestly, “Is there something here you want me to see?”, and if nothing comes to mind, do not invent a sin. Take the human rebukes too. Discipline often arrives through a boss, a spouse or an elder; hear them out before you defend yourself, and thank them if they were right. Change one thing. If he does show you something, a temper, a habit, a misplaced trust, deal with that one thing this week rather than resolving to become a new person. Hold on to the relationship. In the hard week, say to him, “You are my Father”, because the verse rests everything on that.

Textual note. Hebrews follows the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, which reads the second line differently, “and chastises every son whom he receives”, where the Hebrew has “as a father the son in whom he delights.” The sense is the same: the LORD’s discipline is a father’s love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–26 — Blessed Is the One Who Finds Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom is the best thing a person can have, because it is the wisdom by which God made the world. The section opens by calling the one who finds wisdom blessed, and compares her returns with silver, gold and jewels: nothing you desire can match her (vv. 13–15). She holds long life in one hand and riches and honour in the other, her paths are peace, and she is a tree of life, the very thing barred in Eden (vv. 16–18). Then the father lifts his son’s eyes to creation: the LORD founded the earth by this wisdom (vv. 19–20). Kept close, she gives a secure step by day, sweet sleep by night and confidence in the LORD when the storm comes (vv. 21–26).
verseByVerse.theology: The wisdom that holds the universe together is offered to a young man to hold his life together.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who finds wisdom, and the one who gets understanding, for the gain from her is better than gain from silver and her profit better than gold. She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding wisdom makes a person truly well off, because nothing else he could want is worth as much.

Blessed is the one who finds wisdom. A new section opens with a beatitude, a saying that calls someone blessed: truly well off, whatever the circumstances. The language is that of trade: compare the returns, the father says to a young man about to enter the market. Nothing you desire compares with her: not the house, the salary, the reputation or the retirement.

Better than gold. Paul agrees: “godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come” (1 Timothy 4:8). And the wisdom that outweighs every treasure has come to us in a person, Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor. Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; those who hold her fast are called blessed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom gives life first and riches second, and her way is peace; she is the tree of life that was lost in Eden.

Long life is in her right hand. Wisdom is pictured holding gifts in both hands. In her right hand, the hand of greater honour, is long life; in her left, riches and honor.
