Life comes first, riches second: the man who chases riches directly often loses them, and the one who pursues wisdom finds them added. Jesus put it in the same order: “But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).

Her ways are ways of pleasantness. Many imagine a godly life as dreary. The paths of folly are exciting at the start and full of regret; the paths of wisdom are sometimes hard at the start and full of peace.

A tree of life. The phrase takes the reader back to Eden. After the fall God guarded that tree, “lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever” (Genesis 3:22). Now wisdom is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, the very reaching out that was barred in Eden.

The tree restored. The Bible ends where it began, with “the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit”, and “the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2). The way back to the tree is through Christ, who is the wisdom of God.

Does wisdom guarantee riches and long life? No more than verse 2 guarantees old age: the Lazarus of Jesus’ parable was a poor beggar (Luke 16:20). The long life wisdom gives in full is eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens; by his knowledge the deeps broke open, and the clouds drop down the dew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisdom the father urges is the wisdom by which God built the universe, so to live wisely is to live with the grain of creation.

The LORD by wisdom founded the earth. The father lifts his son’s eyes from the marketplace to the universe. “O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all” (Psalm 104:24).

The grain of the universe. Wisdom is not an arbitrary set of rules laid over a neutral world. It is the grain of the universe, like the grain in wood, from the great deeps to the morning dew; folly cuts against it, and the world itself resists the fool.

All things were made through him. The New Testament names this creative wisdom. “All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made” (John 1:3). “For by him all things were created … and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16–17). Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Chapter 8 develops this at length.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not lose sight of these— keep sound wisdom and discretion, and they will be life for your soul and adornment for your neck. Then you will walk on your way securely, and your foot will not stumble. If you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep hold of wisdom, and it will give you a secure step by day and sweet sleep by night.

Keep sound wisdom and discretion. Good judgment is life inside and adornment outside, the double picture of verse 3.

You will walk on your way securely. The wise are not immune from difficulty, but many disasters that wreck lives are the foreseeable results of choices, and wisdom removes a great many stones from the road.

Your sleep will be sweet. When others lie awake in the small hours over a debt or a lie that might come out, the verse promises what money cannot buy. “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). “For he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2).

Asleep in the storm. The most vivid picture of this verse in the Bible is a boat in a storm on Galilee. While the disciples were terrified, Jesus “was in the stern, asleep on the cushion” (Mark 4:38), because he trusted his Father completely. Those who belong to him can learn to sleep the same way.

If you lie awake. If you are a believer who lies awake through insomnia, illness or grief, this is not a rebuke. The verse describes a pattern, and the God who gives sleep also keeps watch with you through the night, for he “will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). Persistent sleeplessness is also worth taking to a doctor; using the help God provides through medicine is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes, for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When disaster strikes, the wise need not panic, because the LORD himself is their confidence.

Do not be afraid of sudden terror. The ESV notes that ruin is literally “storm”, the same storm that struck the fool in chapter 1, “like a storm” (1:27). The storm will come; it will not sweep the wise away.

The LORD will be your confidence. The wise man is safe in the end not because of his own wisdom but because of the LORD. The chapter began with trust (v. 5) and returns to it.

Uncertain wording. “The ruin of the wicked” may mean the storm that overtakes the wicked, or the havoc the wicked bring on others; both fit. And the word translated confidence can also mean “side”, so some translations put the LORD at your side. Either way, the LORD himself is the believer’s security.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Trust in God is tested at the front door. Wisdom turns outward to the neighbour: do not withhold good you could do today, and do not fob a person off with “tomorrow” when you have it with you (vv. 27–28). Do not plot against the neighbour who trusts you, or pick quarrels with someone who has done you no harm (vv. 29–30). Do not envy the violent man who seems to win, for the devious are an abomination to the LORD, while the upright are his friends (vv. 31–32). The chapter closes with three contrasts: curse and blessing on two houses, scorn for the scorner and grace for the humble, and honour inherited by the wise (vv. 33–35).
verseByVerse.theology: Trust in God that does not open the hand to a neighbour is not the trust of verse 5.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it. Do not say to your neighbor, "Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it"—when you have it with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do the good you are able to do for someone today, instead of holding it back or putting it off.

Do not withhold good. Faith in God (v. 5) and honouring him with wealth (v. 9) are tested at the front door. The Hebrew, as the ESV footnote records, reads “from its owners”: the good you could do for someone who needs it belongs, in a sense, to him, so to hold back wages owed or help you could easily give is a kind of theft. God, who has not withheld good from us, does not ask you to meet every need in the world. He asks you not to refuse the need in front of you that is in your power to meet. “So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone” (Galatians 6:10). “Owe no one anything, except to love each other” (Romans 13:8).

Tomorrow I will give it. Postponement is the polite way of withholding good. It sounds generous and costs nothing today, but the need is today, and tomorrow is not promised. “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (27:1).

James on empty words. James saw the same thing in the church: a brother or sister without food, and a believer saying, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” “without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?” (James 2:16). Is there a need you have been saying “tomorrow” to?

verseByVerse.quote: Do not plan evil against your neighbor, who dwells trustingly beside you. Do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not scheme against a neighbour who trusts you, or pick a fight with someone who has done you no harm.

Who dwells trustingly beside you. Your neighbour lives beside you assuming you are safe. To plot against someone who is not on guard is a particular evil: the friendly colleague quietly positioning against you, the partner moving the money.

Do not contend with a man for no reason. Some people pick fights for the pleasure of winning. If he has done you no harm, leave him alone. “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways, for the devious person is an abomination to the LORD, but the upright are in his confidence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not envy the violent man who seems to win, because God detests the devious but shares his friendship with the upright.

Do not envy a man of violence. He often seems to win: he gets his way and takes what he wants. Psalm 73 is the long confession of a believer who nearly slipped this way: “For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (Psalm 73:3). Envy is the first step toward choosing his ways.

An abomination to the LORD. Here is what the envious young man cannot see. The devious person is an abomination to the LORD, one of the strongest words of revulsion in the Old Testament.

The upright are in his confidence. They are in the close circle of friends who share secrets. “The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant” (Psalm 25:14). The violent man has power; the upright man has God’s friendship. Jesus said to his disciples, “but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous. Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor. The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing or curse rests on every home, and he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. This is the gospel in a proverb.

The LORD’s curse and blessing. Three closing contrasts. The wicked man’s house may be large and the righteous man’s small; what matters is whether God’s curse or blessing rests on it. God answers people in kind: the scorner is mocked, the humble are lifted.

To the humble he gives favor. The ESV notes that favor may be rendered “grace”, and that is how the verse passed into the New Testament, where it is quoted twice: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). James introduces it with the words, “But he gives more grace.” Grace is not given to the deserving. It is given to the humble, the people who know they are not deserving. The door to God is low, and only those who bend can get through it.

The wise will inherit honor. The chapter that began with trusting God with all your heart ends by showing where that trust leads. The wise inherit honour as a gift; the fool who grasped at it gets disgrace.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew behind get in the last line is uncertain. The verb usually means to lift up or exalt, so the line may mean that the only promotion fools receive is disgrace. The contrast with the wise is clear either way.

when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet.<sup>25</sup>Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes,<sup>26</sup>for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught.<sup>27</sup>Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it.<sup>28</sup>Do not say to your neighbor, "Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it"—when you have it with you.<sup>29</sup>Do not plan evil against your neighbor, who dwells trustingly beside you.<sup>30</sup>Do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm.<sup>31</sup>Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways,<sup>32</sup>for the devious person is an abomination to the LORD, but the upright are in his confidence.<sup>33</sup>The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous.<sup>34</sup>Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor.<sup>35</sup>The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace.
3.overview:
Where we are. The father has urged his son to dig for wisdom like silver (chapter 2). Now he shows what a life leaning on the LORD looks like: in decisions, money, suffering, sleep and the way you treat the family next door.

The message. Put your whole weight on the LORD instead of on your own cleverness, and he will make your way straight. Wisdom is worth more than anything you could want, for by it God made the world, and it shows itself in open-handed goodness to your neighbour. God scorns the proud, but to the humble he gives grace.

Why it was said. A young man entering the market and public life would be tempted to rely on his own understanding, keep God for the festivals and look after himself first (see the introduction). The father insists that trust must reach every part of life, the barn and the front door included.

How the chapter makes its case. First, trust: keep my teaching and wear steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 1–4); trust the LORD with all your heart and acknowledge him in all your ways (vv. 5–8); honour him with the firstfruits (vv. 9–10); and do not despise his discipline, because it is a father’s love (vv. 11–12). Second, the worth of wisdom: better than gold, a tree of life (vv. 13–18), the wisdom by which the LORD founded the earth (vv. 19–20), giving security by day and sweet sleep by night (vv. 21–26). Third, wisdom turned outward: do not withhold or postpone good, plot against a neighbour or envy the violent, for the LORD curses the wicked but gives favour to the humble (vv. 27–35).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. Jesus is the Son who trusted his Father with all his heart, who “increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52), and who committed his spirit into his Father’s hands on the cross (Luke 23:46). The wisdom by which God founded the earth (v. 19) is the Word through whom “all things were made” (John 1:3), and the tree of life (v. 18) blooms again at the end of the Bible because of him. And verse 34 passed into the New Testament as the gospel in a sentence: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

For us. Bring your next decision, your budget and your hardest week to the Father who did not spare his own Son, and lean your whole weight on him. Then let that trust show at your front door, starting with the need you have been putting off until tomorrow.
3.theology:
Trust in God is wholehearted reliance that does not rest its weight on human understanding (vv. 5-6), and it is expressed in humility (v. 7), generosity (vv. 9-10) and acceptance of discipline (vv. 11-12). God's discipline is evidence of his fatherly love (Heb 12:5-11).

The wisdom by which God created the world (vv. 19-20) is fulfilled in Christ, through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Col 1:16-17). Wisdom is a tree of life, restoring what was lost in Eden (v. 18; Gen 3:22; Rev 22:2).

Love of neighbour is the proof of trust in God (vv. 27-30). God gives grace to the humble (v. 34; Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5). The promises of long life and prosperity describe the general pattern of God's world, not a formula (Job 1:21).
3.examples: A couple choosing whether to move for a new job can pray about it, take advice, think hard, and still not lean their whole weight on their own reading of the future; God promises to level the road, not to show them the map. A family that sets aside its giving at the start of the month, before the bills, is bringing firstfruits. A believer in a hard season need neither shrug it off nor be crushed by it, and may also simply lament. And a neighbour who asks for help today should not hear Come back tomorrow if the help is in our hands now.

keyVerse.quote: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.
keyVerse.note: These verses gather up the whole chapter: everything that follows, from giving the firstfruits to sleeping sweetly to helping a neighbour today, is what whole-hearted trust looks like in practice. They do not forbid thinking, but leaning on our own understanding as if it were God. The God they ask us to trust has shown his heart at the cross, where he did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32).

3.reflection:
Verse 5 asks for trust “with all your heart.” Where are you tempted to trust God for eternity but yourself for the practical things, like money, work or your children? What would it look like to acknowledge him in one decision you face this week?

Verses 9–10 call us to give God the firstfruits, before we know how the harvest will turn out. How does giving first, rather than from what is left over, express trust? How do we keep this from becoming a “give to get” bargain?

Verses 11–12 call hardship a father’s discipline. How can we receive hard things as from a loving Father without either shrugging them off or blaming ourselves for every trouble? How does Christ’s bearing our punishment change the way we see discipline?

Verses 27–28 forbid withholding good or saying “tomorrow” when we could help today. Is there a need you have been postponing? How does God’s grace to the humble (v. 34) move us to be generous to others?

4.title: Keep Your Heart with All Vigilance

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Get wisdom above everything, because what you hold on to ends up holding you. The father widens his address to all his sons and insists that what he gives them is good (vv. 1–2). Then he tells a story about himself: when he was a tender boy his own father taught him, and he passes on the old man’s words (vv. 3–4). Hold fast to them and live; get wisdom and insight, and do not forsake her (vv. 5–6). Wisdom is worth everything you have, and the first step toward her is simply wanting her that much (v. 7). Prize her, embrace her, and she will lift you up and set a crown on your head (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is handed down from grandfather to father to son, and the first step toward it is simply wanting it more than anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O sons, a father's instruction, and be attentive, that you may gain insight, for I give you good precepts; do not forsake my teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father calls all his children to listen, because what he gives them is good, not merely strict.

Hear, O sons. The address has widened from my son to O sons. The private word to one boy is now for every reader, daughters as surely as sons. The ESV notes that gain insight is literally “know insight”: wisdom is known the way a person knows a friend.

I give you good precepts. A young person often assumes that his parents’ instruction is there to limit him. The father asks him to consider that it might be a gift, and warns him not to forsake it, as the men of chapter 2 forsook the paths of uprightness (2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a son with my father, tender, the only one in the sight of my mother, he taught me and said to me, "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live. Get wisdom; get insight; do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth. Do not forsake her, and she will keep you; love her, and she will guard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father hands on what his own father taught him: hold fast to these words and live, and love wisdom, for she will guard you.

When I was a son with my father. The father tells a story about himself. He was once a tender boy too, cherished by his mother, and he asks nothing he did not have to learn himself.

David’s words to Solomon. If the father speaking is Solomon, the grandfather is David, and we have a record of the kind of thing he said: “And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind” (1 Chronicles 28:9).

Love her, and she will guard you. Wisdom is first something to get at a cost, and then someone to love, who in return will guard you. The son who keeps hold of her is kept by her. That is how it always goes with God’s wisdom: what you hold on to ends up holding you.

Wisdom passed on. Three generations: the grandfather who taught, the father who remembers, the son who hears. Wisdom is meant to travel that way, from one generation’s mouth to the next generation’s heart, in words short enough for a boy to carry. What sentences will your children quote to theirs? Not most of what you say; a few things said often and lived out in front of them.

Isn’t newer usually truer? In most of life we assume so. Phones, medicines and cars improve every year, and it is easy to carry that assumption into morals and meaning, as though the latest view of marriage, the self or God must be the best because it is the latest. C. S. Lewis called this “chronological snobbery”: treating an idea as discredited because it has gone out of date, without asking whether anyone ever showed it to be false. Every age has blind spots, and ours can often be seen only with older eyes. That does not make the old automatically right; Jesus rebuked the traditions of the elders when they buried the word of God (Mark 7:8–13). The father is not handing on a family custom but what God has said, which is older than his grandfather and will outlast his grandchildren. And at its centre stands someone neither old-fashioned nor merely new: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8), and he is the one who makes all things new (Revelation 21:5).

Uncertain wording. The only one may mean “only” or “uniquely precious”; the same Hebrew word is used of Isaac, Abraham’s “only son” (Genesis 22:2), though Abraham also had Ishmael. If the speaker is Solomon, he was not Bathsheba’s only son (1 Chronicles 3:5), so the word here probably means that he was her cherished darling.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom, and whatever you get, get insight. Prize her highly, and she will exalt you; she will honor you if you embrace her. She will place on your head a graceful garland; she will bestow on you a beautiful crown."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first step to wisdom is wanting it more than anything else, and the one who prizes her will be lifted up and crowned.

The beginning of wisdom is this. It sounds circular: the beginning of wisdom is to get wisdom. But that is the point. The first step toward wisdom is not cleverness or experience. It is deciding that you want it above everything else. The fool never starts, because he does not think he needs it.

Whatever you get, get insight. This ranks degrees, money, friends and experience beneath this one thing. Jesus told of a merchant “who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). The kingdom and the wisdom of God are not an add-on to a life already full of other priorities. They are worth everything you have.

Prize her highly, and she will exalt you. The language is almost that of courtship, and the grandfather’s words end with a coronation. The person who treasures wisdom is not diminished by submitting to it; he is made royal.

A beautiful crown. Paul saw a crown at the end of his own race: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing” (2 Timothy 4:8).

A practical test. If someone looked at how you spend your money and your hours, would they conclude that wisdom is what you are trying to get?

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 7 is very terse, literally something like the beginning of wisdom: get wisdom. Older translations render it “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom”, taking “beginning” in its sense of “chief”. Either way, wisdom comes first, and getting her is worth any cost.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There are only two roads, and the first step matters more than we think. The father reminds his son that he has taught him and walked the way of wisdom ahead of him, so that his step will be sure whether he walks or runs; instruction is his life, and he must not let go (vv. 10–13). Then, in six urgent commands, he forbids even setting foot on the path of the wicked, whose evil has become an appetite that keeps them awake and feeds them (vv. 14–17). The section ends with the two roads set side by side: the path of the righteous grows like the dawn to full day, while the wicked stumble in a darkness they do not understand (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: One road grows lighter with every step; the other grows darker until a person cannot see what trips him.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, and accept my words, that the years of your life may be many. I have taught you the way of wisdom; I have led you in the paths of uprightness. When you walk, your step will not be hampered, and if you run, you will not stumble. Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hold on to the instruction you were given as to a lifeline, because it will keep your step sure whether life moves at a walk or a run.

Accept my words. The father returns to one son. Accept is stronger than hear: taking a gift into your hands. He has not only taught but led: instruction without example is a map; with example it is a guide. He can say I have led you because he has been on the road himself.

If you run, you will not stumble. Life has steady seasons, when you walk, and seasons at a sprint, when you run and decisions come fast. Wisdom learned in the walking seasons keeps a person from falling in the running ones. A man who has thought through his convictions before the crisis does not have to invent them in it.

Keep hold of instruction. The father talks about instruction the way a man hanging over a cliff talks about a rope: for she is your life. Moses said the same of God’s word: “For it is no empty word for you, but your very life” (Deuteronomy 32:47).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not enter the path of the wicked, and do not walk in the way of the evil. Avoid it; do not go on it; turn away from it and pass on. For they cannot sleep unless they have done wrong; they are robbed of sleep unless they have made someone stumble. For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not take even the first step onto the path of the wicked, for evil practised long enough becomes the thing a person cannot sleep without.

Do not enter the path of the wicked. Verses 14 and 15 say one thing in six ways, and the repetition is deliberate. The danger lies less in a single decision to become wicked than in the first step onto the path, and the second, and then the discovery that one is a long way down it.

Avoid it. The counsel is not “walk down the path a little way to understand it”. Some evil is best understood from a distance: films not to watch, websites not to open, parties not to attend, conversations to walk out of. Pass on.

They cannot sleep unless they have done wrong. A chilling picture of what evil does over time. At first a wicked act keeps a man awake with guilt; in the end, not doing it keeps him awake. Evil has become an appetite. Micah pronounced woe on “those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it” (Micah 2:1). Compare the sweet sleep promised to the wise in 3:24: what a person’s heart loves decides what lets him sleep.

The bread of wickedness. Wickedness is their food. Jesus described what fed him in exactly the opposite terms: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). Every person lives on something. The question is what.

verseByVerse.quote: But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day. The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know over what they stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous life grows steadily brighter like the sunrise, while the wicked stumble in a darkness they do not even understand.

Like the light of dawn. Dawn begins as a grey line on the horizon, then colour, then the sun’s edge, then, steadily, full day. The righteous life is not bright all at once; it grows. That encourages anyone whose faith feels still at the grey-line stage. It is supposed to start there; the question is not how bright the light is but which way it is moving. Paul describes the Christian life the same way: “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

The light of the world. The light has a source. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). The righteous path grows brighter because it leads toward him.

The way of the wicked is like deep darkness. The worst of it is not the stumbling but the not knowing why. Their marriages break and their friendships end, and they blame luck, other people or the system; they cannot see that what trips them is the path they have chosen. “The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12:35).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything comes down to the heart. The father asks for his words to be kept before the eyes and inside the heart, because they are life and medicine to the one who finds them (vv. 20–22). Then comes the centre of the chapter: keep your heart with all vigilance, for every stream of life flows from it (v. 23). From the heart he moves outward through the body: put crooked speech away from the mouth, keep the eyes fixed straight ahead, think carefully about where the feet go next, and swerve neither to the right nor to the left, but turn from evil (vv. 24–27).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole person is kept by keeping the heart, and the heart is kept by what the mouth, eyes and feet are allowed to do.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my words; incline your ear to my sayings. Let them not escape from your sight; keep them within your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep the father’s words always in view and deep in your heart, because they bring life and healing.

Be attentive to my words. The last section moves through the body: ear, eyes, heart, then mouth, eyes and feet. The father wants his words to reach every part of his son.

Let them not escape from your sight. Truth slips away easily. It does not need to be refuted; it only needs to be left unlooked at for long enough. A Bible left closed for a month does not argue with you; it just fades.

Healing to all their flesh. The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads “his” flesh, which makes the promise personal: each person who finds these words finds them life and healing for himself. The father’s words are not only rules; they are medicine.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Guard your heart above everything, because your whole life, what you think, say, choose and love, flows out of it. This is the centre of the chapter, and perhaps the most important single verse for understanding how Proverbs thinks about a person.

Keep your heart. In the Bible the heart is not only feelings but the control room of a person, where he thinks, chooses, loves and believes, and life flows out of it like water from a spring. If the spring is poisoned, every stream downstream is poisoned too.

With all vigilance. Guarding the heart is not protecting your feelings from being hurt. It means watching what goes into it, what it is allowed to love, what it dwells on, and what it is being trained to want. A man does not wake up one day an adulterer; he has let his heart dwell on another woman for months. A person does not become bitter overnight; he rehearsed the grievance a thousand times.

Out of the heart. Jesus taught exactly this: “For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery” (Mark 7:21); and “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45). The problem with human beings is not first their circumstances or their behaviour. It is their hearts.

A new heart. And there is a limit to what anyone can do: no one can make his own heart new. That is what God promises to do, to give a new heart and put his Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26–27). The command to keep the heart is given to people whose hearts God has already begun to change, and when they find they have not kept it, they look to Christ, whose heart was wholly pure in their place, and come back by confession to the mercy that is new every morning.

How do I keep my heart? Watch what it rehearses. Notice what your mind returns to when it is idle, in the shower or at 2 a.m.: a grievance, a fantasy, a fear about money. That is where your heart is being trained. Name it to God. Do not just push the thought away; tell him plainly what you want and what you fear, and pray with the psalmist, “Search me, O God, and know my heart!” (Psalm 139:23). Cut one supply line. If an app, a friendship or an evening habit keeps feeding what you are fighting, change it this week rather than promising to resist it tomorrow. Give it something better to love. A heart is not kept by emptying it but by filling it. Put a verse in front of it in the morning, and turn your thoughts to the Son of God, “who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). A greater love guards the heart best, and Paul promises that “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). You keep watch; he keeps you.

verseByVerse.quote: Put away from you crooked speech, and put devious talk far from you. Let your eyes look directly forward, and your gaze be straight before you. Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure. Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guarded heart shows in a clean mouth, eyes fixed ahead and careful steps that do not swerve from the straight road.

Put away from you crooked speech. After the heart, the mouth, because the mouth is where the heart comes out first. Crooked speech is words that twist: flattery, half-truths, gossip dressed up as concern, sarcasm that wounds. Put them as far from you as you would poison. “Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up” (Ephesians 4:29).

Let your eyes look directly forward. Then the eyes: look straight ahead, like a man on a narrow road who does not glance at every distraction; much temptation begins with the eyes lingering. And the Christian knows what to look at: “let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:1–2). “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

Ponder the path of your feet. Then the feet: think carefully about where the next step goes. Hebrews quotes the line in the form “make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed” (Hebrews 12:13). There the point is that a Christian’s steady walk helps the weaker believers walking behind him.

Do not swerve to the right or to the left. The chapter ends with the language Moses used to Israel: “You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32). There are two ditches, careless sin on one side and proud rule-keeping on the other, and the wise person keeps walking straight ahead, heart guarded, mouth clean, eyes forward, on the road that grows brighter until full day.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated ponder can also mean “make level”, as the ESV notes, and that is the sense Hebrews follows. Either the son is to weigh each step carefully or to smooth the road ahead of him; both mean living deliberately rather than drifting.
