then all your ways will be sure.<sup>27</sup>Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil.
4.overview:
Where we are. The father has shown what trusting the LORD looks like in every part of life (chapter 3). Now he tells his sons what his own father taught him, sets two roads before them, and ends where every life is decided, in the heart.

The message. Get wisdom above everything else, because what you hold on to ends up holding you. There are only two roads, one growing brighter like the dawn and the other sinking into darkness, and the first step decides more than we think. So guard your heart above all, for your whole life flows out of it.

Why it was said. Wisdom in Israel was meant to pass down the generations in the home, from grandfather to father to son (see the introduction). This father knows his son will soon face choices alone, at a run.

How the chapter makes its case. First, an inheritance: the father remembers being a tender boy taught by his own father, and passes on the words: hold fast and live; get wisdom whatever it costs; love her, and she will guard and crown you (vv. 1–9). Second, two paths: keep hold of instruction, which is your life; do not set foot on the path of the wicked, who cannot sleep until they have done wrong, for the path of the righteous shines brighter until full day, while the wicked stumble in deep darkness (vv. 10–19). Third, the heart: keep my words within your heart, keep your heart with all vigilance, and then guard your mouth, eyes and feet, swerving neither right nor left (vv. 20–27).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Jesus is the Son taught by his Father who held fast to every word: “I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me” (John 8:28). He is the light toward which the righteous path grows brighter, “the light of the world” (John 8:12). And the command to keep the heart exposes our need, for “out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts” (Mark 7:21); no one can make his own heart new, and God promises to do it by his Spirit (Ezekiel 36:26–27), through the Son whose heart was wholly pure in our place.

For us. Ask what your heart has been rehearsing this week, and what your children or friends will one day remember you saying. Do not take the first step onto a road you would not want to finish. And if your light is still only a grey line on the horizon, keep walking toward Christ: it is meant to grow until full day.
4.theology:
Wisdom is passed down through the generations in the family (vv. 3-4; 1 Chr 28:9). The first step toward wisdom is to desire it above all else (v. 7; Matt 13:45-46).

Sin grows step by step until it becomes an appetite (vv. 16-17); righteousness also grows step by step, toward full light (v. 18; 2 Cor 3:18; John 8:12).

The heart is the source of all of life, so it must be guarded above all (v. 23; Mark 7:21-23; Luke 6:45). The guarding of heart, mouth, eyes and feet belongs together (vv. 24-27), and the New Testament applies verse 26 to walking steadily for the sake of weaker believers (Heb 12:13).
4.examples: A grandmother who has told her grandchildren the same few sentences about God for years has done what David did for Solomon. A young Christian discouraged that his faith is only a grey line on the horizon can remember that dawn always starts that way. And someone who notices a resentment he has rehearsed for months, or a screen he keeps returning to late at night, has found exactly where verse 23 asks him to stand guard, and where Christ’s mercy meets him when he has failed to.

keyVerse.quote: Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.
keyVerse.note: This is the centre of the chapter and a key to how Proverbs sees a person: the heart is the spring from which thought, word and deed all flow. Guarding the mouth, the eyes and the feet (vv. 24–27) begins here. Jesus taught the same (Mark 7:21), and God promises in the new covenant to give the new heart that no one can make for himself.

4.reflection:
Verses 3–4 describe wisdom passed from grandfather to father to son. What sentences of wisdom were handed on to you, and by whom? What few things, said often and lived out, would you most want to hand on to the next generation?

Verses 14–15 say “do not enter” the path of the wicked in six different ways. Why is the first step onto a wrong path so important? What are some first steps that people often take without noticing?

Verse 18 says the path of the righteous is like the dawn, growing brighter until full day. How does that encourage someone whose faith feels weak or slow to grow? In what ways has your light grown brighter?

“Keep your heart with all vigilance” (v. 23). What feeds your heart most during an ordinary week? Since only God can give a new heart, how do our watchfulness and his grace work together?

5.title: Drink Water from Your Own Cistern

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Honey That Turns to Wormwood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Temptation tells only half the truth, so the father tells the other half. He calls his son to listen, so that his own lips will guard knowledge (vv. 1–2), because the danger ahead also comes through lips: the forbidden woman’s speech drips honey and is smoother than oil (v. 3). But in the end she is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword (v. 4). Her road runs down to death, and the saddest thing is that she does not know it; she wanders without ever stopping to think where she is going (vv. 5–6). The son must learn to judge every pleasure by where it ends.
verseByVerse.theology: Adultery is sweet at the beginning and bitter at the end, and the one who leads others astray is lost herself.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding, that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father calls his son to listen, so that his lips are stocked with knowledge before the forbidden woman’s lips begin to speak.

Your lips may guard knowledge. The danger in this chapter comes through lips: hers “drip honey” (v. 3). A man whose mouth is stocked with truth has an answer ready when flattery comes.

Why so much on this? Chapter 2 warned about the forbidden woman in four verses (2:16–19); chapters 5 and 7 give her a chapter each, and 6:20–35 returns to her in between. The father knows which temptation is most likely to wreck his son.

verseByVerse.quote: For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol; she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexual temptation is sweet at the start and deadly at the end, and the woman who offers it is herself lost, wandering toward death without knowing it.

The lips of a forbidden woman drip honey. Forbidden is literally “strange”, and speech is “palate” (ESV footnotes). The father does not pretend temptation is ugly. If he told his son that sin looks disgusting, the son would decide at the first attractive temptation that his father did not know what he was talking about. So he admits it: it is sweet.

In the end she is bitter as wormwood. In the end changes everything. Wormwood, a plant so bitter that the Bible uses it for grief and judgment, is what the honey becomes, and the smooth speech becomes a sword that cuts both ways. Temptation sells the beginning and hides the end. Before any choice, ask how it tastes in the end. Think past the evening to the morning, past the affair to the divorce court, past the secret to the moment it comes out.

Her steps follow the path to Sheol. Literally her steps “lay hold of” Sheol, the place of the dead (ESV footnote), as if she were grasping at the grave. The tragedy of verse 6 is that she herself is lost: not a mastermind, but wandering without knowing it. The person who leads others into sexual sin has usually never stopped to think where she is going, the very opposite of the command to the son in 4:26, “Ponder the path of your feet”.

Uncertain wording. Verse 6 is compressed. It opens with a word that usually means “lest”, and its verb can be read “she” or “you”, so the King James Version made the son the subject (she keeps him from pondering the path of life), while the ESV and most modern versions make it the woman. The modern reading is more likely, and the point stands either way: her road wanders toward death, and no one on it is thinking about where it goes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stay far away, because adultery costs everything. The father calls all his sons to listen and gives one plain command: do not even go near her door (vv. 7–8). Then he reads out the bill: honour, the best years, strength and the fruit of a lifetime’s work, all handed to strangers who care nothing for him, and a body worn out at the end (vv. 9–11). Last, he puts words into his son’s mouth, the speech of an old man who hated discipline and now stands ruined in front of the whole community (vv. 12–14). The root was never only lust; it was refusing to be taught.
verseByVerse.theology: The father makes his son hear, in advance, the words he will say at the end if he does not listen now.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The safe response to sexual temptation is distance: do not even go near her door.

Do not go near the door of her house. The command, to all sons, for no young man is exempt, is about distance: not “go to her door and resist”, but do not go near it. The strongest men in Scripture, Samson and David among them, fell when they put themselves within reach. Paul’s word is the same: “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). You do not negotiate with this temptation; you leave the building. Paul wrote to people whose bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit who lives in them is the strength to leave.

Name the doors. In practice: the late-night conversation with a colleague that has become personal, the social media account you keep checking, the trip where no one knows you, an app on the phone. Do not go near the door.

verseByVerse.quote: lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless, lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner, and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adultery hands over everything a man has, his honour, his best years, his strength and his wealth, to people who care nothing for him, and leaves him groaning at the end of his life.

Lest you give your honor to others. Now the father reads out the bill: reputation, the best years, money and work, all going “to the house of a foreigner”. Adultery has always been expensive. Today the bill arrives as legal fees, divided property, maintenance payments and a family home sold.

When your flesh and body are consumed. At the end, the body. Sexual sin has physical consequences, sometimes in disease, always in the wearing out of a life spent on it: “the sexually immoral person sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18). The groan at the end of life is the sound of a man who has discovered too late what he spent.

Uncertain wording. Who “the merciless” and the “strangers” are is not said: the woman and those around her, a wronged husband demanding his due (compare 6:34–35), or simply outsiders who end up with what the man squandered. The likely sense is the broadest: what was meant for his own household goes to people who have no mercy on him.

verseByVerse.quote: and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors. I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father lets his son hear the regret he will voice at the end of his life if he will not listen now, and its root is not the woman but contempt for correction.

How I hated discipline. The regret is not only about the woman but about not listening. The sin at the root was despising correction; the adultery grew out of it.

In the assembled congregation. The ruin is public, before the whole community of God’s people. Under Israel’s law adultery was a capital crime, judged before the community (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22), so the man’s cry that he was “at the brink of utter ruin” may well mean he barely escaped with his life. Sexual sin is conducted in secret, but it rarely stays there, and when it comes out it damages not only the man but the congregation that trusted him. That is especially sobering for anyone who leads in a church.

A gift from the future. Every older person who has wrecked his life has some version of this speech, and most could name the teachers who warned them. A young reader can take it as a gift: here is the speech; you do not have to give it. And if you have already given it, it need not be your last word: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). A husband or wife who has been betrayed should hear plainly that the unfaithfulness was not their fault.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Rejoice in the Wife of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s answer to forbidden pleasure is a better pleasure, and a God who sees. The father invites his son to drink from his own well and keep his love for one woman (vv. 15–17), to rejoice in the wife of his youth, and to let her love carry him away all his life (vv. 18–19). Why then be led astray by a stranger (v. 20)? Every road a man takes lies open before the LORD (v. 21), and the man who goes the other way finds that his sins become cords that bind him, until his own lack of discipline leads him astray to death (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The best defence against forbidden pleasure is not less pleasure but delight in the gift God has given.

verseByVerse.quote: Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well. Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets? Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer to forbidden pleasure is not less pleasure but the right one: enjoy the love of your own wife, and keep your love for her alone.

Drink water from your own cistern. The father turns from warning to invitation. In a dry land a man’s own cistern, dug with labour, kept his household alive. The picture is of his wife and the delight of sexual love within marriage, as the Song of Solomon calls a bride “a spring locked, a fountain sealed” (Song of Solomon 4:12). The father does not call sexual desire shameful or tell his son to suppress it. He says: drink, from your own well.

Streams of water in the streets. Verse 16 turns the picture round: a man who sleeps around spills on the public road what was meant to water one home. Sexual love is designed to be exclusive, for yourself alone. That is not a restriction on its joy; it is the condition of it.

Uncertain wording. Verse 16 has no Hebrew word marking a question, and the King James Version read it as a statement, which some took to mean a man’s children spreading abroad. The ESV and most modern versions are surely right to read a question expecting the answer no, since verse 17 at once says “Let them be for yourself alone”.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth, a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands a husband to delight in his wife, body and heart, for the whole of their life together, and to let her love carry him away.

Rejoice in the wife of your youth. A command to be glad in the woman he married young, who will grow old with him. Malachi uses the same phrase to warn men who were abandoning their first wives: “let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth” (Malachi 2:15). The law even freed a newly married man from military service for a year so that he could “be happy with his wife whom he has taken” (Deuteronomy 24:5).

Be intoxicated always in her love. Be intoxicated is literally “be led astray” (ESV footnote), the same verb used of the man who wanders off to sin in verse 23. The father is saying: be led astray, but at home. Let her love be the thing that carries you away.

God designed the marriage bed. The Bible’s frankness here surprises some readers. God is not embarrassed by the marriage bed; he designed it, and Paul tells married couples not to deprive one another (1 Corinthians 7:5).

What this looks like. Rejoicing in a wife of many years is a delight to practise, not a feeling to wait for. Notice her. Tell her, specifically and often, what you admire, as the lover in the Song does: “You are altogether beautiful, my love” (Song of Solomon 4:7). Make time. Put an evening together in the diary before the calendar fills, and protect it as you would a meeting with your boss. Speak well of her in public, and never make her the butt of the joke at a dinner party. Turn toward her, not away. When your eyes or thoughts wander, let that be the signal to come home to her, in conversation, affection and the marriage bed. Keep short accounts. Do not let a quarrel run into a cold week; be the first to say sorry. The strength for this does not come from gritted teeth. Christ nourishes and cherishes the church (Ephesians 5:29) through all her failures and has never tired of her, and a husband who has been loved like that has love to give. The same holds, of course, for wives.

verseByVerse.quote: Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress? For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why trade such delight for a stranger, when the LORD sees every road a man takes and governs where it leads?

Why should you be intoxicated, my son? The word is the same again, “led astray”, and adulteress is literally “a foreign woman” (ESV footnote). Why be led astray by a stranger, when you could be led astray by your wife? This is the chapter’s whole strategy: the best defence against forbidden pleasure is not grim willpower but a greater delight. A husband who keeps pursuing and enjoying his wife has far less appetite for honey from other lips; spouses who neglect each other leave the gate open.

Before the eyes of the LORD. The reason beneath all the others: adultery depends on secrecy, but nothing is secret: “No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13). The woman of verse 6 did not ponder her path. The LORD ponders every path, and the word may mean that he “makes level” them (ESV footnote): he sees the road, and he governs where it leads.

For those who find this painful. The single, the widowed, and those whose marriages are cold or broken may find this chapter painful. Its command to flee still stands for you, and so does its promise that God sees every path (v. 21). The deepest fulfilment of the love the chapter describes is not found in any human marriage but in Christ, who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). That love is offered to every believer, married or not.

verseByVerse.quote: The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin. He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin that feels like freedom turns into a rope, and the man who would not accept discipline is led by his own folly to death.

The cords of his sin. The wicked man thinks he is free; in fact he is tied up, and the ropes are his own sins; every indulgence adds another cord. Jesus said, “everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). Anyone who has fought a pornography habit knows how true this is: it began as a choice and became a cord.

He is led astray. The chapter ends with the word it has been playing on. The man who would not be led astray by his wife’s love is led astray by his own folly, all the way to death. And the cause is named: lack of discipline, the very thing he confessed at verse 12 that he hated. “Desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death” (James 1:15).

Set free. But the cords can be cut. Jesus, having said that whoever practises sin is its slave, went on: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

5.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding,<sup>2</sup>that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil,<sup>4</sup>but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.<sup>5</sup>Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol;<sup>6</sup>she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.<sup>7</sup>And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth.<sup>8</sup>Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,<sup>9</sup>lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless,<sup>10</sup>lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner,<sup>11</sup>and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,<sup>12</sup>and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!<sup>13</sup>I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors.<sup>14</sup>I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."<sup>15</sup>Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well.<sup>16</sup>Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets?<sup>17</sup>Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.<sup>18</sup>Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth,<sup>19</sup>a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.<sup>20</sup>Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress?<sup>21</sup>For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.<sup>22</sup>The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin.<sup>23</sup>He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.
5.overview:
Where we are. The father is still teaching his son in the long opening poems of the book (chapters 1–9). Chapter 4 ended by urging him to keep his heart and “ponder the path of your feet” (4:23, 26); chapter 5 takes the one temptation most likely to wreck that path, the forbidden woman first sketched in 2:16–19, and gives her a whole chapter.

The message. Sexual sin promises sweetness and delivers death, and it costs a man everything he has. But the father’s answer is not fear alone: it is a better joy. God gives husband and wife delight in each other and commands them to enjoy it for life, and the God who sees every path will not let the man who despises correction escape the cords of his own sin.

Why it was said. A young man was about to take his place in the town and its trade, where secret sin was as possible as it is now (see the introduction). Adultery was a capital crime under the law, and the father knows this one sin could undo everything else he has taught.

How the chapter makes its case. Her lips drip honey, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, and she herself wanders toward death unaware (vv. 1–6). Then a command and a bill: do not go near her door, for adultery hands honour, years, strength and wealth to strangers and ends in a groan of regret before the whole community (vv. 7–14). Then the chapter’s real strategy, an invitation: drink from your own well, rejoice in the wife of your youth, be carried away by her love (vv. 15–20). Last, the reason beneath all the others: the LORD sees every path, and the wicked are tied up in the cords of their own sins (vv. 21–23).

Where it leads. To Christ, first by the need the chapter exposes. Israel’s wisest king, who wrote these warnings, was himself led astray by many women (1 Kings 11:1–4), and our hearts wander too. Second, by the pattern of marriage, which Paul says was designed to picture “Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). The faithful husband this chapter calls for is fully seen in Christ, who never once turned from his bride, though his people have been the unfaithful partner (Hosea 3:1). He “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and he cuts the cords of sin: “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

For us. Judge every pleasure by where it ends, and keep your distance from the doors that lead to sin. If you are married, practise delight in your husband or wife rather than waiting to feel it. And whether you are single, married, failing or betrayed, Christ’s faithful love is the deepest joy this chapter points to, and it is offered to you.
5.theology:
Temptation offers sweetness at the start and hides its bitter end (vv. 3-4). Sexual sin is costly in every part of life, and at root it grows from despising correction (vv. 9-14).

Sexual delight within marriage is God's gift and is commanded (vv. 15-19; 1 Cor 7:3-5); delight in that gift is the positive defence against adultery (v. 20). God sees all human ways (v. 21; Heb 4:13), and sin enslaves (v. 22; John 8:34). Marriage points beyond itself to Christ's love for the church (Eph 5:25, 31-32).
5.examples: A married man who notices that a friendship at work has become the place he feels most understood has found one of the doors the father names, and the wise thing is to walk away from it before it opens. A couple who keep making time for each other, years into marriage, are doing what verse 19 commands. And a husband or wife who has already fallen, or been betrayed, should hear both the chapter's warnings and the gospel beyond them: the cords can be cut, and Christ sets free.

keyVerse.quote: For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.
keyVerse.note: Every warning and every invitation in the chapter rests on this verse. Adultery depends on secrecy, and the LORD sees every road a man takes and governs where it leads, which is why the father can call his son both away from the stranger and home to the wife of his youth (v. 18). For a believer the same gaze that exposes is the gaze of a Father who has already covered his child in Christ.

5.reflection:
The father admits that temptation is sweet (v. 3) and then insists on asking how it tastes “in the end” (v. 4). Why is it wiser to tell the whole truth about temptation than to pretend sin is ugly? What helps you think “past the evening to the morning”?

“Do not go near the door of her house” (v. 8). What are the doors to sexual sin in our culture and in your own life, and what would keeping your distance from them look like this week?

The chapter’s main defence against adultery is delight: “rejoice in the wife of your youth” (v. 18). How can married couples practise that delight over many years? How should singles, the widowed and those in hard marriages hear this chapter?

Sin begins as a choice and becomes a cord (v. 22), but “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). How does Christ’s faithful love for his bride give hope both to those who have fallen and to those who have been betrayed?

6.title: Go to the Ant, O Sluggard

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Rash Pledge and the Lazy Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two money traps, promising too much and doing too little, and wisdom’s answer to both is urgent action. A son who has rashly guaranteed a neighbour’s debt is caught by his own words (vv. 1–2), so he must swallow his pride and plead for release at once, escaping like a gazelle from the hunter (vv. 3–5). The sluggard must go to school with the ant, which works with no one watching and stores up in summer for the winter (vv. 6–8). His ruin comes through a little sleep and a little folding of the hands, until poverty arrives like a robber (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom avoids reckless promises and idle hands alike, and both begin as small, pleasant decisions.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, have given your pledge for a stranger, if you are snared in the words of your mouth, caught in the words of your mouth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not bind yourself with a quick promise to pay someone else’s debt, for a moment’s words can trap you for years.

Security for your neighbor. Security and pledge describe what we call co-signing a loan: promising, sealed then with a handshake, to pay if the borrower does not. The Bible does not forbid lending, generosity or bearing another’s burden (“Bear one another’s burdens”, Galatians 6:2). What it warns against, here and repeatedly in Proverbs, is binding yourself to a debt whose size is in someone else’s hands.

Snared in the words of your mouth. The trap was made of words. Many people have lost their homes through a moment’s eagerness to help a friend or look generous; the words took a second, the debt took years. A wise rule many Christians follow: never guarantee more than you could afford to give away outright, and where you can, give rather than guarantee.
verseByVerse.note: Proverbs returns to guaranteeing debts at 11:15, 17:18, 20:16 and 22:26-27.

verseByVerse.quote: then do this, my son, and save yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbor: go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbor. Give your eyes no sleep and your eyelids no slumber; save yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the hand of the fowler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are caught, get free at once: swallow your pride, go to your neighbour and plead for release, and do not rest until it is done.

You have come into the hand of your neighbor. Your future now belongs to someone else’s choices. So go, hurry, and plead with him to release you. Pride will want to keep the promise rather than admit it was foolish. The father says: swallow your pride and get out.

Like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter. A gazelle does not negotiate with the hunter; it runs. Some problems grow quietly while we sleep, and a debt obligation is one of them.

Christ our surety. The New Testament holds a striking reversal of this warning. The one pledge Proverbs tells a son never to make, Christ made for us: he bound himself to pay the debt of people who could not pay. Judah once said to his father about Benjamin, “I will be a pledge of his safety” (Genesis 43:9); Hebrews says that Jesus is “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). He did not run from the obligation; he paid it in full.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind plead urgently is rare. The ESV notes that it may mean “humble yourself”; others take it as “press” your neighbour hard. Both readings point the same way: humble, urgent persistence until you are released.

verseByVerse.quote: Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lazy man is sent to learn from the ant, which works without anyone watching and gathers in summer for the winter ahead.

Go to the ant, O sluggard. From the man who promises too much to the man who does too little. The sluggard appears again and again in Proverbs, usually in comic scenes. Here a grown man is sent to school, and the teacher is an insect. Wisdom is written into creation for anyone willing to consider, and Agur will return to the ants: “the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer” (30:25).

Without having any chief. Two lessons. First, the ant works without a supervisor, while many people work hard only when someone is watching. Paul told Christian workers to labour “heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). They serve a Master who has already promised them the inheritance, so they work for him, watched or not.

She prepares her bread in summer. Second, the ant works ahead, gathering in summer for winter. Wisdom plans for seasons that have not yet arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you arise from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laziness ruins a life not by one big decision but by many small ones, and the poverty it brings arrives as suddenly as a robber.

How long will you lie there, O sluggard? It sounds like a parent at a bedroom door late in the morning. The sluggard does not say, I intend to ruin my life. He says, five more minutes. The word little comes three times: laziness never presents itself as a life decision, and that is what makes it dangerous.

Poverty will come upon you like a robber. The little decisions add up to a sudden arrival, and the sluggard is surprised. He should not be. Verses 10–11 return word for word at the end of the scene in the sluggard’s vineyard (24:33–34), as if the lesson needed saying twice.

Work is not a curse. The New Testament is equally plain: “If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Work is how God provides for us and lets us provide for others, “so that he may have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28).

What it does not mean. The depressed, the exhausted and the sick are not sluggards, and this proverb is not aimed at them. It is aimed at the man who could get up and chooses not to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God hates what tears people apart. A worthless man works by crooked words and secret signals, a wink, a shuffle of the feet, a pointing finger, while his heart plots evil and keeps sowing discord; his end will come suddenly and beyond healing (vv. 12–15). Then comes a list of seven things the LORD hates, moving down the body from haughty eyes and a lying tongue to violent hands, a scheming heart and feet that run to evil, and on to the false witness (vv. 16–19). It builds to its climax in the one who sows discord among brothers, the very sin of the worthless man.
verseByVerse.theology: God's hatred is aimed at what destroys people and community, and the list starts with pride and ends with division.

verseByVerse.quote: A worthless person, a wicked man, goes about with crooked speech, winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his finger, with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord; therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; in a moment he will be broken beyond healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The troublemaker works by secret signals and whispered schemes, spreading division wherever he goes, but his end will come suddenly and beyond remedy.

A worthless person. He works in code: crooked speech, a wink, a movement of the feet (the ESV notes the Hebrew is “scrapes”), a pointing finger, signals to allies behind the backs of his targets. Psalm 35 prays against those who “wink the eye” in hatred (Psalm 35:19). Every office and every church has seen this man: the raised eyebrow in a meeting, the knowing look, the whispered aside.

Continually sowing discord. Beneath the signals is a heart that devises evil, and what it produces is discord: a suspicion planted here, a remark repeated there, friendships split, continually.

In a moment he will be broken. He works slowly and secretly, but his end is sudden, and the man who broke others will be broken beyond healing. God’s patience is not indifference: “While people are saying, ‘There is peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thessalonians 5:3).

verseByVerse.quote: There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked plans, feet that make haste to run to evil, a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD hates the sins that destroy people and community, from the proud look where most of them start to the stirring up of division among his people, where the list reaches its climax.

Six things that the LORD hates. The pattern “six things, seven” is a Hebrew way of building to a climax: the seventh item is the one the list is aiming at. And the language is strong. Some readers are uncomfortable with a God who hates. But a God who loved people and did not hate what destroys them would not be good. A doctor who loves his patient hates the cancer.

The whole person. The list moves down the body: eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet. The whole person can be put to the service of evil.

Haughty eyes. It begins with the look of a person who sees himself above others. Pride comes first because most of the others start there. Jesus told of a Pharisee who looked down on a tax collector, and ended, “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:14). Then a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood. Some readers find it strange that pride stands in the same list as murder. God does not.

Feet that make haste to run to evil. Then the scheming heart and the eager feet. The troublemaker of verse 14 had such a heart, and the gang of chapter 1 had such feet: “their feet run to evil” (1:16).

One who sows discord among brothers. The last two destroy community. A false witness destroys justice. And the seventh, the one the list builds to, picks up the sowing discord of verse 14: the section begins and ends with discord. God hates it most because it attacks what he loves most, the unity of his people.

A word to church members. That should give every church member pause. Gossip, faction, the whispered complaint about the elders, the stirring up of one group against another, all belong on this list. Paul says, “watch out for those who cause divisions” (Romans 16:17), and Jesus pronounced the opposite blessing: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). Ask whether your words this week have stirred up division or made peace.

Does God hate people, or only sins? The last two items are persons, a false witness and a sower of discord, and the Psalms can say of God, “you hate all evildoers” (Psalm 5:5). Scripture means his settled opposition to those who persist in evil, and it is no contradiction of his love, for he “shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Every one of these seven sins was laid on Christ, so that liars, the proud and dividers of churches who turn to him are forgiven and made peacemakers.
verseByVerse.note: Other numerical sayings: 30:15-31, and the "three transgressions, and for four" of Amos 1-2.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–35 — Fire Carried in the Lap
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keep your parents’ teaching close, because adultery is fire. Bound on the heart, the father’s commandment and the mother’s teaching lead, guard and talk with the son, a lamp whose very reproofs are the way of life (vv. 20–23). That light is most needed against the adulteress, whose power begins with desire in the heart and a look from her eyes (vv. 24–26). No one can carry fire against his chest without being burned (vv. 27–29). A thief can repay what he stole; the adulterer destroys himself, earns lasting disgrace and meets a jealous husband whom no gift can satisfy (vv. 30–35).
verseByVerse.theology: Adultery is not a private risk but playing with fire, and it provokes a wound that money cannot settle.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, keep your father's commandment, and forsake not your mother's teaching. Bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck. When you walk, they will lead you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will talk with you. For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life,
verseByVerse.commentary:
A parent’s godly teaching, bound on the heart, becomes a companion that guides by day, guards by night and lights the way to life, even when it corrects.

Keep your father’s commandment. The father returns to his great theme, and the language echoes Moses: “these words that I command you today shall be on your heart”, and “You shall bind them as a sign on your hand” (Deuteronomy 6:6, 8). Parental teaching in Proverbs carries the weight of God’s law because it passes on God’s law, and the mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s.

They will talk with you. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says “it” three times, as if the teaching were a single companion that walks with the son by day, watches at night and talks to him when he wakes. Moses named the same three moments: “when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). That is Scripture stored in the heart. Walking into a meeting, it guides; lying awake, it guards; and on waking, the first thought can be God’s word rather than the day’s anxiety.

The commandment is a lamp. A lamp shows the next step in the dark: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). And the father adds something less comfortable: the reproofs of discipline are the way of life. Correction is part of the light. The person who wants God’s guidance but not his rebukes wants a lamp that shows only pleasant things.

How do I bind them on my heart? Keep a verse with you. Choose one short verse a week, write it on a card or your phone’s lock screen, and say it over until you have it by heart. Use the three moments. Read a few verses before you look at the news in the morning, bring one to mind on the walk or the drive, and let it be your last thought at night instead of tomorrow’s worries. Talk about it at home. Tell your children or a friend what you read today; a word passed on is a word kept. Reach for it when tempted. When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness he answered three times from Deuteronomy, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Even this is not left to our memory alone. God promised a new covenant: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). And Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit “will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). We store the words; he makes them live.

verseByVerse.quote: to preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress. Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes; for the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread, but a married woman hunts down a precious life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light of God’s word is needed most against the adulteress, whose power works through the heart’s desire and a single look, and who costs a man far more than any price.

The evil woman. Here is where the lamp is most needed. Adulteress is literally “the foreign woman” (ESV footnote), and the warning of chapters 2 and 5 returns.

Do not desire her beauty in your heart. The battle is located precisely: in your heart. Adultery is not first an act; it is a desire entertained. Jesus said the same: “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). David’s fall began with a look from a rooftop at “a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful” (2 Samuel 11:2).

Her eyelashes. The weapon named is small: a look held a second too long. The father wants his son to know how little it takes.

The price of a prostitute. The verse compares costs. Sin with a prostitute is costly and degrading, but sin with another man’s wife (the Hebrew is “a man’s wife”) costs far more: it hunts down a precious life. The verse is not approving of prostitution. Paul answers anyone who thinks it harmless: “Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her?” (1 Corinthians 6:16).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases here are uncertain. In verse 24 a change of vowels would turn the evil woman into “the wife of a neighbor”, as the ESV notes; the consonants allow both, and the sense is the same. Verse 26 is compressed, and the ESV notes that it may also mean that “a prostitute leaves a man with nothing but a loaf of bread”. On either reading the point stands: whatever a prostitute costs, a married woman costs a man his life.

verseByVerse.quote: Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched? So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife; none who touches her will go unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adultery is fire carried in your shirt: no one plays with it and escapes being burned.

Can a man carry fire next to his chest? Two questions that answer themselves, so that the son reaches the conclusion himself. Every man who begins an affair believes he will be the exception, keeping it secret and keeping his marriage. He is carrying fire in his shirt and insisting it will not burn. The consequences may be slow or quick, public or private, but there are no exceptions.

verseByVerse.quote: People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry, but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house. He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself. He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away. For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A thief can repay what he took, but the adulterer has stolen what can never be paid back, and he destroys himself in doing it.

People do not despise a thief. A starving man who steals bread gets a measure of sympathy. Still, he must repay sevenfold, a number for full and complete restitution (the law required fourfold or fivefold for stolen livestock, Exodus 22:1, and Zacchaeus promised fourfold, Luke 19:8). It may cost all the goods of his house. But it can be paid. The debt has a limit.

He who commits adultery lacks sense. Adultery is different. The thief was hungry; the adulterer had a wife. The damage is not to his purse but to himself: he who does it destroys himself.

His disgrace will not be wiped away. Even when the sin is forgiven, and it can be, the adulterer’s reputation carries a mark for years. Many a gifted man has discovered that he cannot return to the place of trust he once held.

He will accept no compensation. The final difference from theft: you can repay a thief’s victim, but you cannot pay off a husband whose wife you have taken. What was stolen was not property but a one-flesh union, and “jealousy is fierce as the grave” (Song of Solomon 8:6).

Not a court. The law prescribed death for adultery (Leviticus 20:10), but these verses describe the husband’s fury and the adulterer’s ruin, not a court. That civil penalty belonged to Israel as a nation under God’s own law; in Christ there is forgiveness for adulterers who repent (John 8:11; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

Why the gospel is good news. That is a sobering place to end the chapter, and it is meant to be. But it also shows why the gospel is such good news. The sins that no human compensation can cover, the blood of Christ can. He did not pay in gifts or goods; he paid with his life, and what money could never wipe away, his cleansing does.

When will you arise from your sleep?<sup>10</sup>A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,<sup>11</sup>and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.<sup>12</sup>A worthless person, a wicked man, goes about with crooked speech,<sup>13</sup>winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his finger,<sup>14</sup>with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord;<sup>15</sup>therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; tie them around your neck.<sup>22</sup>When you walk, they will lead you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will talk with you.<sup>23</sup>For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life,<sup>24</sup>to preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress.<sup>25</sup>Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes;<sup>26</sup>for the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread, but a married woman hunts down a precious life.<sup>27</sup>Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned?<sup>28</sup>Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched?<sup>29</sup>So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife; none who touches her will go unpunished.<sup>30</sup>People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry,<sup>31</sup>but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house.<sup>32</sup>He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself.<sup>33</sup>He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away.<sup>34</sup>For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge.<sup>35</sup>He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.
6.overview:
Where we are. The father is still teaching his son in the opening poems of the book (chapters 1–9). After the long warning of chapter 5, he gathers four shorter lessons: three quick portraits of folly, the rash guarantor, the sluggard and the troublemaker, a list of what the LORD hates, and then a return to the adulteress, who will have chapter 7 to herself.

The message. Folly rarely announces itself as ruin. It comes as a handshake, five more minutes in bed, a wink across the room, a look held too long. The LORD hates what destroys people and divides his people, and wisdom acts at once: get free of the rash promise, get up and work, refuse to sow discord, and keep away from the fire of adultery.

Why it was said. The son is stepping into adult life in a small community where neighbours lent and pledged to one another, every household lived by its own labour, and a whisper or an affair could tear a town apart (see the introduction). The father prepares him for money, work, community and marriage in one chapter.

How the chapter makes its case. A son who has guaranteed a neighbour’s debt must humble himself and get free before he sleeps (vv. 1–5). The sluggard must learn from the ant, for a little sleep and a little folding of the hands bring poverty like a robber (vv. 6–11). The worthless man works by secret signals and sows discord, and will be broken suddenly (vv. 12–15). Seven things the LORD hates move down the body from proud eyes to running feet and climax in the one who sows discord among brothers (vv. 16–19). Last, parents’ teaching is a lamp to guard the son from the adulteress, for adultery is fire in the lap and a debt no gift can pay (vv. 20–35).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by a surprising reversal. Every sin on the list of seven was laid on Christ, the one who never sowed discord and makes peace by his cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). The pledge the father forbids, binding yourself to a debt you cannot control, is exactly what Christ did for us: he became “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). And the debt of adultery that no compensation can pay (v. 35), his blood can wash away (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

For us. Ask where you are snared by words you should not have spoken, idle when you could work, or stirring up division in your church. Act today rather than tomorrow. Store God’s word in your heart so that it walks with you, and remember that the one who makes peace has already paid the debts you could never pay.
6.theology:
Wisdom governs money: avoiding reckless financial obligations (vv. 1-5) and working diligently without supervision (vv. 6-11; 2 Thess 3:10; Col 3:23). Christ made the very pledge Proverbs warns against: as guarantor of the new covenant he bound himself to pay his people’s debt (Heb 7:22).

God hates what destroys people, and the list of seven begins with pride and ends with discord among brothers (vv. 16-19; Luke 18:14; Rom 16:17). God's word, stored in the heart, accompanies the believer at every moment (vv. 20-23; Deut 6:6-8).

Adultery begins in the heart (v. 25; Matt 5:28), always burns the one who commits it (vv. 27-29), and does damage that cannot be repaid by human means (vv. 30-35).
6.examples: A young adult asked by a friend to co-sign a car loan can say no kindly, or give what he can afford to lose, rather than hand his future to someone else's choices. Someone who works hard only when the manager is in the office can learn from the ant, and from Paul: we work for a Master who sees. A church member tempted to pass on a complaint about the elders can recognise the seventh thing the LORD hates, and choose to be a peacemaker instead.

keyVerse.quote: For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life
keyVerse.note: The chapter walks through traps of money, work, speech and sex, and this verse names what keeps a son out of all of them: God’s word, passed on by his parents and stored in his heart. It shows the next step in the dark, and its rebukes are part of its light. The new covenant promise is that God writes that word on the heart himself (Jeremiah 31:33).

6.reflection:
Verses 1–5 tell a son to humble himself and get out of a rash promise at once. Why does pride make us slow to admit a foolish commitment? How does Christ’s willingness to become our “guarantor” (Hebrews 7:22) change how you read this warning?

The sluggard’s ruin comes through “a little sleep, a little slumber” (v. 10). Where do small, repeated choices shape your life most, for good or ill? How can we take this seriously without laying it on those who are depressed, sick or exhausted?

The list of things the LORD hates begins with haughty eyes and ends with one who sows discord among brothers (vv. 16–19). Why might God rank division among his people so seriously? What would it look like for you to be a peacemaker in your church this week?

A thief can repay, but the adulterer’s debt cannot be paid in gifts (vv. 30–35). How does this chapter show both the seriousness of sexual sin and the greatness of what Christ has done for those who repent?

7.title: The Young Man Lacking Sense

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Keep My Words as the Apple of Your Eye
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word, guarded and loved, is the son’s protection against the forbidden woman. The father pleads with him to keep and treasure his commandments, for they are life, and to guard them as instinctively as the pupil of his eye (vv. 1–2). They are to be bound on his fingers, shaping what he does, and written on his heart, shaping what he loves (v. 3). Then the son must take wisdom as his sister and insight as his intimate friend (v. 4). A heart already at home with wisdom will see through the smooth words of the adulteress (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The father's defence against seduction is a closer relationship with wisdom than the seductress can offer.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you; keep my commandments and live; keep my teaching as the apple of your eye; bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Guard God’s word as instinctively as you guard your eye, and let it shape both what you do and what you love.

Keep my commandments and live. The last major warning about the forbidden woman opens with the grandfather’s sentence from 4:4, passed on word for word.

The apple of your eye. It is the pupil, so sensitive that anything near it makes you blink. Moses said God kept Israel “as the apple of his eye” (Deuteronomy 32:10). The father wants his son to guard God’s teaching with that same reflex, flinching at anything that threatens it.

Fingers and heart. The fingers stand for what a man does, the heart for what he loves. A man who has God’s word only on his fingers keeps rules he does not love; a man who has it only in his heart has feelings that never become obedience. The father wants both.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call insight your intimate friend, to keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The best defence against a false intimacy is a true one: make wisdom your closest companion, and you will see through the flattering stranger.

You are my sister. Wisdom is to be the son’s sister and intimate friend. In the Song of Solomon “my sister” is a term of tender affection for a bride (Song of Solomon 4:9). The father is not asking his son merely to know about wisdom, but to be close to her, to love her, to be at home with her.

The adulteress with her smooth words. The ESV notes again that these are “the strange” and “the foreign” woman, and again her weapon is smooth words. A young man who has made wisdom his closest friend will recognise a counterfeit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–23 — What the Father Saw from His Window
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A story the father has watched from his window shows how a fall actually happens. A simple young man with nothing at his centre drifts toward her corner as the light fades (vv. 6–9). She meets him dressed to be seen and calculating within, a restless hunter (vv. 10–12). She kisses him, dresses the invitation in religion and flatters him that he is the one she was seeking (vv. 13–15). She offers a luxurious bed, a night of love and the assurance that her husband is far away (vv. 16–20). He follows at once, like an animal to the slaughter, never knowing it will cost his life (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The fall is not sudden; it is a walk that began with a young man choosing which street to take at dusk.

verseByVerse.quote: For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice, and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense, passing along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father has watched a young man with nothing at his centre drift, step by step and as the light fades, toward the house of sin.

At the window of my house. Now a story. The father looks through the lattice, a wooden screen that let a person see out without being seen; what follows he has watched happen. The young man he picks out is not a hardened criminal. He is simple, one of the easily led people of chapter 1, and lacking sense, literally lacking heart: there is nothing at his centre holding him steady. That is the most dangerous condition a young person can be in: not rebellious, just empty.

Passing along the street near her corner. Watch his feet. He does not go to her house, not yet; he is just walking near where sin lives. Maybe he tells himself it is the shorter route. This is how most falls happen: no one wakes up planning adultery, but he chooses the street. It may be the lingering conversation, the website opened “just to see”, the drink with a colleague after everyone else has gone home. Paul’s counsel is to “make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires” (Romans 13:14). Do not walk near her corner.

In the twilight. The light fades as he walks, and so does his judgment. Sin prefers the dark, where no one sees: “people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil” (John 3:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart. She is loud and wayward; her feet do not stay at home; now in the street, now in the market, and at every corner she lies in wait.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She comes to meet him, dressed to be seen and calculating within, a restless hunter waiting at every corner.

The woman meets him. And behold: the father’s voice tightens, as if he wants to shout through the window. Her clothing announces what she is, and her heart is wily, literally “guarded in heart” (ESV footnote). She shows everything on the outside and hides everything on the inside. He is exposed; she is calculating.

At every corner she lies in wait. She is restless, never settled, always out, and she is hunting. The same verb was used of the gang in chapter 1: “let us lie in wait for blood” (1:11). The seductress and the violent man are hunters of the same kind. “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: She seizes him and kisses him, and with bold face she says to him, "I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows; so now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She overwhelms him with a kiss, covers her sin with religion, and flatters him that he is the one she was looking for.

She seizes him and kisses him. She acts before he has said a word. Temptation often works this way: it moves before the person has had time to think, and it behaves as if what is happening is perfectly normal.

I had to offer sacrifices. Her opening line is religious. The sacrifices were “peace offerings” (ESV footnote), and under the law the meat of such an offering had to be eaten that day or the next (Leviticus 7:15–16). She is telling him that a feast of meat is waiting at home and that she has done her duty to God. Religion becomes the cover for sin. Some of the most destructive affairs have been conducted by people who never missed church.

I have found you. Then flattery: to seek you eagerly, and I have found you. You, specifically. For an empty young man, nothing is more intoxicating than being wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen; I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love. For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey; he took a bag of money with him; at full moon he will come home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She offers luxury, pleasure and safety, a perfumed bed, a night of “love” and a husband far away; but what smells like a wedding is a grave.

I have spread my couch with coverings. Everything about the bed is luxurious and imported; she appeals to every sense, and she has prepared.

Myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. Myrrh and aloes appear elsewhere in Scripture in two very different places. The king in Psalm 45 has robes “fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia” on his wedding day (Psalm 45:8). And when Jesus was buried, Nicodemus brought “a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight” (John 19:39). The same scents belong to a wedding and a burial. Her bed smells like a wedding. It is a grave.

Let us take our fill of love till morning. She calls it love. It is not. Chapter 5 described love: rejoicing in the wife of your youth and delighting in her always (5:18–19). She offers a night, till morning. Love is measured in decades; this is measured in hours.

My husband is not at home. Finally the reassurance: the husband is away on a long trip, and no one will find out. Every affair is built on the belief that it will stay hidden. She refers to him coldly, not as “my love” but my husband, a man whose absence is their chance.

verseByVerse.quote: With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him. All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a stag is caught fast till an arrow pierces its liver; as a bird rushes into a snare; he does not know that it will cost him his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Talked out of every objection, he follows her at once, as blind to the cost as an animal walking to its death.

With her smooth talk she compels him. She keeps talking, and every sentence removes an objection. By the end he is not so much persuaded as compelled. There comes a point in temptation where resistance feels impossible. The time to resist was back on the street, one corner ago.

As an ox goes to the slaughter. Three animals tell the same truth. An ox walks placidly to the slaughterhouse, thinking it is going to pasture. A stag is caught and waits for the arrow. A bird rushes into a snare, eagerly. None of them knows what is happening: he does not know that it will cost him his life.

Samson and Joseph. The Bible has its own case study. Samson laid his head on Delilah’s knees, and “his strength left him” (Judges 16:19). And it has its counter-example. When Potiphar’s wife caught Joseph by his garment and said, “Lie with me,” “he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house” (Genesis 39:12). Joseph lost a coat and kept his life. The young man in Proverbs 7 kept his coat and lost everything.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of the middle line, the stag caught fast, is difficult, and gives the probable reading. Read as it stands, the line seems to speak of a fool in fetters, as in the King James Version, which pictures a fool going to the stocks. Either way it is a third picture of a creature walking unawares into captivity and death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — Many a Victim Has She Laid Low
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The story is told to arm the sons. The father turns from the window and calls them to listen: do not let the heart turn aside to her ways, and the feet will not stray into her paths (vv. 24–25). Her victims are many, and many were stronger than this young man, so no one may think himself safe (v. 26). The house that looked like a bedroom is the road to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The strong have fallen here too, so no reader may assume he is the exception.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O sons, listen to me, and be attentive to the words of my mouth. Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father turns from the window to his sons: the fall starts in the heart, so guard the heart before the feet go astray.

And now, O sons, listen to me. The story is over. The father has not told it to entertain his sons but to arm them.

Let not your heart turn aside. Two steps again: first the heart turns aside, then the feet stray. The fall begins inside. James describes the same order: “each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14). This is why the father spent so much of the book on the heart. Guard it, and the feet will follow.

In practice. That means paying attention to where the heart’s imagination drifts, and turning it back early. It means friends who ask hard questions: “exhort one another every day”, “that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). And it means prayer, because Jesus said, “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41). He said it as one who knew temptation from the inside: he “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). The young man at the window had no one; the believer has a High Priest who stood where he stands and did not fall, and who gives mercy and grace in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).

verseByVerse.quote: for many a victim has she laid low, and all her slain are a mighty throng. Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her victims are countless, and many were stronger than this young man; her house is not a bedroom but the road down to death.

Many a victim has she laid low. The final warning is in the numbers. Many have fallen here, and her slain are a mighty throng. She has brought down people who were stronger, wiser and more gifted than the young man on the street. Samson was strong; David was a man after God’s own heart. No one is too strong for this temptation: “let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12).

The chambers of death. The chapter that began with a perfumed bed ends in the chambers of death. The bedroom was the way into the grave.

God is faithful. But the Bible’s last word on temptation is not death: “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape” (1 Corinthians 10:13). There is always a door out, and very often it is the door of your own house, which you can walk back through before dark. And for those who have already gone into her house, the Christ who went down into death for sinners came up again, and brings back with him all who turn to him.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you;<sup>2</sup>keep my commandments and live; keep my teaching as the apple of your eye;<sup>3</sup>bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.<sup>4</sup>Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call insight your intimate friend,<sup>5</sup>to keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words.<sup>6</sup>For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice,<sup>7</sup>and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense,<sup>8</sup>passing along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house<sup>9</sup>in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.<sup>10</sup>And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart.<sup>11</sup>She is loud and wayward; her feet do not stay at home;<sup>12</sup>now in the street, now in the market, and at every corner she lies in wait.<sup>13</sup>She seizes him and kisses him, and with bold face she says to him,<sup>14</sup>"I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows;<sup>15</sup>so now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.<sup>16</sup>I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen;<sup>17</sup>I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.<sup>18</sup>Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love.<sup>19</sup>For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey;<sup>20</sup>he took a bag of money with him; at full moon he will come home."<sup>21</sup>With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him.<sup>22</sup>All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a stag is caught fast<sup>23</sup>till an arrow pierces its liver; as a bird rushes into a snare; he does not know that it will cost him his life.<sup>24</sup>And now, O sons, listen to me, and be attentive to the words of my mouth.<sup>25</sup>Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths,<sup>26</sup>for many a victim has she laid low, and all her slain are a mighty throng.<sup>27</sup>Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death.
7.overview:
Where we are. This is the father’s last and fullest warning about the forbidden woman, after 2:16–19, chapter 5 and 6:20–35. It is also the last of his speeches before Wisdom herself takes the stage in chapter 8, and it prepares for the two rival invitations of chapter 9, where Folly speaks almost exactly as this woman does.

The message. Sexual sin does not usually ambush a strong man; it gathers up an empty one who has wandered near its door. It comes dressed in religion, flattery and luxury, promises love and secrecy, and leads to death. So keep God’s word close and dear, make wisdom your intimate friend, and do not let your heart turn aside even one street toward her.

Why it was said. The father is preparing a young man for a town at dusk, with its market, its streets and its festival meals (see the introduction). His son’s greatest danger is not rebellion but drift, and the time to resist is long before the door.

How the chapter makes its case. First the father’s plea: keep my teaching as the apple of your eye, and call wisdom your sister (vv. 1–5). Then a story told from his window. A young man lacking sense walks toward her corner as night falls (vv. 6–9); she meets him dressed to be seen, loud and wily (vv. 10–12), seizes and kisses him, and covers the invitation with talk of sacrifices and vows (vv. 13–15). She offers a perfumed bed, a night of love and a husband safely away (vv. 16–20), and he follows her like an ox to the slaughter (vv. 21–23). Last, the father turns to his sons: do not let your heart go her way, for her victims are many and her house is the road to death (vv. 24–27).

Where it leads. To Christ, first by the need the chapter exposes: every one of us has walked toward some corner we should have avoided. Second, by contrast with the true Son. Where the young man had nothing at his centre, Jesus treasured his Father’s words; he “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), and he went down into “the chambers of death” (v. 27) not as a victim of folly but to bring sinners back from it. The man who could not resist one evening’s temptation is rescued by the one who resisted every temptation.

For us. Watch the streets you walk, the screens you open and the evenings you spend, because falls begin with drift. Keep God’s word dear, keep friends who ask hard questions, and pray for help before the moment comes. And if you have already gone through her door, Christ is still the way of escape, and the way home.
7.theology:
Sin works gradually and through small choices: a street chosen at dusk (vv. 8-9). Temptation appeals to every sense, flatters, uses religion as cover, and promises secrecy (vv. 13-20). The heart turns before the feet stray (v. 25; Jas 1:14).

The defence against a false closeness is real closeness to wisdom (v. 4), God's word treasured and written on the heart (vv. 1-3), flight rather than negotiation (Gen 39:12), watchful prayer (Matt 26:41), and the faithfulness of God who provides a way of escape (1 Cor 10:13). No one is strong enough to be safe from this sin (v. 26; 1 Cor 10:12).
7.examples: A young man who notices that his evening walks, or his late-night scrolling, keep taking him past the same corner can change the route before he has to fight the battle at the door. A Christian who finds himself using church language to excuse what he knows is wrong is doing what the woman did with her peace offerings (v. 14). And anyone who has already gone through her door can still turn round and go home: the way of escape is real, and the Christ who rose from death brings home those who turn to him.

keyVerse.quote: Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths
keyVerse.note: This is the lesson the father draws from everything he saw from his window. The young man’s fall began long before her door, when his heart turned and his feet followed it down the wrong street. Guard the heart, and the feet are kept; and the heart is best guarded by loving wisdom more (v. 4), as the true Son loved his Father’s words.

7.reflection:
The young man was not rebellious but “lacking sense”, literally lacking heart (v. 7), and he drifted toward her corner at dusk (vv. 8–9). What are the “streets near her corner” in our culture? Why is drift often more dangerous than open rebellion?

The woman wraps her invitation in religion (v. 14), flattery (v. 15) and the promise of secrecy (vv. 19–20). Which of these do you think is most persuasive today, and why?

The father’s defence is to treasure God’s words like the apple of your eye and to call wisdom your sister (vv. 2–4). What practical habits help God’s word become something we love and not only rules we keep?

Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). How does it help in temptation to know that he stood where we stand and did not fall? What hope does the gospel offer to someone who has already gone through her door?

8.title: Wisdom Calls: I Was Beside Him

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Wisdom Calls at the Crossroads
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom calls openly to everyone, and what she offers is worth more than anything else. She does not whisper at dusk like the woman of chapter 7 but stands on the heights, at the crossroads and by the city gates, where all must pass (vv. 1–3). Her call goes out to all people, even the simple and the foolish, who most need what she gives (vv. 4–5). Every word she speaks is true and straight, with nothing twisted or hidden (vv. 6–9). So take her instruction instead of silver, for nothing you could want compares with her (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The seductress of chapter 7 whispered at a corner in the dark; Wisdom calls in the open, to everyone, and has nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.quote: Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice? On the heights beside the way, at the crossroads she takes her stand; beside the gates in front of the town, at the entrance of the portals she cries aloud:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom calls out openly, where everyone passes and every decision is made, in sharp contrast to the whisper at dusk in chapter 7.

Does not wisdom call? Chapter 7 ended in the chambers of death. The young man lacking sense went looking for a voice at dusk and found the wrong one. Wisdom was calling all along.

On the heights. The seductress lay in wait “at every corner” (7:12), in the twilight. Wisdom stands on the heights, where she can be seen, at the crossroads, where decisions are made, and beside the gates, where everyone passes (see the city gate). One whispers in the dark; the other calls aloud in the open. Every reader stands at that crossroads, and the question is whether he is listening.

verseByVerse.quote: "To you, O men, I call, and my cry is to the children of man. O simple ones, learn prudence; O fools, learn sense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom invites everyone, and above all the simple and the foolish, who lack the very thing she offers.

To the children of man. Wisdom’s call is universal, and she calls the very people who seem least likely to respond: the simple and the fools. She does not wait for them to improve before she invites them; the invitation is precisely for those who lack what she offers. This is how grace works. Jesus said he came to call not the righteous but sinners (Mark 2:17), and Wisdom’s voice sounds exactly like his.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, for I will speak noble things, and from my lips will come what is right, for my mouth will utter truth; wickedness is an abomination to my lips.
