All the words of my mouth are righteous; there is nothing twisted or crooked in them. They are all straight to him who understands, and right to those who find knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom’s words are true, right and straight, with nothing hidden or twisted, and they are plain to anyone humble enough to understand.

I will speak noble things. Every word Wisdom uses of her speech contrasts with the seductress. Hers were smooth words and flattery; Wisdom’s are noble things, what is right, truth. The lips of the forbidden woman dripped honey (5:3); Wisdom’s lips find wickedness detestable.

Nothing twisted or crooked in them. You never have to read Wisdom’s words twice to find the trick. And they are straight to him who understands: the words are clear, but it takes an understanding heart to see how clear they are. To the proud they seem foolish or narrow; to the humble, obvious.

Does it hide its ending? Here is a test for any voice, whether a friend, an advertisement or your own desires: does it need to hide its ending, as the seductress hid the chambers of death? Wisdom never does.

verseByVerse.quote: Take my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold, for wisdom is better than jewels, and all that you may desire cannot compare with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is worth more than any wealth, so when you must choose, choose her.

Take my instruction instead of silver. As in 3:14–15, the key word is instead. She is not saying, have both. She is saying, if you must choose, choose me. The honest businessman who loses a deal because he would not lie has taken instruction instead of silver. The student who will not cheat for a grade has taken knowledge rather than gold. Wisdom says they have the better bargain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom is strong and generous, and she loves those who love her. She lives with prudence and knowledge, and because the fear of the LORD is hatred of evil, she hates pride, arrogance and crooked speech (vv. 12–13). Counsel and strength are hers, and every king or ruler who governs justly does so by her (vv. 14–16). Those who seek her find her (v. 17). She brings riches and honour that endure, fruit better than gold, but only along the paths of justice, and she gives those who love her an inheritance (vv. 18–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Every just ruler governs by a wisdom that is not his own, and that wisdom gives herself to anyone who loves her.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, wisdom, dwell with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion. The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom lives with good sense and hates evil, above all pride, because to fear the LORD is to hate what he hates.

I, wisdom, dwell with prudence. Prudence, knowledge and discretion are Wisdom’s companions, and whoever takes her in finds she brings her family: good sense, foresight, the ability to plan well.

The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil. Here is a definition that should surprise anyone who thinks of the fear of the LORD as merely a feeling. You cannot revere God and be comfortable with what he hates. A person who says he fears God but enjoys cruelty, lies easily and laughs at purity has not understood the words. “Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good” (Romans 12:9).

Pride and arrogance. The first things on Wisdom’s hate list are pride and arrogance, just as haughty eyes stood first among the seven things the LORD hates (6:17). Pride is the opposite of wisdom because pride will not learn.

verseByVerse.quote: I have counsel and sound wisdom; I have insight; I have strength. By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just; by me princes rule, and nobles, all who govern justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is strong as well as good, and every ruler who governs justly does so with wisdom borrowed from God.

I have strength. Wisdom is not weak. Many people think of goodness as soft and of power as belonging to the ruthless. Wisdom says she holds both the counsel and the strength.

By me kings reign. Every just government has ruled by wisdom not its own. Kings think their power comes from armies, elections or birth. It comes from God: “he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise” (Daniel 2:21), and “there is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1).

Borrowed wisdom. That is a humbling truth for anyone in authority, whether a president, a manager, an elder or a parent: the wisdom to rule well is borrowed. And it is a comforting truth for everyone under authority: no ruler is outside the rule of the one whose robe bears the name “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16).

Textual note. The ESV notes that many manuscripts read all who “govern the earth” in verse 16.

verseByVerse.quote: I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me. Riches and honor are with me, enduring wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold, even fine gold, and my yield than choice silver. I walk in the way of righteousness, in the paths of justice, granting an inheritance to those who love me, and filling their treasuries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom loves those who love her, and she rewards them with lasting riches gained justly, an inheritance rather than a windfall.

I love those who love me. Wisdom is not a cold principle but someone who returns love. Put this beside chapter 1, where those who ignored her call “will seek me diligently but will not find me” (1:28). The same words, opposite outcomes, and the difference is the heart. The people of chapter 1 sought rescue from the storm; the people of chapter 8 seek Wisdom because they love her. Anyone who seeks God for God’s sake will find him.

Enduring wealth and righteousness. Wisdom does bring riches and honour, but look at the adjective, enduring, and the word beside it, righteousness. The riches of folly are quick and passing; Wisdom’s are slow and lasting. Her fruit and her yield are the language of a harvest, something that grows over seasons.

In the paths of justice. She fills treasuries, but only by walking in the paths of justice; Wisdom never makes anyone rich by crooked means. And what she gives is an inheritance, something received as a gift and kept in a family. Isaiah extends the same invitation in the voice of the LORD: “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” “Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live” (Isaiah 55:2–3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–31 — Before the Beginning of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s wisdom is older than the world, and creation itself was made by it and in joy. Before anything was made, the LORD had Wisdom with him (vv. 22–23). She was brought forth before the depths and springs, before the mountains and hills, before the first dust of the earth (vv. 24–26). She was there as he set the heavens in place, drew the horizon on the deep, fixed the sea’s limit and marked out the earth’s foundations (vv. 27–29). Beside him like a master workman, she was his daily delight, rejoicing in his world and delighting in the children of man (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom here is a poetic figure, but the New Testament gives her place and work to the eternal Son, through whom all things were made and in whom the Father delights.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old. Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s wisdom is older than the world: before he made anything at all, his wisdom was with him, the first principle of all his work.

The LORD possessed me. Proverbs 8 is poetry. Wisdom is personified, that is, pictured as a person, as Folly is in chapter 9: a woman calling in the streets. The point is that God’s wisdom is older than the world and that everything was made by it. God was never without his wisdom.

Set up. This is the word God uses of his King: “I have set my King on Zion” (Psalm 2:6). Before there was an earth, Wisdom was enthroned. Read in the light of Christ, the line recalls Micah’s ruler to be born in Bethlehem, “whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” (Micah 5:2), and Jesus’ prayer, “glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5).

In the beginning was the Word. The New Testament leads us from this chapter to Christ, though it never quotes it directly. What Proverbs says of God’s wisdom in a poem, the apostles say of the Son plainly: Paul calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). But the New Testament is careful how it says this. John does not say the Word was made at the beginning; he says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Son is not the first of God’s works; he is the one “through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6). When the risen Christ calls himself “the beginning of God’s creation” (Revelation 3:14), he means its source and ruler, not its first product. In the same way Paul calls the Son “the firstborn of all creation” and at once explains, “For by him all things were created” (Colossians 1:15–16). Firstborn means the heir who holds the highest rank (Psalm 89:27), not the first thing made.

Where Christians differ. Who is Wisdom in this chapter? Some Christians read it as a direct description of the eternal Son. Others read Wisdom as a poetic personification of God’s own wisdom. In the fourth century Arius and his followers went further, using the Greek translation “created” (see below) to argue that the Son of God was a creature, the first and greatest thing God made. The church rejected that teaching at the Council of Nicaea in 325, and rightly.

This commentary’s view. Wisdom here is a poetic personification of God’s wisdom, as Folly is in chapter 9, fully embodied in Christ but not a statement about the Son’s origin, for he had no beginning. Arius misused this verse: he took a line of poetry about God’s wisdom and turned it into a statement about when the Son began, which it was never meant to be.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind possessed usually means to get or acquire, but it is sometimes used of God making or bringing forth (Genesis 14:19), so translations differ. The ESV notes that it may be rendered “fathered”, and that the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint) read “created”; it also notes that work is literally “way”. The poem’s point does not hang on the choice: wisdom was God’s before anything was made.
verseByVerse.note: Wisdom speaks as present with God before creation, language the New Testament echoes of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains had been shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth, before he had made the earth with its fields, or the first of the dust of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the oceans, the springs, the mountains or the first speck of dust, God’s wisdom already was.

Brought forth. This is birth language, and the poem uses it to say that Wisdom did not come after the world. Before the oceans, before a single spring, Wisdom was. The Nicene Creed, the church’s fourth-century confession, says of the Son that he is “begotten, not made”, and that is the right direction to take this language when it is applied to Christ: not that he had a beginning, but that he is eternally from the Father, as a son is from a father.

Before the mountains had been shaped. The poem goes down the list of the oldest things anyone can imagine. Mountains seem eternal; Wisdom is older. The first of the dust of the world, the very first grain of soil, came after her. Everything a person can see or touch is younger than the wisdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: When he established the heavens, I was there; when he drew a circle on the face of the deep, when he made firm the skies above, when he established the fountains of the deep, when he assigned to the sea its limit, so that the waters might not transgress his command, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom was present as God built the world, spreading the heavens, drawing the horizon and setting the sea its bounds, so that creation is ordered, not chaos.

I was there. Wisdom was not a spectator in the stands but present at the work. God drew a circle on the face of the deep, the horizon, where the sky seems to meet the waters. Genesis says that at the beginning “darkness was over the face of the deep” (Genesis 1:2). Wisdom saw God mark out order in that darkness.

He assigned to the sea its limit. To the ancient mind the sea was the great symbol of chaos. God speaks and it stops: “Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed” (Job 38:11); “I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass” (Jeremiah 5:22).

In a human life. Wisdom does the same in a human life. The commands of God that seem to limit us are like the shoreline: without them, chaos floods everything. A person who throws off every limit does not become free; he becomes a flood that wrecks his own life and others’.

Where Christians differ. Proverbs 8 is poetry and does not say how long the work of creation took. Faithful Christians who read the days of Genesis as long ages or as a literary framework do so out of reverence for Scripture too, and deserve respect.

This commentary’s view. Genesis does say how long: God made all things in six ordinary days (Genesis 1; Exodus 20:11).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew of verse 28 is uncertain, but the picture is clear: God fixed the skies and the springs of the deep in their places.

verseByVerse.quote: then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always, rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom was at God’s side as he made the world, his joy, rejoicing in all he made and delighting above all in human beings.

Beside him, like a master workman. Here the poem reaches its warmest point. Wisdom was close at God’s side, like the skilled craftsman at the builder’s elbow. John says, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), and speaks of “the only God, who is at the Father’s side” (John 1:18).

I was daily his delight. The mood of creation was joy. Wisdom was rejoicing before him always. Creation was not a grim task. It was carried out in delight, the Father delighting in his Wisdom and Wisdom rejoicing before him.

My beloved Son. When Jesus was baptised, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). And Jesus spoke of the glory the Father had given him “because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). The delight of verse 30 is older than time.

Delighting in the children of man. Wisdom’s delight moved outward, to the inhabited world and above all to human beings. Of all that God made, Wisdom took special pleasure in them. Read that in the light of the gospel. The Son who was the Father’s delight before the world began delighted in the children of man so much that he became one of them. He “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7). The Wisdom who rejoiced over the world at creation came into that world to save it. That is how much God’s wisdom delights in you.

Uncertain wording. The rare Hebrew word behind master workman may instead mean a little child, as the ESV notes, a picture of Wisdom playing at God’s side; and I was daily his delight may mean “daily filled with delight” (ESV footnote). On every reading Wisdom is close to God and full of joy as he makes the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–36 — Whoever Finds Me Finds Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wisdom that made the world now calls for a decision. Wisdom turns back to her sons: blessed are those who keep her ways, hear her instruction and do not neglect it (vv. 32–33). The blessed life belongs to the one who listens daily, watching at her gates like someone waiting for a door to open (v. 34). The chapter ends with two ways: For whoever finds me finds life and the favour of the LORD, while whoever misses her wounds himself, and all who hate her love death (vv. 35–36).
verseByVerse.theology: Life and death depend on one thing: whether a person finds wisdom, and in the fullest sense that means finding Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O sons, listen to me: blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction and be wise, and do not neglect it. Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having shown that she made the world, Wisdom turns back to her sons: the blessed life belongs to those who listen to her daily and wait at her door.

And now, O sons. It is the phrase the father used after the story of the seductress (7:24). After the vision of creation, Wisdom comes back to the crossroads and draws the conclusion: listen to me. The wisdom that made the world is the wisdom that will make your life.

Do not neglect it. The danger for most people is not open rejection of wisdom but neglect: letting the voice go unheard because other voices are louder and closer.

Watching daily at my gates. The picture is of someone waiting outside a house every morning for the door to open, like a servant waiting for his master, or a lover for the beloved. The blessing belongs to the person who makes seeking wisdom a daily habit, not something he turns to only in a crisis.

Waiting on Christ. For a Christian, waiting at Wisdom’s doors means waiting on Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). And it is never a wait at a locked house. He has promised, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Every morning, someone’s gate. The picture may seem quaint. It is not. Most of us already keep a morning vigil: the phone reached for before we are fully awake, the feed checked, the inbox opened, and all of it again a dozen times before lunch. Some of the cleverest people alive are paid to make sure we keep coming back, and what we return to every day slowly shapes what we love. So the question is not whether we will watch daily at some gate, but at whose. A feed wants your attention so that it can sell it; Wisdom wants your attention so that she can give you life (v. 35). And the gospel adds a last surprise. In Jesus’ story of the lost son, the one watching the road was not the son but the father, who saw him while he was still a long way off, and ran (Luke 15:20). Those who wait at Wisdom’s doors find that someone has been watching for them first.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To find wisdom is to find life itself and the LORD’s favour; to miss her is to wound yourself, and to hate her is, in the end, to choose death.

Whoever finds me finds life. This is the promise the chapter has been building toward: not only a better life, but life itself, and favor from the LORD, which is grace.

He who fails to find me injures himself. No one else needs to punish the fool; he wounds himself.

All who hate me love death. The last phrase is stark. Nobody thinks he loves death. The young man of chapter 7 thought he loved pleasure. But to reject the source of life is, whether one knows it or not, to choose death: “whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him” (John 3:36).

Life in the Son. “Whoever has the Son has life” (1 John 5:12). “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). To find Wisdom, finally, is to find Christ.

A choice with a face. So the chapter ends where the book always ends up, at a choice between two ways. But here the choice has a face. The Wisdom who stood beside the Father at creation, delighting in the children of man, stands at the crossroads and calls. Whoever finds him finds life.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice?<sup>2</sup>On the heights beside the way, at the crossroads she takes her stand;<sup>3</sup>beside the gates in front of the town, at the entrance of the portals she cries aloud:<sup>4</sup>"To you, O men, I call, and my cry is to the children of man.<sup>5</sup>O simple ones, learn prudence; O fools, learn sense.<sup>6</sup>Hear, for I will speak noble things, and from my lips will come what is right,<sup>7</sup>for my mouth will utter truth; wickedness is an abomination to my lips.<sup>8</sup>All the words of my mouth are righteous; there is nothing twisted or crooked in them.<sup>9</sup>They are all straight to him who understands, and right to those who find knowledge.<sup>10</sup>Take my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold,<sup>11</sup>for wisdom is better than jewels, and all that you may desire cannot compare with her.<sup>12</sup>"I, wisdom, dwell with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion.<sup>13</sup>The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate.<sup>14</sup>I have counsel and sound wisdom; I have insight; I have strength.<sup>15</sup>By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just;<sup>16</sup>by me princes rule, and nobles, all who govern justly.<sup>17</sup>I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me.<sup>18</sup>Riches and honor are with me, enduring wealth and righteousness.<sup>19</sup>My fruit is better than gold, even fine gold, and my yield than choice silver.<sup>20</sup>I walk in the way of righteousness, in the paths of justice,<sup>21</sup>granting an inheritance to those who love me, and filling their treasuries.<sup>22</sup>"The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old.<sup>23</sup>Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth.<sup>24</sup>When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water.<sup>25</sup>Before the mountains had been shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth,<sup>26</sup>before he had made the earth with its fields, or the first of the dust of the world.<sup>27</sup>When he established the heavens, I was there; when he drew a circle on the face of the deep,<sup>28</sup>when he made firm the skies above, when he established the fountains of the deep,<sup>29</sup>when he assigned to the sea its limit, so that the waters might not transgress his command, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,<sup>30</sup>then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always,<sup>31</sup>rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man.<sup>32</sup>"And now, O sons, listen to me: blessed are those who keep my ways.<sup>33</sup>Hear instruction and be wise, and do not neglect it.<sup>34</sup>Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors.<sup>35</sup>For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD,<sup>36</sup>but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death."
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 ended in “the chambers of death” (7:27), with a young man following a whisper at dusk. Now, in the longest and highest of her speeches (compare 1:20–33), Wisdom herself calls aloud in broad daylight. It is the summit of the opening poems, and prepares for the rival feasts of chapter 9.

The message. God’s wisdom calls to everyone, even the simple and the foolish, offering words that are true, a rule that is just, riches that last and, in the end, life itself. This wisdom is no human invention: it was with the LORD before the world began, at his side as he made it, his daily delight, and delighting in human beings. Whoever finds her finds life and the LORD’s favour; whoever hates her loves death.

Why it was said. The son has just heard the seductress’s smooth words; he needs to hear a better voice. And he needs to know that the wisdom his parents pass on is not merely family advice or a tradition shared with Israel’s neighbours (see the introduction), but the wisdom by which the Creator made and still orders the world.

How the chapter makes its case. Wisdom calls in public to all, and her words are straight and worth more than silver or jewels (vv. 1–11). She hates pride, gives kings and rulers their just rule, and loves and enriches those who love her (vv. 12–21). Then the poem rises to its height: before the depths, the mountains or the first dust of the world, Wisdom was with the LORD, beside him like a master workman, his delight, and rejoicing in the children of man (vv. 22–31). So listen to her and wait daily at her doors, for whoever finds her finds life (vv. 32–36).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him. The chapter is poetry, and Wisdom is a personification of God’s own wisdom, not a direct description of the Son or a statement about when he began, for he had no beginning (see the note on vv. 22–23). But what the poem says of God’s wisdom the New Testament says plainly of Christ: he is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), and in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). The wisdom that delighted in the children of man came to live among them, and Jesus calls at the crossroads as Wisdom did: “Come to me” (Matthew 11:28).

For us. Every day many voices call. Choose the one that never hides its ending, value it above money, and listen to it daily, not only in a crisis. To find Christ is to find life and the favour of God, and he has promised never to turn away anyone who comes.
8.theology:
God's wisdom is universally offered (vv. 4-5), perfectly truthful (vv. 6-9), and the source of all just authority (vv. 15-16; Dan 2:21; Rom 13:1). The fear of the LORD includes hatred of evil (v. 13).

Wisdom existed before creation, and God made the world by it (vv. 22-31). She is a poetic figure, God’s wisdom pictured as a woman, not a direct portrait of the Son, but the New Testament gives this language its full meaning in Christ. It identifies Christ as the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24; Col 2:3), through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3; Col 1:16-17; Heb 1:2). Verse 22 must not be read, as Arius read it, to make the Son a creature; the Son is eternally with the Father (John 1:1; 17:5), begotten, not made.

The Father's eternal delight in his Wisdom (v. 30; Matt 3:17; John 17:24) overflows in delight in humanity (v. 31), fulfilled when the Son became man (Phil 2:6-7). Finding Wisdom is finding life; rejecting her is loving death (vv. 35-36; John 17:3; 3:36).
8.examples: God's commands work like a shoreline: they look like limits, but they are what keeps the chaos out. And the blessed life is pictured as someone who waits at Wisdom's door every morning, not only when trouble comes.

keyVerse.quote: For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter builds to this promise. The Wisdom who called at the crossroads and stood beside the LORD at creation offers not just a better life but life itself, and God’s favour, which is grace. The New Testament shows where that wisdom is finally found: “Whoever has the Son has life” (1 John 5:12).

8.reflection:
Wisdom calls in public, “on the heights” and “at the crossroads” (vv. 2–3), while the woman of chapter 7 whispered at dusk. What voices compete for your attention each day, and how can you tell which of them “hide their ending”?

“The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil” (v. 13), and the first things Wisdom hates are pride and arrogance. Why is pride the great enemy of wisdom? Where might it be keeping you from learning?

Verses 22–31 picture God’s wisdom with him before creation, his delight, and “delighting in the children of man” (v. 31). How does the New Testament’s teaching that Christ is “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24) help you read this poem? What does it tell you about how God regards human beings?

“Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my gates” (v. 34). What gate do you watch first each morning? What would it look like this week to wait daily on Christ, the one who promised never to cast out anyone who comes to him?

9.title: Wisdom Has Built Her House

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom’s invitation is a feast already prepared, offered free to anyone who knows he needs it. Wisdom has built a solid house and done all the work of the banquet herself: the meat slaughtered, the wine mixed, the table laid (vv. 1–2). She does not wait for guests to find her, but sends her young women to call from the heights of the town to the very people most at risk, the simple and those who lack sense (vv. 3–4). Her offer is simply to come and eat, and the meal changes the guest: leave your simple ways, live, and walk in the way of insight (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom's invitation is a feast already prepared, offered free to people who have nothing to bring but their need.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars. She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom has done all the work herself: the house is built and the table laid before a single guest is called. The first nine chapters end with two pictures meant to be seen side by side: two women, two houses, two feasts.

She has hewn her seven pillars. Her pillars are cut from stone, and seven often stands for completeness: the house is finished and solid, nothing temporary. Proverbs will later say, “The wisest of women builds her house” (14:1), and Jesus spoke of the wise man “who built his house on the rock”, the house that “did not fall” (Matthew 7:24–25).

She has set her table. Everything is ready before anyone is invited, and the host has paid the cost. Jesus told a parable that sounds almost exactly like this. A king prepared a wedding feast for his son and sent word: “See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast” (Matthew 22:4). The gospel is not an invitation to come and help prepare the meal. It is an invitation to a table already set.

A further echo. Many Christians have heard an echo here, though not the verse’s own meaning. The New Testament speaks of a house God is building, with Christ Jesus as “the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:20–21). The house wisdom builds is finally God’s dwelling among his people.

Uncertain wording. No one knows exactly what the seven pillars refer to: a fine house with pillars round its courtyard, the seven days of creation (8:22–31), or simply completeness, the likeliest. Mixed her wine probably means wine blended with spices, though some think of wine mixed with water. Either way the point is plain: the house is solid and the feast carefully prepared.

verseByVerse.quote: She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom does not wait to be found; she sends her messengers to call the simple, the very people most likely to walk into Folly’s house.

She has sent out her young women. Her invitation goes out to find people, calling “from the highest places in the town”, where the voice carries furthest. In the parable of the great banquet the master said, “Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city”, and then, “Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:21, 23).

Whoever is simple. That is exactly the young man of chapter 7, who was “lacking sense” (7:7). Wisdom invites the very person most likely to walk into Folly’s house, and she does not demand that he become wise first. The qualification for her feast is knowing you need it, just as Jesus said, “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17).

Wisdom’s messengers today. Every Christian who speaks of Christ to a friend is one of Wisdom’s messengers, calling from wherever he stands in the town. He does not need to be eloquent; he only passes on an invitation he once received.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed. Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom’s offer is food to be received, not a course to be passed, and taking it changes the direction of a life: leave, live, walk.

Come, eat of my bread. Wisdom is not only studied but received, as food becomes part of a body. Isaiah’s great invitation sounds the same: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1).

The bread of life. Jesus took these words onto his own lips: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:51). The poem does not name him, but the gospel shows what this bread finally is: Christ himself, “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), who gives not only food but his own life. The Bible’s last invitation is still Wisdom’s: “let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (Revelation 22:17).

Leave your simple ways, and live. No one can sit at Wisdom’s table and keep his old life unchanged. Grace is free, but it does not leave a person where it found him: by the Spirit it turns a life around.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says literally leave the simple ones, and the ESV notes the alternative Leave the company of the simple. Either a way of life or companions may be meant; both are true, for “Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise” (13:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How a person takes correction shows whether he can be taught, and so which table he will sit at. Between the two feasts come sayings about the scoffer and the wise. Correct a scoffer and you will be insulted; correct a wise man and he will love you and grow wiser still (vv. 7–9). The reason lies at the root: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and to know the Holy One is insight, the motto of 1:7 returning to close the first nine chapters (v. 10). Wisdom brings life (v. 11), and each person answers for his own choice: no one else can be wise for you, and no one else will bear your scoffing (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: How a person takes correction shows which banquet he is heading for.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury. Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you. Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same rebuke is hated by the scoffer and welcomed by the wise, so how a person takes correction shows what is in his heart. These sayings interrupt the two banquets to explain why some accept Wisdom’s invitation and others do not.

Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse. The scoffer is the person who mocks what is serious. Correct him and you get abuse: insults, anger, perhaps worse. Jesus said the same: “do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you” (Matthew 7:6).

Reprove a wise man, and he will love you. The same rebuke produces opposite reactions, and the reaction reveals the heart.

He will be still wiser. The Hebrew simply says give to a wise man, as the ESV notes. The wise man is not the one who knows the most but the one who keeps learning.

Your own response. So turn the test on yourself: when someone last pointed out a fault in you, did you love them for it or resent them? A believer can bear correction without despair, because his standing rests on Christ, not on being found faultless. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (27:6), and the psalmist welcomed a righteous man’s rebuke as “a kindness” and “oil for my head” (Psalm 141:5).

What it does not mean. Not that we write off anyone who bristles once, or stop offering the gospel to mockers; only that we stop pressing correction on someone who has shown he will trample it.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight. For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life. If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom begins with reverent awe of the LORD and grows into knowing the Holy One himself; it leads to life, and each person answers for whether he takes it.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. The motto of 1:7 returns, framing the first nine chapters like a door at each end, and something is added: wisdom is not only fearing God but knowing him personally. The goal of Proverbs is not a clever life but a life that knows God.

The Holy One. “Holy” can sound like a word for stained glass. At root it means set apart: God is not a larger version of us but in a class of his own, utterly pure. So fear and knowledge stand together; no one knows this God casually. Isaiah saw him and cried, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). Yet the Holy One has made himself knowable. Peter said to Jesus, “we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God” (John 6:69), and that Holy One died so that sinners “have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). When you open Scripture, remember whom you are coming to know: not an idea, but the Holy One who has brought you near. See Holiness in the Theological Dictionary.

Years will be added to your life. Folly’s guests are among the dead (v. 18); Wisdom’s have years added.

If you are wise, you are wise for yourself. No one else can be wise for you, and no one else will bear your scoffing. Your parents’ faith will not save you, and your friends’ folly will not excuse you. “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself” (Ezekiel 18:20).

If you scoff, you alone will bear it. Parents need to hear this half. A son or daughter who scoffs bears it alone; a father or mother who taught faithfully is not made guilty by a child’s choices, and may keep praying for that child with hope.

Does wisdom always lengthen life? As a pattern, yes: the wise avoid much that cuts lives short. But Abel, John the Baptist and Stephen died young and righteous, so the proverb states how God’s world usually works, not a timetable for each life (see the introduction). Its fullest meaning lies beyond the grave: “whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Folly copies Wisdom’s invitation word for word, but her table is stolen and her house is a grave. She is loud and knows nothing; where Wisdom built and prepared, Folly simply sits at her door, yet she has taken a seat on the same heights and calls to people who are walking straight on their way (vv. 13–15). Her words are Wisdom’s words exactly, so the simple cannot tell the two apart by what they hear (v. 16). The difference lies in what is served, stolen water and secret bread that are sweet only because they are forbidden (v. 17), and in where the house leads: her guests are already among the dead (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Folly copies Wisdom's invitation word for word, but her table is set with stolen goods in a house of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing. She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town, calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folly has nothing to teach and has prepared nothing, yet she takes the same high seat as Wisdom and calls to people who are doing well.

The woman Folly is loud. Folly is pictured as a woman, like Wisdom, and looks very like the forbidden woman of chapter 7, who was also “loud” (7:11). She is seductive, and she knows nothing: she has a great deal to say and nothing to teach.

She sits at the door of her house. Wisdom has built, hewn, slaughtered, mixed, set and sent: six verbs of work. Folly sits. She has built and prepared nothing.

On the highest places of the town. And yet she has found a seat exactly where Wisdom’s messengers called (v. 3). Her voice is just as easy to hear.

Who are going straight on their way. Her target is not the lost but those walking a good road, to pull them off it. No one is so far along the straight road that he is beyond her reach: “let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12).

Uncertain wording. Seductive comes from the same root as simple, and the ESV notes the alternative full of simpleness. It may say what she does or what she is; probably both: Folly is a simpleton who makes simpletons.
verseByVerse.note: Folly is pictured as a rival woman, imitating wisdom’s invitation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says, "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folly’s invitation sounds exactly like Wisdom’s, but she offers stolen pleasures made sweet by secrecy, and her guests are already among the dead.

Whoever is simple, let him turn in here! Here is the chilling detail: Folly’s invitation is Wisdom’s word for word (v. 4), from the same heights, to the same people. False teaching borrows the vocabulary of the gospel, and sin promises life, freedom and fulfilment, the very things God offers. The simple person cannot tell the two invitations apart by their words, only by what is served and by where the house leads.

Stolen water is sweet. Wisdom offered meat and mixed wine; Folly offers water and bread, and it is stolen. She has nothing of her own. Her whole appeal is that it is forbidden: the water is no better, and the bread is pleasant because it is eaten in secret. Since the father pictured the marriage bed as water from “your own cistern” (5:15), stolen water probably hints at adultery, though Folly’s table holds every forbidden thing.

The oldest temptation. The fruit in Eden was “a delight to the eyes”, and the woman took it (Genesis 3:6), its attraction sharpened by the fact that God had said no. Paul describes the same perverse effect: “sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness” (Romans 7:8). In an affair, a theft or a secret habit, the secrecy is half the pleasure.

But he does not know that the dead are there. Her guests see a party. They do not see what the father has shown since chapter 2: the dead are there. The Hebrew word is rephaim, the shades of the dead, as at 2:18; her guests are already in Sheol, the place of the dead. They think they are dining; they are buried.

Proverbs 9 in one sentence. “For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23): stolen water that ends in death, or bread given free that ends in life. Both hostesses are calling now, in the same words. But only one has paid for the feast herself, and in the gospel the host paid with his own life. “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

How can I tell the two voices apart? Not by the words, but by what is served and where it leads. Does it need to be kept secret? Does it leave me emptier each time? Folly’s table depends on the dark; Wisdom’s feast is set in the open.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars.<sup>2</sup>She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.<sup>3</sup>She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town,<sup>4</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,<sup>5</sup>"Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed.<sup>6</sup>Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."<sup>7</sup>Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury.<sup>8</sup>Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you.<sup>9</sup>Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.<sup>10</sup>The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight.<sup>11</sup>For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.<sup>12</sup>If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.<sup>13</sup>The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing.<sup>14</sup>She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town,<sup>15</sup>calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,<sup>16</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says,<sup>17</sup>"Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."<sup>18</sup>But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 closes the long poems that open the book. After the father’s warnings against the adulteress (chapters 5–7) and Wisdom’s account of creation (chapter 8), and before the short sayings begin in chapter 10, the whole section is gathered into one last scene: two women, two houses, two feasts.

The message. Every life is an answer to an invitation. Wisdom, who has done all the work herself, calls the simple to her table to eat freely and live; Folly calls the same people in the same words, offering stolen pleasures in a house of the dead. What decides which table we sit at is whether we will be taught, and that begins with the fear of the LORD and the knowledge of the Holy One.

Why it was said. The young men of Israel, like every generation, heard many voices in the streets and at the gate (see the introduction). The father knows that Folly will not sound like folly; she will borrow Wisdom’s words. So he lets his son hear both invitations side by side before he goes out to meet them.

How the chapter makes its case. First Wisdom’s banquet (vv. 1–6): the house built, the feast ready, the simple called to leave, live and walk. Then, between the feasts, why people answer so differently (vv. 7–12): the scoffer hates correction and the wise man loves it, for “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (v. 10). Last, Folly’s feast (vv. 13–18): she has prepared nothing, yet calls from the same heights in Wisdom’s very words, offering stolen water, and her guests are in Sheol.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God revealed in him. Wisdom’s banquet is the shape of the gospel invitation: Jesus told of a king whose dinner was ready, the oxen slaughtered, who sent his servants into the streets to call the poor and the outcast (Matthew 22:4; Luke 14:21). Then he called himself the meal: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The generous host of Proverbs 9 shows what God is like, and in Christ the host paid for the feast with his own life, giving his flesh “for the life of the world” (John 6:51). Folly offers life and ends in death; he went into death so that his guests might live.

For us. Both voices are calling today, and they sound alike. Judge them by what is served and where the house leads. Ask how you take correction, for that shows which table you are walking toward. And come to Christ’s table as you are: the only qualification is knowing you need it.
9.theology:
Chapters 1 to 9 close with two invitations. Wisdom's feast is prepared at the host's cost and offered freely to the needy (vv. 1-6), as the gospel banquet is (Matt 22:2-4; Luke 14:16-23; John 6:35; Rev 22:17); accepting it means leaving the old way (v. 6).

The response to correction reveals the heart (vv. 7-9), and the fear of the LORD stands at both ends of the first nine chapters (v. 10; 1:7). Each person answers for his own response (v. 12; Ezek 18:20).

Folly imitates Wisdom's words (v. 16), offers only what is stolen and secret (v. 17; Gen 3:6; Rom 7:8), and leads to death (v. 18; Rom 6:23).
9.examples: The same rebuke can be hated by one person and loved by another, and the difference shows which table each is heading for. Wisdom works, building and preparing; Folly only sits and calls. And the guests at her table think they are dining when they are already buried.

keyVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the chapter and the closing door of chapters 1–9, which opened with the same motto (1:7). It explains why some accept Wisdom’s invitation and others refuse it: wisdom begins not with cleverness but with reverent awe of God, and grows into knowing the Holy One himself. That Holy One has made himself known in Jesus, “the Holy One of God” (John 6:69).

9.reflection:
Wisdom has done all the work of her feast before a single guest arrives (vv. 1–2), and Jesus told a parable in which everything was ready before the invitation went out (Matthew 22:4). Why is it so hard for us to believe that God’s grace is a table already set, rather than a meal we must help to prepare?

Verses 7–9 say that the way we respond to correction shows what kind of person we are. Think of the last time someone pointed out a fault in you. How did you respond, and what helps a Christian receive correction without either resentment or despair?

Folly uses Wisdom’s exact words (v. 16). Where today do you hear sin or false teaching borrowing the language of life, freedom or love? How can we tell the two invitations apart?

“Stolen water is sweet” (v. 17). Why does secrecy make wrong things feel more attractive? What does it look like to bring a secret habit into the light, and how does the promise of life at Wisdom’s table help?

10.title: The Proverbs of Solomon: Two Ways in Two Lines

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Righteous and the Wicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The two ways of chapters 1–9 now walk into the family, the purse and the memory a life leaves behind. The new heading opens Solomon’s collection with a saying about parents: a son’s wisdom or folly is never private (v. 1). Wealth gained by wickedness does not profit, for the LORD feeds the righteous and thwarts the craving of the wicked (vv. 2–3). A slack hand brings poverty, and a son who sleeps through harvest brings shame (vv. 4–5). The righteous carry blessing on their heads and leave a memory that goes on blessing, while the wicked hide violence behind their words and leave a name that rots (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: From here the book speaks in two-line contrasts, and the first ones set the two ways side by side in the family, the purse and the memory a life leaves behind.

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A child’s wisdom gladdens his parents and his folly grieves them, because no one’s choices are private.

The proverbs of Solomon. With a new heading the book changes shape. After nine chapters of a father’s long speeches, from here to the middle of chapter 22 come short sayings, most of them two-line contrasts: the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the lazy. The first nine chapters were the lecture; these are the tools, to be picked up, turned over and carried into the day. One or two pondered will do more good than a chapter skimmed.

A wise son makes a glad father. The first tool is aimed at the family, where a son’s choices land first.

The Son who made his Father glad. Only one Son ever made his Father wholly glad. At the Jordan the Father said of Jesus, “with you I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22), and Jesus could say, “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). He is the wise Son this verse describes, whose obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19), and he came for the foolish sons and daughters who grieve their parents and God, as the father running to the prodigal shows (Luke 15:20).

Are the proverbs promises? Mostly they are patterns, true as a rule (see the introduction). Proverbs says the diligent grow rich (v. 4), and also that injustice sweeps away the poor man’s harvest (13:23); Ezekiel describes a righteous father whose son turns violent (Ezekiel 18:5–13). So a hard-working believer who is still poor has not disproved the book or failed God. And parents whose child has turned away should hear this verse as a description of their sorrow, not a verdict on their parenting. God himself said, “Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me” (Isaiah 1:2). The Bible’s certainties rest on God’s promises in Christ, not on a formula for children or money.
verseByVerse.note: The first collection of Solomon’s one-verse proverbs (10:1–22:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death. The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth gained wrongly cannot save or satisfy, but the LORD provides for the righteous and frustrates the wicked.

Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit. Dishonest gain is real money, but it cannot buy what matters or save its owner from death. Jesus warned, “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15).

But righteousness delivers from death. The righteous life keeps a man from the violent or shameful ends of the wicked. In the light of the New Testament it points further, to the righteousness God gives in Christ, which delivers from death itself (Romans 5:17–21). It is not salvation by good works.

The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry. The LORD first appears in these sayings as provider and judge. The wicked have cravings that God thwarts: they get what they wanted and find it does not satisfy, or they never get it at all.

Who the righteous are. From here to chapter 15 nearly every saying sets the righteous against the wicked, and we may hear “righteous” as “respectable” or even “self-righteous”. In Proverbs it is a word about how you treat people. Timothy Keller often pointed out, drawing on Bruce Waltke, that in Proverbs the righteous are willing to take a loss themselves so that the community gains, while the wicked are willing to let the community lose so that they gain. That exposes us: underneath, most of us are quietly keeping ourselves first. Only one man was righteous all the way down: Jesus, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). His righteousness is counted to us as a gift, and then it begins to remake us in his likeness. So look this week for one place where you can absorb a cost, of time, money or credit, so that someone else is better off. See Justification in the Theological Dictionary.

Does no righteous person ever go hungry? David said, “I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread” (Psalm 37:25). That is the pattern of God’s care. Yet Hebrews speaks of the faithful who went about “destitute, afflicted, mistreated” (Hebrews 11:37). A proverb states how God’s world generally works, not a guarantee against every hardship. But even in hunger the righteous are never abandoned, and their Father, who knows what they truly need, has promised to provide it (Matthew 6:33).

verseByVerse.quote: A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich. He who gathers in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps in harvest is a son who brings shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laziness leads to want and diligence to plenty, and the wise seize the season of work while it lasts.

A slack hand causes poverty. One hand is loose, not gripping the tool; the other is keen and hard at work. Laziness is not the only cause of poverty, and Proverbs says much about the oppressed poor and the unjust rich. But it is one cause, and a young person can do something about it.

He who gathers in summer. Harvest does not wait. There are a few weeks when the crop must be brought in, and a son who sleeps through them has lost the year, and shames the family that bears his name. Life has harvests too: the years of study, the early career, the season when children are young and must be taught. They do not come back.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous carry blessing and leave a memory that goes on blessing others, while the wicked hide violence and leave a name that rots.

Blessings are on the head of the righteous. They rest there visibly, like a crown. The wicked man’s mouth, by contrast, hides something: he talks pleasantly, and violence lies behind the words.

The memory of the righteous is a blessing. A righteous memory goes on blessing others after death: the grandmother whose prayers are still remembered, the father whose honesty is still quoted. Abel was killed at the beginning of history, and “through his faith, though he died, he still speaks” (Hebrews 11:4). “He will be remembered forever” (Psalm 112:6).

The name of the wicked will rot. It will rot, like meat left out. No one names his son after a notorious traitor.

Uncertain wording. The second line of verse 6 can also be read, as the ESV notes, “but violence covers the mouth of the wicked”. Then it means that the violence he planned will come back over his own face. Either reading fits Proverbs: the wicked hide harm in their words, and the harm returns on them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–21 — The Mouth of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Most of these sayings are about the mouth, because speech is where wisdom and folly show themselves first. The wise receive instruction while the fool babbles his way to ruin, and the person of integrity walks securely (vv. 8–10). The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, and love covers offences that hatred keeps stirring (vv. 11–12). The wise store up knowledge and learn from words; the fool learns only from the rod (vv. 13–14). Money protects, but it amplifies what a person already is (vv. 15–16). Rejecting reproof harms others, hatred is wrong whether hidden or voiced, and the more we talk the more we sin, while righteous lips feed many (vv. 17–21).
verseByVerse.theology: What comes out of a person's mouth either gives life to others or does them harm, and restraint is half of wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise of heart will receive commandments, but a babbling fool will come to ruin. Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out. Whoever winks the eye causes trouble, and a babbling fool will come to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise listen and live with nothing to hide, while the babbling fool and the schemer talk and plot their way into trouble.

The wise of heart will receive commandments. The wise man takes in, receiving commandments because he knows he needs them; the fool pours out. The babbling fool, literally the fool of lips, is too busy talking to hear anything, and he talks himself into ruin.

Whoever walks in integrity walks securely. Integrity means being whole, the same person in public and in private, and that person walks securely. He does not have to remember which story he told to whom. The man with a crooked way is living with a time bomb: he will be found out.

Whoever winks the eye. The winking eye is the signal of the schemer we met in 6:13. The second line repeats verse 8 word for word; some truths are worth saying twice within a few lines.

Textual note. Some ancient translations have a different second line in verse 10, but the one who rebukes boldly makes peace, and a few modern versions follow them. The Hebrew text, which the ESV follows, repeats verse 8.

verseByVerse.quote: The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A righteous person’s words refresh and give life, and love refuses to keep reopening wounds that hatred keeps stirring.

The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life. In a dry land a fountain is where people come to stay alive. The righteous person’s speech is like that: people come away from talking with him refreshed, encouraged, set right. The second line repeats verse 6.

Hatred stirs up strife. It stirs, like someone poking embers back into flame, and keeps old grievances alive. Love covers. It does not pretend the offence did not happen, and it does not cover crimes that must be exposed. But it declines to keep uncovering what has been forgiven. “Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates close friends” (17:9).

Rivers of living water. Jesus promised that this fountain would flow from everyone who comes to him: “Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). A believer’s mouth can become a fountain of life because the Spirit of life lives in him.

Love covers all offenses. Peter took this proverb straight into the life of the church: “Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). And behind every Christian’s covering love stands the love of God, who covered our sins at the cost of his Son.

Is there an offence you keep stirring? What would it mean to cover it today?

verseByVerse.quote: On the lips of him who has understanding, wisdom is found, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks sense. The wise lay up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise learn through words and store up knowledge, while the senseless learn only through pain and talk themselves into trouble.

A rod is for the back of him who lacks sense. There are two ways to learn. The person with understanding learns through words; wisdom is on his lips because it has gone in through his ears. The person who lacks sense will not learn through words, so he learns through the rod, through pain. The question is whether a person learns from instruction or from consequences.

The wise lay up knowledge. They store it like provisions. The fool spends his words as fast as he gets them, and every sentence brings disaster a step closer. Some people are one remark away from losing a job or a friend, and they make the remark.

verseByVerse.quote: A rich man's wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin. The wage of the righteous leads to life, the gain of the wicked to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Money really does protect, and poverty really does expose, but wealth only makes a person more of what he already is.

A rich man’s wealth is his strong city. Money does protect people. The rich can afford lawyers, doctors and a cushion against disaster; the poor have none, and one broken car can ruin them. Proverbs is not naive about that.

A second line added. But the book does not leave it there. In 18:11 the same first line comes back with a second line added: “A rich man’s wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his imagination.” The fortress is real, and it is also partly imaginary. Money protects against many things, but not against death, grief, judgment or an empty heart. That is why Paul tells the rich not to be haughty, “nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God” (1 Timothy 6:17).

The wage of the righteous leads to life. The righteous man’s wages go toward life: his family fed, his neighbour helped, God honoured. The wicked man’s gain leads to more sin: more greed, more indulgence, more distance from God. Money is an amplifier. It makes a person more of what he already is.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who rejects reproof leads others astray. The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever utters slander is a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing correction leads others astray as well as yourself, and hatred is wrong whether it is hidden behind a smile or spoken as slander.

He who rejects reproof leads others astray. A person who will not take correction harms others too. A father who never admits he was wrong teaches his children to do the same; a leader who will not be corrected takes a whole organisation down with him. Whether a person can be taught is never his own business alone.

The one who conceals hatred has lying lips. Verse 18 names two ways to handle hatred, and both are wrong. Hide it behind a smile, and you are a liar. Let it out as slander, and you are a fool. The only real answer is not to hide it or voice it, but to have it removed from the heart, which only God can do.

verseByVerse.quote: When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent. The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Much talk brings much sin, so the wise hold their tongues, and the words of the righteous are precious food for many.

When words are many, transgression is not lacking. The more a person talks, the more chances there are to say something wrong. James says, “let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger” (James 1:19), and “if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2).

Whoever restrains his lips is prudent. The wise person restrains his lips, like reining in a horse, and that self-control is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:23), not mere willpower. Ask God for it, and keep a guard on your lips.

The tongue of the righteous is choice silver. The contrast is between the tongue of one and the heart of the other. The righteous man’s words are valuable because his heart is; the wicked man’s heart is worth little, so his words are too. Speech is only as good as the heart it comes from.

The lips of the righteous feed many. The verb is a shepherd’s word: righteous lips tend and pasture many with counsel, encouragement, truth and the gospel itself. The fool cannot feed even himself, and dies starving for the sense that was on offer. The Good Shepherd fed his flock with words of eternal life (John 6:68), and those who speak his words share his work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–32 — The Blessing and the Stronghold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by looking to the future: what the righteous hope for will come, and what they stand on will hold. Lasting riches come from the blessing of the LORD, which adds no sorrow (v. 22). A fool treats wrongdoing as a joke, but the dread of the wicked will come on him, and when the storm passes only the righteous are left standing (vv. 23–25). A lazy man is as irritating as smoke in the eyes, while the fear of the LORD lengthens life (vv. 26–27). The hope of the righteous brings joy, the LORD’s way is their stronghold, and they will never be removed (vv. 28–30). Their mouths bring forth wisdom and know what is fitting (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter ends by looking to the future: what the righteous hope for will come, and what they stand on will hold.

verseByVerse.quote: The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lasting riches are the LORD’s gift, and what he gives does not bring sorrow with it.

The blessing of the LORD makes rich. This saying puts diligence in its place: riches that last come from the blessing of the LORD, without the sorrow that so often attaches to money: the anxiety, the family fights, the guilt of how it was gained. “Godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:6).

Is this a promise of wealth? No. God’s blessing is the true riches. Many faithful believers are poor (Luke 6:20; James 2:5); the proverb is not a prosperity formula.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the second line may be read, “and toil adds nothing to it”. That would not contradict verse 4, which praised the diligent hand; it would say that diligence without God’s blessing achieves nothing lasting. “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Either way: work hard, and rest in the knowledge that the increase is his.

verseByVerse.quote: Doing wrong is like a joke to a fool, but wisdom is pleasure to a man of understanding. What the wicked dreads will come upon him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted. When the tempest passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What a person enjoys shows what he is, and when the storm comes the wicked are swept away while the righteous stand.

Doing wrong is like a joke to a fool. What a person laughs at reveals what he loves. For the fool, wrongdoing is entertainment: the prank that humiliates someone, the joke about cheating, the laughter at sin on a screen. For the man of understanding, wisdom is where the pleasure is.

What the wicked dreads will come upon him. The wicked man pushes down a fear that one day he will answer for what he has done, and he is right. The righteous man’s desire will be granted.

When the tempest passes. The storm comes to both; the difference is what is left standing. Jesus told of two houses in the same storm. One “did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock”, and the other fell, “and great was the fall of it” (Matthew 7:25, 27). The rock is Jesus and his words.

verseByVerse.quote: Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him. The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be short.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lazy worker is a constant irritation to those who rely on him, but reverence for God tends toward a long life.

Like vinegar to the teeth. A comic picture any manager will recognise: send a lazy man on an errand, and the experience is like sour vinegar on your teeth or smoke in your eyes: irritating, painful and impossible to ignore. A Christian employee’s reliability is part of his witness, whether or not anyone thanks him for it.

The fear of the LORD prolongs life. Verse 27 states the general pattern again (9:11). A life lived in reverence toward God avoids many of the things that shorten lives: violence, addiction, reckless living, the stress of guilt. And ultimately the fear of the LORD leads to a life that has no end.

verseByVerse.quote: The hope of the righteous brings joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish. The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless, but destruction to evildoers. The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous can rejoice in hope now, because the LORD himself is their fortress and they will never be uprooted.

The hope of the righteous brings joy. The wicked expects a future built on his own plans, and it will perish. The righteous hopes in God, and that hope brings joy even now, before it is fulfilled. “Hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts” (Romans 5:5).

The way of the LORD is a stronghold. The same way of the LORD is two different things to two different people: a fortress to the blameless, destruction to evildoers. God’s ways do not change; what differs is whether a person walks in them or against them. The same sun that makes a rooted plant grow withers one with no roots.

The righteous will never be removed. The righteous are rooted. “Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever” (Psalm 125:1). Circumstances will shake them; they will not be removed from God’s hand (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.quote: The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off. The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked, what is perverse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous speak wisdom and know what fits the moment, while twisted speech will be cut off.

The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom. Wisdom is brought forth as a tree bears fruit; it grows out of the righteous person’s mouth naturally. The perverse tongue, the tongue that twists truth, is like a branch that will be cut off.

The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable. They know what is fitting: when to speak and when to be quiet, what will help and what will wound, how to say a hard thing kindly. That skill is learned over years of listening to God and to people. The wicked mouth knows only what is twisted. “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Colossians 4:6).

10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 opens Solomon’s main collection (10:1–22:16), and the book changes shape. After nine chapters of a father’s long speeches and Wisdom’s calls, the two ways now come in short two-line sayings, most of them contrasts between the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the foolish.

The message. The choice between Wisdom’s house and Folly’s is made on ordinary days, in the family, at work, with money and above all with the mouth. The righteous give life to others and their lives last; the wicked take, hide what they are, and leave a name that rots. Over both stands the LORD, who feeds, blesses and keeps the righteous and brings the hopes of the wicked to nothing.

Why it was said. These sayings were coined to be remembered and carried into the field, the market and the city gate (see the introduction). They train the young, and everyone else, to see what the fear of the LORD looks like in the small choices that make up a life.

How the chapter makes its case. The first sayings set the two ways side by side in the family, the purse and the memory a life leaves (vv. 1–7). Most of the middle is about speech: the wise receive while the fool babbles, the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, love covers all offences, and many words bring sin (vv. 8–21). The chapter ends looking ahead: the blessing of the LORD makes rich, the storm sweeps the wicked away, and the righteous will never be removed (vv. 22–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. Only one Son ever made his Father wholly glad: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22). Only one mouth was perfectly a fountain of life, so that officers sent to arrest him came back saying, “No one ever spoke like this man!” (John 7:46). Measured against these sayings, every one of us has babbled, stirred strife and kept ourselves first. The righteousness the chapter describes is finally his, counted to those who trust him, and his Spirit then makes their mouths fountains too (John 7:38).

For us. Take one or two of these sayings into the week rather than skimming them all. Ask what your words have done to the people around you today, whether you are stirring an old offence or covering it, and where your hope finally rests. The God who adds no sorrow to his blessing has given his Son, and those who stand on him will not be moved.
10.theology:
The two ways of chapters 1-9 are now applied to everyday life in compressed sayings. Proverbs describe the general pattern of God's world, not guarantees for every case (v. 3; Ps 37:25; Heb 11:37).

Human diligence matters (vv. 4-5), but lasting wealth is the LORD's blessing (v. 22; Ps 127:2). Speech reveals the heart (v. 20) and either gives life or does harm (vv. 11, 21). Love covers offences (v. 12; 1 Pet 4:8). Wealth gives real protection, but it is a false security for anyone who trusts in it (v. 15; 18:11). The hope of the righteous will not perish (v. 28; Rom 5:5).
10.examples: Think of the person whose words you go to when you are dry: that is what verse 11 means by a fountain of life. Ask how your name will be remembered when you are gone: as a blessing, or as something rotten (v. 7). And try saying less for a day, asking the Spirit for restraint, and notice how much you are glad you did not say.

keyVerse.quote: The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.
keyVerse.note: No subject in this chapter gets more attention than the mouth, and this verse gathers it up: words either give life to others or hide harm. The next verse shows the heart behind both, hatred that stirs strife and love that covers. Jesus promised that rivers of living water would flow from everyone who comes to him (John 7:38).

10.reflection:
Verse 1 says a son’s choices bring gladness or sorrow to his parents. How do our choices affect others more than we admit? How should parents whose child has turned away read this verse, in the light of God’s own words in Isaiah 1:2?

“The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life” (v. 11). Whose words have been a fountain of life to you, and what made them so? What would change if your words were like that for the people you live and work with?

“Love covers all offenses” (v. 12; 1 Peter 4:8). What is the difference between covering an offence and hiding a wrong that must be exposed? Is there an old offence you keep stirring that you could cover today?

Verses 4 and 22 set hard work beside “the blessing of the LORD”. How do diligence and dependence on God fit together in your work, your money and your rest?

11.title: A Just Weight Is His Delight
11.text: <sup>1</sup>A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight.<sup>2</sup>When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom.<sup>3</sup>The
