will himself be watered.<sup>26</sup>The people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it.<sup>27</sup>Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it.<sup>28</sup>Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.<sup>29</sup>Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind, and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart.<sup>30</sup>The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise.<sup>31</sup>If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 continues Solomon’s main collection, begun in chapter 10. The sayings still come in two-line contrasts between the righteous and the wicked, but here they move out of the home and into the market, the neighbourhood and the city.

The message. Righteousness is never merely private. God cares about the scales at the market stall as much as the prayers in the temple: a just weight is his delight. How we trade, speak about our neighbours, keep confidences and use what we have either blesses the people around us or tears them down, and it comes back to us. The generous are enriched, the hoarder is cursed, and the God who weighs hearts will see that evil does not go unpunished.

Why it was said. Israel’s towns ran on face-to-face trade, sworn guarantees and the reputation a person carried through the city gate (see the introduction). Rigged weights, gossip and hoarding in a famine could ruin a neighbour, and these sayings trained God’s people to live as his in the places where money and words change hands.

How the chapter makes its case. First, honest scales and a rejoicing city (vv. 1–11): the LORD hates a false balance, riches fail on the day of wrath, and a city is lifted by the upright and overthrown by the wicked. Next, the neighbour (vv. 12–22): the wise neither sneer nor spread secrets, seek many counsellors, avoid rash guarantees and show kindness, and evil will not go unpunished. Last, the open hand (vv. 23–31): one who waters will himself be watered, trust in riches falls, the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and if even the righteous are repaid on earth, the wicked certainly will be.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. The God who delights in a just weight weighs hearts too (v. 20), and on that scale no one’s ways are blameless except Christ’s. So the God of honest scales did not tip the balance; he paid the full weight himself: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). And the open hand of verses 24–25 is a small copy of his: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (2 Corinthians 9:15).

For us. Look at the scales in your own work. Guard what you say about people who are not in the room. And because God has given you his Son, give freely, trusting him to choose the currency in which he repays.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Honest Scales and a Rejoicing City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Righteousness is public: it is measured in the marketplace and felt by a whole city. The LORD hates a rigged scale and delights in an honest one, and pride brings disgrace while the humble have wisdom (vv. 1–2). Integrity guides the upright, but riches cannot help on the day of wrath, and the wicked are trapped by their own crookedness and cravings (vv. 3–6). At death the hopes of the wicked end, and the trouble they plan for the righteous often lands on themselves (vv. 7–8). The godless can ruin a neighbour with his mouth, but when the righteous prosper the whole city rejoices, lifted by their blessing and torn down by the words of the wicked (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Righteousness is public: it is measured in the marketplace and felt by a whole city.

verseByVerse.quote: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight. When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD hates cheating in business and delights in honest dealing, and he brings down the proud while giving wisdom to the humble.

A false balance. In the ancient market, goods were weighed on a balance against stones of a set weight (see weights and scales). A dishonest trader kept two sets of stones in his bag, a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling. The law had forbidden it: “You shall have just balances, just weights” (Leviticus 19:36). Amos denounced merchants eager to “make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances” (Amos 8:5).

An abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight. God calls the rigged scale an abomination, a word often used of idolatry, and the honest weight his delight. God cares about the till at the corner shop, and is pleased by an accurate invoice, an honest tax return, a fair price for a used car: “A just balance and scales are the LORD’s” (16:11).

When pride comes, then comes disgrace. Disgrace follows pride as thunder follows lightning. The humble have wisdom because they are willing to learn. “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

In everyday work. What are the scales in your work: the timesheet, the expense claim, the grade you give a student? For those he has already made his own, each of these, honestly kept, can be the LORD’s delight.

verseByVerse.quote: The integrity of the upright guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them. Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death. The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness. The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the treacherous are taken captive by their lust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Integrity guides and rescues the upright, the wicked are destroyed by their own crookedness, and money cannot help on the day of God’s wrath.

The integrity of the upright guides them. A person of integrity has a built-in guide. When a hard decision comes, he does not have to calculate what he can get away with; he already knows what he will do. The treacherous man has no such guide, and his crookedness eventually turns on him.

Riches do not profit in the day of wrath. The second line of verse 4 repeats 10:2; the first names the moment when riches fail. Zephaniah said, “Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD” (Zephaniah 1:18). Many people prepare financially for every day except that one; only the righteousness God gives in Christ will stand on it.

The wicked falls by his own wickedness. Verses 5 and 6 make the same point: the wicked are destroyed less by God’s thunderbolts than by their own choices. Their own cravings become the chains. Sin carries its own punishment inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wicked dies, his hope will perish, and the expectation of wealth perishes too. The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked walks into it instead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hopes of the wicked die with them, but the righteous are rescued, and the trouble meant for them often falls on the wicked.

When the wicked dies, his hope will perish. Everything the wicked man hoped for was on this side of the grave, so at the grave it all ends. The righteous man’s hope does not stop at death; that is where it is finally realised.

The righteous is delivered from trouble. Sometimes the trouble meant for the righteous lands on the wicked. The book of Esther is a whole story built on this proverb: Haman built a gallows for Mordecai, and in the end “they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Esther 7:10).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that wealth in verse 7 may also be read strength or iniquity. Whichever he trusted, his hope dies with him.

verseByVerse.quote: With his mouth the godless man would destroy his neighbor, but by knowledge the righteous are delivered. When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish there are shouts of gladness. By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is overthrown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked do harm with words, but the righteous bless their whole community, which rejoices when they do well.

With his mouth the godless man would destroy his neighbor. His weapon is slander, lies and rumour, which can destroy a neighbour’s reputation, marriage or career. The defence is knowledge: knowing the truth, knowing God, and being known for integrity, so that the lie does not stick.

The city rejoices. When the righteous prosper, communities are better off; when a corrupt official falls or a crime boss is jailed, the streets celebrate.

By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted. The upright bless their city: they pay fair wages, keep their word, care for the poor and pray for their leaders. The wicked tear it down, again by the mouth: corruption, propaganda, lies. God told the exiles in Babylon, “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you”, “for in its welfare you will find your welfare” (Jeremiah 29:7), and Jesus called his disciples “the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — The Neighbour, the Secret and the Kind Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How a person treats the people around him, in speech, trust and kindness, comes back to him. The wise do not belittle a neighbour or spread his secrets (vv. 12–13). Communities are kept safe by many counsellors, and households by refusing rash guarantees for strangers (vv. 14–15). A gracious woman gains an honour that violent men cannot seize, and kindness benefits the kind while cruelty wounds the cruel (vv. 16–17). The wicked earn wages that deceive, while those who sow righteousness reap a sure reward, for the LORD delights in blameless ways and assures us that evil will not go unpunished (vv. 18–21). And beauty without discretion is wasted, like gold in a pig’s snout (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: How a person treats the people around him, in speech, trust and kindness, comes back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever belittles his neighbor lacks sense, but a man of understanding remains silent. Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise do not belittle their neighbours or spread their secrets; they know when to keep quiet.

Whoever belittles his neighbor lacks sense. The sneer or the joke at someone’s expense feels clever, but shows a lack of sense. The man of understanding, tempted to cut someone down, keeps quiet. “Do not speak evil against one another, brothers” (James 4:11).

Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets. The slanderer goes from house to house and group to group, passing on what he was told in confidence. The law had said, “You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people” (Leviticus 19:16). The trustworthy person is a locked safe: you can tell him your struggle and know it will not be talked about at the church lunch on Sunday.

A test to put to yourself. Could the people you spoke about this week hear it all and still trust you? Where they could not, the way back is confession, to God and often to them.

What it does not mean. Keeping a thing covered never means hiding abuse, a crime or a threat to someone’s safety. Telling those who can protect the vulnerable, including the authorities, is not slander but love.

verseByVerse.quote: Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm, but he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Communities stand by listening to many advisers, and households are kept safe by refusing to guarantee strangers’ debts.

Where there is no guidance, a people falls. Nations fall, and companies, churches and families too, when one person makes decisions and listens to no one. Safety lies in many counsellors. The wise leader surrounds himself with people who can tell him he is wrong, and the same applies to personal decisions (15:22).

Whoever puts up security for a stranger. This is the warning of 6:1–5 again. Striking hands was the handshake that sealed a guarantee. To guarantee a stranger’s debt is to hand your financial future to someone you do not know. The one who hates doing it is not stingy; he is wise.

The one who became surety. What is folly for us, Jesus did in love: he became “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22), taking on the debt of strangers and enemies and paying it in full.

verseByVerse.quote: A gracious woman gets honor, and violent men get riches. A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Graciousness and kindness win what force cannot and bless the one who shows them, while cruelty harms the cruel.

A gracious woman gets honor, and violent men get riches. Two kinds of gain stand side by side. Violent, ruthless men do get rich; the book is not naive about that. But a gracious woman gets something they cannot take by force: honour, freely given. They may have more money; she has more of what money cannot buy.

A man who is kind benefits himself. Kindness looks like giving something away, but it comes back: friends, peace of mind, a good name, a softer heart. The cruel person, who thinks he is winning, is damaging his relationships, his conscience and his soul. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” (Matthew 5:7).

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked earns deceptive wages, but one who sows righteousness gets a sure reward. Whoever is steadfast in righteousness will live, but he who pursues evil will die. Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those of blameless ways are his delight. Be assured, an evil person will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wickedness pays deceptive wages, but righteousness is a sowing with a sure harvest, for the LORD delights in the blameless and will punish evil.

The wicked earns deceptive wages. His pay looks real, but it promises more than it delivers and does not last. The righteous man’s reward is sure, and he sows: righteousness is like planting, and the harvest comes later, but it comes.

Whoever is steadfast in righteousness will live. Two words matter: steadfast and pursues. The righteous man keeps going in one direction over years; the wicked man chases evil. Both are committed, and each arrives where his road leads, at life or at death.

Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD. The pair from verse 1, abomination and delight, now describes hearts. God weighs the heart the way an honest trader weighs grain, and on that scale no one’s ways are blameless but Christ’s. His perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him (2 Corinthians 5:21), and in him they are the LORD’s delight.

Be assured, an evil person will not go unpunished. God gives his word on it. That comforts the victim still waiting for justice and warns the wrongdoer who thinks he got away with it. “He will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6).

Are the children of believers automatically saved? No. Grace is not inherited (John 1:13). But God does bless the households of those who fear him, and children raised in a godly home are under real promises and means of grace (Acts 2:39). The proverb gives a pattern, not a guarantee for each child.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beauty without good sense is a fine thing wasted, like a gold ring dragged through the mud.

Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout. The picture is meant to shock. A gold nose ring was fine jewellery. Put it in a pig’s snout, and it is still gold, but it is wasted, rooting through the mud. Beauty without discretion, without good sense and moral judgment, is like that: real, but attached to something that drags it through the dirt.

Beyond beauty. The proverb applies to men as well, and to every gift: intelligence without integrity, talent without character. Peter says the lasting beauty is “the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious” (1 Peter 3:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — One Who Waters Will Be Watered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who gives freely is the one who ends up rich, and the greatest thing a wise person can win is another soul. The desires of the righteous end in good (v. 23). In God’s world the generous grow richer and the stingy grow poorer; whoever waters others is watered, and the merchant who hoards grain in a famine is rightly cursed (vv. 24–26). Those who seek good find favour, those who trust in riches fall, and the righteous flourish like a green leaf (vv. 27–28). The man who troubles his home inherits the wind, the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and if even the righteous are repaid on earth, the wicked certainly will be (vv. 29–31).
verseByVerse.theology: The one who gives freely is the one who ends up rich, and the greatest thing a wise person can win is another soul.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the righteous ends only in good, the expectation of the wicked in wrath. One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want. Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered. The people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In God’s world the generous end up richer and the grasping poorer: whoever refreshes others will be refreshed.

The desire of the righteous ends only in good. Because their desires are aimed at God and his ways, they finish in good. The expectations of the wicked finish in wrath.

One gives freely, yet grows all the richer. By ordinary arithmetic, giving makes you poorer; in God’s world it often goes the other way. The one who clutches what he should give suffers want: not always in money, though often in that too, but always in joy, friendship and the favour of God.

One who waters will himself be watered. A farmer who waters his neighbour’s field in a drought finds that rain falls on his own. Paul put it this way: “whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6). And Jesus: “give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap” (Luke 6:38); “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

The people curse him who holds back grain. In a famine, a merchant with a full warehouse can hold his grain back until the price rises. The people curse him, and rightly; Amos condemned those who “trample on the needy” (Amos 8:4). Today it is price-gouging in a crisis. The one who sells at a fair price when he could have squeezed people has a blessing on his head.

The giver who gave first. The open hand begins with God, who gave first: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (2 Corinthians 9:15). Christ, who was rich, became poor for us (2 Corinthians 8:9); those who have received like that can afford to give.

What it does not mean. This is not a scheme for getting rich by giving, as some preachers claim. The poor widow who gave her two small coins went home as poor as she came, and Jesus praised her above all the rich givers (Mark 12:41–44). God’s repayment is sure, but he chooses its currency.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it. Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People find what they look for, and those who lean on money fall while the righteous flourish.

Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor. Whoever looks for ways to do good finds favour (the ESV notes “acceptance”) with God and people; whoever goes looking for trouble finds it, and it finds him back.

Whoever trusts in his riches will fall. The key word is trusts. Having riches is not condemned; leaning on them is, because money is not strong enough to hold the weight. Jesus said, “how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God!”, and “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person” to enter it (Mark 10:24–25), not because God hates wealth, but because wealth is so easy to trust.

The righteous will flourish like a green leaf. A leaf is not strong, but it is alive, fed by a root the eye cannot see. The righteous are strong the same way, through the life of God flowing into them.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind, and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise. If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who wreck their homes end with nothing, the righteous give life and win others, and if God repays even the righteous, the wicked will not escape.

Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind. A man who brings trouble into his home, through anger, neglect, drink or reckless spending, will have nothing to hold at the end, and the fool ends up working for the wise man he despised.

The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. This is the image from Eden and from 3:18. Other people are nourished and live because of what grows from a righteous life.

Whoever captures souls is wise. To capture a soul is to win a person, to draw him to wisdom and life, and here it is the mark of the wise. As it stands, it most likely means winning people over by a good life. Jesus’ call to fish for people is a fair application rather than the proverb’s first meaning: he called fishermen and said, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19). “Those who turn many to righteousness” will shine “like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:3). The wisest investment a person can make is in another person’s soul.

If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked. Peter quotes the verse to Christians under persecution, in the words of the Greek Old Testament, which differ from the Hebrew: “If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” (1 Peter 4:18). If God disciplines even his own people in this life, the judgment of the wicked is certain. That should drive every reader to the one place where sin has already been fully repaid: the cross, where the righteous One bore what the ungodly deserved, so that the ungodly who trust him are saved after all.

Uncertain wording. The line about capturing souls is hard in Hebrew. The phrase can elsewhere mean taking a life, and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads it quite differently, so some think a copying slip lies behind it. The familiar he that winneth souls is wise comes from the King James Version. The likeliest sense is still that the wise win people over.

11.theology:
God's standards apply in the marketplace; honest business is his delight (v. 1; Lev 19:35-36). Sin carries its own punishment (vv. 5-6), and God will certainly judge evil (v. 21; Rom 2:6).

Righteousness has public effects on a whole community (vv. 10-11; Jer 29:7). In God’s world the generous are enriched (vv. 24-25; 2 Cor 9:6; Luke 6:38), and trust in riches fails (v. 28; Mark 10:24-25).

Winning others to wisdom is the mark of the wise (v. 30; Dan 12:3; Matt 4:19). If God disciplines even the righteous, his judgment on the wicked is certain (v. 31; 1 Pet 4:18).
11.examples: Before a major decision, ask who your counsellors are, and whether any of them ever disagrees with you. And when a crisis gives you the chance to squeeze people, a fair price is a small act of righteousness that a whole town notices.

keyVerse.quote: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight.
keyVerse.note: This verse sets the tone for the chapter: God’s standards reach into the marketplace, and righteousness is measured in ordinary dealings with other people. The pair “abomination” and “delight” returns in verse 20, where God weighs not goods but hearts. On that scale only Christ is found blameless, and in him those who trust him become the LORD’s delight.

11.reflection:
Verse 1 says that honest business is the LORD’s “delight”. What are the “scales” in your daily work, and where are you tempted to tip them slightly in your favour?

Verses 10–11 say that a whole city is lifted by the blessing of the upright. What would it look like for your church, or for you, to “seek the welfare of the city” where God has placed you (Jeremiah 29:7)?

Verses 12–13 contrast the slanderer with the person who keeps a confidence. Could the people you spoke about this week hear everything you said? What helps us become people others can trust with their struggles?

“One who waters will himself be watered” (v. 25). How has God’s generosity to you in Christ shaped the way you give? Why is this verse not a formula for getting rich by giving?

12.title: A Good Word Makes Him Glad
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.<sup>2</sup>A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns.<sup>3</sup>No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved.<sup>4</sup>An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like 12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 continues Solomon’s main collection (10:1–22:16). Chapters 10 and 11 have set the righteous and the wicked side by side in the family, the market and the city; now the contrasts turn to what lies underneath a life, its root, and to the words that come out of it.

The message. What holds a life steady is not seen: a heart that loves correction and a root in God. And what comes out of that root, especially in words, either wounds or heals. Lies win for a moment; truth lasts. The fool is sure he is right and the wise man listens; anxiety weighs a heart down and a good word lifts it. At the end, the path of righteousness is life, and on it there is no death.

Why it was said. In Israel a person’s word was everything: in the law court at the city gate, in a sworn bargain, in the household (see the introduction). A false witness could take a life. These sayings trained the young to build a life that would stand, and a tongue that could be trusted.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the root of the righteous (vv. 1–12): whoever loves correction loves knowledge, the righteous will never be moved, a good wife is a crown, and honest work and modest living beat display. Next, words that cut or heal (vv. 13–23): the fool is right in his own eyes, rash words are like sword thrusts but the tongue of the wise heals, and truthful lips endure forever. Last, the path where there is no death (vv. 24–28): the diligent rule, a good word lifts anxiety, the righteous guide their neighbours, and the path of righteousness leads to life.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes, by pattern and by the hope of verse 28. James says that “no human being can tame the tongue” (James 3:8), and these sayings leave us in no doubt that we have wounded with words and bent the truth. Only one man always spoke the truth and never wounded rashly: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). He is the good word to the anxious, and he made the last line of the chapter plain: “if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John 8:51).

For us. Ask how you take correction, and who has permission to tell you no. Count the cost of the life you display to others. Think of someone carrying a weight you cannot see, and give them a good word today. And walk the path of righteousness in Christ, knowing it does not end in death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Root of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Stability grows from what cannot be seen: a teachable heart, a good marriage, honest work and a root in God. Whoever loves correction loves knowledge, the LORD favours the good, and the root of the righteous will never be moved (vv. 1–3). A good wife is her husband’s crown, and a shameful one is rot in his bones (v. 4). Just thoughts and rescuing words build a house that stands, while the plans and words of the wicked lie in ambush and fall (vv. 5–8). Better to be modest and fed than to play the great man and go hungry; the righteous care even for their animals, work the land in front of them, and bear fruit from a root God has planted (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Stability grows from what cannot be seen: a teachable heart, a good marriage, honest work and a root in God.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid. A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns. No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one becomes wise without loving correction, and the life God favours is rooted so deeply that it cannot be moved.

Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge. Nobody gains knowledge without being corrected, because learning means finding out you were wrong. So a person who loves knowledge must also love the discipline that brings it. A person who hates correction has shut the only door to learning, and that is why Proverbs, which rarely uses so blunt a word, calls him stupid. Few people love correction naturally; the Spirit teaches it, as a believer sees the “peaceful fruit of righteousness” it yields (Hebrews 12:11).

A good man obtains favor from the LORD. The LORD is not neutral about character. The good man obtains favour; the schemer is condemned. God looks past a person’s success to his heart and his plans.

No one is established by wickedness. Wickedness can build something that looks solid, but it has no foundation. The righteous have a root, and a root is what holds a tree when the wind comes. The picture is of the man in Psalm 1, “like a tree planted by streams of water” whose “leaf does not wither” (Psalm 1:3). What keeps a believer standing in a storm is what was growing in secret before it came.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wife of strong character is her husband’s honour, and one who brings shame slowly eats away at him from within.

An excellent wife is the crown of her husband. A wife of strength and character is his crown. The same phrase opens the great poem at the end of the book: “An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels” (31:10).

Like rottenness in his bones. The other side is painful: a wife who brings shame is a decay no one outside may see, eating away at his strength from inside.

Husbands too. The principle applies to husbands as much as to wives: every spouse is a crown or a slow decay to the other, and most are some of each on different days. Where you have been the decay, the way back is confession and the forgiveness of Christ, who loved his bride before she was any crown (Ephesians 5:25).

verseByVerse.quote: The thoughts of the righteous are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful. The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them. The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand. A man is commended according to his good sense, but one of twisted mind is despised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Character is formed in the mind before it shows in deeds, and in time the righteous stand while the wicked fall.

The thoughts of the righteous are just. The righteous person’s thoughts are already bent toward what is fair; the wicked person’s counsels, his plans and advice, are already deceitful before a word is spoken. Character is formed in the mind long before it shows in the hands.

The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood. Words can ambush. A false accusation, a lie in court, a rumour that ruins someone: the wicked use words the way the gang of chapter 1 used an ambush (1:11). The upright use their mouths to rescue, both themselves and others.

The house of the righteous will stand. A house in Proverbs is a family and its future as well as a building. The wicked are overthrown and are no more; the house of the righteous stands, often for generations.

A man is commended according to his good sense. In the long run people recognise sense, and a twisted mind too. Reputation is not always fair in the short term, but over years it tends to settle on what a person actually is.

verseByVerse.quote: Better to be lowly and have a servant than to play the great man and lack bread. Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel. Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense. Whoever is wicked covets the spoil of evildoers, but the root of the righteous bears fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Modest sufficiency beats empty display, and righteousness shows in kindness to animals, honest work and fruit from God’s planting.

Better to be lowly and have a servant. One man lives modestly and is well provided for. Another plays the great man, spends to look important, and has nothing to eat: the car on finance, the house beyond the budget, the credit card paying for the image. Better to be thought ordinary and have bread on the table.

The life on display. Thorstein Veblen, an American economist writing in 1899, coined the phrase conspicuous consumption for spending whose real purpose is to be seen. Since then we have all joined in: the holiday chosen partly for the photographs, the kitchen partly for the visitors, a whole life arranged for an audience it barely knows. Underneath the display is a hunger for a verdict, to be seen as someone, and no display can settle it, because the audience keeps changing and its verdict is never final. The gospel gives what the display was reaching for. The one who had every right to honour “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), so that people who are nobody in the world’s eyes could be called children of God. Someone who has been seen like that, all the way down, and loved, can afford to be thought ordinary.

Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast. A righteous person’s goodness reaches all the way down to his animals: he feeds his ox or donkey, rests it, and does not beat it. The law said, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4), and God ended the book of Jonah by asking whether he should not pity Nineveh, “and also much cattle” (Jonah 4:11). How a person treats creatures that cannot repay him or complain reveals his heart.

The mercy of the wicked is cruel. Even their mercy is cruel: their best kindness still has an edge of contempt in it.

Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread. The farmer who works the field in front of him eats. The man who chases worthless pursuits, get-rich schemes, fantasies and endless distractions, lacks sense.

The root of the righteous bears fruit. The wicked man wants what other crooks have taken. The righteous man’s provision grows from the inside, from what God has planted, while the wicked man’s comes from grabbing.

Uncertain wording. Verse 12 is hard in Hebrew: the word translated spoil usually means a net, or what a net catches, and the line is very compressed, so translations differ. The contrast is still clear: the wicked grab, the righteous grow. In verse 9, and have a servant can also be read and works for himself; either way, modest sufficiency beats empty display.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Words can cut or heal, and truth outlasts every lie. The evil man is trapped by his own lips, while a man’s words and work come back to him (vv. 13–14). The fool is right in his own eyes and shows his irritation at once; the wise listen to advice and let an insult pass (vv. 15–16). A truthful witness speaks honestly, rash words wound like a sword while the wise tongue heals, and truthful lips endure forever while a lie lasts a moment (vv. 17–19). Those who plan peace have joy, no final harm comes to the righteous, the LORD hates lying lips and delights in the faithful, and the prudent do not need to announce all they know (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Words can cut or heal, and truth outlasts every lie.

verseByVerse.quote: An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous escapes from trouble. From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man's hand comes back to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked are caught in the trap of their own words, while what a person says and does comes back to him.

An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips. The snare is made of his own words: the lie that needs another lie, the boast that gets checked, the angry email that gets forwarded. The righteous man escapes because he said nothing that needs escaping from.

The work of a man’s hand comes back to him. A man’s words are like seeds, and he eats what grows from them: kind words bring kindness back, harsh ones conflict. His work comes back to him too.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the first line may also be read, “In the transgression of the lips, there is an evil snare”. Either way the trap is set by the speaker’s own mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice. The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fool is sure he is right and reacts at once to every slight, while the wise listen to advice and let insults pass.

The way of a fool is right in his own eyes. The fool’s problem is that he is sure he is right. The book of Judges ends with a whole nation in that condition: “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25), and the result was chaos. “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death” (14:12).

A wise man listens to advice. The wise man is not the one who is always right, but the one who assumes he might be missing something. Before a big decision, who have you asked who might tell you no?

The prudent ignores an insult. The fool’s irritation is on his face and in his voice at once; he cannot let anything pass. The prudent man is not a doormat; he simply does not need to answer every slight. The supreme example is Christ: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

What it does not mean. A slight to your pride can be overlooked; abuse or harm to yourself or others should be named and brought to those who can help.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence, but a false witness utters deceit. There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Careless words wound deeply while wise words heal, and truth outlasts every lie.

Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence. The setting is a courtroom, but a person truthful in everyday speech will be an honest witness when it matters. The ESV notes that speaks is literally “breathes out”: truth or lies come out of a person as naturally as breath, because they are what is inside.

Rash words are like sword thrusts. Words spoken without thinking go in like a blade. Many people carry scars from a sentence said to them decades ago by a parent, a teacher or a spouse, a sentence the speaker has probably forgotten. James says, “no human being can tame the tongue”, and “From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so” (James 3:8, 10).

The tongue of the wise brings healing. A word of apology, encouragement or blessing can reach a wound that nothing else touches. If you have wounded someone with words, the healing will very likely also have to come through words.

Truthful lips endure forever. Every lie has a short shelf life: it works for a moment, then must be maintained, defended and finally exposed. The truth simply stays true. Behind every truthful word stands the God whose “faithfulness” “endures forever” (Psalm 117:2), and the Son who is “the truth” (John 14:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy. No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peacemaking brings joy, God turns all that befalls the righteous to good, and he hates lies and delights in the faithful.

Those who plan peace have joy. Schemer and peacemaker both make plans, but only the one who plans peace finds joy in it. Planning a reconciliation, a kindness, a way to heal a rift, fills the heart in a way plotting never does.

Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD. Abomination and delight again (11:1, 20). God hates lying because he is the God of truth, and lying is the native language of the devil, who is “a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). “Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self” (Colossians 3:9). That includes the small lies: the excuse for being late, the exaggerated story, the “I’m fine”. God delights in those who act faithfully, whose words and deeds can be relied upon. “Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another” (Ephesians 4:25).

A prudent man conceals knowledge. He does not have to show everything he knows. He waits for the right moment, keeps confidences, and does not need to win every conversation. The fool announces whatever is in his head, and what is in his head is folly.

Does no ill really befall the righteous? Read alone, verse 21 seems untrue: righteous people get cancer, lose children and are persecuted. But nothing that befalls the righteous is finally ill for them, because God turns it to good: “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28). That does not make the loss less real or the grief wrong; death and pain are still enemies. It means they do not have the last word. The same event can be a disaster to a wicked man and a means of purifying a righteous one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–28 — The Path Where There Is No Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter moves from a weighed-down heart to a path on which death itself does not have the last word. The diligent end up leading, while the lazy end up working under others (v. 24). Anxiety presses the heart down, and a good word lifts it (v. 25). The righteous guide their neighbours, while the way of the wicked leads them astray; the lazy man fails to finish even the meal he has caught, while diligence is itself a treasure (vv. 26–27). And the chapter ends with one of the book’s most hopeful lines: on the path of righteousness there is life, and no death (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter moves from a weighed-down heart to a path on which death itself does not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labor. Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laziness ends in servitude while diligence leads, and a heart weighed down by anxiety is lifted by a good word.

The hand of the diligent will rule. The irony is sharp. The lazy man avoids work to stay free and ends up doing forced labor under someone else; the diligent man takes on work willingly and ends up leading. Avoiding effort does not avoid work; it only decides who will give the orders.

Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs him down. This is a tender proverb. Anxiety sits on the heart and presses it down, and anyone who has lived with it knows how physical that feels. The proverb does not tell the anxious man to try harder or pull himself together. It says that a good word lifts him.

A good word makes him glad. First, for the anxious: God has spoken a good word to you. Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God’s hand, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). Second, for everyone else: you can be the good word to someone carrying a weight you cannot see.

When anxiety settles in. If anxiety has settled in for months, so that good words do not lift it, that is not a failure of faith. Talking to your pastor and seeking out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up, alongside prayer and the company of the church, is a wise use of God’s gifts, not a lack of trust; and if a doctor prescribes medicine, taking it is no failure of faith either. If anxiety or despair ever brings thoughts of ending your life, tell someone and get help the same day.

verseByVerse.quote: One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray. Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth. In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous guide their neighbours, diligence finishes what it starts, and the path of righteousness leads to a life death cannot end.

One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor. The righteous person shows others the way simply by walking it, while the wicked lead their companions off the road. “Do not be deceived: ‘Bad company ruins good morals’” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Whoever is slothful will not roast his game. The lazy man goes hunting, catches something, and then cannot be bothered to cook it. The effort is wasted at the last step. Unfinished degrees, half-built projects, good intentions never followed through: the sluggard is often not lazy about starting, only about finishing.

In its pathway there is no death. The chapter ends on one of the book’s most hopeful lines: on the path of righteousness there is life, and no death. The Old Testament does not often speak so directly about what lies beyond the grave, but this proverb reaches toward it. Death is not the end of the righteous man’s path.

Never see death. Jesus made the promise explicit: “if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John 8:51). And at the tomb of Lazarus: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?” (John 11:25–26). No one walks the path of righteousness perfectly; Christ walked it for us, and his righteousness is counted ours (Romans 5:19). On that path, through him, death has lost its sting.

Uncertain wording. All three verses are hard in places. The ESV notes that verse 26 may begin “The righteous chooses his friends carefully”, which fits too, and that verse 27 may end “but diligence is precious wealth”: the habit of finishing is itself a treasure. The second line of verse 28 is difficult Hebrew; some early translations read a contrast, that the other way leads to death, while the ESV follows the Hebrew as it stands. Either way, the path of righteousness is the path of life.

12.theology:
Stability comes from being rooted in God (vv. 3, 12; Ps 1:3). No one becomes wise without being willing to be corrected (vv. 1, 15). Righteousness extends even to care for animals (v. 10; Deut 25:4; Jonah 4:11).

Speech wounds or heals (v. 18; Jas 3:8-10); God hates lies and delights in faithfulness (v. 22; Eph 4:25). The prudent absorb insults, as Christ did (v. 16; 1 Pet 2:23). Nothing that happens to the righteous harms them in the end (v. 21; Rom 8:28).

A good word lifts anxiety (v. 25; 1 Pet 5:7). The path of righteousness leads beyond death (v. 28; John 11:25-26).
12.examples: Husbands should read verse 4 and ask whether they honour their wives as the crown they are. And somebody you will see today is carrying a weight you cannot see; a sentence of encouragement from you may be exactly what lifts it.

keyVerse.quote: In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
keyVerse.note: The chapter ends on one of the most hopeful lines in Proverbs. Everything before it, the root that cannot be moved, the truthful lips that endure, the good word that lifts the heart, belongs to a path that leads to life and not to death. The Old Testament rarely speaks so directly of what lies beyond the grave, and Jesus made the promise plain: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25).

12.reflection:
“Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid” (v. 1). Why is correction so hard to receive? Who in your life has permission to tell you that you are wrong, and how do you usually respond?

Verse 9 contrasts the modest man who has enough with the man who plays the great man and lacks bread. Where are you tempted to live for an audience? How does being known and loved by God free us from needing to be seen as someone?

“There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing” (v. 18). Can you remember words that wounded you, or healed you? Is there someone you need to speak a healing word to, or ask forgiveness of?

“Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad” (v. 25). What good word has God spoken to you in Christ that lifts your anxiety? Who around you might need a good word from you this week?

13.title: Hope Deferred Makes the Heart Sick
13.text: <sup>1</sup>A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.<sup>2</sup>From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence.<sup>3</sup>Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.<sup>4</sup>The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.<sup>5</sup>The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace.<sup>6</sup>Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.<sup>7</sup>One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.<sup>8</sup>The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.<sup>9</sup>The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out.<sup>10</sup>By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom.<sup>11</sup>Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.<sup>12</sup>Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.<sup>13</sup>Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded.<sup>14</sup>The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.<sup>15</sup>Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin.<sup>16</sup>Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly.<sup>17</sup>A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.<sup>18</sup>Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored.<sup>19</sup>A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.<sup>20</sup>Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm.<sup>21</sup>Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.<sup>22</sup>A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous.<sup>23</sup>The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.<sup>24</sup>Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him.<sup>25</sup>The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.
13.overview:
Where we are. We are in the main collection of Solomon’s sayings (10:1–22:16), where the long speeches of chapters 1–9 give way to two-line proverbs, most of them setting the wise beside the fool and the righteous beside the wicked. Chapter 13 opens, as the book did, with a father and a son.

The message. A life is shaped by what it listens to, what it says and how it waits. The teachable son, the guarded mouth, the patient hand and the companion of the wise are on the road to life; the scoffer, the loose tongue, quick money and the company of fools lead to ruin. The chapter is also honest: waiting can make the heart sick, injustice can sweep away the harvest of the poor, and only God’s word is a fountain that does not fail.

Why it was said. These sayings trained young people in Israel’s farming towns for adult life: work, money, speech, friendships, inheritance and the raising of children, all lived before the LORD (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First, the mouth and the purse: a son who hears, lips that are guarded, appearances that deceive, pride that breeds strife and wealth that is gathered little by little (vv. 1–11). Then the heart that waits: hope deferred makes it sick, a desire fulfilled is a tree of life, and the word of God and the teaching of the wise keep a person out of death’s snares (vv. 12–19). Last, the circles a life moves in: the friends we walk with, the grandchildren we leave behind, the poor whom injustice robs, and the children we love enough to discipline (vv. 20–25).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. The wise son who hears his father’s instruction (v. 1) is fully seen only in Jesus, who said, “I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me” (John 8:28). The deferred hope of verse 12 runs through the whole Old Testament and is fulfilled in him, and the tree of life it pictures stands at the end of the Bible, beside the river that flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Revelation 22:1–2).

For us. Ask whose voice you are listening to, what your mouth is doing to the people around you, and whom you are walking with. If you are waiting with a sick heart, bring the ache to God without pretending; in Christ no hope placed in him will be put to shame.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Guarded Mouth and the Honest Purse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Restraint and patience keep a life; haste and a loose mouth ruin it. A wise son listens, while the scoffer has already decided not to (v. 1). The mouth feeds its owner good or harm, and the one who guards it guards his life (vv. 2–3). The sluggard’s desires go hungry, and the righteous are protected by their integrity (vv. 4–6). Appearances deceive: the rich may be poor and the poor rich, and wealth both ransoms and endangers (vv. 7–8). The light of the righteous shines on, pride breeds only strife, and money gained hastily dwindles while money gathered little by little grows (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Mouth and money are both kept by restraint and patience, and both are ruined by haste.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke. From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence. Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom begins with an ear open to correction and shows in a guarded mouth.

A wise son hears. The chapter opens, as the book did, with a son and a father. The scoffer has already dismissed the speaker, so rebuke bounces off him.

The fruit of his mouth. Good words bear fruit their speaker eats: friendships, trust, peace. The treacherous man’s appetite is for something else, violence, and that is what he feeds on.

Whoever guards his mouth. Opens wide his lips pictures a mouth with no gate at all. The man who guards his mouth has a gatekeeper, and the Spirit, whose fruit is self-control (Galatians 5:23), keeps that gate. One unguarded sentence has ended careers and marriages. James goes further: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless (James 1:26).

verseByVerse.quote: The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied. The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace. Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Desire without diligence gets nothing, and a life is guarded by righteousness or toppled by sin.

The sluggard craves. He craves, often intensely: the house, the qualifications, the good marriage. He simply does not do what gets them. Laziness does not kill desire; it only guarantees frustration.

The righteous hates falsehood. He does not merely avoid lies; he hates them, in himself and in others.

Righteousness guards. Righteousness is pictured as a bodyguard, and sin as an enemy that knocks a man flat. A blameless life does not make anyone invulnerable, but it removes a great many dangers that sin would have brought with it.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that brings shame (v. 5) may be rendered “stench”: the Hebrew verb can mean either. Either way, the wicked man’s life gives off something that repels the people around him.

verseByVerse.quote: One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth is not always where it seems, and even real wealth both rescues a man and makes him a target.

One pretends to be rich. Appearances deceive both ways. One man drives the expensive car and is drowning in debt; another lives quietly and has saved for decades.

The church at Laodicea. The proverb is most deeply true in spiritual things. The church at Laodicea said, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17). Paul described the apostles as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything (2 Corinthians 6:10).

The ransom of a man’s life. Wealth can pay a ransom when a rich man is kidnapped or sued. But it is also why he is a target. The poor man hears no threat: nobody bothers to rob a man with nothing.

Uncertain wording. The verbs of verse 7 may mean “pretends to be” or, as the ESV notes, “makes himself” rich or poor: either pretence is exposed, or the grasping man ends with nothing while the generous man stays rich. In verse 8, hears no threat is the Hebrew phrase translated “does not listen to rebuke” in verse 1; most take it as the ESV does.

verseByVerse.quote: The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out. By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom. Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous shine on while the wicked’s lamp goes out; pride breeds strife, and quick money melts while patient gathering grows.

The light of the righteous. A righteous life is a light that shines gladly. The wicked man has a lamp, a smaller thing, and it will be put out. A lamp burning in a house meant the family was alive and present; a lamp gone out meant the house was empty. The light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine (Job 18:5).

Insolence. Pride produces one crop: strife. The proud will not take advice or admit fault, so every disagreement becomes a war. James asks, What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? (James 4:1). Where there is constant conflict, look for pride first, and look for it in the mirror.

Wealth gained hastily. Quick money, from a scam, a gamble, a windfall or a get-rich-quick scheme, tends to disappear as fast as it came. Whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished (28:20).

Whoever gathers little by little. Honest work and patient saving increase wealth, and so it is with character, a marriage and a knowledge of Scripture: whoever wants them instantly rarely gets them at all.

Uncertain wording. Hastily renders a Hebrew word that usually means breath or vanity, as in Ecclesiastes: wealth with nothing solid behind it. The ESV notes that it may mean “by fraud”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heart that waits needs a word that gives life. “Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life” (v. 12): the Bible names the ache of waiting honestly. What sustains a person in the meantime is the word: whoever despises it destroys himself, and the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life that keeps him out of death’s snares (vv. 13–14). Good sense, prudence and a faithful messenger bring favour and healing (vv. 15–17). Heeding correction leads to honour, and fools miss the sweetness they crave because they will not turn from evil (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The heart can sicken while it waits, and God's word is what keeps it alive until the desire is met.

verseByVerse.quote: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long waiting makes the heart sick and fulfilment revives it; God names that ache honestly and points it to a hope that will not fail.

Hope deferred makes the heart sick. Few sentences in the Bible are more honest about waiting. Think of the infertile couple who hoped each month, the single person who hoped for marriage year after year, the parent praying for a child who has walked away, the medical result or the reconciliation that does not come. The proverb does not tell them to feel differently. It says: this is what happens, and God knows it.

But we had hoped. The disciples on the road to Emmaus spoke with sick hearts: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel (Luke 24:21). They said it to the risen Jesus himself, walking beside them unrecognised. Their hope had not failed; it had been fulfilled beyond anything they imagined. The psalmist spoke to his own heart in the same condition: Why are you cast down, O my soul, Hope in God; for I shall again praise him (Psalm 42:5).

A desire fulfilled is a tree of life. Fulfilled hope is like the tree of Eden. Not every earthly desire is granted in this life. The saints of Hebrews 11 all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). But the tree of life stands at the end of the Bible, beside the river, and no hope placed in Christ will be disappointed there. If we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience (Romans 8:25).

When the heart stays sick. If long waiting slides into depression, talk to a biblical counsellor and see a doctor; medicine is no failure of faith. Thoughts of ending your life need help the same day.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded. The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Despising God’s word destroys a person; revering it is a fountain that keeps him from death’s traps.

Whoever despises the word. The ESV notes that this may be “a word” and “a commandment”, any piece of good instruction. But in the whole Bible the supreme word is God’s, and the one who despises it destroys himself. God says, this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isaiah 66:2).

A fountain of life. Wise teaching has a practical purpose: to help a person turn away from the snares of death. It shows where the traps are before you step in them. Think of the parents, teachers or pastors whose words kept you out of a snare you did not even see at the time.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly. A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good sense and prudence win trust, and a faithful messenger heals where a false one brings disaster.

Every prudent man acts. People trust good sense; the prudent man thinks before he acts. The fool flaunts his folly, spreading it out for display like a merchant with his goods.

A wicked messenger falls. A messenger who distorts his message causes disaster. A faithful envoy brings healing, because he delivers the message as it was given. Paul described the gospel ministry this way: we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20). Christ himself is the faithful witness (Revelation 1:5), who spoke the Father’s message without loss. Every Christian who speaks of him is an envoy, and healing comes when the message is told without additions or subtractions.

Uncertain wording. The ESV marks the second line of verse 15 as a probable reading; the Hebrew says the way of the treacherous “is rugged” or “is an enduring rut”. Either picture works: a rocky road, or a rut worn so deep that a person cannot climb out.

verseByVerse.quote: Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored. A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing correction ends in disgrace and accepting it in honour; fools crave sweetness but will not leave the evil that blocks it.

Poverty and disgrace come. Ignoring instruction costs both money and reputation. At the time accepting correction feels humiliating and refusing it feels dignified; in the long run it is the other way round.

Sweet to the soul. The first line echoes verse 12; the second explains why fools never taste that sweetness. They want the good life, and they hate the very idea of giving up what ruins it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A life is shaped by its company and shapes the lives that follow it. Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, while the companion of fools suffers harm, and disaster pursues sinners (vv. 20–21). A good man leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren, though the proverb admits that injustice can sweep away even the harvest of the hard-working poor (vv. 22–23). The loving parent disciplines his child diligently, and the righteous have enough while the wicked go hungry (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: A life is shaped by the company it keeps, and it shapes the generations that come after it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We become like the company we keep, and sin’s consequences hunt the sinner down.

Walks with the wise. We become like those we spend time with, not immediately, but surely. Walk with fools and you will not merely be influenced; you will suffer harm, because fools bring their consequences on everyone near them. Paul quoted a proverb of his own day: Bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33).

The slide in Psalm 1. Psalm 1 traces the slide from walking to standing to sitting: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers (Psalm 1:1).

The Wise One to walk with. Jesus called his disciples first so that they might be with him (Mark 3:14), and the council later recognized that they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13).

A test worth running. Are the people you spend most time with making you wiser?

What it does not mean. This is not a call to avoid sinners. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, but as their physician, not as a companion in their folly (Luke 5:31–32). The question is who is shaping whom.

Disaster pursues sinners. The picture is of something chasing a man: he may outrun his consequences for a while, but they follow him. Moses warned, be sure your sin will find you out (Numbers 32:23).

verseByVerse.quote: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous. The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good life blesses generations, and not all poverty is laziness: injustice can sweep away the harvest of the hard-working poor.

An inheritance. A good man thinks two generations ahead. Planning well for a family’s future is godly, but the best inheritance is not financial: a name, a faith, a pattern of prayer and honesty that grandchildren remember. Timothy inherited a faith that dwelt first in his grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5).

The sinner’s wealth is laid up for the righteous. The sinner, meanwhile, is storing up wealth that will pass out of his hands, often to the very people he despised.

Swept away through injustice. The poor man’s field would yield much food: he has worked it. But injustice sweeps his harvest away: unjust taxes, stolen land, corrupt officials, withheld wages. The book that praises diligence admits that diligence is not always enough in a crooked world. James thunders against rich men whose labourers’ wages were kept back by fraud and are crying out against you (James 5:4). So be slow to judge the poor, and quick to oppose the injustice that keeps them poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him. The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaving a child uncorrected is not kindness but neglect; love disciplines diligently.

He who loves him. The parent who never disciplines is not kind; the proverb says he hates his son, leaving him without the correction he needs. A child never told no is being set up for a painful life. The loving parent is diligent to discipline him; the ESV notes that it may be read, “disciplines him early”, before patterns harden.

What the rod stands for. The rod stands for discipline as a whole: correction and consequences, including physical correction. Whatever form discipline takes, the Bible never licenses cruelty, rage or abuse. The same Scriptures say, Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger (Ephesians 6:4), and Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged (Colossians 3:21). Discipline given in anger serves the parent; discipline given in love serves the child.

The Father who disciplines. Behind every parent stands the Father who disciplines his children: God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? (Hebrews 12:7).

No guarantee. No discipline, however faithful, guarantees the outcome. Parents are responsible for faithfulness, not for their child’s heart, which only God can change. And no parent is perfectly faithful: the Father who disciplines also forgives, and Christ’s obedience covers failing parents who come to him in confession (1 John 1:9).

Enough. The righteous may not feast, but they have enough, and that is a gift. Paul had learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content (Philippians 4:11). The wicked man’s belly suffers want, sometimes because he is poor, and often because nothing is ever enough for him.

Where Christians differ. Does this mean physical punishment today? Many Christians read the rod as a figure for discipline of every kind and hold that physical correction now does more harm than good. Others, including most of the Reformed tradition, take the rod at its word: measured physical correction, alongside instruction, is one God-given means for young children. Faithful Christian parents differ on this question, and neither side should despise the other.

This commentary’s view. The proverbs do speak of a real rod, but what Scripture requires of every parent is loving, consistent discipline; whether to use measured physical correction is left to wise parents. Where it is used, it is never given in anger, never to injure or humiliate, always with explanation and restored affection, and parents must also keep the law of the land they live in. Any discipline that frightens or harms a child is abuse, not the rod of Proverbs, and a child or parent caught in it should seek help and safety at once.

13.theology:
Restraint in speech and patience with money are marks of wisdom (vv. 3, 11). True wealth and poverty are not always as they appear (v. 7; 2 Cor 6:10; Rev 3:17).

God knows the sickness of deferred hope, and the believer's hope, though sometimes deferred for a lifetime, ends at the tree of life (v. 12; Heb 11:13; Rom 8:25). God's word is to be revered (v. 13; Isa 66:2), and those who carry the gospel bring healing when they deliver it faithfully (v. 17; 2 Cor 5:20).

Companions shape character (v. 20; Ps 1:1). Poverty can be caused by injustice as well as laziness (v. 23; Jas 5:4). Loving discipline is essential to parenting, and never permits harshness (v. 24; Eph 6:4; Heb 12:7).
13.examples: Parents might ask whether they know who their children walk with (v. 20). And everyone might ask what their grandchildren will inherit from them that cannot be spent (v. 22).

keyVerse.quote: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
keyVerse.note: The chapter is about the long road of a wise life, and this verse names honestly what the long road costs: waiting hurts. It also points to where the road ends, at the tree of life, which the Bible sets again beside the throne of God and of the Lamb (Revelation 22:2).

13.reflection:
Verse 1 contrasts the son who listens with the scoffer who has stopped listening. Whose correction do you find hardest to hear, and why?

“Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise” (v. 20). Who has shaped you most, for good or ill? How can our church help each other walk with the wise, and with Christ himself?

“Hope deferred makes the heart sick” (v. 12). What are you or people you love waiting for? How do the Emmaus road and the tree of life in Revelation 22 speak to a sick heart without making light of it?

Verse 23 says injustice can sweep away the harvest of the poor, and verse 24 calls loving discipline diligent. How do these two verses keep us from easy judgments, about the poor and about other parents?

14.title: Whoever Oppresses a Poor Man Insults His Maker
14.text: <sup>1</sup>The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down.<sup>2</sup>Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways
