Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness.<sup>23</sup>In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty.<sup>24</sup>The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly.<sup>25</sup>A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful.<sup>26</sup>In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge.<sup>27</sup>The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.<sup>28</sup>In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined.<sup>29</sup>Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly.<sup>30</sup>A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.<sup>31</sup>Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.<sup>32</sup>The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death.<sup>33</sup>Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools.<sup>34</sup>Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.<sup>35</sup>A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.
14.overview:
Where we are. We are still in Solomon’s main collection of two-line sayings (10:1–22:16). Chapter 13 ended with the household and its children; chapter 14 begins with a woman building her house and ends with a whole nation.

The message. Every life is being built up or torn down from the inside, by choices often hidden from everyone else. The fear of the LORD is the foundation that holds: it gives a person strong confidence, a refuge for his children, a fountain of life, and even a refuge in death. Without it a road can feel right all the way to the grave, and how we treat the poor shows what we really think of the God who made them.

Why it was said. Israel’s young people lived in close-knit towns where a household’s reputation, a witness in the gate and the treatment of the poor neighbour shaped everyone’s life (see the introduction). These sayings taught them to look beneath appearances.

How the chapter makes its case. First, houses and hearts: a household built or demolished, a messy but fruitful barn, the scoffer who cannot find wisdom, fools who mock guilt, the private heart, and the way that seems right but ends in death (vv. 1–14). Then the prudent and the poor: the simple believe everything, the poor are avoided, and blessing rests on the one who is generous to them (vv. 15–24). Last, the fear of the LORD as a fountain of life, reaching into a person’s temper, his treatment of the poor, his death and the life of his nation (vv. 25–35).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. The guilt offering that fools mock (v. 9) pointed to the Servant who would make an offering for guilt (Isaiah 53:10). The way that seems right and ends in death (v. 12) is answered by the one who said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The heart no stranger can enter (v. 10) is known by a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, and the refuge the righteous find in death (v. 32) is opened by the one who rose from it.

For us. Ask what you are building with your own hands at home, and test the roads that feel right against God’s word. Treat the poor as bearers of God’s image, because the Son of God became poor for us. And let the fear of the LORD, not the fear of death, have the last word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Houses Built and Torn Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Homes and lives are built or torn down from the inside, often out of sight. A wise woman builds her household and folly pulls it down with her own hands, and uprightness shows whether a person fears the LORD (vv. 1–3). A clean but empty barn yields nothing (v. 4). Honest witnesses, scoffers who cannot find wisdom and fools who deceive themselves and mock guilt are set against the prudent and upright (vv. 5–9). The heart has depths no stranger shares (v. 10). The impressive house falls while the humble tent flourishes, a way can seem right and end in death, laughter can hide an ache, and everyone eats the fruit of his own ways (vv. 11–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Homes and lives are built or torn down by choices made from the inside, often out of sight of everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down. Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises him. By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back, but the lips of the wise will preserve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Homes are built or torn down by the character of those inside, and conduct shows whether a person fears the LORD.

The wisest of women. In 9:1 Wisdom was pictured as a woman building her house; here a real woman does the same. A house in Proverbs means a household: a family, its atmosphere, its future. A wise woman builds it day after day through small acts of care, patience and prayer.

Folly with her own hands tears it down. No enemy is needed. Bitterness, a sharp tongue, contempt, the refusal to forgive: a person can dismantle her own home brick by brick without intending to. The proverb applies equally to husbands, and where we have pulled them out, the God who forgives can rebuild (Psalm 127:1).

Whoever walks in uprightness. Uprightness is the visible evidence that a person fears God. And the devious man, whatever he says in church, despises God: crooked conduct is a statement about what someone thinks of the God who sees it.

A rod for his back. The fool’s mouth makes the stick he will be beaten with, while the wise are protected by their words.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 3 can be read, as the ESV notes, “In the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride”: his proud speech is itself the rod. Either way, his words turn on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fruitfulness brings mess, and whoever insists on a spotless life must accept an empty one.

Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean. A farmer who wants a spotless barn can have one: get rid of the oxen. But then there is no ploughing and no harvest.

Anything fruitful is messy. Children bring noise, broken things and sleepless nights. A church full of new believers brings problems a tidy, empty church never has. A growing business has complications a failing one does not. Is there a mess in your life you resent, when it really comes with something God is using to feed you and others?

verseByVerse.quote: A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies. A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding. Leave the presence of a fool, for there you do not meet words of knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lies come as easily as breath to the false witness, and the scoffer never finds wisdom because he mocks its source.

A false witness. He breathes out lies because falsehood has become his nature.

A scoffer seeks wisdom. He does seek wisdom, and does not find it, because he seeks it while mocking the very things that would teach him. He wants the benefits of wisdom without bowing to its source. For the man of understanding, who has begun with the fear of the LORD, knowledge comes easily, because he is humble enough to receive it.

Leave the presence of a fool. Sometimes the wise thing is simply to leave. Some conversations produce nothing but folly, and staying in them only lets the folly rub off on you.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools is deceiving. Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prudent see where their road leads; fools deceive themselves and laugh at guilt, while the upright find acceptance.

Discerning his way. The prudent man knows where he is going and why. The fool’s folly is deceiving, and chiefly it deceives the fool himself: he believes his own story about where his road leads.

The guilt offering. It was the sacrifice by which an Israelite acknowledged wrongdoing and made it right (Leviticus 5:14–6:7). Fools find the idea laughable. Among people who take guilt seriously, there is reconciliation, with God and with each other.

Mocking guilt today. Modern people mock guilt in their own ways, calling it repression or old-fashioned religion. But the person who cannot take his own guilt seriously can never know the joy of having it taken away. The whole sacrificial system pointed to the final guilt offering, Christ himself, the Servant of whom Isaiah said, when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring (Isaiah 53:10). In him, who bore our guilt and obeyed in our place, the upright find their acceptance.

Uncertain wording. The first line of verse 9 is hard Hebrew. It may mean that fools mock at guilt (or the guilt offering), or that guilt mocks fools, who never find the forgiveness it should lead them to. The second line, the ESV notes, is literally “but among the upright is acceptance”. The contrast is clear either way: fools make light of guilt, and the upright find favour.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every heart has depths no other person can fully reach, and God alone knows them completely.

The heart knows its own bitterness. This is a lonely sentence, and a true one. Friends can sit with you, and should: weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). But there is a place inside each person where he is alone. Who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? (1 Corinthians 2:11). It should make us slow to say “I know exactly how you feel” to a grieving person.

The one who does know. The LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). There is no bitterness so private that God does not see it, and no joy so personal that he does not share it. And Christ, who took on a human heart, is a high priest who is not unable to sympathize with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15). The place where no stranger can come is exactly where he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What lasts depends on whom a household serves, not how strong it looks, and a road can feel right all the way to death.

House and tent. The wicked have a house, solid and impressive; the upright have a tent, flimsy and temporary. Yet the house is destroyed and the tent flourishes.

There is a way. The road that leads to death does not look like it. It seems right, reasonable, even good. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says “ways of death”, plural. There are many such roads: the respectable career that pushes God to the edge, the religion of good deeds that never needs a Saviour, the relationship everyone says is fine. Jesus said, what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God (Luke 16:15). The only safe test is God’s word.

Living your truth. Our culture has a phrase for the way that seems right: my truth. It is usually meant kindly. It honours experience and refuses to let anyone else tell me who I am. But it quietly asks something no one can carry: that each person be the final judge of his own road, with nothing outside him able to say he has gone wrong. Then the person who most needs a warning is the one no one may warn. The proverb is gentler and harder. It assumes that a sincere person can walk calmly towards death, convinced all the way. And it points, surprisingly, to the gospel. Outside Jerusalem there was once a road that seemed to every onlooker to lead only to death: a man condemned, mocked and nailed to a cross. Its end was life, for him and for all who trust him. The way that seems right can end in death; the way that looked like death was the way of life, and the one who walked it says, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).
verseByVerse.note: Repeated word for word in 16:25.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief. The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laughter can hide an aching heart, earthly joy ends, and everyone is filled with the fruit of his own ways.

Even in laughter. Behind many laughing faces is an aching heart; the life of the party may be the loneliest person in the room. The proverb calls us to look past appearances, and to be gentle. It is also honest about life in a fallen world: every earthly joy has an end, and even the happiest marriage ends one day in a parting.

Blessed are those who mourn. Jesus said, Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matthew 5:4). The proverb says earthly joy may end in grief; the gospel promises that for believers, grief ends in joy.

The backslider in heart. He is the person whose heart has turned back from God. The same phrase is used of him and of the good man: each is filled with the fruit of his ways. Everyone eats what he grows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Simple, the Prudent and the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prudent person tests what he hears, refuses to despise the poor, and works rather than talks. The simple believe everything, while the wise give thought to their steps, turn from evil and are crowned with knowledge (vv. 15–18). Evil will one day bow before good (v. 19). The poor man is avoided even by his neighbours and the rich man has many friends, but despising a neighbour is sin, and the blessing rests on the one who is generous to the poor (vv. 20–21). Those who plan good meet steadfast love and faithfulness, toil brings profit, and mere talk brings poverty (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: The prudent person tests what he hears, does not follow the crowd in despising the poor, and works rather than talks.

verseByVerse.quote: The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps. One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless. A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated. The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prudent person tests what he hears and thinks before he steps, while the simple believe anything and drift into folly.

The simple believes everything. This speaks straight to an age of viral rumour. The simple believe every forwarded message, health scare, conspiracy and flattering salesman. The prudent person gives thought: he checks, weighs, waits.

Testing spiritual claims. The same applies to spiritual claims. Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John 4:1). The Bereans received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so (Acts 17:11): they tested even what an apostle told them.

Cautious. The ESV notes that is cautious may be “fears”, that is, fears the LORD. The wise man is careful because he takes God and consequences seriously. The fool is reckless and careless, and often proud of it, calling his recklessness courage.

Quick temper. Verse 17 names two kinds of troublemaker: the hot-headed man who blows up, and the cold schemer who plots. Both damage everyone around them.

The simple inherit folly. The simple person does not need to work at becoming a fool; he inherits folly by drifting. Knowledge is a crown, and no one wins it by drifting.

verseByVerse.quote: The evil bow down before the good, the wicked at the gates of the righteous. The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends. Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evil will one day bow to good; meanwhile the world courts the rich, but God calls despising the poor sin and blesses generosity.

The evil bow down. For now the wicked often seem to be in charge. The proverb looks to the end, when the order is reversed and evil bows before good, at the gates of the righteous, where a town’s business and justice were done. The last day will show it fully.

The poor is disliked. The poor man is avoided even by his neighbours, because he may ask for something; the rich man is surrounded by friends, many of them friends of his money. Proverbs is not approving of this. It shows it so that we recognise it in ourselves.

Whoever despises his neighbor. Despising a neighbour, including the poor neighbour everyone avoids, is sin. James rebuked a church that gave the rich visitor a good seat and told the poor man, You stand over there, and asked, have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts? (James 2:3–4). The blessing is on the one who is generous to the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Do they not go astray who devise evil? Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness. In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty. The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who plan good meet God’s loyal love, and honest toil produces what talk never will.

Devise good. Both kinds of people devise, make plans. Those who plan evil go astray. Those who plan good meet steadfast love and faithfulness, the two great covenant words of 3:3. The ESV notes that meet may be “show”. Both are true: the one who plans good both receives and gives God’s loyal love.

Mere talk. Every workplace knows the person with endless ideas who does nothing. All toil, even the dull and unnoticed kind, produces something.

The crown of the wise. For the wise, wealth can be a crown, an honour they use well. For fools, whatever they have only produces more foolishness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–35 — The Fear of the LORD Is a Fountain of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Reverence for God reaches into every part of life, from the courtroom to the grave. A truthful witness saves lives (v. 25). The fear of the LORD gives strong confidence, a refuge for one’s children and a fountain of life (vv. 26–27). A king’s glory is his people, patience shows great understanding, and a tranquil heart gives life while envy rots the bones (vv. 28–30). Oppressing the poor insults their Maker, while generosity honours him (v. 31). The righteous find refuge in death, wisdom rests in the understanding heart, righteousness exalts a nation, and a wise servant wins his king’s favour (vv. 32–35).
verseByVerse.theology: Reverence for God reaches into a person's temper, his view of the poor, his death, and the life of his nation.

verseByVerse.quote: A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful. In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD gives strong confidence, a refuge for one’s children and a fountain of life.

A truthful witness saves lives. In a courtroom one honest witness can save an innocent man, and one lie can destroy him.

Strong confidence. The person who fears God fears nothing else in the same way. And the benefit reaches his children: a home where God is honoured, a model of faith, prayers offered for them for decades. It is a refuge, not a guarantee, for children still make their own choices. But a parent’s faithfulness is never wasted, even when a child wanders.

A fountain of life. This is nearly identical to 13:14, with the fear of the LORD in place of the teaching of the wise. The two belong together: wise teaching is a fountain only because it flows from reverence for God.

verseByVerse.quote: In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined. Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly. A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A leader’s glory is his people’s flourishing, patience shows understanding, and envy rots a person from within.

A multitude of people. A king’s greatness is measured by his people, not merely by his palace. Every leader’s glory is the flourishing of the people entrusted to him. And the King of kings will be glorified by a people no one can number.

Slow to anger. This is how God describes himself: a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger (Exodus 34:6). The person who is slow to anger reflects God, and shows great understanding, because he takes time to see the whole situation. The hot-tempered man exalts folly. Patience is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22), grown in those who have first known God’s patience with them.

A tranquil heart. Body and soul are closely bound. A heart at peace with God and content gives life to the flesh; the ESV notes it may be “healing”. Envy makes the bones rot. The envious man thinks he is damaging the one he envies; in fact he is rotting his own bones. Where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice (James 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every poor person bears God’s image, so to crush the poor insults God and to help them honours him.

Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker. The poor man was made by God in God’s image: So God created man in his own image (Genesis 1:27). To crush him is to show contempt for the one whose image he bears. The same truth appears in 17:5: Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker.

He who is generous to the needy honors him. Every act of kindness to a poor person is an act of worship. Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD (19:17). How we treat the cleaner, the refugee or the employee who cannot complain is how we treat God.

Christ and his needy brothers. Jesus went further, identifying himself with his needy brothers (many think he means his disciples, others the needy in general; either way the point about him stands): as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40). John will not let anyone separate love for God from love for people: he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20). And we give freely because Christ first gave to us: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death. Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked fall by their own evil, but the righteous find shelter even in death.

Refuge in his death. Death, the thing every human being dreads, becomes for the righteous a place of refuge. Death is still an enemy, the last one Christ will destroy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and believers grieve it; but the righteous man is not destroyed by death. He is sheltered in it. The New Testament fills in the picture: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Philippians 1:21); we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The believer walks through death into the arms of God.

Wisdom rests. Wisdom is at home, at rest, in the heart of a wise man; the ESV notes the line may mean that wisdom “rests quietly” there. It does not need to show off. And yet a truly wise person cannot be completely hidden, even in a crowd of fools.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads in his integrity instead of in his death, from very similar Hebrew letters, and some modern versions follow it; the ESV keeps the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people. A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness lifts a nation up and sin disgraces it.

Righteousness exalts a nation. A nation is lifted up not by military or economic strength alone, but by righteousness: justice in its courts, honesty in its business, care for its weakest. And sin is a reproach to any people, whatever its size or history. Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD (Psalm 33:12).

Christians and their nation. That gives Christians a reason to pray for their nation and to live righteously in it, not to make it the kingdom of God, but because righteousness is good for every people.

A servant who deals wisely. A servant who acts wisely wins his king’s favour; the one who acts shamefully faces his anger. Every Christian serves a King who has already shown him favour, and he serves best when he is sure of it.

14.theology:
Homes are built or destroyed by the character of those in them (v. 1). Human perception is unreliable: a way can seem right and lead to death (v. 12; 16:25), so every claim must be tested (v. 15; 1 John 4:1). The heart has depths only God fully knows (v. 10; 1 Sam 16:7; Heb 4:15).

Every human being bears God's image, so treatment of the poor is treatment of God (v. 31; Gen 1:27; Matt 25:40). The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life (v. 27) and a refuge for the next generation (v. 26). The righteous have hope in death (v. 32; Phil 1:21). Righteousness exalts nations (v. 34).
14.examples: Before you forward the next alarming message, give it the thought verse 15 asks for. And ask who the person is that you tend to avoid because he might need something (v. 20); he bears his Maker's image.

keyVerse.quote: Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.
keyVerse.note: The chapter keeps returning to the poor neighbour whom everyone avoids (vv. 20–21, 31), and this verse gives the reason he matters: he bears his Maker’s image. It turns ordinary kindness into worship, and it prepares for Christ, who became poor for our sake and counts what is done to the least of his brothers as done to him.

14.reflection:
“The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down” (v. 1). What small, daily choices build up or tear down a home? Where might you need God to rebuild what you have pulled down?

“There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death” (v. 12). Which roads seem right in our culture, or in your own life, that God’s word calls into question? How does the cross turn this proverb upside down?

Verses 20, 21 and 31 deal with the poor. Why are the poor so easily avoided, even by neighbours? What would it look like for you or your church to honour God by the way you treat the needy?

Verses 26–27 and 32 speak of the fear of the LORD as confidence, a refuge for children and a refuge in death. How does fearing God set us free from other fears?

15.title: A Soft Answer Turns Away Wrath
15.text: <sup>1</sup>A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.<sup>2</sup>The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly.<sup>3</sup>The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.<sup>4</sup>A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit.<sup>5</sup>A fool despises his father's lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man!<sup>12</sup>A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise.<sup>13</sup>A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed.<sup>14</sup>The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly.<sup>15</sup>All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast.<sup>16</sup>Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it.<sup>17</sup>Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it.<sup>18</sup>A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention.<sup>19</sup>The way of a sluggard is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway.<sup>20</sup>A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish man despises his mother.<sup>21</sup>Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense, but a man of understanding walks straight ahead.<sup>22</sup>Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed.<sup>23</sup>To make an apt answer is a joy to a man, and a word in season, how good it is!<sup>24</sup>The path of life leads upward for the prudent, that he may turn away from Sheol beneath.<sup>25</sup>The LORD tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries.<sup>26</sup>The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD, but gracious words are pure.<sup>27</sup>Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household, but he who hates bribes will live.<sup>28</sup>The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things.<sup>29</sup>The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.<sup>30</sup>The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones.<sup>31</sup>The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise.<sup>32</sup>Whoever ignores instruction despises himself, but he who listens to reproof gains intelligence.<sup>33</sup>The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
15.overview:
Where we are. We are in the middle of Solomon’s main collection (10:1–22:16), in the run of chapters where nearly every proverb is a sharp contrast. Chapter 14 ended with a nation and its king; chapter 15 turns to the tongue, the table and the God who sees and hears everything.

The message. The LORD sees every place and every heart, so the words we speak, the worship we offer and the homes we keep all lie open before him. A gentle word heals, a harsh one wounds; a simple prayer from an upright heart pleases him more than costly religion from a crooked one; a little with the fear of the LORD and love around the table is richer than a fortune with trouble. The way up is always down: humility comes before honour.

Why it was said. These sayings trained young people for life in Israel’s homes, markets and courts, where angry words, bribes, proud neighbours and empty sacrifices were everyday temptations (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First, the tongue and the eyes of the LORD: a soft answer, a gentle tongue, and the God who sees everywhere, even the depths of death, and who loves the prayer of the upright (vv. 1–12). Then what makes a life rich: a glad heart, a hungry mind, a little with the fear of the LORD, a dinner of herbs where love is, good counsel and a word in season (vv. 13–23). Last, the upward path: the LORD tears down the proud and defends the widow, hears the righteous, refreshes with good news, and teaches humility before honour (vv. 24–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The soft answer has never been spoken more powerfully than when Jesus prayed for those crucifying him (Luke 23:34). He is the Servant given the tongue of those who are taught to speak a word in season to the weary (Isaiah 50:4), the bearer of the good news that refreshes the bones (Isaiah 52:7), and the one who humbled himself to death on a cross and was exalted (Philippians 2:8–9): humility before honour, fulfilled.

For us. Lower your voice when anger rises, and listen before you answer. Do not hide behind religious activity; bring God a simple, honest prayer, through the blood of Jesus. Value love around the table above what is on it, and take the low road of humility, trusting the God who exalts in his own time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Tongue and the Eyes of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD who sees everything hears every word and every prayer. A soft answer turns away wrath while a harsh word stirs up anger, and the wise make knowledge attractive (vv. 1–2). The eyes of the LORD are in every place, watching the evil and the good (v. 3). A gentle tongue is a tree of life, a fool despises correction, and the house of the righteous holds real treasure (vv. 4–7). The LORD hates the sacrifice of the wicked but delights in the prayer of the upright, and he loves those who pursue righteousness (vv. 8–9). Even Sheol lies open before him, so the hearts of people certainly do, and the scoffer who avoids correction walks towards death (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD who sees everything, down to the hidden heart, hears every word and every prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A gentle answer cools anger and a harsh one inflames it; the wise make knowledge attractive, while fools pour out folly.

A soft answer. Someone comes at you angry: a customer, a teenager, a spouse. Answer in kind, and the anger doubles. Answer softly, and very often it drains away. A soft answer is not a weak one. It may say something hard. It simply refuses to add heat: it lowers the voice, acknowledges the other person’s frustration and does not reach for the sharpest word available. A harsh word is petrol on a small fire.

With gentleness and respect. Peter tells Christians who are challenged about their faith to answer with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Gentleness is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:23): when a sharp reply rises, ask God for gentleness, lower your voice and see what happens.

Why does gentleness feel like losing? In a polarised age the soft answer looks like surrender. If the other side is not merely mistaken but dangerous, lowering your voice feels like betraying your cause, and your own side will tell you so. So the temperature rises, online and around dinner tables, exactly as the proverb predicts. Underneath there is often fear: if I do not win this exchange, something I depend on, my standing, my tribe, my sense of being right, is under threat. Secure people do not need to shout, and the gospel gives that security at the root. A Christian’s standing does not hang on winning the argument, because the verdict that matters has already been given in Christ. And the soft answer has the strongest pedigree there is. The one who could have called on more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53) prayed for the men driving in the nails, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). That was not weakness. It was the power that turned away wrath for ever.

Commends knowledge. The wise man makes knowledge attractive; people want to hear more. The fool pours out folly, like water from an overturned jar, with no control and no end.

verseByVerse.quote: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing anywhere is hidden from the LORD: that is a warning to the evil and a comfort to the good.

The eyes of the LORD are in every place. There is nowhere God does not see: not the locked office, the hotel room on a business trip, the browser in private mode, or the thought no one will ever hear. Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Psalm 139:7).

Keeping watch on the evil and the good. For the evil, nothing is hidden and nothing will be forgotten: no creature is hidden from his sight (Hebrews 4:13). For the good, no act of faithfulness goes unnoticed: the prayer said alone, the kindness nobody thanked you for, the temptation resisted with no one watching. God was watching. How would today change if you lived it knowing that the LORD’s eyes are on this room?

verseByVerse.quote: A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit. A fool despises his father's instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent. In the house of the righteous there is much treasure, but trouble befalls the income of the wicked. The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so the hearts of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Words heal or crush, and the home of the righteous is rich in what money cannot buy.

A gentle tongue. A gentle tongue gives life to the people around it, and a twisted tongue breaks the spirit. Some people have been broken inside by years of harsh, mocking or manipulative words from someone close to them.

His father’s instruction. The fool’s contempt starts at home. The prudent man, whatever his age, heeds reproof.

Much treasure. The righteous man’s house holds treasure, not necessarily money, but everything that makes a home rich: peace, love, faith, stability. The wicked man has income, perhaps a large one, and trouble comes with it: legal battles, family conflict, anxiety, the constant need for more.

Spread knowledge. Wise people scatter knowledge like seed. A fool’s heart is unstable, so his words are too.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the gentle tongue of verse 4 may be a “healing” tongue; the Hebrew word can mean either. The second line of verse 7 is compressed, and the ESV notes it may be read “the hearts of fools are not steadfast”.

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him. The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who pursues righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rejects costly worship from an unchanged life and welcomes the simple prayer of the upright.

The sacrifice of the wicked. A wicked man brings a costly sacrifice, and God calls it an abomination. An upright man simply prays, with nothing in his hands, and God finds it acceptable. God is not impressed by religious activity cut off from a changed life. He said through Isaiah, What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? (Isaiah 1:11), and through Samuel, Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22).

A warning and an encouragement. This warns anyone who uses church attendance, giving or religious duty as cover for a life he has no intention of changing. And it encourages the person who feels he has nothing to offer God but a simple prayer. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Psalm 51:17). Yet the upright are not heard because their prayers are good enough. Believers draw near to God by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19), the one sacrifice that never needs repeating.

Pursues righteousness. From worship the proverb turns to the whole way of life. He loves the one who pursues righteousness: not the one who has fully arrived, but the one chasing it. And his love comes first. We pursue righteousness because he loves us, not to earn his love (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: There is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die. Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man! A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever refuses correction walks towards death, for the God who sees into death itself sees every human heart.

There is severe discipline. A person who leaves God’s way does not escape discipline; it becomes severe. God corrects gently at first, and more firmly if gentle correction is ignored. The one who hates reproof altogether cuts himself off from the correction that could save him.

Sheol and Abaddon. Sheol is the realm of the dead; Abaddon is a word for destruction, the deepest place of ruin. Even these lie open before the LORD, like a book on a table. If God sees the depths of death, how much more the human heart?

How much more the hearts! No motive is hidden from him, no secret resentment, no self-deception. That is terrifying for anyone trying to hide from God, and freeing for anyone who has stopped trying. There is no point pretending to the one who already knows everything, and no need to, because he loved us knowing it.

A scoffer. The scoffer avoids the very people who could help him: a wise friend, a pastor, a counsellor, because they might tell him something he does not want to hear. So he surrounds himself with people who agree with him, and stays a scoffer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Better a Dinner of Herbs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What makes a table or a life rich is not what is on it, but reverence for God and love around it. The heart shapes the face, the mind feeds on what it seeks, and a cheerful heart has a continual feast (vv. 13–15). Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with trouble, and better a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox with hatred (vv. 16–17). The hot-tempered stir up strife while the patient quiet it, and the sluggard’s path is all thorns (vv. 18–19). A wise son gladdens his father, plans succeed with many advisers, and a word in season is a joy (vv. 20–23).
verseByVerse.theology: What makes a table or a life rich is not what is on it, but reverence for God and love around it.

verseByVerse.quote: A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed. The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly. All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A heart that has found its joy in God can feast even in hard days.

A glad heart. The face shows the heart. Proverbs does not pretend the believer is never crushed: A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones (17:22).

Feed on folly. Everyone is hungry for something. The man of understanding goes looking for knowledge; the mouths of fools feed on folly: gossip, trivia, scandal, entertainment that empties the mind. What a person feeds on, he becomes.

A continual feast. Here evil means hard and miserable, not wicked. Two people can live through similar circumstances very differently, and often the difference is what is in their hearts. A cheerful heart is not denial. It has found something to rejoice in that circumstances cannot take. Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice (Philippians 4:4). Paul wrote that from prison.

A word to the depressed. This is no rebuke to a believer living with depression. Sorrow of heart that crushes the spirit (v. 13) is named here as a real affliction, not a sin, and The LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little with the fear of the LORD and love around the table is richer than a fortune with trouble and hatred.

Better is a little. A small income with the fear of the LORD beats a fortune with trouble attached: anxiety, family fights, a guilty conscience, the fear of losing it. Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” (Hebrews 13:5).

A dinner of herbs. On one table there is a bowl of vegetables and a family that loves each other. On the other is a roast from the fattened ox, the most expensive meal there was, eaten in cold silence or open hostility. Which table would you rather sit at?

In everyday life. This is a word to anyone chasing a bigger house, a better car or a more impressive holiday at the cost of the relationships inside the home. The children will not remember what was on the table. They will remember whether there was love around it.

verseByVerse.quote: A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention. The way of a sluggard is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some people bring conflict into every room and others calm, and the sluggard’s road is all obstacles.

A hot-tempered man. He does not merely react to strife; he stirs it up. The person slow to anger actively quiets it, and so reflects God, who is slow to anger (Exodus 34:6).

A hedge of thorns. The sluggard’s road is blocked with thorns: everything is hard, every task has a reason it cannot be done today. Part of this is excuse, thorns of his imagination. Part is real: tasks put off grow into tangles. The upright person’s path is a level highway, not because life is easy, but because he deals with things as they come.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish man despises his mother. Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense, but a man of understanding walks straight ahead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fool despises even the mother who raised him, while the man of understanding keeps to the straight road.

Despises his mother. The first line repeats 10:1, but the second is sharper. In chapter 10 a foolish son was a sorrow to his mother; here a foolish man despises her. It is one thing to cause a mother grief, and worse to hold her in contempt. And this fool is a grown man, still treating the woman who raised him with scorn.

Folly is a joy. The man without sense finds folly fun. The man of understanding is not distracted by what is merely entertaining; he walks straight ahead, keeping to the road.

verseByVerse.quote: Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed. To make an apt answer is a joy to a man, and a word in season, how good it is!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Plans succeed when tested by wise counsel, and the right word at the right moment is a joy.

Without counsel plans fail. A plan made alone is a plan made with one set of blind spots. Many advisers bring many angles. The person too proud to ask for advice will watch his plans fail; the person who seeks it often finds problems before they happen (compare 11:14).

A word in season. Almost everyone has known the right word at the right moment: a friend who knew what to say at the funeral, a teacher’s sentence that changed a direction. The same words at the wrong time do nothing, or harm.

Christ’s word in season. The Servant of the LORD in Isaiah, whom the New Testament shows to be Jesus, says, The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary (Isaiah 50:4). Jesus spoke exactly that word: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The word in season comes from someone who has first been listening, to God and to the person in front of him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–33 — The Path That Leads Upward
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The road of wisdom climbs, and the way up is always by the way down. The path of life leads upward, away from Sheol (v. 24). The LORD tears down the house of the proud and protects the widow’s boundaries, hates wicked schemes and loves gracious words (vv. 25–26). Greed for unjust gain troubles a household, and the righteous think before they answer (vv. 27–28). The LORD is far from the wicked but hears the righteous, and good news refreshes the whole person (vv. 29–30). Whoever accepts reproof gains understanding, for the fear of the LORD is the school of wisdom, and humility comes before honour (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology: The road of wisdom climbs, and the way up is always by the way down: humility before honour.

verseByVerse.quote: The path of life leads upward for the prudent, that he may turn away from Sheol beneath. The LORD tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom’s path climbs towards life, and the LORD brings down the proud while he guards the vulnerable.

The path of life. The path of the wise climbs, towards life and towards God; the other direction goes down to Sheol. Paul puts it this way: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is (Colossians 3:1).

The widow’s boundaries. In the ancient world a widow was among the most vulnerable people there were. A powerful neighbour could move her boundary stones a few feet each year and take her land, and she had no husband to defend her. But she has the LORD, who maintains her boundaries himself. He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18). And the proud man’s house, built partly on what he took, God tears down.

Mary’s song. Mary sang the same reversal: he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate (Luke 1:52). That is a comfort to the vulnerable and a summons to everyone who has power over them.

verseByVerse.quote: The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD, but gracious words are pure. Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household, but he who hates bribes will live. The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God judges thoughts as well as deeds, greed troubles a home, and the righteous think before they speak.

The thoughts of the wicked. The schemes of the wicked are an abomination to God before they are ever carried out. And gracious words are pure in his sight: clean, like refined metal.

Unjust gain. The greedy man thinks he is providing for his family. In fact he is troubling it, bringing stress, danger, shame and eventually ruin into his home. The man who hates bribes, who will not take the under-the-table payment or the corrupt deal, will live. Integrity at work protects the family at home.

Ponders how to answer. The righteous person thinks before he answers; the wicked person’s mouth pours out, again the image of an overturned jar. In an age of instant replies, the discipline of pausing to consider how to answer is rare and precious.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous. The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is near to those who turn to him and far from those who cling to wickedness.

Far from the wicked. God is everywhere (v. 3), and yet he is far from the wicked. The distance is not in space but in relationship. The difference is not that the righteous are sinless, but that they have turned towards him. A heart that holds on to its wickedness and prays anyway is praying into a wall. A heart that turns to God in repentance finds him close enough to hear a whisper. Your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:6).

Good news. The light of the eyes may be the bright face of a friend, or simply the joy of seeing clearly. And good news refreshes the bones; the ESV notes that the Hebrew is “makes fat”, the ancient picture of health and strength.

The best news. There is no better news than the gospel. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news (Isaiah 52:7). The angel said to the shepherds, Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people (Luke 2:10). That is the news that refreshes the bones.

verseByVerse.quote: The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise. Whoever ignores instruction despises himself, but he who listens to reproof gains intelligence. The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accepting correction is the way to wisdom, and humility always comes before honour.

Life-giving reproof. Reproof rarely feels life-giving. But the person whose ear accepts correction ends up living among the wise, as one of them.

Despises himself. A person who ignores instruction thinks he is defending himself. The proverb says he despises himself, treating his own life as worthless by refusing what would improve it. Real self-respect listens.

Humility before honor. The fear of the LORD is not just the beginning of wisdom; it is the whole school. And humility comes before honor, always in that order. The way up is down.

He humbled himself. No one showed this more than Christ. He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9). That obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19), and the same path is open to everyone who follows him: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Peter 5:6).

15.theology:
God sees everything, including the hidden heart (vv. 3, 11; Ps 139:7-8; Heb 4:13). Worship is acceptable only from a life turned toward God; simple prayer from the upright pleases him more than costly sacrifice from the wicked (vv. 8-9, 29; 1 Sam 15:22; Ps 51:17).

Speech can defuse anger, give life or crush the spirit (vv. 1, 4, 23). Contentment and love are better than wealth (vv. 16-17; Heb 13:5). God defends the vulnerable against the proud (v. 25; Deut 10:18; Luke 1:52).

The good news refreshes the whole person (v. 30; Isa 52:7). Humility precedes honour, supremely in Christ (v. 33; Phil 2:8-9; 1 Pet 5:6).
15.examples: Ask what your mind has been feeding on this week (v. 14). Notice the person at work or church who quietly settles strife, and thank God for him. And the next time a sharp reply rises, try the soft answer and see what happens to the anger in the room.

keyVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s soft answers, simple prayers, humble tables and teachable ears all grow from this root: reverence for God, which makes a person humble. The verse states the pattern the whole Bible follows, and that Christ fulfilled supremely when he humbled himself to the cross and was exalted.

15.reflection:
“A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (v. 1). Think of a recent conflict. What would a soft answer have sounded like? What makes it so hard to give one, and how does the gospel make us secure enough to try?

“The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good” (v. 3). Where do you find this verse a warning, and where a comfort?

Verses 16–17 prefer a little with the fear of the LORD, and a dinner of herbs where love is, to great wealth with trouble. What would change in your home if you really believed this?

“Humility comes before honor” (v. 33). How did Jesus live this out? What might taking the low road look like for you this week?

16.title: The Heart of Man Plans His Way
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD.<sup>2</sup>All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit.<sup>3</sup>Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established.<sup>4</sup>The LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble.<sup>5</sup>Everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination to the LORD; be assured, he will not go unpunished.<sup>6</sup>By steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the LORD one turns away from evil.<sup>7</sup>When a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.<sup>8</sup>Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues with injustice.<sup>9</sup>The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.<sup>10</sup>An oracle is on the lips of a king; his mouth does not sin in judgment.<sup>11</sup>A just balance and scales are the LORD's; all the weights in the bag are his work.<sup>12</sup>It is an abomination to kings to do evil, for the throne is established by righteousness.<sup>13</sup>Righteous lips are the delight of a king, and he loves him who speaks what is right.<sup>14</sup>A king's wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it.<sup>15</sup>In the light of a king's face there is life, and his favor is like the clouds that bring the spring rain.<sup>16</sup>How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver.<sup>17</sup>The highway of the upright turns aside from evil; whoever guards his way preserves his life.<sup>18</sup>Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.<sup>19</sup>It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud.<sup>20</sup>Whoever gives thought to the word will discover good, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD.<sup>21</sup>The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness.<sup>22</sup>Good sense is a fountain of life to him who has it, but the instruction of fools is folly.<sup>23</sup>The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious and adds persuasiveness to his lips.<sup>24</sup>Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body.<sup>25</sup>There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.<sup>26</sup>A worker's appetite works for him; his mouth urges him on.<sup>27</sup>A worthless man plots evil, and his speech is like a scorching fire.<sup>28</sup>A dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends.<sup>29</sup>A man of violence entices his neighbor and leads him in a way that is not good.<sup>30</sup>Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass.<sup>31</sup>Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life.<sup>32</sup>Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city.<sup>33</sup>The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.
16.overview:
Where we are. We are at the midpoint of Solomon’s main collection (10:1–22:16). After six chapters of mostly contrasting pairs, chapter 16 opens with a cluster of sayings about the LORD himself, and then a group about the king, before returning to everyday wisdom.

The message. We truly plan, choose and speak, but the LORD weighs our motives, establishes our steps and governs everything, down to the fall of the dice. That is not a reason to stop planning but to plan humbly: commit your work to him, trust him with the outcome, and walk in the humility, honesty and self-control that please him. Pride, however secure it feels, goes before a fall.

Why it was said. Israel’s young men would make plans, trade, speak before officials and serve kings (see the introduction). They needed to know that none of this happened outside the rule of the LORD, and that his justice reaches the market scales and the royal court alike.

How the chapter makes its case. Nine sayings set our plans inside God’s purpose: he gives the answer of the tongue, weighs the spirit, establishes committed work, rules even over the wicked, covers iniquity by steadfast love and faithfulness, and directs our steps (vv. 1–9). Then the ideal king: just in judgment, honest in his weights, delighted by truth, his favour like spring rain (vv. 10–15). Then wisdom better than gold, pride before a fall and gracious words like honey (vv. 16–24). Last, destructive people, the crown of grey hair, the greater victory of self-control, and the lot that falls as the LORD decides (vv. 25–33).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise, pattern and the character of God revealed in him. The steadfast love and faithfulness that cover iniquity (v. 6) met at the cross, where God put forward his Son as a propitiation (Romans 3:25). The cross is also the supreme case of verses 1–9: evil men did what they planned, and Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). And the just king of verses 10–15, whom Israel’s kings never fully were, is the Son of David who judges the poor with righteousness and in whose face the light of God shines (Isaiah 11:4; 2 Corinthians 4:6).

For us. Plan carefully, then hand the outcome to God and stop carrying what he has promised to carry. Let him search your motives, and ask who is allowed to tell you that you are proud. Rule your own spirit by his Spirit, and rest in the truth that nothing, not even what looks like chance, falls outside your Father’s hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Man Plans, the LORD Establishes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Human planning is real and responsible, but it always happens inside the purpose of a sovereign God. People plan, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD, and he weighs motives that look pure to us (vv. 1–2). Work committed to him is established, and he has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble (vv. 3–4). Pride will not go unpunished, iniquity is covered by steadfast love and faithfulness, and when a man’s ways please the LORD he can make even enemies to be at peace (vv. 5–7). Better a little with righteousness than great gain with injustice, for man plans his way but the LORD establishes his steps (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Human planning is real and responsible, but it always happens inside the purpose of a sovereign God.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD. All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We make our plans, but our words are in God’s hands, and he weighs motives we think are pure.

The plans of the heart. Verses 1–9 are one of the Bible’s richest meditations on human choice and God’s sovereignty. A man plans and prepares what he will say, but what actually comes out when the moment arrives, the answer of the tongue, is in God’s hands. Jesus built a promise on it: do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour (Matthew 10:19).

Still worth planning. This does not make planning pointless; it makes it humble. Prepare, and then pray.

The LORD weighs the spirit. We give ourselves the benefit of every doubt. But the LORD puts motives on the scale (the ESV notes it may be “spirits”, every one of them), and his reading often differs from ours. Paul knew this: For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me (1 Corinthians 4:4). A clear conscience is good, but it is not the final verdict. That is a reason for humility about ourselves, and for leaving other people’s motives to God.

Weighed and found pure. On that scale none of our motives is found pure. Christ’s were, and his righteousness is counted to those who trust him (Philippians 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established. The LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hand your work to the LORD and he will establish it, for nothing, not even wickedness, lies outside his purpose.

Commit. The word pictures rolling a heavy load onto someone stronger. The work is still yours to do, but you give its outcome to God. Commit your way to the LORD; trust him, and he will act (Psalm 37:5). This is not a promise that every plan will turn out as drawn up, but that plans placed in God’s hands will be established, made firm, in the shape he intends.

How do I commit my work to the LORD? Take a real piece of work: the exam, the job application, the hard conversation on Thursday. Hand it over by name. Before you begin, tell God what it is, what you hope for and what you fear, and say plainly that the outcome is his. Then do the work well, as for him, without cutting corners; committing it to God is no substitute for preparing. Hold the result open. Decide beforehand that a no will not mean he has failed you, and a yes will not prove that you were clever. Hand it back when it returns. At 2 a.m., when the worry picks the load up again, put it down again: Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you (Psalm 55:22). You can do this because Jesus did it first. In Gethsemane he laid the hardest work ever given into his Father’s hands, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42), and on the third day the Father established it.

Even the wicked. This hard verse does not say God makes people wicked, or that he is the author of evil; Scripture everywhere holds people responsible for their sin. It says that nothing, not even wickedness, is outside God’s purposes. The wicked have a place in his plan: the day of trouble, the day of judgment. Joseph’s brothers meant their evil fully, and Joseph could still say, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The same God who uses the evil of wicked men will judge it. For a believer suffering at the hands of the wicked, this verse is a rock: the wicked are not outside God’s control, and neither is your life.

Where Christians differ. All agree that God is not the author of sin and that people are responsible for it. Arminian Christians hold that God permits evil and free choices but does not ordain them; the Reformed tradition reads this verse, with Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23, as teaching that God ordains whatever comes to pass.

This commentary’s view. God ordains all that happens, sinful acts included, without being the author of sin, and his purpose includes the means, so human choices and prayers are real (see Sovereignty and providence in this commentary’s positions).

Uncertain wording. For its purpose translates a short Hebrew phrase that can also mean “for its answer”, that is, for its fitting end, or (as older versions took it) “for himself”. All three readings say that nothing God made is purposeless.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination to the LORD; be assured, he will not go unpunished. By steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the LORD one turns away from evil. When a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God judges hidden pride and covers iniquity by his own steadfast love and faithfulness.

Arrogant in heart. Arrogance need not show itself in words or deeds to be judged; it is enough that it is in heart. The second half repeats the solemn promise of 11:21: be assured. Pride will not escape.

Iniquity is atoned for. The Hebrew word behind atoned (to cover) appears in Proverbs only here and in verse 14, where a wise man will appease a king’s wrath. How is iniquity covered? By steadfast love and faithfulness (in Hebrew, hesed and emet), the words God used to describe himself (Exodus 34:6). Many take the line to mean the love and faithfulness a repentant person shows, and the second line points partly that way. But no human kindness can pay for sin. In the end it is covered by God’s own loyal love and truthfulness. Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other (Psalm 85:10).

Love and faithfulness met at the cross. God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25), that is, a sacrifice that turns away his wrath. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). And the second line shows the fruit: the forgiven person, living in the fear of the LORD, turns away from evil.

When a man’s ways please the LORD. God can turn even hostile people towards peace. It is not guaranteed; Jesus pleased the Father perfectly and was crucified. But again and again God softens the hearts of opponents towards those who walk with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues with injustice. The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We plan our way, but the LORD directs each step.

Better is a little. Like 15:16, this weighs a small honest income against a great one made by injustice. The first lets you sleep; the second will eventually be taken from you, one way or another.

The LORD establishes his steps. The nine verses close where they began (v. 1). A person plans his way, the general direction; God establishes his steps, each one. He works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11). That frees a believer from both anxiety and passivity. Plan carefully, then trust the one who directs the steps.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — The Throne and the King's Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ideal king rules justly under God, and his favour is life. His verdicts carry the weight of an oracle and do not go wrong (v. 10). Honest scales and weights belong to the LORD, so a ruler must protect them (v. 11). Righteousness establishes the throne, and the good king loves those who speak the truth (vv. 12–13). His anger is deadly and a wise man calms it, while his favour is like the clouds that bring the spring rain (vv. 14–15). Israel’s kings rarely matched this picture, and so it became a longing for the King to come.
verseByVerse.theology: The ideal king rules justly under God, and his favour is life; the book points beyond every earthly throne to the King who never judges wrongly.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle is on the lips of a king; his mouth does not sin in judgment. A just balance and scales are the LORD's; all the weights in the bag are his work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king must judge as though speaking for God, because justice belongs to the LORD.

An oracle. A group of proverbs about the ideal king begins here. His verdict is to carry divine authority, and his judgment is not to go wrong. Israel’s kings rarely lived up to this, and Proverbs knows it. So the verse is both a standard for every ruler and a longing for a king who would truly meet it: the Son of David of whom Isaiah said, with righteousness he shall judge the poor (Isaiah 11:4).

A just balance. Justice comes from God. The honest scale and weights belong to him, and a ruler who allows cheating in the market is tampering with something that is not his (compare 11:1).

Uncertain wording. Oracle translates a word that elsewhere almost always means the divination God forbade (Deuteronomy 18:10). Here it seems to be used positively, of a verdict so decisive it sounds like a word from heaven. Whether it describes what a king should be or what the ideal king is, the point is the same: a ruler is answerable to God for his judgments.

verseByVerse.quote: It is an abomination to kings to do evil, for the throne is established by righteousness. Righteous lips are the delight of a king, and he loves him who speaks what is right. A king's wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it. In the light of a king's face there is life, and his favor is like the clouds that bring the spring rain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness establishes a throne, and a good king’s favour is life.

The throne. A good king finds evil repulsive, not because it harms his image, but because his throne rests on righteousness. Authority of every kind that does wrong undermines itself.

Righteous lips. A wise leader wants honest advisers, not flatterers. If you lead anything, do you love the person who tells you the truth?

A king’s wrath. An ancient king’s anger could mean execution. A wise man knows how to calm it, with truth, humility and good timing. Paul says the governing authority does not bear the sword in vain (Romans 13:4). The wise respect that power without flattering it.

The light of a king’s face. The king’s look of approval is like the spring rains that made the harvest possible. Every earthly king is a small and imperfect picture of the true one. The priestly blessing prayed, the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Numbers 6:25), and God has now given the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). His favour is not rain for one season’s crop, but life that does not end.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom, humility and gracious speech are worth more than anything pride could win. Getting wisdom is better than gold, and the upright guard their lives by keeping to a road that turns from evil (vv. 16–17). Pride goes before destruction, and it is better to be lowly with the poor than to share the spoil of the proud (vv. 18–19). Whoever attends to the word finds good and whoever trusts the LORD is blessed (v. 20). Wisdom starts in the heart and makes speech sweet and persuasive, and gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and health to the body (vv. 21–24).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom, humility and gracious speech are worth more than anything pride could win.

verseByVerse.quote: How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver. The highway of the upright turns aside from evil; whoever guards his way preserves his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is worth more than gold, and the upright guard their lives by turning from evil.

Better than gold. The psalmist says of God’s words, More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold (Psalm 19:10). Between a large sum and understanding how to live before God, there is no contest.

The highway of the upright. The upright do not wander into evil and then try to get out; their whole road turns aside from it. Guarding the road is guarding the life.

verseByVerse.quote: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pride blinds a person until the fall comes, so lowliness is better than the spoils of the proud.

Pride goes before destruction. Usually shortened to “pride comes before a fall”, this describes a pattern seen in every generation: the executive who thought the rules did not apply to him, the preacher who stopped being accountable. Pride makes a person stop listening, stop watching and stop depending on God, and then the fall comes. And the proud person cannot see it; it is usually visible to everyone else first. So the wise question is not “Am I proud?” but “Who in my life is allowed to tell me I am?”

The vice we now call a virtue. For most of Christian history pride stood at the head of the deadly sins. Today we tell children to be proud of themselves, and the word has become a compliment. Much of what we mean is harmless: gladness in good work, a refusal to be crushed. But C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, put his finger on the thing this proverb means. Pride, he argued, is competitive by its very nature: it takes no pleasure in having something, only in having more of it than the next person. That is why it never rests. A culture of rankings, follower counts and constant comparison feeds it every hour, and leaves us swollen or crushed depending on whom we have just measured ourselves against. The gospel does not cure pride by telling us we are worthless. It ends the competition. If my worth is a gift, settled by the one who humbled himself to the point of death on a cross for me, I no longer need to be above anyone, and I can stop measuring. And God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9): the way up really is down.

A lowly spirit. It would be easy to join the proud sharing out the spoil; it is better to be with the lowly. Jesus began his teaching with the same reversal: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gives thought to the word will discover good, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD. The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Attention to the word goes with trust in the LORD, and sweetness makes truth persuasive.

Gives thought to the word. The ESV notes that this may be “to a matter”: anyone who thinks carefully about a matter finds good. But the richest reading is the word of God, and the second line points that way. Careful attention and trust belong together. Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD (Jeremiah 17:7).

Sweetness of speech. How a wise person speaks matters as well as what he says. Kindness and grace in how truth is put make it more persuasive. Truth delivered harshly is often rejected, not because it is untrue, but because of how it was said.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense is a fountain of life to him who has it, but the instruction of fools is folly. The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious and adds persuasiveness to his lips. Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wise speech begins in a wise heart, and gracious words are as sweet and strengthening as honey.

A fountain of life. Good sense keeps giving life to its owner, like a spring that does not run dry. When fools try to teach, what they teach is folly.

The heart of the wise. Wise speech starts not with technique but in the heart. No communication course can substitute for being a wise person.

A honeycomb. Honey was the sweetest thing an Israelite knew, and a source of quick strength. Gracious words are like that: sweet to receive and genuinely strengthening. Those who have received God’s gracious words have honey to give.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–33 — The Whisperer, the Gray Head and the Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the whisper that ruins a friendship to the dice in the lap, nothing falls outside the LORD’s rule. A way can seem right and end in death, and hunger drives the worker on (vv. 25–26). Four portraits show destructive people at work: the worthless man whose speech scorches, the whisperer who separates friends, the violent man who drags his neighbour in, and the schemer with his winks and pursed lips (vv. 27–30). Grey hair gained in righteousness is a crown, and ruling one’s spirit is greater than taking a city (vv. 31–32). The lot is cast, but its every decision is from the LORD (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: From the whisper that ruins a friendship to the dice in the lap, nothing falls outside the LORD's rule.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death. A worker's appetite works for him; his mouth urges him on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A road that seems right can still end in death, and hunger keeps the worker working.

There is a way. This repeats 14:12 word for word, because it is so easily forgotten. Here, after proverbs about trust in the LORD, it reminds us that there is no neutral ground: if we do not trust God, we are trusting what seems right to us.

A worker’s appetite. Hunger is a good motivator. God built the need for food into us, and it keeps a great many people diligent. If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10) is not cruelty; it lets the appetite do its work.

verseByVerse.quote: A worthless man plots evil, and his speech is like a scorching fire. A dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends. A man of violence entices his neighbor and leads him in a way that is not good. Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Destructive people work through scorching words, whispers and secret signals; the wise recognise them and refuse to become them.
