he will seek at harvest and have nothing.<sup>5</sup>The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.<sup>6</sup>Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find?<sup>7</sup>The righteous who walks in his integrity— blessed are his children after him!<sup>8</sup>A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes.<sup>9</sup>Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"?<sup>10</sup>Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright.<sup>12</sup>The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both.<sup>13</sup>Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread.<sup>14</sup>"Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts.<sup>15</sup>There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.<sup>16</sup>Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners.<sup>17</sup>Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.<sup>18</sup>Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war.<sup>19</sup>Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler.<sup>20</sup>If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness.<sup>21</sup>An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end.<sup>22</sup>Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you.<sup>23</sup>Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good.<sup>24</sup>A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way?<sup>25</sup>It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows.<sup>26</sup>A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them.<sup>27</sup>The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts.<sup>28</sup>Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld.<sup>29</sup>The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair.<sup>30</sup>Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts.
20.overview:
Where we are. We are still in Solomon’s main collection (10:1–22:16). Chapter 19 ended with judgment ready for scoffers; chapter 20 opens with wine that mocks and closes with blows that cleanse, and in between it keeps returning to the hidden heart and the God who sees it.

The message. No one can see all the way into his own heart, and no one can make it clean (v. 9), but the LORD sees it all. He made the eye and the ear (v. 12), he hates double standards (vv. 10, 23), he directs our steps beyond our understanding (v. 24), and his lamp searches our innermost parts (v. 27). So we can leave revenge and our future in his hands, and let him cleanse us, even when the cleansing hurts.

Why it was said. Israel’s markets ran on weights and haggling, its kings sat in judgment, and wine, vows and disputes over inheritance were part of ordinary life (see the introduction). The young needed to learn that the God of the covenant was present at the market stall, the table and the throne, and in the secret places of their own hearts.

How the chapter makes its case. First, wine, strife and the deep heart: drink and quarrels, the sluggard’s empty field, the deep water of human motives, the rare faithful man, the king who winnows evil, the question no one can answer with a yes, and the double standards God hates (vv. 1–11). Then the seeing eye and the mouth full of gravel: the LORD who made eye and ear, the lying buyer, the rash guarantor, deceit that turns to grit, and counsel against the babbler (vv. 12–19). Last, wait for the LORD: honour for parents, haste over an inheritance, no private revenge, steps directed by God, rash vows, the lamp of the LORD, the throne upheld by steadfast love, and the blows that cleanse (vv. 20–30).

Where it leads. To Christ above all by the need it exposes. “Who can say, ‘I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin’?” (v. 9). No one but Christ could. His obedience is counted to all who trust him, and “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). The king upheld by steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 28) finds his fulfilment in the King who came “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). And the call to wait for the LORD instead of repaying evil (v. 22) is the road Christ walked, who “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

For us. Let God’s lamp search you, and do not blow it out. Keep honest weights in business and in judging others, hand your grudges to the Judge, and when your path makes no sense, trust the one who directs your steps.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Wine, Strife and the Deep Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one sees all the way into his own heart, and no one can make it clean. Wine mocks those it leads astray, the fool loves a quarrel, and the sluggard who will not plough in the cold finds nothing at harvest (vv. 1–4). A person’s motives lie deep like water and need understanding to draw them out, and faithfulness is far rarer than talk of it, though the integrity of the righteous blesses his children (vv. 5–7). The king winnows evil with a look, and then comes the question no one can answer with a yes: who can say his heart is pure? (vv. 8–9). God hates double standards, and even a child shows himself by what he does (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: No one sees all the way into his own heart, and no one can make it clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drink promises cheer and then makes a fool of the drinker, and whoever lets it lead him astray is not wise.

Wine is a mocker. Wine is pictured as a person, and the portrait is sharp. It is a mocker: it promises cheer and then makes a fool of the drinker. Strong drink is a brawler: it starts fights, loosens tongues and turns ordinary men violent. Noah, the righteous survivor of the flood, “drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent” (Genesis 9:21). Chapter 23 paints the drunkard’s misery in full (23:29–35).

Whoever is led astray by it is not wise. The proverb condemns being led astray by it. The ESV notes that the last phrase may be read “will not become wise”: a person in the grip of drink stops growing. “Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18).

Not abstract. For anyone who has seen alcohol destroy a family, this verse is not abstract. And if you are beginning to need a drink rather than enjoy one, the mocker has already started laughing. Tell someone: a pastor, a biblical counsellor, your doctor.

Must Christians abstain from alcohol? Many hold that they should, for the sake of those who struggle, for their own safety and as a witness (Romans 14:21); and abstaining is right for anyone who cannot drink with control. But Scripture calls wine God’s gift (Psalm 104:15), Jesus made it (John 2:1–11), and Paul forbids drunkenness, not wine (Ephesians 5:18). The better reading is that moderate drinking is permitted, drunkenness forbidden, and abstinence a free and often wise choice. Faithful Christians differ here, and neither should judge the other (Romans 14:3).

verseByVerse.quote: The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life. It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling. The sluggard does not plow in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not provoke real power carelessly, count it honour to stay out of a quarrel, and do the hard work now or reap nothing later.

The terror of a king. A king’s anger can be as deadly as a lion’s growl (the same picture as 19:12), so the wise do not provoke real power carelessly.

Keep aloof from strife. The world thinks the man who wins every argument is strong; the proverb gives the honour to the man who stays out of it. That is not cowardice: it takes more self-control to walk away than to fight. And every fool will be quarrelling; it is almost the mark by which you recognise him.

The sluggard does not plow in the autumn. In Israel the ploughing was done in autumn, when the rains came and the weather turned cold and unpleasant. The sluggard stays indoors, and at harvest he goes looking for a crop that was never planted. Every harvest in life requires an unpleasant ploughing season: study before the exam, saving before retirement, discipline before maturity.

verseByVerse.quote: The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find? The righteous who walks in his integrity— blessed are his children after him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real motives lie deep and need patient understanding to draw them out, faithfulness is rarer than talk of it, and a parent’s integrity blesses the next generation.

Like deep water. A person’s real motives lie deep, like water at the bottom of a well. Most people cannot see them, and often the person himself cannot. But a man of understanding will draw it out, like someone lowering a bucket on a long rope.

Drawing it out. This is the skill of a good counsellor, pastor, parent or friend: asking the questions that help another person discover what is really going on inside. Not telling him, but drawing it out. Whose deep water could you patiently draw up this week by listening rather than talking?

A faithful man who can find? Talk about loyalty is cheap; a person who keeps his word when it costs him is rare. Jesus asked a sobering question of the same kind: “when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

Blessed are his children after him. A father’s integrity blesses the next generation with a good name, a model to follow and the fruit of his prayers. The most lasting thing a parent gives is not money but a life of integrity lived in front of the children.

verseByVerse.quote: A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes. Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king sifts evil with a look, and before such a judge no one can claim a clean heart, or make his own heart clean.

Winnows all evil with his eyes. A farmer winnows grain by tossing it in the wind so the chaff blows away; a wise judge, with a look, separates the truth from the lies. Earthly kings do this imperfectly. The King who will sit on the final throne does it perfectly.

Who can say? Straight after the king who sees all evil comes the question that silences everyone. The answer is no one, not the most moral or the most religious. “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

I have made my heart pure. Notice I have made. No one is pure, and no one can make himself pure; self-improvement cannot clean a heart. Only God can: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10). And he does: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). No one can say it of himself. Christ could, and his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD. Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God detests double standards, in the market and in the heart, and even a child shows his character by what he does.

Unequal weights and unequal measures. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is “Two kinds of” weights: one set for buying, one for selling (see weights and scales). The verse comes back almost exactly at verse 23, and the principle appeared at 11:1. Double standards in business are detestable to God, and so are double standards in life: one rule for me and another for everyone else, one set of weights for my faults and another for yours.

Even a child makes himself known. Character shows early, and parents should watch what their children do, not only what they say. Actions reveal character, and, as the alternative reading below shows, they can also hide it. “You will recognize them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16), given enough time to see the fruit.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes a different reading of verse 11: “Even a child can dissemble in his actions, though his conduct seems pure and upright” (to dissemble is to pretend). Both are true of children, and of adults.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — The Seeing Eye and the Mouth Full of Gravel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who made the eye and the ear watches the market and the mouth. He gave sight and hearing, and the eyes he made are for opening, not for sleep (vv. 12–13). The buyer who runs down the goods and then boasts of his bargain is caught, and wise words are rarer than jewels (vv. 14–15). The man who guarantees a stranger’s debts is a bad risk, and bread gained by deceit tastes sweet and turns to gravel (vv. 16–17). Plans need counsel, and the babbler who carries others’ secrets will carry yours (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who made eyes and ears sees the buyer's lie, and makes the cheat's gain turn bitter.

verseByVerse.quote: The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both. Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD made our eyes and ears, so they are gifts to thank him for and to use as he intends, and the eyes he made are for opening, not for loving sleep.

The hearing ear and the seeing eye. Every eye that sees and every ear that hears was made by God. That is a reason for gratitude: sight and hearing are gifts, not rights. And it is a reason for sober thought: the God who made the eye sees, and the God who made the ear hears (Psalm 94:9), and he intends them to be used for what he made them for. When Moses complained that he could not speak, the LORD answered, “Who has made man’s mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?” (Exodus 4:11).

Love not sleep. Sleep is good; loving it is dangerous, because the one who loves sleep comes to poverty. Open your eyes, get up, face the day, and there will be bread.

verseByVerse.quote: "Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts. There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hears the bargain-hunter’s little lie, and wise words are rarer and more precious than jewels.

“Bad, bad,” says the buyer. A scene from any market. The buyer frowns at the item: poor quality, far too expensive, cheaper elsewhere. The seller lowers the price, and the buyer walks away and tells his friends what a bargain he got.

Bargaining and lying. The proverb does not condemn bargaining; it exposes the lie. Many who would never tell an outright lie think nothing of misrepresenting a car they are selling or running down a house they want to buy. The God who hates unequal weights (v. 10) also hears the buyer’s “Bad, bad”.

The lips of knowledge. Gold and gems are plentiful enough in the market. What is truly rare is a mouth that speaks knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners. Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever guarantees a stranger’s debts is a bad risk, and gain won by deceit tastes sweet before it turns to grit.

Take a man’s garment. A piece of hard-headed financial advice, repeated at 27:13. If a man is foolish enough to guarantee a stranger’s debts, do not lend to him without collateral: take his cloak as security. A man with such poor judgment is a bad risk.

Bread gained by deceit. Imagine biting into fresh bread and finding your mouth full of grit and stones. That is what dishonest gain becomes. At first it is sweet: the money from the fraud, the promotion won by lying, the grade from cheating. Afterward it turns to gravel: guilt, exposure, broken trust, a conscience that grinds.

Fleeting pleasures. Moses chose “rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin” (Hebrews 11:25). Sin’s pleasure is real, but it is fleeting, and it leaves gravel.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the last phrase of verse 16 may be “for an adulteress” instead of for foreigners. Either way the guarantor has shown poor judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Big plans need wise counsel, and whoever carries other people’s secrets to you will carry yours to others.

Plans are established by counsel. No sensible king goes to war on a whim, and the same is true of the battles of ordinary life: starting a business, confronting a problem, making a big move. Plans are established by counsel (compare 24:6).

A simple babbler. The first line is from 11:13; the second draws the practical conclusion: do not keep company with a person who cannot keep his mouth shut. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is “with one who is simple in his lips”. If he is telling you other people’s secrets, he is telling other people yours.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leave vengeance and direction to God, and let him search the heart with the lamp he has put inside it. Cursing parents ends in darkness, and wealth grabbed too early is not blessed (vv. 20–21). Do not repay evil but wait for the LORD, who also hates false scales (vv. 22–23). Our steps are from the LORD, beyond our understanding, so vows must be made with thought, not in haste (vv. 24–25). A wise king separates out the wicked, the human spirit is the LORD’s lamp searching the inner self, and steadfast love upholds a throne (vv. 26–28). Every age has its glory, and even painful blows can cleanse the innermost parts (vv. 29–30).
verseByVerse.theology: Leave vengeance and direction to God, and let him search the heart with the lamp he has put inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness. An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever curses his parents puts out his own light, and wealth grabbed too early is not blessed.

If one curses his father or his mother. Under the law, cursing a parent was a capital crime: “Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death” (Exodus 21:17). God takes the honour of parents that seriously. The lamp going out pictures a life that ends in darkness.

An inheritance gained hastily. Think of the prodigal son demanding his inheritance before his father was dead. Wealth grabbed before it is rightly due, or acquired too quickly, rarely brings blessing; what comes fast often goes fast, and brings ruin with it.

Honouring parents today. The death penalty for cursing parents ended with Israel’s civil law, but the duty to honour them stands (Ephesians 6:2). Honouring does not mean obeying sin or tolerating abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not pay back evil yourself; trust the LORD to deal with it, for his scales are true and yours are not.

Do not say, “I will repay evil.” When someone wrongs us, we want to get him back. The proverb forbids even saying it. Instead, wait for the LORD. That is not passivity but trust that God sees the wrong, cares about justice and will act. And it is freedom: you do not have to carry the weight of evening the score.

Vengeance is mine. Paul takes up the principle: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). Is there a wrong you have been planning to repay? Hand it to the God who has forgiven you, and ask his Spirit for patience to wait.

The way Christ did it. “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). He bore the wrath our own wrongs deserved. People who have been forgiven that much can afford to let the Judge settle the rest.

How do I leave it with him? Tell God exactly what was done. Waiting is not pretending you were not hurt; the psalms name wrongs in detail, and so may you. Refuse the small repayments. Revenge is seldom dramatic: the cold shoulder at work, the story told so others think less of him, the help quietly withheld. Decline each one as it comes. Hand it over again. When the conversation replays at 2 a.m., do not rehearse your reply; say, “Lord, this is yours”, as often as it returns. Pray for him. Jesus says, “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44); start with one honest sentence of blessing.

False scales. The repetition of verse 10, right after the call not to take revenge, may be deliberate. Revenge is a kind of false scale: we weigh the other person’s offence heavily and our own lightly. God’s scales are true.

Does “wait for the LORD” forbid the courts? It forbids private revenge. The magistrate is God’s servant to punish evil (Romans 13:4), so seeking justice lawfully is not revenge.

verseByVerse.quote: A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way? It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD directs our steps beyond our understanding, which frees us from needing to see the whole road and warns us against rash promises to him.

A man’s steps are from the LORD. If God directs every step, no one can fully understand his own path; we see a few steps ahead at best. Jeremiah prayed, “I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps” (Jeremiah 10:23).

How then can man understand his way? That is a relief rather than a burden. You do not have to understand your whole life to walk it faithfully. In the confusing season, the closed door, the unexpected turn, you may not understand your way, but the one directing your steps does.

It is a snare to say rashly, “It is holy.” Some people make promises to God in a moment of emotion, “I dedicate this to you” or “If you get me through this, I will…”, and think about them only afterward. It becomes a trap. Jephthah vowed that “whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me” would be offered up, and his daughter came out (Judges 11:31). “It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5:5). Think first; then promise.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them. The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts. Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise ruler deals firmly with evil, God searches the inner self through the spirit he gave us, and steadfast love and faithfulness are what truly uphold a throne.

A wise king winnows the wicked. The picture comes from the threshing floor, where a heavy wheel was rolled over the grain to separate it from the husk. A wise ruler separates out the wicked in the same way and deals with them firmly: justice is not soft on evil.

The lamp of the LORD. God has placed a lamp inside every human being. The ESV notes that the Hebrew word is “breath”, the breath of life God breathed into man. With it he searches all his innermost parts. That is the conscience, and more than the conscience: the human capacity to know oneself, which God uses to shine light into the corners we would rather keep dark.

Do not blow it out. When you feel inner discomfort about something you have done, that may be the lamp of the LORD. Do not blow it out. “Who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?” (1 Corinthians 2:11). And God searches deeper than we can ever search ourselves.

Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king. A king is kept on his throne not finally by armies but by steadfast love and faithfulness, the two words that sum up how God keeps covenant with his people: “Steadfast love and faithfulness meet” (Psalm 85:10). The one King whose throne is upheld forever came “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair. Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every age has its own glory, and painful correction can reach and cleanse the depths of a person.

The glory of young men. The young have strength, energy and courage; the old have gray hair, the sign of experience, wisdom and a long life (16:31). Neither should despise the other; a church or family that honours both is strong.

Blows that wound cleanse away evil. The chapter ends on a hard truth: pain can cleanse. Discipline that hurts, the wound of correction, the painful consequence, can reach the innermost parts and make them clean in a way that gentle words sometimes do not. “For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness” (Hebrews 12:11).

What it does not mean. A believer in a painful season may be under the strokes of a loving Father, cleansing something deep. But not every pain is correction for a particular sin, as Jesus said of the man born blind (John 9:3). And the verse never excuses anyone who wounds another in the name of discipline: abuse is not God’s refining, and anyone suffering it should seek safety at once.

20.theology: No one can make his own heart pure (v. 9), but God cleanses all who confess (1 John 1:9). He sees the deep motives no one else can (vv. 5, 27), hates double standards (vv. 10, 23), and directs our steps beyond our understanding (v. 24). So his people leave vengeance to him (v. 22), make vows with thought (v. 25), and receive even painful discipline as his cleansing (v. 30).
20.examples:
The chapter's pictures stay in the mind: Noah uncovered in his tent, the sluggard who would not plow in the cold autumn rain, the bucket lowered into the deep water of a heart, the buyer's "Bad, bad" and his boast afterward, the mouthful of gravel, and Jephthah's rash vow.

Two of them are for this week. Hand over to God a wrong you have been planning to repay. And when the lamp of conscience shows you something you would rather not see, do not blow it out.

keyVerse.quote: Who can say, ‘I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin’?
keyVerse.note: The chapter keeps looking beneath the surface, at deep motives, hidden double standards and the lamp that searches the innermost parts, and this question is where that search ends: no one can claim a clean heart, or make one. It exposes our need and points to Christ, the only one who could say it, whose blood cleanses all who confess their sins.

20.reflection:
“The purpose in a man’s heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out” (v. 5). How can we become better at drawing out what is really going on in someone else, or in ourselves?

“Who can say, ‘I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin’?” (v. 9). Why is it so tempting to think we can clean ourselves up? How does the gospel answer this question?

“Do not say, ‘I will repay evil’; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you” (v. 22). What do the small, everyday forms of revenge look like in your life? How does Christ’s example in 1 Peter 2:23 help us wait?

Verses 10, 14, 17 and 23 deal with honesty in buying, selling and earning. Where are you most tempted to use “unequal weights”, in business or in judging others?

21.title: The Victory Belongs to the LORD
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.<sup>2</sup>Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart.<sup>3</sup>To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.<sup>4</sup>Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin.<sup>5</sup>The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty.<sup>6</sup>The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death.<sup>7</sup>The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just.<sup>8</sup>The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.<sup>9</sup>It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.<sup>10</sup>The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.<sup>11</sup>When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge.<sup>12</sup>The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.<sup>13</sup>Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.<sup>14</sup>A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath.<sup>15</sup>When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.<sup>16</sup>One who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead.<sup>17</sup>Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich.<sup>18</sup>The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright.<sup>19</sup>It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman.<sup>20</sup>Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling, but a foolish man devours it.<sup>21</sup>Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor.<sup>22</sup>A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust.<sup>23</sup>Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble.<sup>24</sup>"Scoffer" is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride.<sup>25</sup>The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor.<sup>26</sup>All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.<sup>27</sup>The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent.<sup>28</sup>A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure.<sup>29</sup>A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.<sup>30</sup>No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD.<sup>31</sup>The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
21.overview:
Where we are. We are near the end of Solomon’s main collection of two-line sayings (10:1–22:16). Chapter 20 said that “a man’s steps are from the LORD” (20:24); chapter 21 puts even the king’s heart in his hand.

The message. The LORD rules everything, from the heart of a king to the outcome of a war, and he weighs every heart. So what he looks for is not religious show but a just and merciful life: righteousness and justice more than sacrifice (v. 3), an ear open to the poor (v. 13), a hand that gives and does not hold back (v. 26). Plans, wisdom and preparation all matter, but none of them can stand against him, and none of them wins without him (vv. 30–31).

Why it was said. The first hearers lived under kings who could make or ruin them, beside a temple whose sacrifices were easy to treat as cover for crooked dealing (see the introduction). These sayings put the king under God, and put the worshipper’s daily life under the same scrutiny as his offering.

How the chapter makes its case. First, God and the heart: the king’s heart steered like water, every heart weighed, justice above sacrifice, and four short-cuts to gain that come to nothing (vv. 1–8). Then mercy and justice, framed by two sayings about a quarrelsome home: the merciless neighbour, the ear closed to the poor, the secret bribe, the joy and terror of justice, and the wicked caught in their own trap (vv. 9–19). Last, the shape of a wise life: saving, pursuing righteousness, guarding the tongue, giving, worshipping without hypocrisy, and the climax: no wisdom avails against the LORD, and the victory is his (vv. 20–31).

Where it leads. To Christ, chiefly by the character of God that the cross reveals. The rulers gathered against Jesus did only “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28): God turned the worst crime in history into the victory of salvation. The chapter also exposes our need, for the LORD weighs the heart (v. 2), and only one man has done righteousness and justice perfectly (v. 3). And verse 18, where the wicked becomes a ransom for the righteous, is turned upside down at the cross: the Righteous One came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

For us. Pray for the leaders who worry you; their hearts are in God’s hand. Do not let church activity stand in for honest dealing on Monday, and do not close your ear to the cry you would rather not hear. Make the horse ready, plan, work and prepare, and then rest, because the victory belongs to the LORD, and in Christ he has already won it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The King's Heart in the LORD's Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rules even the most powerful heart and weighs every heart, so what he wants is a just life, not a religious substitute for one. The king’s heart is water channelled by the LORD’s hand, and our own ways, which always look right to us, are weighed by him (vv. 1–2). Righteousness and justice please him more than sacrifice, while pride, the lamp the wicked steer by, is plain sin (vv. 3–4). Then four sayings show where crooked roads to gain end: haste in poverty, lying wealth in a vanishing breath, violence in the flood that sweeps away its users, and guilt in a twisted path while the pure walk straight (vv. 5–8).
verseByVerse.theology: No heart, not even a king's, is outside God's direction, and no religious act replaces a just life.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even a king’s heart is steered by the LORD, and every heart is weighed by him.

The king’s heart. Picture a farmer sending irrigation water this way or that with a movement of his hoe. The most powerful person in the land, whose decisions seem to shape history, is like that water in God’s hand.

God turns kings’ hearts. Scripture shows it again and again. Ezra praised the LORD “who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king” of Persia (Ezra 7:27). Nebuchadnezzar, the proudest king on earth, was humbled “until you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will” (Daniel 4:32).

The LORD weighs the heart. Almost the same as 16:2, and placed after the king’s heart it applies the same truth to everyone: God weighs what is actually inside. The scales we use on ourselves are always flattering.

A comfort in a frightening world. No president, dictator or board of directors is outside God’s hand. That is why Paul urges prayer “for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life” (1 Timothy 2:2). Pray for the leaders who worry you.

Is the king still responsible? Yes. God used Assyria’s king for his purpose and then punished him for his arrogant heart (Isaiah 10:5–15); Herod and Pilate did what God had planned, and were guilty (Acts 4:27–28). God steers without forcing, and is never the author of sin.

verseByVerse.quote: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God wants a just life more than any offering, and the pride that guides the wicked is sin.

Righteousness and justice. God commanded sacrifices, but never as a substitute for a righteous life. A worshipper who cheats his workers on Monday and brings an offering at the weekend has misunderstood God completely. “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). “For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). Micah asked what the LORD requires, and answered: “to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).

Religious activity today. Today’s equivalent is religious activity: attendance, giving, serving on committees. All good, and none of it can cover for a life of injustice. Where we have failed here, as all have, the answer is not more ritual but Christ, who did justice and loved kindness perfectly in our place, and then offered himself as the one sacrifice that takes sin away.

Haughty eyes. Pride shows in the eyes and lives in the heart. It is the lamp the wicked walk by, the light they steer their lives with. The verdict is simple: it is sin.

Uncertain wording. The word for lamp is almost identical to the word for newly broken ground, and the ESV notes that it may mean “the ploughing”: pride is what the wicked cultivate. Either way, it is sin.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death. The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just. The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Haste, lies and violence all end in loss; patient work and a straight path last.

The plans of the diligent. Two paths to wealth, and only one works. Careful planning and steady work lead surely to abundance. The hasty want it now: the shortcut, the gamble, the scheme. Everyone who goes that way ends poor. Patience is not only a virtue; it is a financial strategy.

A lying tongue. Money made by lies is like breath on a cold morning: visible for a second and gone. The liar thinks he is seeking treasure; he is running into a trap. “What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (James 4:14). If life itself is a vapour, riches gained by lying are a vapour within a vapour.

The violence of the wicked. The violence the wicked use against others becomes the flood that carries them off. And the root cause is named: they refuse. Their problem is not that they do not know what is just; they will not do it.

The way of the guilty. Guilt bends a person’s path: the guilty must twist and turn to avoid being found out. The pure can walk in a straight line because they have nothing to hide.

Textual note. In verse 6 most Hebrew manuscripts read “a vapor for those who seek death”, while some, with the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), read a snare of death (ESV note). The sense is much the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Cry of the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mercy and justice reveal what a heart is. The section is framed by two sayings about a quarrelsome home, where a corner of the roof and then a desert are better (vv. 9, 19). Between them stand the wicked man who desires evil and shows his neighbour no mercy, the scoffer whose punishment teaches the simple, and the Righteous One who watches the wicked man’s house (vv. 10–12). The ear closed to the poor will cry and not be heard; a secret gift can buy off anger; justice done brings joy to some and terror to others (vv. 13–15). Drifting from wisdom ends among the dead, the love of pleasure ends in poverty, and the wicked fall into the trouble they meant for the upright (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: A person who will not hear the poor will one day find that he is not heard.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife. The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes. When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge. The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hard heart shows at home and towards the neighbour, and God watches the wicked man’s house and brings it down.

A corner of the housetop. Israel’s houses had flat roofs, and a cramped shelter up there, exposed to the weather, is better than a spacious house full of conflict. The saying appears again word for word at 25:24, and in a sharper form at verse 19.

A quarrelsome wife. The proverb, written for young men, is honest about a real misery, and it applies to husbands as much as wives. A home can be large and comfortable and still unbearable. What kind of atmosphere do you create at home: the kind people are glad to come back to, or the kind that drives them up to the roof?

The soul of the wicked. Wickedness is at bottom a matter of desire. The wicked man does not merely do evil; he wants it. And those who live near him get no mercy.

When a scoffer is punished. A near repeat of 19:25. The simple learn by watching others punished; the wise learn by being taught. Better to be the second kind of learner.

The Righteous One observes. God observes the house of the wicked, watches closely, and in his time brings it down. The wicked man thinks no one is watching his house. Someone is.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 12 says only “a righteous one”. Some translations take it as a righteous man who considers the wicked man’s house and learns from its ruin. The ESV capitalises it as God, since throwing the wicked down is his work, and that is the more likely reading.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered. A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath. When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever shuts out the cry of the needy will not be heard himself, and our reaction to justice shows whose side we are on.

The cry of the poor. To close the ear to need is a choice, and God answers it in kind: the day will come when he is the one crying out, and no one will answer.

The rich man and Lazarus. Jesus told of a rich man who “feasted sumptuously every day”, while at his gate lay a poor man named Lazarus, “who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table” (Luke 16:19–21). After death the rich man cried out for mercy, and none came. “For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy” (James 2:13). And John asks, “if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?” (1 John 3:17).

Is there a cry you have closed your ear to? The poor are not always at the gate. Sometimes they are in an appeal letter, a news story, or a struggling colleague.

A gift in secret. This is an observation, not a recommendation. The second line is literally “a bribe in the bosom”, tucked inside the robe. A quiet gift can calm anger. There is a legitimate form of this, as when Jacob sent gifts ahead to Esau (Genesis 32:20), and a corrupt one, which Proverbs condemns (17:23). The proverb describes how people work and leaves the reader to use it rightly.

When justice is done. A just verdict brings joy to one group and terror to another, and how a person reacts shows which group he belongs to. The final day of justice will be exactly this: joy for those who belong to the Judge, terror for those who do not.

verseByVerse.quote: One who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead. Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich. The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright. It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drift and the love of pleasure end in loss, and the wicked fall into the trouble they planned for the upright.

One who wanders. He wandered: not a dramatic rebellion, just a drift off the path. And he ends up resting, but in the assembly of the dead. Folly offers rest and delivers death.

Whoever loves pleasure. Wine and oil were ancient luxuries, and good gifts of God: “wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine” (Psalm 104:15). The problem is not enjoying them but loving them. A person who lives for pleasure, spending on every comfort and experience, will be poor, and often poor in more than money.

A ransom for the righteous. This is not about payment for sin. It describes God’s justice turning the plans of the wicked back on them, so that the trouble they planned for the righteous falls on them instead, as Haman was hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai (Esther 7:10). God said to Israel, “I give Egypt as your ransom” (Isaiah 43:3).

The gospel reversal. The gospel turns even this proverb upside down. There the Righteous One came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Christ, who was no traitor, took the place of traitors, so that traitors could be brought home.

A desert land. Verse 9 said a corner of the roof; now it is the desert, with its heat and loneliness. Constant fretting makes any home a wilderness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom gathers, gives, guards its tongue and prepares well, but it wins only because the LORD gives the victory. The wise store up while the fool devours, and those who pursue righteousness and kindness find life and honour (vv. 20–21). Wisdom takes walls that strength cannot, a guarded tongue keeps out of trouble, and the scoffer is defined as pride in action (vv. 22–24). The sluggard craves all day while the righteous gives freely (vv. 25–26). Wicked worship is worse when it is a cover, the false witness perishes while the careful listener’s word lasts, and bluff is set against careful thought (vv. 27–29). The climax puts all human wisdom and preparation under the LORD (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Prepare the horse, and trust the LORD for the victory, for no plan can succeed against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling, but a foolish man devours it. Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise keep reserves, and those who pursue righteousness find life and honour too.

Precious treasure and oil. The wise man’s house has reserves; the fool devours everything as soon as it comes in. The difference between them is not how much they earn, but what they do with it.

Righteousness and kindness. The person who pursues righteousness and kindness finds three things: life, honour, and righteousness itself. The pursuit is rewarded with more of what was pursued. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6). Most people chase honour and miss it; those who chase righteousness find honour as well.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust. Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. "Scoffer" is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom achieves what force cannot, a guarded tongue avoids trouble, and scoffing is pride.

The city of the mighty. Wisdom beats brute power, in war and in life. The strong trust their strongholds; the wise find a way over.

Whoever keeps his mouth. A near repeat of 13:3. Most of the trouble a person gets into could have been avoided by keeping quiet.

“Scoffer” is the name. The proverb gives a definition, piling up words for pride: arrogant, haughty, arrogant pride. That is what a scoffer is. His mockery is not wit; it is pride wearing a smile.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor. All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sluggard is consumed by wants he will not work for, while the righteous gives freely.

The desire of the sluggard. The sluggard is killed not by lack of desire but by desire that never turns into work. The unfulfilled craving eats him alive.

He craves and craves. One spends his day craving, the other giving. The craver never has enough. The giver, who seems to have less because he gives it away, is the one who is full. Jesus said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

The righteous gives and does not hold back. Which describes your average day: craving or giving? An open hand is the Spirit’s work in those who have been given everything in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent. A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure. A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worship used as cover is doubly hateful to God, lies do not last, and the upright think rather than bluff.

The sacrifice of the wicked. Verse 3 said justice is better than sacrifice; this goes further. A wicked man’s sacrifice is already an abomination (15:8). It is worse still when he brings it with evil intent: using religion to cover a crime, buy favour, or look respectable.

A false witness. The liar perishes (compare 19:5, 9). The man who hears, who listens carefully before he speaks, gives testimony that lasts. Careful listening makes for truthful speaking.

A bold face. The wicked man bluffs and brazens it out. The upright man does something harder: he gives thought to his ways. Bluff hides a man; careful thought builds his life.

Uncertain wording. In verse 29 the Hebrew is written one way and traditionally read another, giving two verbs: the upright gives thought to his ways, or “establishes” them (ESV note). Both fit: he considers his path and so makes it firm.

verseByVerse.quote: No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing succeeds against the LORD, so prepare well and trust him for the outcome, because the victory is his.

No wisdom. Wisdom, understanding, counsel: the verse says no to all three. No human wisdom can succeed against the LORD. When the rulers gathered against Jesus, they thought they were in control, but the church said in prayer that they had done only “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28). The greatest crime in history accomplished God’s plan of salvation.

The horse is made ready. The war horse was the tank of the ancient world. The proverb does not say, do not prepare it. It says, prepare it, and know that the victory belongs to the LORD. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). David said to Goliath, “the battle is the LORD’s” (1 Samuel 17:47).

The balance of the book. This is the balance of the whole book. Work hard, plan well, study, prepare, get advice, saddle the horse. Then trust God with the outcome, because it is his. The farmer ploughs and waits for rain. What is the horse you need to make ready this week, and have you handed its victory to the LORD?

21.theology:
God is sovereign over the hearts of rulers (v. 1) and over every plan against him (v. 30). Human preparation is right, but the outcome belongs to God (v. 31; Ps 20:7).

A just life matters more to God than religious ritual (vv. 3, 27; Mic 6:8; Hos 6:6). Refusing mercy to the poor brings judgment without mercy (v. 13; Luke 16:19-25; Jas 2:13). Righteousness and generosity are pursued and rewarded (vv. 21, 26; Matt 5:6).

The chapter's last verse finds its fullest answer at the cross. The rulers took counsel against the LORD and his Anointed (Ps 2:2; Acts 4:25–28), and what looked like their victory and his defeat was the reverse: through the cross Christ disarmed the powers and triumphed over them (Col 2:15). The horse must still be made ready, but the believer works knowing that the decisive battle is already won.
21.examples:
The pictures to remember are the farmer turning irrigation water with his hoe, breath on a cold morning, the corner of the roof and the desert, and the rich man with Lazarus at his gate.

The practice is simpler: pray for the leaders who worry you, do not cheat on Monday and then bring an offering on Saturday, ask whether your day is spent craving or giving, and saddle the horse while trusting the LORD for the victory.

keyVerse.quote: The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The chapter begins with the king’s heart in God’s hand and ends here, with every human plan and preparation under his rule. The verse holds together the whole balance of Proverbs: work hard and prepare well, then trust the outcome to the LORD, who alone gives the victory.

21.reflection:
“The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (v. 1). Which leaders, at home or abroad, worry you most? How does this verse change the way you think about them and pray for them?

Verse 3 says righteousness and justice please the LORD more than sacrifice, and verse 27 warns against worship brought with evil intent. Where might religious activity be tempting us to overlook how we treat people during the week?

“Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered” (v. 13). Whose cry is easiest for you to shut out, and what would opening your ear look like this month?

Verses 30–31 tell us to make the horse ready and still trust the LORD for the victory. Where do you tend to err: by failing to prepare, or by trusting your preparation? How does the cross, where God’s plan won through human evil, steady you?

22.title: Train Up a Child in the Way He Should Go
22.text: <sup>1</sup>A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold.<sup>2</sup>The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.<sup>3</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.<sup>4</sup>The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life.<sup>5</sup>Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them.<sup>6</sup>Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.<sup>7</sup>The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender.<sup>8</sup>Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail.<sup>9</sup>Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.<sup>10</sup>Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease.<sup>11</sup>He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend.<sup>12</sup>The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor.<sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!"<sup>14</sup>The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it.<sup>15</sup>Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.<sup>16</sup>Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty.<sup>17</sup>Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge,<sup>18</sup>for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips.<sup>19</sup>That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.<sup>20</sup>Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge,<sup>21</sup>to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you?<sup>22</sup>Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate,<sup>23</sup>for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.<sup>24</sup>Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man,<sup>25</sup>lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.<sup>26</sup>Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts.<sup>27</sup>If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?<sup>28</sup>Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set.<sup>29</sup>Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
22.overview:
Where we are. This chapter closes Solomon’s main collection of two-line sayings (10:1–22:16) and opens a new one, “the words of the wise” (22:17–24:22). Chapter 22 shows what trusting the LORD looks like in name, money, children and neighbours.

The message. A good name and the fear of the LORD are worth more than riches, because rich and poor alike were made by one Maker (v. 2), and the LORD himself pleads the cause of the poor (v. 23). Wisdom shapes children early, avoids the slavery of debt, shares bread, chooses friends carefully and leaves the neighbour’s boundary alone. And all of it has one aim: “That your trust may be in the LORD” (v. 19).

Why it was said. The first hearers lived where the rich could crush the poor at the gate, where a boundary stone could be shifted at night and debt could end in slavery (see the introduction). The new collection also speaks to young men being trained to carry messages and serve before kings (vv. 21, 29), for whom honesty and skill were everything.

How the chapter makes its case. First, a good name, rich and poor: one Maker of all, humility, the training of a child, the borrower’s slavery and the generous eye (vv. 1–9). Then folly and its cure: the scoffer driven out, the sluggard’s absurd lion, the pit of forbidden women, and folly bound up in a child’s heart (vv. 10–16). Last, the words of the wise begin, written so that the reader may trust the LORD, with their first sayings: do not rob the poor, avoid angry friends and rash pledges, leave the ancient landmark, and do skilful work (vv. 17–29).

Where it leads. To Christ, first by the character of God he reveals. The LORD who pleads the cause of the poor (v. 23) came near in the Son who “became poor” for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and who is now our advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). The chapter also exposes our need: folly is “bound up in the heart of a child” (v. 15), and discipline can restrain it but cannot give a new heart, which only the Spirit of Christ gives. And the purpose of the whole collection, trust in the LORD (v. 19), finds its resting place in him.

For us. Choose your name over your profit, and see every person, rich or poor, as made by the same Maker. Train children patiently and leave the outcome to God, who alone gives new birth. Stay out of needless debt, keep your hand open, and do your daily work skilfully, as for the King who always notices.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Good Name, Rich and Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Character outweighs wealth, because “the LORD is the Maker of them all” (v. 2). A good name is worth choosing over riches, and rich and poor share one Maker (vv. 1–2). The prudent take shelter when they see danger, humility and the fear of the LORD bring true reward, and those who guard their souls keep far from the crooked road (vv. 3–5). A child trained early carries it into old age (v. 6). Then money and power: the borrower serves the lender, injustice reaps calamity, and the generous eye that shares bread is blessed (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Character, reputation and the shaping of a child are worth more than money, and every rich and poor person was made by the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good reputation is worth more than wealth, and rich and poor stand equal before the God who made them both.

A good name. The verb matters: to be chosen. Life presents the choice again and again. Sign the misleading contract and make money, or refuse and keep your name. Cut the corner no one will notice, or do the job right. A good name is built slowly by thousands of such choices, and it can be destroyed by one.

What a good name is. A name means a reputation for integrity, the trust people place in your word. When the early church needed men to handle money, they looked for “seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom” (Acts 6:3). “A good name is better than precious ointment” (Ecclesiastes 7:1). Money can be lost and regained; a name, once lost, is very hard to recover, though the Lord who restored Peter still restores those who return to him.

The rich and the poor. Rich and poor live in the same town and sit, or should sit, in the same church. Beneath all the differences of income is the deepest equality: the LORD is the Maker of them all. Job said of his servant, “Did not he who made me in the womb make him?” (Job 31:15).

One Maker of all. That truth humbles the rich, who owe their existence to the same Maker as the beggar, and it lifts the poor, who bear the same image as the millionaire. In God’s presence there is no first class.

verseByVerse.quote: The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prudent heed warning signs and keep away from the crooked road, and humility with the fear of the LORD brings God’s blessing.

The prudent sees danger. The prudent see storm clouds and take shelter; the simple keep walking and get soaked. Prudence is paying attention to warning signs: the debt rising, the relationship getting too close, the symptom that keeps coming back. The same proverb appears again at 27:12.

The reward for humility. Humility and the fear of the LORD go together, and they lead to riches, honour and life.

What humility is. We tend to hear humility as low self-esteem or a modest manner. Proverbs ties it to the fear of the LORD, and that is the clue. Humility is what happens to someone who has really seen God: he stops acting as the centre of things, because he has met the one who is. The proud must keep defending their place; the humble have been put in theirs and found it safe, for “to the humble he gives favor” (3:34).

Humility shown to us. The Son of God, “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), “laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist” (John 13:4), and went lower still, to the cross, for proud people. This week humility may look like asking for help you would rather not need, or letting someone else have the credit without mentioning your part. See also Humility in the Theological Dictionary.

Thorns and snares. The crooked path is full of hazards that snag and trap. The person who cares about his soul keeps far not only from the trap but from the road it lies on.

Does humility guarantee riches? No. This is the usual fruit of wise living under God’s favour, not a formula; Proverbs itself says, “Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it” (15:16).

Uncertain wording. Verse 4 is compressed, and the ESV notes that it may be read, “The reward for humility is the fear of the LORD”: humility is rewarded with deeper reverence for God, and with it everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Training that shapes a child early usually lasts for life, but this is a proverb, not a guarantee that parents control the outcome.

A painful verse. Few verses in Proverbs are quoted more, or hurt more, because many faithful parents have watched a child walk away from the faith they taught. So it must be read carefully.

Train up a child in the way he should go. First, what it says. Train up pictures shaping a young life from the start, when it is most easily shaped, and early training goes deep: habits, convictions, instincts, a love of Scripture and prayer planted in childhood very often last a lifetime. Timothy had known “from childhood” “the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation” (2 Timothy 3:15).

What this looks like. Training is mostly ordinary. Moses pictured it: “You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Keep a small daily habit. A Bible story and a short prayer, kept up for years, does more than an occasional grand effort. Welcome the questions. When a child asks in the car why God let the dog die, answer honestly, or say, “Let’s find out together.” Say sorry to your children. When you have shouted unfairly, confess it and ask their forgiveness; they learn the gospel by watching a parent who needs it. Bring them among God’s people. Let them see other adults who love Christ, and sit with you under his word. None of this saves a child, and you are not his saviour. But you are bringing him to the one who said, “Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:14).

A proverb, not a guarantee. Second, it is a proverb: it describes how God’s world generally runs, not what happens in every case. The book itself says a wise father can have a foolish son (17:21). Children are not machines; each makes his own choices before God (9:12). The verse is not a promise that parents can control the outcome, and not a verdict that the parents of a wandering child must have failed.

Even when he is old. Third, a word to the parent whose child has left. The seed planted is not lost. Many who wander come back, often much later, to what they were taught. Keep praying. The God who is a Father has prodigal children too, and waits at the end of the road for them.

Only God gives new birth. Parents plant and water, but only God gives new birth (John 3:8; 1 Corinthians 3:6), so a child’s wandering is not proof that you failed, and a child’s faith is not your achievement. Where a parent did fail, as every parent does in some way, there is forgiveness in Christ for that too, and freedom to keep loving a wayward child without carrying his choices as your own.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew reads literally "according to his way", which most take as the way he ought to go; some also hear in it training suited to each child's age and nature.

verseByVerse.quote: The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Debt takes away freedom, injustice reaps its own ruin, and the generous person who shares with the poor is blessed.

The borrower is the slave. A blunt statement of how debt works. The one who owes is not free: his decisions, his time and his future belong partly to the one he owes. Many people live as slaves to consumer debt without calling it that. The proverb does.

Borrow rarely. Debt is not always sin; a mortgage can be wise. But the verse is a reason to borrow rarely and carefully, and to get free when you can. “Owe no one anything, except to love each other” (Romans 13:8).

Whoever sows injustice. What you plant, you harvest. Plant injustice, and calamity grows: “they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hosea 8:7). And the rod of his fury, the power the unjust man used to beat others down, breaks in his hand.

A bountiful eye. Bountiful is literally “good”: a good eye (ESV note). A generous person looks at others with kindness, sees their need, and shares his bread. Generosity begins with how we see people.

Uncertain wording. The second line of verse 8 is terse. Most take it, as here, to mean that the oppressor’s power to strike will fail; some take the rod as the punishment that falls on him. Either way, injustice does not last.
verseByVerse.note: After v. 8 the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver, which Paul echoes (2 Cor 9:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Folly Bound Up in a Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Folly must be driven out, whether from a group, a heart or a child. Remove the scoffer and quarrels cease; a pure heart and gracious speech win a king’s friendship; the LORD watches over knowledge and overturns the traitor’s words (vv. 10–12). The sluggard invents a lion in the street to avoid work, and the flattering mouth of the forbidden woman is a pit (vv. 13–14). “Folly is bound up in the heart of a child”, and loving discipline drives it out, while the man who gets rich by oppressing the poor or flattering the rich ends in poverty (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: No child is born wise, and no excuse is too absurd for a lazy man.

verseByVerse.quote: Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease. He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend. The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remove a persistent scoffer and strife goes with him, a pure heart and gracious speech win trust, and God guards the truth against the treacherous.

Drive out a scoffer. Sometimes one person is the source of all the conflict in a group, and a church or team that tolerates a persistent scoffer will never have peace. There is a time when love requires removing someone who will not stop sowing strife.

Purity of heart. A pure heart and gracious speech, the inner and the outer, win the friendship of those in high places. People in power are surrounded by flatterers and schemers, and they value someone pure and gracious. And the King of kings says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

The eyes of the LORD. God guards true knowledge, keeping it from being lost, and he overturns the words of the treacherous. Lies may seem to win for a while, but God is watching over the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!" The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lazy invent absurd excuses to avoid work, and the flattery of the adulteress is a pit that swallows those already under God’s displeasure.

“There is a lion outside!” Why will the sluggard not go to work? There might be a lion in the middle of town! It is absurd, and that is the point. The lazy man’s excuses are often ridiculous, but he states them with complete seriousness. A similar line appears at 26:13.

We all have lions. “The weather is bad.” “I’m not in the right frame of mind.” “It won’t work anyway.” “Someone else would do it better.” What lion have you been using to avoid something you know you should do? Name it to the Lord, whose Spirit gives the strength to walk past it.

The mouth of forbidden women. The Hebrew is “strange” women (ESV note), as in chapters 2, 5 and 7. Their mouth, their flattery, is a deep pit, easy to fall into and almost impossible to climb out of. And the second line is sobering: falling into it can itself be a mark of God’s judgment. Sometimes God’s anger against persistent sin takes the form of giving a person over to it (Romans 1:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him. Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children are born with folly tied into their hearts and need loving discipline, and those who get rich by injustice end poor.

Folly is bound up. Children are not born innocent and wise, needing only to be left alone to flourish. Folly is bound up in their hearts, tied in tight, as anyone who has watched a two-year-old knows. David confessed, “Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity” (Psalm 51:5). Selfishness and rebellion do not need to be taught.

Are children born good? Much modern parenting assumes so, and blames whatever goes wrong on what was done to the child. Jean-Jacques Rousseau gave the idea its classic form at the start of Émile: everything is good as it comes from its Maker, and everything degenerates in human hands. But anyone who has watched two toddlers and one toy knows better. Augustine, in his Confessions, describes a baby too young to speak turning pale with jealousy as another infant was fed, and concludes that what is innocent in infants is the weakness of their limbs, not their wills. Proverbs agrees, and rescues parents from two errors: the romantic thinks a child needs only freedom, the moralist only rules. He needs love and correction both, and beneath them what no parent can give: a new heart. So the parent’s task is not to produce a good child but to bring a needy one to the Saviour who said, “Let the little children come to me” (Matthew 19:14).

The rod of discipline drives it far from him. So children need discipline, loving correction that loosens what is tied in their hearts and drives it away, in the careful way described at 13:24. Its aim is to free the child from folly, not to vent the parent’s frustration.

Whoever oppresses the poor. Two ways of getting ahead by injustice: squeezing the poor, and buying favour with the rich. Both end in poverty. God is not mocked.

Where Christians differ. Is the rod literal? Many hold that it commends measured physical discipline of young children; others read it figuratively, and some think physical discipline always unwise.

This commentary’s view. The rod stands for discipline of every kind, and the words speak of a real rod. Scripture requires loving, consistent discipline; whether to use measured physical correction with young children is left to wise parents. Where it is used, it comes with explanation, never in anger or to injure (Ephesians 6:4). Anything that frightens or harms a child is abuse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Words of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new collection, “the words of the wise” (v. 17), begins with its purpose: “That your trust may be in the LORD” (v. 19). The teacher calls for ear and heart, promises that wisdom stored within will be ready on the lips, and has written “thirty sayings” so that the learner can give true answers to those who send him (vv. 17–21). The first saying is for the poor, whose cause the LORD pleads (vv. 22–23). Then come warnings against angry friends and rash pledges, a command to leave the ancient landmark, and praise for the skilful worker who will stand before kings (vv. 24–29).
verseByVerse.theology: The sayings of the wise are given so that the reader's trust will rest in the LORD, and they begin with the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge, for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips. That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new collection begins, calling for an open ear and a ready tongue, and its whole purpose is that the reader should trust the LORD.

Incline your ear. A new section begins here and runs to 24:22: the words of the wise. The sayings become longer, often two or three verses, and return to direct commands, like the father’s speeches of chapters 1 to 9. The opening calls for ear and heart together, hearing and applying.

Ready on your lips. Wisdom is to be stored within and kept ready on your lips: learned so well that it comes out when needed. The Christian who has Scripture ready on his lips in a moment of temptation, grief or counsel knows how pleasant that is.

That your trust. Here is the purpose of all the practical advice that follows: that your trust may be in the LORD. The sayings about money, anger, food and work are not a self-help programme; every wise habit is an act of faith in the God who designed life to work this way. And the teacher says, even to you. This is personal.

Did the Bible copy an Egyptian book? Parts of this section resemble the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope (see the introduction). Wisdom was shared across the ancient world, and the author may have used and reshaped such sayings. Inspiration does not mean the writer used no sources (Luke 1:1–4); the Spirit guided what he wrote, and verse 19 gives the purpose no Egyptian text had: That your trust may be in the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: A new collection, “the words of the wise” (22:17–24:22). Parts of its opening section are similar to an Egyptian wisdom text, the Instruction of Amenemope.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge, to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The teacher has written his sayings down so that the learner will know what is true and can be trusted to report it faithfully.

Thirty sayings. The teacher has put his sayings into writing, a collection designed to be learned and passed on.

A true answer. The purpose is not only personal. The student learns what is right and true so that he can bring back a reliable answer to those who sent him, like a messenger who returns with an accurate report. Wisdom makes a person trustworthy, someone whose word can be relied on.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word behind thirty is uncertain. As written it looks like a word for “formerly”, and it was traditionally read as one the KJV renders “excellent things”. Most modern translations read thirty, a small change of vowels, partly because Amenemope has thirty chapters and roughly thirty sayings can be counted in 22:17–24:22. Either way, these are chosen words to be learned.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not take advantage of the poor because they cannot fight back, for the LORD himself takes up their case.
