Do not rob the poor. The first of the thirty sayings is about the poor, and that is surely deliberate. Why would anyone rob the poor? Because he is poor: he cannot fight back. He has no lawyer, no influence, no voice. The gate was where the courts sat, so crushing the afflicted at the gate means using the legal system against people who cannot defend themselves.

The LORD will plead. But the poor man does have a lawyer: the LORD will plead their cause. The law said of widows and orphans, “If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:23). God is “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5). The man who robs the poor has made the most dangerous enemy in the universe. The saying returns at 23:10–11: “their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you.”

Our advocate. The God who pleads for the helpless has come near in Christ, who “became poor” for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9) and is our “advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1). Those who have been defended by him should be the last to crush anyone who cannot defend himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not make a close friend of a hot-tempered man, because anger is catching.

Make no friendship. Choose friends carefully, and do not choose a hot-tempered one. Angry people are not beyond love, but close friendship with them is dangerous.

Lest you learn his ways. Anger is contagious. Spend enough time with an angry man and you will learn his ways: reacting as he reacts, seeing slights where he sees them, raising your voice as he does. “Bad company ruins good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33). And you become entangled in his quarrels and their consequences. Who are you learning your ways from?

verseByVerse.quote: Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts. If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not guarantee other people’s debts, or you may lose even your bed.

Who give pledges. The warning against guaranteeing debts returns, now as one of the thirty sayings (compare 6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18).

Why should your bed be taken? When the borrower cannot pay, the creditor comes to you, and if you have nothing, he takes your bed. You end up sleeping on the floor for someone else’s debt. Count the cost before you sign.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set. Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Respect boundaries rightly set long ago, and do your work with skill, because skilful work is noticed.

The ancient landmark. Boundary stones marked each family’s land, set when the land was first divided. Moving one a few feet was an easy, secret way to steal a neighbour’s inheritance, often from someone too weak to object. The law forbade it: “You shall not move your neighbor’s landmark, which the men of old have set” (Deuteronomy 19:14). The saying is repeated and applied to the fatherless at 23:10.

The principle reaches further. Respect what has been rightly established by those before you. Not every old boundary is sacred, but some are, and moving them for personal gain is theft.

A man skillful in his work. A man who is truly skillful at what he does, whether craftsman, scribe, builder or nurse, will be noticed and promoted. Daniel and his friends were found “ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters”, and “they stood before the king” (Daniel 1:19–20).

Skilful work. Christian work should be skilful work, done as for the Lord. Whether or not a king ever notices, the King of kings always does.

22.theology:
All human beings share one Maker, so the poor have the same dignity as the rich (v. 2; Job 31:15). Reputation and character outweigh wealth (v. 1). Children are born with folly bound in their hearts and need loving discipline (v. 15; Ps 51:5). Early training shapes a life, though proverbs describe patterns rather than guarantees (v. 6; 17:21).

The purpose of practical wisdom is trust in the LORD (v. 19). God is the advocate of the poor against their oppressors (vv. 22-23; Exod 22:22-24; Ps 68:5). Debt enslaves (v. 7), character is shaped by companions (vv. 24-25), and excellent work honours God (v. 29).

The LORD who pleads the poor man's cause (v. 23) is seen most fully in Christ, who preached good news to the poor (Luke 4:18) and is his people's advocate (1 John 2:1). The one Maker of rich and poor (v. 2) became poor himself, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9).
22.examples:
Think of a reputation built by thousands of small choices, or of the millionaire and the beggar who have one Maker. Think of a credit card that has quietly become a master, or of the sluggard's lion in the street, or of a two-year-old's heart.

Above all, remember that the poor man has the LORD as his lawyer (v. 23), and that the parent of a child who has walked away is praying to a Father who waits for his own prodigals.

keyVerse.quote: That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.
keyVerse.note: The verse states the purpose of all the practical wisdom around it: the sayings about money, children, friends and work are meant to lead us to trust God. It turns Proverbs from a self-help manual into a call to faith, addressed personally, “even to you”.

22.reflection:
“A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches” (v. 1). Where are you most often tempted to trade a little of your name for a little gain? What helps you choose well?

Verse 6 is a proverb, not a guarantee. How should that shape the way parents train their children, and the way the church treats parents whose children have wandered?

“The borrower is the slave of the lender” (v. 7). How has debt, or freedom from it, affected you or people you know? What would wise steps look like for your household?

Verse 23 says the LORD pleads the cause of the poor. How does knowing Christ as our advocate change the way we treat people who cannot defend themselves?

23.title: My Son, Give Me Your Heart
23.text: <sup>1</sup>When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you,<sup>2</sup>and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite.<sup>3</sup>Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food.<sup>4</sup>Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist.<sup>5</sup>When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven.<sup>6</sup>Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies,<sup>7</sup>for he is like one who is inwardly calculating. "Eat and drink!" he says to you, but his heart is not with you.<sup>8</sup>You will vomit up the morsels that you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words.<sup>9</sup>Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words.<sup>10</sup>Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless,<sup>11</sup>for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you.<sup>12</sup>Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge.<sup>13</sup>Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die.<sup>14</sup>If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol.<sup>15</sup>My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad.<sup>16</sup>My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right.<sup>17</sup>Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day.<sup>18</sup>Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.<sup>19</sup>Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way.<sup>20</sup>Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat,<sup>21</sup>for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags.<sup>22</sup>Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.<sup>23</sup>Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding.<sup>24</sup>The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him.<sup>25</sup>Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice.<sup>26</sup>My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways.<sup>27</sup>For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well.<sup>28</sup>She lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind.<sup>29</sup>Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes?<sup>30</sup>Those who tarry long over wine; those who go to try mixed wine.<sup>31</sup>Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly.<sup>32</sup>In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.<sup>33</sup>Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things.<sup>34</sup>You will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast.<sup>35</sup>"They struck me," you will say, "but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink."
23.overview:
Where we are. We are in “the words of the wise” (22:17–24:22), the collection that began by stating its aim: “That your trust may be in the LORD” (22:19). Chapter 22 ended with the skilful man who “will stand before kings”; chapter 23 follows him to the king’s table.

The message. Whatever wins the heart rules the life, so guard your heart against every appetite that wants it: rich food at a powerful man’s table, the money that sprouts wings, envy of sinners, the wine that sparkles, the woman who lies in wait. At the centre stands the father’s plea, “My son, give me your heart” (v. 26). Those who give it, and keep on in the fear of the LORD, have a future that will not be cut off (v. 18), and the helpless have a Redeemer who is strong (v. 11).

Why it was said. These sayings were shaped for young men entering public life, where banquets, patrons, money and drink came with strings attached, and the fatherless could easily lose their fields (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First, appetite, wealth and the fatherless: restraint at a ruler’s table, riches that fly away, the stingy host, and the orphan’s field guarded by a strong Redeemer (vv. 1–12). Then a glad father and a future hope: loving discipline, a father’s joy, the cure for envy, honour for aged parents, and truth never sold (vv. 13–25). Last, the heart and the cup: “give me your heart”, the prostitute’s pit, and Scripture’s fullest portrait of drunkenness (vv. 26–35).

Where it leads. To Christ, first by pattern. The Redeemer of verse 11 is the go’el, the near kinsman who bought back family land and defended his own; God takes that role for the fatherless, and Christ fills it by sharing our flesh and blood and buying back those who could not free themselves (Hebrews 2:14–17; Galatians 4:4–5). The chapter also exposes our need: no son has ever given his father an undivided heart (v. 26) except Christ, who gave it in our place. And the future that will not be cut off (v. 18) is secured by his resurrection, while the enslaved drinker of verse 35 needs exactly what he offers: “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

For us. Notice what is pulling at your heart, whether money, food, drink, envy or a forbidden person, and give your heart to God, who first gave his heart to you in his Son. Decide when enough is enough before the next pay rise. Honour your parents in their old age. And if something has mastered you, tell someone today: a slave can be set free.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Appetite, Wealth and the Fatherless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Appetite, greed and false hospitality are traps, but the helpless have a strong Redeemer. At a powerful man’s table, watch carefully and put a knife to your throat if you are greedy, because rich food can be bait (vv. 1–3). Do not wear yourself out for wealth: it sprouts wings and flies off (vv. 4–5). Do not eat with a stingy host whose words say “Eat and drink!” while his heart counts the cost (vv. 6–8). Do not waste wisdom on a fool, and do not move the landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, “for their Redeemer is strong” (vv. 9–11). A fresh call to hear and apply leads into what follows (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Appetite, greed and false hospitality are traps, and the fatherless have a Redeemer strong enough to defend them.

verseByVerse.quote: When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite. Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At a powerful person’s table, keep a firm grip on your appetite, because lavish hospitality is often bait.

Observe carefully. A young man is invited to dine with someone powerful: a king, an official, a wealthy patron; today, the chief executive’s dinner or the invitation that could open doors. Be alert.

A knife to your throat. A startling image: if you cannot resist good food and drink, treat it as seriously as a knife at your throat. Self-control at a powerful man’s table is not a matter of manners. A man who overindulges, drinks too much, talks too freely or looks too eager has put himself in the host’s power. And self-control is the Spirit’s fruit (Galatians 5:22–23), which he supplies to those who ask.

Deceptive food. Why deceptive? Because rich hospitality often has a purpose: to gain influence, extract information or create an obligation. Daniel, at the table of Babylon’s king, “resolved that he would not defile himself with the king’s food” (Daniel 1:8). There are tables where the food is a hook.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 1 can mean what is before you or “who” is before you (ESV note). Both fit: watch the food, and watch the man who serves it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist. When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not wear yourself out chasing wealth, because riches fly away, and only God can hold you secure.

Do not toil to acquire wealth. This is not a command against hard work; Proverbs praises diligence constantly. It is a command against making wealth the goal you wear yourself out for. There is a point where a wise person says: enough.

Be discerning enough to desist. Many never find that point: always one more promotion, a bigger house, a larger pension. They sacrifice health, marriage and children on the altar of acquiring more than they will ever need.

It sprouts wings. You look at your money, and in the moment you look, it grows wings and flies off like an eagle. A market crash, a lawsuit, an illness, inflation, a thief: wealth is not a possession you hold but a bird perched near you for now.

The rich fool. Jesus told of the rich fool: “Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20). Paul tells the rich not to set their hopes “on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy”, and to be “rich in good works”, “so that they may take hold of that which is truly life” (1 Timothy 6:17–19).

How do I know when to stop? Decide what is enough before the next pay rise. Name a level of income or a size of house that would truly be enough, and settle in advance where anything beyond it will go: to giving, to others, to freeing up time. Count the cost of the promotion. Before you say yes, ask who pays for it: your evenings, your wife or husband, the children’s Saturdays, your Sunday. Keep one day the job does not get. A weekly rest is a confession that God, not your effort, holds you up. Ask the people at home. They usually know before you do when work has become the thing you serve. Underneath is the question of what makes you secure. We can stop because the one thing we most need is already ours and cannot fly away: “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5). In Christ you are not working your way to safety. You are already held.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies, for he is like one who is inwardly calculating. "Eat and drink!" he says to you, but his heart is not with you. You will vomit up the morsels that you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be taken in by a grudging host whose words welcome you while his heart counts the cost.

A man who is stingy. Stingy is literally “whose eye is evil” (ESV note), the opposite of the “good eye” of the generous man (22:9). He offers you food, but begrudges every mouthful.

His heart is not with you. His words say “Help yourself!” while inside he counts the cost. What a man truly is, is what goes on inside him, not what he says. Everyone has sat at a table like that and felt the chill beneath the welcome.

You will vomit up. When you realise what was really going on, the meal turns your stomach, and all your polite compliments were wasted.

A misused verse. The old rendering “as he thinketh in his heart, so is he” (v. 7) is often taken to mean that our thoughts create our reality. In context it describes a stingy host who counts the cost of every bite while urging you to eat. It is a warning about hypocrisy, not a principle of positive thinking.

Uncertain wording. The first line of verse 7 is one of the hardest in Proverbs, built on a rare word. The ESV takes it as inwardly calculating and notes another reading, “as he calculates in his soul, so is he”; some translate “like a hair in the throat”, something that makes you gag, which would fit verse 8. Either way, his welcome is false.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words. Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you. Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not waste wisdom on someone who will scorn it, and never take advantage of orphans, for God himself is their strong Redeemer.

In the hearing of a fool. Some people cannot be helped by good advice, because they will only despise it. Wisdom knows when speaking is useful and when it is only casting pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6).

The fields of the fatherless. The warning of 22:28 returns, applied to orphans, whose fields no father will defend. But they do have someone: their Redeemer.

Their Redeemer is strong. The word is go’el, the kinsman-redeemer, the close relative whose duty was to buy back family land and defend his family, as Boaz did in the book of Ruth: “If you will redeem it, redeem it” (Ruth 4:4). Here God himself is the Redeemer of those who have no one, and he is strong. Job, in his darkest hour, said, “For I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25). Whoever takes advantage of an orphan has made the Redeemer his opponent.

Our near kinsman. The kinsman-redeemer pattern reaches its height in Christ, who shared our flesh and blood to become our near kinsman (Hebrews 2:14–17) and bought back those who could not free themselves (Galatians 4:4–5).

Apply your heart. A fresh call to attention, heart and ear together, introduces the next sayings: hearing that goes all the way in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — A Glad Father and a Future Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wise son brings joy, and the one who fears the LORD has a future. Loving discipline will not kill a child; it may save him from death (vv. 13–14). A father’s inmost being rejoices when his son speaks what is right (vv. 15–16). The cure for envy of sinners is to keep on in the fear of the LORD, because “Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off” (vv. 17–18). So steer the heart away from drunkards and gluttons, listen to father and mother into their old age, buy truth and never sell it, and give your parents the joy of a righteous child (vv. 19–25).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD looks to a future the envied sinner does not have, and a wise child is a parent's joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die. If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Loving discipline will not destroy a child; it may save him from a life that runs towards death.

Do not withhold discipline. Parents sometimes hold back discipline because they fear it will harm the child. The proverb reassures them: loving correction will not destroy him. What will harm him is growing up without it. The same balance as 13:24 and 22:15 must be kept: discipline is always for the child’s good.

Save his soul from Sheol. What is at stake is not only the child’s behaviour but his soul. A child who never learns that wrong has consequences, never learns to submit to authority, never hears “no”, is being prepared for a life that runs towards destruction.

How does discipline save his soul? Sheol here is death, a life ruined and cut short by folly. Discipline cannot give a child a new heart; only God does that. But it is a means God uses to restrain folly and point a child towards life.

Where Christians differ. Does this mean physical punishment today? Many Christians read the rod as a figure for discipline of every kind and hold that physical correction now does more harm than good. Others, including most of the Reformed tradition, take the rod at its word: measured physical correction, alongside instruction, is one God-given means for young children.

This commentary’s view. The proverbs do speak of a real rod, but what Scripture requires of every parent is loving, consistent discipline; whether to use measured physical correction is left to wise parents. Where it is used, it is never given in anger, never to injure or humiliate, always with explanation and restored affection, and parents must also keep the law of the land they live in. Any discipline that frightens or harms a child is abuse, not the rod of Proverbs.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad. My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A father’s deepest joy is a son whose heart is wise and whose lips speak what is right.

My heart too will be glad. The father’s heart is bound to his son’s: he feels the son’s wisdom inside.

My inmost being. Literally “My kidneys” (ESV note), the Hebrew way of speaking of the deepest feelings. When the son speaks rightly, his father’s joy goes all the way down; there are few joys like hearing your child say something wise and true. And the heavenly Father delights in his children in the same way: “he will rejoice over you with gladness” (Zephaniah 3:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not envy sinners; keep on fearing the LORD, because his people have a future that will not be cut off.

Let not your heart envy. Envy of sinners is a real temptation. They seem freer, richer, happier; they seem to get away with things. The psalmist almost slipped because of it. The cure is not to study the sinner’s life more closely but to keep going in the fear of the LORD all the day, steadily, every hour.

Surely there is a future. The envied sinner’s success does not last; the person who fears God has a future. The psalmist saw it when “I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17). And he could say, “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).

A hard present with a certain future. For the Christian, the future is guaranteed by the resurrection of Christ. Whatever the sinner has now, the believer’s hope will not be cut off. Which is better: a good present with no future, or a hard present with a certain one?

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way. Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat, for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Steer your heart deliberately, and keep out of the company of heavy drinkers and gluttons, whose way ends in rags.

Direct your heart. The heart does not naturally steer towards wisdom; it must be deliberately turned onto the right way.

Be not among drunkards. Excess in food and drink is not merely unhealthy; it leads to poverty and a lethargy that ends in rags. And the warning is about company: do not be among them. The crowd you eat and drink with shapes your habits. Jesus warned, “watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life” (Luke 21:34).

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old. Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep listening to your parents and honouring them in old age, and get the truth at any cost and never trade it away.

Listen to your father. A word for grown children. Your father gave you life; keep listening to him. And your mother, when she is old, when she repeats herself, moves slowly, needs help, forgets things: do not despise her. The temptation to treat aged parents with impatience or contempt is real. The fifth commandment has no age limit.

Buy truth. Truth is something to buy, to pay for, whatever it costs: time, effort, pride, popularity. And once you have it, do not sell it. There will be offers: a little of the truth traded for a promotion, for acceptance, for peace in the family, for an easier life.

What would you not sell the truth for? And what have you, perhaps, already sold a little of? If so, the God of truth forgives those who confess, and his Spirit makes them faithful again.

verseByVerse.quote: The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him. Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A child’s righteousness is his parents’ purest joy, so give them that joy.

The father of the righteous. A parent’s purest joy is not in a child’s success but in his character.

Let your father and mother be glad. Give your parents that gladness. It is a beautiful motive for a young person: not only obeying God for himself, but bringing joy to the people who gave him life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–35 — The Heart and the Cup
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The father asks for the heart, because the rival loves that want it lead to ruin. “My son, give me your heart” is the centre of the chapter (v. 26). The prostitute and the adulteress are a deep pit and a narrow well, a robber lying in wait who multiplies betrayal (vv. 27–28). Then comes the fullest portrait of drunkenness in Scripture: six questions about woe and wounds, answered by those who linger over wine; the sparkle that bites like a serpent; the distorted mind, the spinning world, and the slave’s first thought on waking: “I must have another drink” (vv. 29–35).
verseByVerse.theology: The father asks for the heart, because the heart that is given to God is kept from the prostitute’s pit and the drunkard’s cup.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways. For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well. She lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father asks for his son’s whole heart, because a heart not given to him will be captured by the woman who lies in wait.

Give me your heart. Here is the centre of the chapter, and in a sense of the whole book. The father does not ask first for obedience, effort or good behaviour. He asks for the heart, and everything else will follow: a son who has given his heart to his father will want to watch his ways and walk in them.

The gospel invitation. Read it as God’s voice, and it is the invitation of the gospel. God does not want our rule-keeping without our hearts; he wants us. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). No one gives it wholly: Christ alone gave the Father an undivided heart, and he gave it in our place.

How do I give him my heart? The heart in Proverbs is the control room: what you love, think about and steer by. Notice where it already goes. Your daydreams, your bank statement and where your eyes go when you are bored show what has your heart now. Give him the first of your attention. Before the phone in the morning, a psalm and a few words of prayer say who comes first. Bring rival loves to him at once. When you feel the pull of the colleague who flirts, the win you must have, or the grudge you enjoy, tell him straight away, before it settles. Let your eyes follow his ways. The verse joins heart and eyes: a heart given to God shows in what you choose to watch and to want. And this is a response, not a purchase. He gave his heart first, in his Son: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). The heart is won back by being loved, not by being ordered.

A deep pit. The reason the father asks for the heart at once now appears: a heart not given to him will be given to someone else. The prostitute is a deep pit; the adulteress, literally “a foreign woman” (ESV note), is a narrow well, easy to fall into and almost impossible to climb out of.

She lies in wait. She is a hunter, lying in wait. And she increases the traitors: every man who falls to her has betrayed a wife, a family, a vow, and his God. Sexual sin multiplies betrayal.

Uncertain wording. In verse 26 the Hebrew is written one way and traditionally read another: observe my ways, or “delight in” them (ESV note). The two belong together, for the eyes watch what the heart delights in.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who tarry long over wine; those who go to try mixed wine. Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly. In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lingering over drink leads to woe, quarrels and wounds, and wine that looks beautiful bites like a snake in the end.

Who has woe? The Bible’s fullest portrait of drunkenness opens with six questions, like a riddle. Anyone who has lived with an alcoholic, or been one, recognises every line.

Those who tarry long. The answer: those who tarry long, who stay and keep drinking. Not the person who has a glass with dinner, but the one who lingers, and the one who goes looking for new kinds of drink to try. Isaiah pronounced woe on those “who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them” (Isaiah 5:11).

Do not look at wine. The warning starts with the eyes, and the attraction is described honestly. The father does not pretend it is unappealing. He says that for some people the only safe thing is not to look.

In the end. The same words as 5:4, where the forbidden woman, sweet at first, turns bitter in the end. The sparkle hides fangs. What goes down smoothly bites like a snake: liver disease, lost jobs, broken families, violence, death on the roads.

Does the Bible forbid all alcohol? No. Wine is among God’s gifts (Psalm 104:15), and Jesus made it at a wedding (John 2:1–11). What Scripture condemns is drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18) and lingering over drink. For some, especially those who have struggled with it, not drinking at all is the wise and free choice, and no one should press a drink on them (Romans 14:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things. You will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast. "They struck me," you will say, "but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drink distorts the mind and finally enslaves, so that the drinker reaches first for what is destroying him, yet even this slavery can be broken.

Strange things. Drunkenness distorts perception and loosens the tongue. Many a person has said something drunk that destroyed a relationship he spent years building.

On the top of a mast. The room is spinning, like a ship’s mast swaying in a storm. He cannot find anything steady.

“I must have another drink.” The saddest line. He wakes with bruises he cannot remember, and his first thought is not “I must stop” but I must have another drink. That is addiction, described thousands of years ago with perfect accuracy: the substance that has hurt him is the thing he reaches for first.

Disease or sin? Our culture calls addiction either a disease, so that blame is cruel, or a choice: he could stop if he wanted to. Each sees something true. The drinker in these verses is plainly in bondage, waking to reach for the thing that is killing him, and plainly responsible, the man who tarried long over the wine. Scripture holds both together in one word: slavery. A slave really is bound, and he also serves his master with his own hands. Christian counsellors have long pointed out that beneath the bottle there is usually a kind of worship: something trusted to give the relief, courage or peace that only God can give. That is why neither scolding nor a diagnosis on its own sets anyone free, good as wise medical help is. What frees a slave is a stronger master who buys him back and then lives with him. “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

I will not be dominated by anything. Paul said, “I will not be dominated by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12). But the gospel meets the addict where he is: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Mark 2:17). The cry of the enslaved is Paul’s: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25).

Not a hopeless verdict. If this describes you or someone you love, it is not a hopeless verdict but a diagnosis, and diagnosis is where help begins. Tell someone today: a pastor or biblical counsellor, and a doctor too, because stopping heavy drinking suddenly can be medically dangerous, and using medical help is no failure of faith. Bring it all to Christ, who sets captives free.

Uncertain wording. The word translated mast occurs only here, and the ESV notes “of the rigging”. Either way, he lies high on something that pitches and rolls.

23.theology:
Wealth is uncertain and must not become the goal of life (vv. 4-5; 1 Tim 6:17-19). God is the strong Redeemer of the fatherless (vv. 10-11; Job 19:25). The fear of the LORD has a future hope that cannot be cut off (vv. 17-18; Ps 73:17, 26).

God asks first for the heart (v. 26). Drunkenness enslaves and distorts (vv. 29-35; Eph 5:18; 1 Cor 6:12), yet Christ came as a physician for the sick and delivers those enslaved (Mark 2:17; Rom 7:24-25).
23.examples:
The chapter moves from the chief executive's dinner and the host who says "Eat and drink!" while counting the cost, to money growing wings, to God the Redeemer standing guard over the orphan's field.

At home it asks for patience with a mother who repeats herself in old age, and for truth bought and never sold. And at its centre is the call to give God the heart, set against the drunkard in his spinning room whose first waking thought is another drink.

keyVerse.quote: My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways.
keyVerse.note: Every warning in the chapter, about food, money, envy, sex and drink, is about what will capture the heart, and here the father asks for the heart itself. It is the centre of the chapter and close to the centre of the whole book, and read as God’s voice it is the invitation of the gospel.

23.reflection:
“Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist” (v. 4). How do you know when enough is enough? What practical steps could help you stop before work and money take more than they should?

“Let not your heart envy sinners” (v. 17). Whom are you most tempted to envy, and how does the promise that “surely there is a future” (v. 18) answer that envy?

The father says, “My son, give me your heart” (v. 26). What shows where your heart is going now, and what would it look like to give it to God this week, knowing that he gave his heart first?

Verses 29–35 describe drunkenness as a kind of slavery. How should a church care for someone who is enslaved, to drink or to anything else, with both honesty and hope?

24.title: The Righteous Falls Seven Times and Rises Again
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them,<sup>2</sup>for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble.<sup>3</sup>By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established;<sup>4</sup>by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches.<sup>5</sup>A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might,<sup>6</sup>for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory.<sup>7</sup>Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth.<sup>8</sup>Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer.<sup>9</sup>The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind.<sup>10</sup>If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small.<sup>11</sup>Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.<sup>12</sup>If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work?<sup>13</sup>My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste.<sup>14</sup>Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off.<sup>15</sup>Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home;<sup>16</sup>for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity.<sup>17</sup>Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles,<sup>18</sup>lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him.<sup>19</sup>Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked,<sup>20</sup>for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out.<sup>21</sup>My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise,<sup>22</sup>for disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both?<sup>23</sup>These also are sayings of the wise. Partiality in judging is not good.<sup>24</sup>Whoever says to the wicked, "You are in the right," will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations,<sup>25</sup>but those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them.<sup>26</sup>Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips.<sup>27</sup>Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house.<sup>28</sup>Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips.<sup>29</sup>Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."<sup>30</sup>I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense,<sup>31</sup>and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.<sup>32</sup>Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.<sup>33</sup>A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,<sup>34</sup>and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
24.overview:
Where we are. This chapter completes “the words of the wise” (22:17–24:22) and adds a short appendix, “These also are sayings of the wise” (24:23–34), before the proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men begin in chapter 25.

The message. Wisdom builds what lasts, and it does not look away. It refuses to envy violent men, builds a house and fills it, stands firm in adversity, and rescues those being led to death, because the God who weighs the heart knows when we only pretend not to know (vv. 11–12). The righteous fall again and again, yet rise (v. 16); they neither gloat over an enemy nor fret over the wicked, they judge fairly, refuse revenge, and keep their vineyard from sliding into ruin a little sleep at a time.

Why it was said. The first hearers, like us, were tempted to envy prosperous wrongdoers, look away from victims, pay back injuries and let ordinary duties slide (see the introduction). These sayings answer each temptation with the God who sees the heart.

How the chapter makes its case. First, built by wisdom: do not envy evil men; wisdom builds a house and wins its battles with counsel; adversity tests strength; and the wise must rescue those stumbling to the slaughter (vv. 1–12). Then seven times he rises: wisdom is sweet and gives a future, the righteous rise after every fall, and they neither gloat nor fret (vv. 13–22). Last, more sayings of the wise: impartial judging, honest answers, first the field and then the house, no revenge, and the sluggard’s ruined vineyard (vv. 23–34).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and the pattern it sets. No one has always rescued those being taken away to death, and none of us can say, “we did not know” (v. 12). But when we were the ones on that road, Christ saw, came and took our place. The righteous man who falls and rises (v. 16) finds his deepest fulfilment in the Righteous One who went down into death and rose on the third day, and in whom every fallen believer rises again, as Peter did. And the refusal to gloat or repay (vv. 17, 29) takes flesh in the one who “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23).

For us. Stop envying people whose hearts devise violence, and ask God for strength before the day of adversity comes. Do not scroll past those being led to death; act for the one within your reach. If you have fallen again, rise, because Christ prays for you. And go out to your own vineyard today: pull one thorn, and set one stone back in the wall.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom builds what lasts, and the God who weighs the heart calls the wise to rescue the perishing. Do not envy evil men or long for their company, for their hearts plan violence (vv. 1–2). Wisdom builds a house and fills its rooms with lovely riches; it multiplies strength and wins battles through counsel, while the fool has nothing to say at the gate (vv. 3–7). Schemers and scoffers earn their names (vv. 8–9). Adversity shows how small our strength is (v. 10). Then the climax: rescue those being taken away to death, because the one who weighs the heart will not accept the excuse, “we did not know this” (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom builds, strengthens and refuses to look away from those being led to death.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them, for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not envy evil men or long for their company, because behind their success lie violence and trouble.

Be not envious of evil men. The warning of 23:17 comes back with an addition: nor desire to be with them. Envy of the wicked does not stay envy. It becomes a longing to belong to their circle, to share their freedom and success: the same pull the gang exerted in chapter 1.

Their hearts devise violence. Look past the success to the heart and lips, and you find violence and trouble. The life that looked enviable from outside is poison from inside.

verseByVerse.quote: By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Homes and every human work are built and filled by wisdom, not first by money or cleverness.

By wisdom a house is built. A house, a family, a business, a church: all built by wisdom and made firm by understanding. Not by money first, or cleverness, or luck.

The rooms are filled. The riches here are precious and pleasant: not only valuable but lovely to live with. Think of a home where wisdom lives: laughter, peace, stored-up memories, faith, good conversation, hospitality. Those are the treasures that fill rooms built by wisdom. A large house built by folly can be empty in every room.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might, for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory. Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is greater strength than force, it wins through good counsel, and it is beyond the fool.

Full of strength. The wise man may not be physically powerful, but he knows what to do, how and when. Knowledge multiplies whatever might he has.

Wise guidance. Battles are won by good planning and good advice (compare 11:14; 20:18). A general who listens to his advisers beats one who trusts only himself. The same is true of every struggle a person faces: an illness, a financial crisis, a troubled child. Get counsel.

Wisdom is too high for a fool. In the city gate, where the elders gathered to decide matters, the fool has nothing to contribute. Wisdom is out of his reach, like fruit on a high branch.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer. The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin begins in the planning, and schemers and scoffers earn the name and disgust they deserve.

A schemer. The man who keeps planning evil soon gets a name for it: people call him a schemer.

The devising of folly. Even planning folly is sin; the ESV notes that devising may be “scheming”. Sin does not begin when the act is done; it begins in the plotting. And the scoffer, the mocker of everything good, is not merely disliked; he is an abomination to mankind.

verseByVerse.quote: If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adversity shows how small our strength is, and sends us to God’s.

If you faint in the day of adversity. Adversity reveals strength. Anyone can look strong when life is easy; if you collapse the moment trouble comes, your strength was small all along. In Hebrew the saying is a play on words: the day of tsarah (distress) shows that your strength is tsar (narrow, small).

Your strength is small. That can sound harsh, but it is an honest mirror, and it drives a believer to the right source. Human strength is small; God’s is not. “He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength”, and “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:29, 31). Paul discovered that the Lord’s “power is made perfect in weakness”, so that he could say, “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

A larger strength. So the proverb is not a command to grit your teeth and be tough. It is an invitation to find strength larger than your own before the day of adversity comes. “And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise must rescue those being led towards death, because God, who weighs the heart, sees through the excuse that we did not know.

Rescue those. There are people being led towards death, through injustice, violence, addiction, despair or their own folly, and the wise are commanded to act: rescue, hold back. Not to observe, not to feel sorry, but to intervene.

Who is being taken away today. The applications are wide: the unborn, the trafficked, the persecuted, the neighbour sinking into suicidal despair, the friend drinking himself to death, and above all the person without Christ walking towards eternal death. Which of them is within your reach? If someone may be about to take his own life, do not wait: stay with him and get help the same day.

We did not know this. The proverb refuses the excuse. God weighs the heart. He knows whether we truly did not know, or chose not to know, or knew and looked away. The priest and the Levite in Jesus’ parable saw the wounded man and “passed by on the other side” (Luke 10:31). “So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17). Deliberate ignorance is not innocence in God’s eyes.

The comfort of not knowing. After the Second World War many ordinary Germans said they had not known what was being done to their Jewish neighbours. Some truly did not; many, historians have shown, knew enough to know they should not ask. We face a stranger form of the temptation: no generation has known more about others’ suffering, or had more ways of scrolling past it. Being informed and feeling sad is not the same as caring.

Our rescuer. But before this verse judges us, it describes our rescuer. When we were the ones being taken away to death, Christ did not plead that he had not known. He saw, he came, and he took our place on that road. God forgives those who confess their looking away, and Christ sends those he has rescued, in his Spirit’s strength, to the next person stumbling to the slaughter.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom gives a future that the wicked cannot take away, so the righteous neither gloat nor fret. Wisdom is as sweet to the soul as honey, and it brings a hope that will not be cut off (vv. 13–14). Plots against the righteous fail, “for the righteous falls seven times and rises again” (vv. 15–16). Do not rejoice when an enemy falls, for the LORD hates gloating (vv. 17–18). Do not fret over evildoers or envy them, for their lamp will be put out (vv. 19–20). Fear the LORD and the king, and keep away from those bent on revolt (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The righteous are not those who never fall but those who keep getting up, and they do not gloat when others fall.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste. Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is sweet to the soul as honey is to the mouth, and it brings a sure future.

Eat honey. After a heavy warning, a sweet invitation. Honey is good; enjoy it. God gave good things to be tasted.

Wisdom is such to your soul. Wisdom is like honey to the soul: sweet, nourishing, delightful. The psalmist said of God’s words, “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 119:103). Many think of God’s wisdom as bitter medicine. The proverb says: taste it, it is honey.

There will be a future. The second half repeats the promise of 23:18 word for word: your hope will not be cut off. Wisdom is sweet now, and it gives a secure future.

verseByVerse.quote: Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home; for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Plots against the righteous fail, because though they fall again and again, God raises them up.

Seven times. Here is why ambushing the righteous fails, and it must be read carefully. It does not say the righteous never fall. They fall seven times, a number meaning again and again: into hardship, into failure, into sin. What makes them righteous is not that they never go down, but that they rise again. The wicked stumble once and stay down; the righteous keep getting up, because God keeps lifting them. “Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise” (Micah 7:8).

Peter rose again. Peter fell as badly as a disciple can fall, denying Jesus three times. But Jesus had said to him beforehand, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). He rose. If you have fallen, perhaps for the seventh time, the question is not whether you fell but whether you will rise. And the one who prayed for Peter prays for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not take pleasure in an enemy’s downfall, because God is displeased with gloating.

Do not rejoice. The natural response when an enemy comes to disaster is satisfaction: “He got what he deserved.” The proverb forbids even the inner gladness: let not your heart be glad. It is a remarkable command for the Old Testament, and it points straight to Jesus: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

Lest the LORD see it. The second line is surprising. If you gloat, God may be so displeased that he turns his anger away from your enemy, and perhaps towards you. The point is not that we should hide our gladness to make sure the enemy suffers. It is that gloating over someone’s fall is itself an ugly sin, which God will not reward. God himself says, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11). Neither should we.

verseByVerse.quote: Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked, for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not burn with anger or envy at the success of evildoers, because they have no future.

Fret not yourself. This echoes Psalm 37: “Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers!” (Psalm 37:1). To fret is to get heated and anxious, to lie awake angry that the wicked are doing well. It burns the fretter, not the wicked.

No future. Whatever the evil man has now, it ends (compare 13:9). The righteous have a future that will not be cut off (v. 14); the wicked have only a present. There is nothing there to envy.

What to do when fretting starts. Psalm 37 gives the steps. Turn from the feed. If the news, or a former colleague’s holiday photos, keeps you stewing over who is getting away with it, stop looking for a while. Take the complaint into God’s presence. Asaph was nearly lost “until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17). Say to God what is eating you, and then read what he says about how it ends: the lamp of the wicked will be put out (v. 20). Do the next good thing. “Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land and befriend faithfulness” (Psalm 37:3). Fretting fixes your eyes on someone else’s field; work your own. Be still and wait. “Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way” (Psalm 37:7). The cross is why that is not wishful thinking. There the wicked seemed to win completely, and on the third day God raised the Righteous One. The future promised to the righteous in verse 14 is secured in him.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise, for disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear God first, respect rightful authority, and keep away from rebels.

Fear the LORD and the king. The fear of the LORD comes first, and then respect for rightful authority. Peter says the same, in the same order: “Fear God. Honor the emperor” (1 Peter 2:17). “Pay to all what is owed to them”, “respect to whom respect is owed” (Romans 13:7).

Disaster will arise suddenly. Those who rebel against God and rightful authority bring sudden disaster on themselves, and on those who join them. Keep away from the revolt.

Must we obey every government? We honour and obey rulers (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:17), but the LORD comes first: when a ruler commands sin, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29; compare Daniel 3). The verse warns against rebellion, not against refusing to sin.

Uncertain wording. Those who do otherwise is literally “those who change” (KJV “them that are given to change”), most likely rebels. The both of verse 22 may mean the LORD and the king, or both kinds of rebel. Either way, revolt ends in disaster.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A short appendix of “sayings of the wise” (v. 23) teaches honest justice and faithful work. Partiality in judging is wrong: calling the wicked righteous brings curses, while rebuking them brings blessing (vv. 23–25). An honest answer is like a kiss, and a wise person puts the field in order before building the house (vv. 26–27). Do not bear false witness against a neighbour or plan to pay him back (vv. 28–29). The chapter ends with an eyewitness story: a sluggard’s vineyard overgrown with thorns and its wall broken down, and the lesson that ruin comes by “a little sleep, a little slumber” (vv. 30–34).
verseByVerse.theology: Honest words and ordered work build a life; neglect lets thorns take it over quietly.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are sayings of the wise. Partiality in judging is not good. Whoever says to the wicked, "You are in the right," will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations, but those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Justice must be impartial: calling the guilty innocent brings a curse, while honest rebuke brings blessing.

Partiality in judging. A new heading introduces a short appendix of further sayings. The first is about justice: a judge must not play favourites. The law said, “You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17). That applies wherever anyone judges others: the parent between children, the teacher marking work, the church leader settling a dispute.

“You are in the right.” A judge who acquits the guilty is not merely wrong; he is cursed by peoples. Calling evil good destroys public trust.

Those who rebuke the wicked. The one with the courage to tell the guilty they are in the wrong is blessed. Honest judgment takes courage, and God honours it.
verseByVerse.note: Another short collection of “sayings of the wise” (24:23–34).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips. Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An honest answer is an act of friendship, and wise people secure their living before they build their house.

An honest answer. An honest answer is like a kiss, a sign of true friendship: honesty is a form of love. The friend who gently tells you the truth is showing you love.

Prepare your work outside. First the field, which provides a living; then the house. Do not build the beautiful home before you have the income to support it. Jesus asked, “which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost” (Luke 14:28)?

verseByVerse.quote: Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips. Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not speak falsely against a neighbour, and do not plan to pay him back for what he has done.

Be not a witness. This is the ninth commandment in proverb form: do not testify against a neighbour without cause, or deceive with your lips.

As he has done to me. The voice of revenge sounds reasonable, even like justice. The proverb forbids even saying, “I will do to him as he has done to me.” Personal revenge is not ours to take (compare 20:22).

The golden rule. Jesus turned this completely around. Not “do to him as he has done to me”, but “whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them” (Matthew 7:12). The golden rule is the opposite of revenge. “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17). And Christ lived it: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down. Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A neglected vineyard falls to ruin without any enemy, and the wise learn from what they see.

The field of a sluggard. The chapter ends with an eyewitness story, like the father’s in chapter 7. The vineyard is overgrown with thorns, and with the wall down, animals and thieves could get in.

Neglect needs no action. No enemy had attacked the vineyard. No drought had struck. It had simply been left alone, and that is the terrifying thing about neglect: it requires no action at all. Thorns grow by themselves; walls fall by themselves. A marriage left untended, a prayer life abandoned, a child not taught, a body not cared for, a faith not fed: none needs to be attacked to be ruined. It only needs to be left.

I saw and considered it. He did not just see a mess and walk on. He considered it and received instruction. Wise people learn from what they see in other people’s lives. Is there a neglected vineyard you have watched fall apart, and what did it teach you about your own?

verseByVerse.quote: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruin comes not by one big decision but by small postponements, and then it arrives suddenly.

A little sleep. The ruin of the vineyard did not come from one big decision to let it go. It came from a little sleep, a little slumber, a little rest: every day a small postponement, every season the work put off a bit longer. The words repeat 6:10–11 almost exactly.

Like a robber. And one day poverty arrives, sudden and unstoppable. The sluggard is surprised. No one who walked past his vineyard is.

In everyday life. What is the vineyard in your life where the wall is starting to crumble? Today, with the Lord’s help, is a better day than tomorrow to pull the first thorn and lay the first stone back in place.
verseByVerse.note: Repeats 6:10–11.

24.theology:
Wisdom builds lasting homes (vv. 3-4). Human strength fails in adversity, but God gives strength to the faint (v. 10; Isa 40:29-31; 2 Cor 12:9-10). God holds people responsible for rescuing those in mortal danger and sees through the excuse that we did not know (vv. 11-12; Jas 4:17).

The righteous are marked not by never falling but by rising again through God's grace (v. 16; Mic 7:8; Luke 22:32). Gloating over an enemy's fall displeases God (vv. 17-18; Ezek 33:11; Matt 5:44). Revenge is forbidden (v. 29; Matt 7:12). Neglect alone brings ruin (vv. 30-34).

The rising of the righteous (v. 16) rests on more than their own toughness. The Righteous One himself went down into death for the unrighteous and was raised (Acts 3:14–15; 1 Pet 3:18), and because he rose, those who are his will rise too, from every fall and at last from the grave (1 Cor 15:20–22). He is also the one who did what verse 11 commands: he came to rescue those being led away to death.
24.examples:
Picture rooms filled with riches that are precious and pleasant, and strength found out on the day of adversity. Hear the excuse "We didn't know," and notice the quiet gladness that rises when an enemy stumbles.

Then remember Peter, who fell and rose; an honest answer given like a kiss; the field prepared before the house; and the vineyard ruined without any enemy at all.

keyVerse.quote: for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity.
keyVerse.note: The verse explains why plots against the righteous fail, and it is honest: the righteous fall again and again, yet God keeps raising them. It holds out hope to every believer who has fallen, and finds its fullest meaning in the risen Christ, in whom his people rise.

24.reflection:
“By wisdom a house is built” (v. 3). What “precious and pleasant riches” do you want to fill your home with, and what would it take to build that by wisdom rather than money or effort alone?

“Rescue those who are being taken away to death” (v. 11). Who within your reach is being led towards harm or death, and what would it mean not to say, “we did not know this” (v. 12)?

“The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (v. 16). How does this verse, and Christ’s prayer for Peter, speak to someone who feels he has fallen too often to get up?

The sluggard’s vineyard was ruined by “a little sleep, a little slumber” (v. 33). Where in your life, whether prayer, marriage, children, health or work, is the wall beginning to crumble, and what is the first stone to set back?

25.title: A Word Fitly Spoken
25.text: <sup>1</sup>These also are proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.<sup>2</sup>It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.<sup>3</sup>As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable.<sup>4</sup>Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel;<sup>5</sup>take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.<sup>6</sup>Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great,<sup>7</sup>for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be put lower in the presence of a noble. What your eyes have seen<sup>8</sup>do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame?<sup>9</sup>Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal another's secret,<sup>10</sup>lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end.<sup>11</sup>A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver.<sup>12</sup>Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear.<sup>13</sup>Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters.<sup>14</sup>Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.<sup>15</sup>With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone.<sup>16</sup>If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it.<sup>17</sup>Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you.<sup>18</sup>A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow.<sup>19</sup>Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips.<sup>20</sup>Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda.<sup>21</sup>If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink,<sup>22</sup>for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.<sup>23</sup>The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks.<sup>24</sup>It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.<sup>25</sup>Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.<sup>26</sup>Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.<sup>27</sup>It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory.<sup>28</sup>A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls.
25.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 25 opens a new collection, proverbs of Solomon “which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied” (v. 1), running to the end of chapter 29. After the words of the wise (22:17–24:34), we are back at court, among kings, nobles, messengers and neighbours.

The message. Wisdom is fitness: the right word at the right moment, the right place at the table, the right measure of a good thing, and the self-control that makes all of these possible. Pride, haste, gossip, false witness and the unguarded heart all spoil what could have been golden. And the most fitting answer of all is the one no one expects: bread for a hungry enemy (vv. 21–22).

Why it was said. Hezekiah was a king who “trusted in the LORD” (2 Kings 18:5) and set about renewing Judah’s worship and life; gathering Solomon’s wisdom for a new generation of officials and households was part of that work (see the introduction). These sayings trained men who would stand before kings, carry messages, settle disputes and live close to their neighbours.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the court: God’s glory in what he hides and a king’s in what he searches out, a throne cleared of the wicked, humility that waits to be called up, and disputes settled quietly and in person (vv. 1–10). Then a string of pictures about words and the people who speak them: golden apples, cold snow at harvest, rainless clouds, a soft tongue that breaks bone, honey in measure, and the false witness, the faithless friend and the tactless singer (vv. 11–20). Last, the surprising kindness that heaps coals on an enemy’s head, the backbiter and the quarrelsome home, good news from far away, the muddied spring, and the city without walls (vv. 21–28).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. He is the one who humbled himself and was told by his Father, as it were, “Come up here” (vv. 6–7; Philippians 2:8–9), and whose words were always fitly spoken (v. 11; Isaiah 50:4). Above all, verses 21–22 describe what God did in his Son: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The hungry enemy he fed was us.

For us. Ask where your words have been true but unfitting, where you have pushed yourself forward, or where your walls are down. Then take the bread to the person who has wronged you, not to win, but because you were once God’s enemy and he fed you with his own Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Glory of Kings and the Wisdom of Restraint
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: True greatness belongs first to God, then to kings who serve justice, and it is never seized by pushing yourself forward. God is glorious in what he hides, a king in searching it out, and even a king’s heart is beyond his subjects’ reach (vv. 2–3). A throne lasts when the wicked are cleared away from it, as dross from silver (vv. 4–5). So do not claim the place of the great; wait to be called up (vv. 6–7). And when you have a grievance, do not rush to court or betray a secret to win, but take it to your neighbour himself (vv. 7–10).
verseByVerse.theology: God's glory hides what is too deep for us; human wisdom searches, waits to be honoured, and settles disputes privately.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hezekiah’s men gathered and preserved more of Solomon’s wisdom for a new generation.

The men of Hezekiah. A new collection begins (chapters 25–29). Hezekiah, king of Judah more than two centuries after Solomon, had men at his court gather and copy out further proverbs of Solomon. He was one of Judah’s most faithful kings: “He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel”, and “held fast to the LORD” (2 Kings 18:5–6). Part of his reformation was preserving God’s word for the next generation.

A debt to faithful copyists. The men of Hezekiah are unnamed, but every reader of these chapters owes them a debt. Faithful copying, preserving and passing on of Scripture is an act of love for people not yet born.
verseByVerse.note: Hezekiah reigned about 715–686 BC, more than two centuries after Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out. As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable. Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel; take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is glorious in what he hides, a king in what he searches out, and a throne lasts only when the wicked are removed.

The glory of God to conceal. God is glorious in what he hides: the depths of his purposes, the reasons for suffering, the workings of providence we cannot trace. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us” (Deuteronomy 29:29). “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33).

The glory of kings is to search things out. A ruler is glorious in searching out: investigating a case, discovering the truth, understanding his realm. God does not need to search; kings must, because they do not know. So a believer may be humble about what God has not revealed, and eager to investigate everything he has placed within our reach. Science, scholarship, justice and the study of Scripture are all royal work.

Does every discovery make God smaller? Many assume that each time we explain something, God loses a little ground (see the note on Genesis 1:1). This proverb pictures it differently. God hides things as a father hides treasure for his children to find, and their finding it is their glory, not his defeat. Many founders of modern science expected order in nature because they believed in a wise Creator. Explaining an engine has never done away with the engineer.

As the heavens for height. Even a king’s heart is too deep for his subjects to read. How much less can anyone fathom the heart of God.

Take away the dross. A silversmith cannot make a fine vessel until the impurities are removed, and a king cannot rule justly while surrounded by wicked advisers. Every leader should look at the people closest to him and ask whether they are silver or dross.

The secret now told. The greatest hidden thing was God’s purpose to save, “the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints” (Colossians 1:26), laid open in a crucified and risen Christ. And he is the one King whose throne has no dross around it: “the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom” (Hebrews 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be put lower in the presence of a noble. What your eyes have seen do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not push yourself into the place of honour, and do not rush to accuse a neighbour over what you think you saw.

“Come up here.” Jesus built a parable on this proverb: “go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’” And he drew the conclusion: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:10–11).

The one who took the lowest place. Jesus lived his parable. “He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:8–9). Those who belong to him can take the low seat, because their honour is secure in him.

Do not hastily bring into court. You saw something and you are sure. But what if you misunderstood, or your neighbour has a side you did not see? You may end up the one put to shame. Jesus urged, “Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court” (Matthew 5:25), and Paul told the Corinthians, “To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Corinthians 6:7). This is no reason to stay silent about crime or abuse, which must be reported; the warning is against accusing on a quick look and a sure feeling.

Uncertain wording. “What your eyes have seen” ends verse 7 in the Hebrew. The ESV takes it with verse 8; it can instead close verse 7, so that the noble is someone you have seen with your own eyes. The counsel is the same either way.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus told a parable along these lines.

verseByVerse.quote: Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal another's secret, lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take a quarrel to the person himself, and never win it by betraying a secret.

Argue your case. Take a dispute to the person directly, not to the court of public opinion, and never use another’s private information as ammunition. Jesus gave the same order: go to your brother “between you and him alone” (Matthew 18:15).

Lest he who hears you. A person who reveals secrets to win an argument may win it and lose his reputation for good. Everyone who hears him learns that he cannot be trusted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Words are powerful, for good or ill, and the people who speak them prove reliable or worthless when it matters. A word that fits is golden, and so is a wise rebuke to an ear that listens (vv. 11–12). A faithful messenger refreshes like snow-cooled water at harvest, while the boaster is a cloud with no rain (vv. 13–14). Patience and a soft tongue persuade where force fails (v. 15). Even good things, honey and friendship, need measure (vv. 16–17). Then come those who hurt: the false witness, the faithless friend, and the one who sings cheerful songs to the grieving (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Words and presence can refresh or wound, and the difference is timing, truth and restraint.

verseByVerse.quote: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver. Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word that fits its moment is as beautiful as golden fruit set in silver.

A word fitly spoken. A fitting word suits the moment, the person and the need. The same sentence can be gold in one setting and lead in another: comfort offered too soon to the grieving, correction given in public, a joke at the wrong moment. Wisdom knows not only what to say but when and how.

A wise reprover. A rebuke can be jewellery, on two conditions: a wise reprover and a listening ear.
