Gracious words. People “marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth” (Luke 4:22). Christ’s words always fitted, because he always saw the person in front of him (Isaiah 50:4).

Uncertain wording. “Fitly” renders a rare Hebrew expression, probably “in its right circumstances” or “at the right time”, and “apples of gold” may be golden fruit or gold ornaments shaped like fruit. The point is plain: a word that suits its moment is precious.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters. Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reliable messenger refreshes those who send him; a man who promises gifts and never gives them is a cloud without rain.

The cold of snow. Not snow falling, which would ruin the harvest (26:1), but a drink cooled with snow from the mountains, handed to a labourer in the summer heat. So is a faithful messenger to the one who sent him. Christ was his Father’s faithful messenger (John 17:8), and a Christian who faithfully carries his word refreshes the heart of his Master.

Clouds and wind without rain. In a dry land clouds raise hope of rain, and when none falls the disappointment is bitter. So with the man who talks of the gift he will give and never gives it. Jude uses the same picture for false teachers: “waterless clouds, swept along by winds” (Jude 12). Is there a promise of help you have not kept? Keep it if you still can; the God who keeps every promise to you forgives the ones you have broken.

verseByVerse.quote: With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Patient, gentle speech moves people whom force and anger never will.

With patience a ruler may be persuaded. Shouting at a stubborn authority usually hardens it; patience and a gentle word can wear down resistance that seemed unbreakable. Abigail turned David and his armed men from bloodshed with a humble, well-chosen speech (1 Samuel 25).

A soft tongue will break a bone. Gentleness is not weakness. Bone is the hardest thing in the body, and a soft tongue breaks it.

verseByVerse.quote: If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good things, including a friend’s company, are best enjoyed in measure.

Eat only enough. Honey is good (24:13), but too much makes you sick. Food, pleasure, entertainment, even rest: good gifts are enjoyed with thanks and with limits.

Let your foot be seldom. Friendship is sweet too, but the friend who is always at your door and never gives you space becomes wearying. Wise friends leave before they are too much.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow. Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips. Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda.
verseByVerse.commentary:
False witnesses, faithless friends and tactless comforters all wound people when they most need help.

False witness. Three weapons: one crushes, one cuts, one pierces from a distance. False testimony does all three: it crushes a reputation, cuts relationships, and wounds from far away, where the victim cannot answer.

A treacherous man. A bad tooth fails you exactly when you bite down, a foot slips exactly when you put weight on it, and a treacherous friend fails you exactly when you lean on him. Choose friends you can put weight on.

Songs to a heavy heart. Cheerful songs sung to someone in grief are like taking away his coat in the cold, or pouring vinegar on soda so that it fizzes: well meant, perhaps, but they make things worse. Christians sometimes rush to say “Everything happens for a reason” to people in deep pain. “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Often it is best to sit quietly and say little. Even at the tomb of Lazarus, knowing he would raise him, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — Burning Coals and Broken Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom shows itself in surprising mercy and in a guarded life. The chapter’s high point is kindness to a hungry enemy, which may burn his conscience and which the LORD rewards (vv. 21–22); Paul builds on it in Romans 12. Then come the backbiter who brings angry faces and the home ruined by quarrels (vv. 23–24), the refreshment of good news from far away and the dismay of a righteous man who gives way (vv. 25–26), and a closing warning: glory, like honey, sickens in excess, and a life without self-control is a city with its walls down (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Kindness to an enemy is the strongest answer to evil, and self-control is the wall around a life.

verseByVerse.quote: If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meet your enemy’s need with kindness, not revenge; it may burn his conscience, and the LORD will reward you.

Give him bread. The Old Testament here anticipates the Sermon on the Mount: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). The answer to an enemy is not revenge, nor even neutrality, but practical kindness.

Burning coals. Not a cleverer way to hurt him. The likely sense is the burning shame and conviction that kindness produces: he expected retaliation and got bread, and it sears his conscience. Kindness may melt his hostility and bring him to repentance.

Overcome evil with good. Paul quotes these verses and concludes: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:20–21). God himself did exactly this: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The hungry enemy he fed was us. Is there an enemy you could feed this week?

What it does not mean. Not that you must stay within reach of someone who is harming you. Kindness can be shown from a safe distance, and seeking protection or reporting abuse is not revenge (Romans 13:4).

Uncertain wording. Scripture never explains the coals. Some read them as judgment: if the enemy will not repent, kindness increases his guilt. Others point to an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried coals on his head as a sign of shame. Paul’s use shows that the aim is the enemy’s good, not his harm.

verseByVerse.quote: The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks. It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Backbiting brings angry faces as surely as wind brings weather, and a quarrelsome home is worse than a corner of the roof.

The north wind. As surely as a certain wind brings rain, a tongue that talks behind people’s backs brings angry faces. The people talked about find out, and the storm comes.

A corner of the housetop. Word for word the same as 21:9: better a cramped corner of a flat roof in peace than a house full of quarrelling. The book addresses sons, so it names the wife, but husbands are warned too (Colossians 3:19).

Uncertain wording. In Israel the north wind is usually cold and dry, and rain comes from the west (Luke 12:54), so some take the word of a north-westerly wind, and some older versions read “drives away rain”. The ESV’s reading best fits the second line.

verseByVerse.quote: Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country. Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good news from far away refreshes like cold water, but a righteous man who caves in to the wicked fouls the spring.

Cold water to a thirsty soul. In a world without phones a family might wait months for news of a son far away. When the messenger finally said, “He is well”, it was like cold water to a parched throat.

Good news from a far country. There is no better news from a far country than the gospel: God has sent his Son, sins are forgiven, death is defeated. “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news” (Isaiah 52:7). And Christ came from the far country himself to bring it.

A muddied spring. A spring is where people come for clean water. A righteous person who compromises his integrity under pressure muddies it for everyone who depends on him.

verseByVerse.quote: It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory. A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chasing your own glory sickens like too much honey, and a life without self-control is a city with its walls down.

It is not good. Honey again (compare v. 16), now set beside glory: sweet in its place, sickening in excess. Jesus asked, “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (John 5:44).

A man without self-control. An unwalled city was helpless before any raiding band. So is a person without self-control: anger, lust, greed, gluttony, laziness and every passing impulse walk in and take what they want.

The wall around a life. Self-control is the Spirit’s gift: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Christ had all power at his arrest and held it back for our sake (Matthew 26:53); his Spirit now rebuilds the walls in his people. Where is your wall broken down? That is where the enemy is walking in.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the second line of verse 27 is uncertain; the Hebrew is very compressed. Most translations take it, as here, as matching the first line.

25.theology:
God's glory includes what he conceals (v. 2; Deut 29:29; Rom 11:33). The preservation of Scripture is a work of faithful people (v. 1). Humility waits to be exalted (vv. 6-7; Luke 14:8-11). Disputes are to be settled privately and quickly (vv. 8-10; Matt 5:25; 18:15).

Fitting speech is precious (v. 11), and compassion must be sensitive to the grieving (v. 20; Rom 12:15). Kindness to enemies overcomes evil (vv. 21-22; Rom 12:20-21). The counsel to take the lower seat (vv. 6-7) was lived out by Christ himself, who humbled himself to the cross and was given the name above every name (Phil 2:5–11). And the God whose glory it is to conceal (v. 2) is also glorious in revealing: his plan, hidden for ages, is now made known in Christ (Col 1:26–27). Self-control is a life's wall and a fruit of the Spirit (v. 28; Gal 5:23).
25.examples: Hezekiah's scribes copy for readers not yet born; the humble guest takes the lowest seat; a fitting word is apples of gold in silver, and an empty promise a cloud with no rain. Then come the hard cases: cheerful clichés said too soon to the grieving, bread for a hungry enemy, and a life as open as a city with no walls.

keyVerse.quote: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver.
keyVerse.note: The chapter is about fitness: the right word, the right place, the right measure, and the right answer even to an enemy. This verse names that quality and shows its beauty. It also points to the one whose every word fitted the moment, who knew “how to sustain with a word him who is weary” (Isaiah 50:4).

25.reflection:
“It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out” (v. 2). How does this verse help you hold together humility about what God has not revealed and eagerness to study what he has given us to understand?

Verses 11–20 describe words that are golden and words that wound, including cheerful songs sung to a heavy heart (v. 20). Think of a time someone spoke a word that fitted your need exactly. What made it fit, and how can we learn to speak like that?

Paul quotes verses 21–22 in Romans 12 and adds, “overcome evil with good.” Who is the “enemy” in your life who might be hungry or thirsty in some way, and what would feeding him look like? How does God’s kindness to us as his enemies (Romans 5:10) change the way we see that person?

“A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls” (v. 28). Where are the walls of your life most often broken through, and how does the Spirit build them up again?

26.title: Answer Not a Fool According to His Folly
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool.<sup>2</sup>Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight.<sup>3</sup>A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.<sup>4</sup>Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself.<sup>5</sup>Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.<sup>6</sup>Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence.<sup>7</sup>Like a lame man's legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools.<sup>8</sup>Like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honor to a fool.<sup>9</sup>Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools.<sup>10</sup>Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard.<sup>11</sup>Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly.<sup>12</sup>Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.<sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!"<sup>14</sup>As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed.<sup>15</sup>The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth.<sup>16</sup>The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly.<sup>17</sup>Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears.<sup>18</sup>Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death<sup>19</sup>is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I am only joking!"<sup>20</sup>For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases.<sup>21</sup>As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.<sup>22</sup>The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body.<sup>23</sup>Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart.<sup>24</sup>Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart;<sup>25</sup>when he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart;<sup>26</sup>though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.<sup>27</sup>Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling.<sup>28</sup>A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.
26.overview:
Where we are. We are still in the proverbs of Solomon copied by Hezekiah’s men (25:1–29:27). Chapter 25 ended with the city whose walls are down (25:28); chapter 26 shows three kinds of people whose walls are down: the fool, the sluggard and the troublemaker.

The message. Folly is not a lack of brains but a way of life that will not be taught, and it ruins everything it touches: honour, messages, proverbs, friendships and peace. Yet the chapter’s sharpest warning falls on someone who looks far more respectable: “Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him” (v. 12). The deadliest folly is to be sure you need no help.

Why it was said. These sayings trained men who would appoint messengers, hire workers, judge disputes and keep peace among neighbours (see the introduction). They needed to recognise a fool before trusting him, and to recognise the fool in themselves.

How the chapter makes its case. Three galleries of portraits. First the fool (vv. 1–12): honour does not fit him, a causeless curse cannot land on you, and wisdom knows when to answer him and when not (vv. 4–5); give him a message or a proverb and the result is useless or dangerous, and he goes back to his folly like a dog to its vomit; but the man wise in his own eyes is worse. Then the sluggard (vv. 13–16), with his lion in the road, his bed, his dish and his theories. Last the troublemakers (vv. 17–28): the meddler, the “only joking” deceiver, the whisperer who feeds a quarrel, the hater whose warm lips glaze an evil heart, and the flatterer, until every pit-digger falls into his own pit.

Where it leads. To Christ, first by the need it exposes. Verse 12 sets every reader before the question of whether he knows his own folly, and Jesus said, “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). He is also the pattern the chapter longs for: he answered fools and kept silent before them with perfect judgment (vv. 4–5), and in him lips and heart always matched (1 Peter 2:22), though he was betrayed with the warmest of lips (vv. 23–26). And by promise: no causeless curse can land on those for whom he became a curse (v. 2; Galatians 3:13).

For us. Ask which portrait looks most like you, and especially whether you are wise in your own eyes. Then bring that folly to Christ, who became our wisdom. Refuse to feed a quarrel, stop saying “only joking”, and speak the truth in love instead of flattering.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Portrait of the Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Folly ruins whatever it touches, but the man wise in his own eyes is worse still. Honour fits a fool as snow fits summer, though a causeless curse can no more land on you than a darting bird (vv. 1–3). Wisdom knows when to answer a fool and when to keep silent (vv. 4–5). Give a fool a message, a proverb or honour, and it proves useless or dangerous, like cut-off feet, lame legs, a stone tied into a sling, a thorn in a drunkard’s hand, or a random archer (vv. 6–10). He returns to his folly like a dog to its vomit, and yet there is more hope for him than for the self-satisfied (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The fool is out of place in honour, useless with wise sayings, and bound to repeat his folly; only the man who is sure of his own wisdom is worse.

verseByVerse.quote: Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool. Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight. A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honour does not fit a fool, an undeserved curse cannot harm you, and a fool who will not listen must learn by pain.

Snow in summer. Verses 1–12 are a gallery of portraits of the fool. In Israel the rains fall in winter and the grain harvest comes in the dry season, so rain at harvest was so unexpected that Samuel could call down thunder and rain at wheat harvest as a sign of the LORD’s displeasure (1 Samuel 12:17–18). Honour given to a fool is like that: it does not belong, and it does damage, whether by promoting someone without character or by giving authority to one who will misuse it.

Like a sparrow in its flitting. A word of comfort among the fools. A curse spoken without cause is like a small bird darting about: it never lands. An unjust curse, slander, or a claim of spiritual power over you has no power to settle on you. When Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel, Balaam could only say, “How can I curse whom God has not cursed?” (Numbers 23:8).

The curse that did land. The curse our sin deserved was not causeless, and it did land, on Christ: he “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). So for those in him every curse is causeless now. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

A rod for the back of fools. Animals that will not respond to reason are directed by force. The fool has made himself like them: he will not listen to words, so pain has to teach him.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sometimes a fool should be left unanswered and sometimes answered, and wisdom knows which.

Answer not a fool. One of the book’s most famous pairs. Do not answer a fool on his own terms: if he shouts or mocks, do not do the same, or you sink to his level.

Answer a fool. Verse 5 says the opposite: answer him in a way that exposes his folly, or he will go away thinking he was right.

Is the Bible contradicting itself? No. It is teaching how proverbs work (see the introduction): both statements are true, and wisdom is knowing which fits this fool, on this day. Sometimes an answer would only drag you down; sometimes silence would leave a lie standing to mislead others.

Jesus did both. When the chief priests demanded to know his authority, he first answered with a question that exposed their dishonesty (verse 5): “The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?” When they refused to reply, he declined to say more (verse 4): “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matthew 21:25, 27). Before Pilate and Herod he kept a silence no fool could move (Mark 15:5; Luke 23:9). The next time someone foolish provokes you, ask not only “What is true?” but “Will answering help, or only make me like him?”
verseByVerse.note: The pairing was noticed early: the rabbis of the Talmud debated these two verses and settled the matter by applying them to different situations.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence. Like a lame man's legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honor to a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trusting a fool with a message, a proverb or honour is useless and self-defeating.

By the hand of a fool. Without post or telephone, a message travelled only as well as its carrier. Sending a fool is like cutting off your own feet: the message will not arrive, or arrives garbled, and you swallow the harm yourself (“drinks violence”). Compare the faithful messenger of 25:13.

A lame man’s legs. A proverb in a fool’s mouth is there but does nothing. A fool can quote wise sayings, even Bible verses, but cannot use them.

Binds the stone in the sling. A sling is meant to release a stone. Tie the stone in, and the sling is useless, or the stone flies back at you. Honouring a fool is that absurd.

Uncertain wording. The word for “sling” occurs only here; some take it as a heap of stones, but the sling fits the picture of something self-defeating.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fool with a wise saying is dangerous, and so is hiring someone you know nothing about.

Like a thorn. Verse 7 said a proverb in a fool’s mouth is useless; this says it can be dangerous. A drunkard waving a thorn branch hurts himself and everyone near him. A fool who wields a saying or a verse of Scripture without understanding can do real damage: condemning people who need comfort, excusing sin, justifying cruelty. Scripture in the wrong hands becomes a weapon.

Like an archer. Hiring a fool or a drunk you know nothing about is like an archer shooting at random: someone is going to get hurt.

Uncertain wording. Verse 10 is among the most obscure lines in Proverbs; older English versions made it a saying about God the Creator rewarding fools, and the ESV notes another reading, “hires a fool or passersby”. Most modern translations agree on the sense: careless hiring does widespread harm.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly. Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fool keeps returning to his folly, yet the man who is sure of his own wisdom is in a worse state still.

A dog that returns. A disgusting image, and meant to be: the fool suffers for his folly and goes back to it, the same addiction or explosive temper, again and again. Peter quotes this proverb of those who had known the way of righteousness and turned back: “What the true proverb says has happened to them: ‘The dog returns to its own vomit’” (2 Peter 2:22). What do you keep going back to? Naming it honestly to God is the first step; the Spirit Christ gives is the power to leave it.

Wise in his own eyes? After eleven verses of fools comes someone worse. The fool might one day realise he is a fool; the self-satisfied man cannot be taught, because he already knows.

Why the self-satisfied are worse off. That is why Jesus said the tax collectors and prostitutes, who knew their need, were entering the kingdom ahead of the religious experts (Matthew 21:31). “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). The most dangerous place to stand is certainty that you do not need to change, and the most hopeful is to know you are a fool who needs a Saviour. “Never be wise in your own sight” (Romans 12:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — A Portrait of the Sluggard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Laziness is finally a matter of self-deception. Four quick sketches build the portrait. The sluggard invents danger to avoid going out: “There is a lion in the road!” (v. 13). He turns in bed like a door on its hinges, all motion and no progress (v. 14). He is too tired to lift his hand from the dish to his mouth (v. 15). And he is sure he is wiser than seven men who can answer sensibly (v. 16). The last sketch links him with the man of verse 12: wise in his own eyes, and therefore the hardest of all to help.
verseByVerse.theology: The lazy man has excuses, turns in bed without getting up, tires of feeding himself, and is sure he is right.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!" As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed. The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth. The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sluggard invents excuses, makes no progress, and is too lazy even to feed himself, yet he thinks himself wiser than everyone.

“There is a lion in the road!” The first sketch is the excuse already met at 22:13: an imagined danger that conveniently keeps him at home.

A door turns on its hinges. Pure comedy: the sluggard turns over in bed, plenty of motion and no progress, fixed to his bed as a door to its frame.

Buries his hand in the dish. This sharpens 19:24. There the sluggard would not bring his hand back to his mouth; here it wears him out. Laziness grows until even eating seems too much effort.

Than seven men. The fourth sketch matters most. The sluggard thinks he knows better than seven sensible people together. He has a theory for why work is pointless and effort does not pay, and he will not be argued out of it. That links him with the man of verse 12: wise in his own eyes, and so the hardest of all to help.

What it does not mean. Not that every tired or unmotivated person is a sluggard. Depression, illness and exhaustion can look like laziness; they call for compassion and often a doctor’s help, not a lecture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–28 — Firebrands, Whispers and a Glazed Pot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Troublemakers wound with words, but evil comes back on those who plan it. The meddler grabs a stray dog by the ears, and the deceiver who says “I am only joking!” is a madman throwing firebrands (vv. 17–19). Gossip is the wood that keeps quarrels burning, and it tastes delicious (vv. 20–22). Warm words can glaze an evil heart, and a hater’s gracious speech must not be believed, though he will be exposed in the end (vv. 23–26). The chapter closes with the pit-digger falling into his own pit, and the reminder that lying and flattery are forms of hatred (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Destructive speech hides behind jokes, whispers and warm words, and it ends by burying the one who uses it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears. Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I am only joking!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not meddle in other people’s quarrels, and do not hurt people and then call it a joke.

Meddles in a quarrel. A last gallery: troublemakers. In Israel dogs were not pets but half-wild scavengers roaming the streets. Grab a passing one by the ears and you will be bitten, and cannot safely let go. So with quarrels that are none of your business. Peter lists the “meddler” alongside the murderer and the thief (1 Peter 4:15). This does not forbid peacemaking when it is invited and fitting; it forbids the busybody who wades in uninvited and makes things worse.

Like a madman. A madman hurling burning sticks and arrows does deadly harm. So does the man who hurts someone with a lie, a prank or a cruel remark, and then, seeing the damage, says, “I am only joking!”

“I am only joking!” The joker claims innocence, but the arrows still land. Paul says there should be no “crude joking”, “but instead let there be thanksgiving” (Ephesians 5:4). If you have said “only joking” after hurting someone, the words did not pull the arrow out. An apology might.

verseByVerse.quote: For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases. As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife. The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Quarrels die when no one feeds them with gossip, yet gossip is hard to resist because it tastes so good.

For lack of wood. A quarrel with no gossip feeding it dies down. Many conflicts would end on their own if people stopped carrying the stories back and forth. You may not be able to put out a quarrel, but you can refuse to be its fuel.

Charcoal to hot embers. Some people are fuel: a quarrelsome man keeps strife burning as charcoal keeps embers glowing. In the conflicts around you, do you feed the fire or starve it?

Delicious morsels. Repeated word for word from 18:8. Here it explains why the whisperer keeps finding listeners: gossip tastes good, and what is swallowed stays deep inside. So the fire never runs short of wood.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart. Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart; when he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart; though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Warm words can cover a heart full of hatred, so do not judge by tone alone; in the end the disguise will be exposed.

Glaze. A cheap clay pot can be coated with a shiny glaze so that it looks like fine ware. So “fervent lips”, warm and enthusiastic words, can glaze an evil heart. Jesus said to religious hypocrites, “you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones” (Matthew 23:27).

Whoever hates disguises himself. A secret hater may speak very graciously: “believe him not”. There are “seven abominations”, a whole heart full of them, behind the pleasant words. The psalmist knew such a man: “His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart” (Psalm 55:21). Wisdom does not judge by tone alone.

Betrayed with a kiss. The warmest of lips once served the darkest heart: “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). The one Judas betrayed is the only man whose lips and heart always matched: “neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22).

Exposed in the assembly. The disguise will not last. “Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known” (Luke 12:2). The glaze eventually cracks.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “glaze” comes from a change of vowels; the Hebrew otherwise reads “silver of dross”, a silvery coating over clay. The picture is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling. A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evil schemes come back on those who plan them, and lies and flattery, however friendly they seem, are forms of hatred.

Whoever digs a pit. “He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head” (Psalm 7:15–16). Haman, hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai, is the classic case. And the greatest pit ever dug, the cross, became the place where Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15).

A flattering mouth. The liar may seem friendly, but lying is a form of hatred: you do not deceive people you truly love. Flattery feels pleasant, but it “works ruin”, blinding people to their faults. Paul warns of those who “by smooth talk and flattery” “deceive the hearts of the naive” (Romans 16:18), and says of his own ministry, “we never came with words of flattery” (1 Thessalonians 2:5).

In everyday life. Who tells you only what you want to hear? And to whom are you doing that? Real love tells the truth, even when flattery would be easier.

26.theology:
Proverbs must be applied with discernment, not mechanically, as the paired sayings of vv. 4-5 show (Matt 21:24-27). The man who is certain of his own wisdom is harder to help than the fool (v. 12; Rom 12:16). A causeless curse has no power over those God blesses (v. 2; Num 23:8).

Hypocrisy, deceptive joking, gossip and flattery are forms of hatred that will be exposed and will rebound on those who practise them (vv. 18-28; Matt 23:27; Luke 12:2; Ps 7:15-16).

The dog that returns to its vomit (v. 11; 2 Pet 2:22) shows that folly cannot cure itself, and the man wise in his own eyes (v. 12) shows that it will not ask for a cure. Both need what the chapter cannot give: a new heart. That is the gift of Christ, who became to us wisdom from God (1 Cor 1:30), and in whom The old has passed away (2 Cor 5:17).
26.examples: The chapter is a gallery: rain on the harvest, a curse that flutters and never lands, Scripture as a thorn in a drunkard's hand, a door swinging on its hinges, a passing dog grabbed by the ears, "I'm only joking!", a fire with no wood, and glaze on a cheap pot.

keyVerse.quote: Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
keyVerse.note: After eleven verses about fools, the chapter turns on the reader with a twist. The man who is sure of his own wisdom is worse off than the fool, because he will not be taught and sees no need of help. It is the doorway to the gospel, which is good news only for those who know they need it.

26.reflection:
Verses 4 and 5 give opposite advice about answering a fool. What does this pair teach about how to read Proverbs? Think of a situation where silence was wiser, and one where an answer was needed.

“There is more hope for a fool than for” the man wise in his own eyes (v. 12). Why is self-satisfaction so dangerous? Where are you most tempted to think you need no correction?

Verses 13–16 laugh at the sluggard’s excuses. What “lion in the road” do you tend to use to avoid what you should be doing?

Verses 17–28 describe meddlers, jokers, whisperers and flatterers. Which of these does the most harm in families or churches you know, and what would it look like to starve that fire of wood (v. 20)?

27.title: Iron Sharpens Iron
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring.<sup>2</sup>Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.<sup>3</sup>A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both.<sup>4</sup>Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?<sup>5</sup>Better is open rebuke than hidden love.<sup>6</sup>Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.<sup>7</sup>One who is full loathes honey, but to one who is hungry everything bitter is sweet.<sup>8</sup>Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home.<sup>9</sup>Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel.<sup>10</sup>Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity. Better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away.<sup>11</sup>Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me.<sup>12</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.<sup>13</sup>Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for an adulteress.<sup>14</sup>Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing.<sup>15</sup>A continual dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike;<sup>16</sup>to restrain her is to restrain the wind or to grasp oil in one's right hand.<sup>17</sup>Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.<sup>18</sup>Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored.<sup>19</sup>As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man.<sup>20</sup>Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man.<sup>21</sup>The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise.<sup>22</sup>Crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him.<sup>23</sup>Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds,<sup>24</sup>for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?<sup>25</sup>When the grass is gone and the new growth appears and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered,<sup>26</sup>the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field.<sup>27</sup>There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.
27.overview:
Where we are. We are in the third chapter of the proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men (25:1–29:27). After the portraits of fools, sluggards and troublemakers in chapter 26, chapter 27 turns to the people who make us better: honest friends, near neighbours, a wise son, and the one who sharpens us face to face.

The message. You do not own tomorrow, and you cannot see yourself clearly alone, so live humbly and let others in. The friend who wounds you with the truth loves you more than the enemy who kisses you; one person sharpens another; praise tests you more than hardship does; and what has been entrusted to you, your “flock”, needs your steady attention, because riches and crowns do not last.

Why it was said. These sayings were gathered for people whose lives depended on close relationships and careful work: households, neighbours, farmers and herdsmen, in a world where a bad harvest or a broken friendship could mean ruin (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First, humility and true friendship (vv. 1–10): do not boast about tomorrow or praise yourself; a fool’s provocation and jealousy are crushing burdens; faithful wounds are better than an enemy’s kisses; stay in your nest, and keep old friends and near neighbours. Then life face to face (vv. 11–22): a wise son gladdens his father, the prudent take cover, loud blessings and quarrelsome homes wear us down, iron sharpens iron, the heart reflects the man, the eyes are never satisfied, praise is a furnace, and folly survives even the mortar. Last, a small shepherd’s poem (vv. 23–27): know well your flocks, for riches do not last, and faithful care yields enough.

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need the chapter exposes. He is the friend whose wounds are faithful (v. 6), who rebuked Peter and then restored him, and who says, “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19). He is the Son who made his Father’s heart glad (v. 11). He alone fills the eyes that are never satisfied (v. 20; John 6:35). And the closing poem finds its fulfilment in the Good Shepherd, who knows the condition of every one of his sheep (John 10:14).

For us. Hold your plans for tomorrow loosely, and stop praising yourself. Thank the friend who has told you the truth, and become that friend for someone else. Ask who sharpens you, and whom you sharpen. And look closely this week at the flock entrusted to you, in the strength of the Shepherd who knows you by name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Tomorrow, Praise and Faithful Wounds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Humility about tomorrow and about ourselves opens the way to true friendship. No one owns tomorrow, and self-praise is worth nothing (vv. 1–2). A fool’s provocation is heavier than stone, and jealousy more crushing than anger (vv. 3–4). Open rebuke is better than hidden love: a friend’s wounds are faithful, an enemy’s kisses false (vv. 5–6). Hunger makes even bitter things sweet, and a man away from home is a bird away from its nest (vv. 7–8). A friend’s honest counsel is like perfume, so keep old friends, and value a neighbour who is near over a brother far away (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Honest friends who wound us are worth more than flatterers who kiss us, and none of us owns tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tomorrow belongs to God, so plan humbly, and let others do the praising.

Do not boast about tomorrow. We talk about next year as if it were certain, but any day may bring a phone call, a diagnosis, an accident, or a blessing no one saw coming.

Planning humbly. This is not a call to stop planning, but to plan humbly. James takes up the point: “you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (James 4:14), and he tells believers to say, “If the Lord wills.” Tomorrow is not ours, but it is not empty: it belongs to a Father who already knows what it holds (Matthew 6:34). Is there something you are postponing, a reconciliation, an apology, a conversation about Christ, on the assumption that there will be a tomorrow?

Let another praise you. Everyone discounts self-praise; praise from a stranger with no reason to flatter means something. “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (2 Corinthians 10:18). The social media age has made self-promotion a way of life, but the proverb still stands. Even Christ said, “I do not seek my own glory” (John 8:50), and left his honour to his Father.

verseByVerse.quote: A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both. Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fool’s provocation wears a person down more than heavy labour, and jealousy is more relentless than anger.

A fool’s provocation. A provoking fool is heavier than stone or wet sand. The constant needling, unreasonable demands and pointless arguments wear a person down more than physical labour. The proverb is a kind of sympathy for anyone who lives or works with such a person.

Who can stand before jealousy? Anger is destructive, but it often burns out. Jealousy settles in and does not let go; a jealous rival or colleague will pursue a grievance for years. “Jealousy is fierce as the grave” (Song of Solomon 8:6). Jealousy that checks, controls and isolates a husband or wife is not love but danger: seek help from a wise pastor or counsellor, and if you feel unsafe, get to safety and contact the authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A friend who tells you a hard truth loves you more than an enemy who flatters you with affection.

Open rebuke. A friend who sees you walking into disaster and says nothing, so as not to upset you, has not really loved you. Love that will not risk the friendship to tell the truth is not strong enough.

The wounds of a friend. A friend’s wounds are “faithful”: they come from loyalty, they hurt, and they heal. An enemy’s kisses are “profuse”: many, warm and false. The most notorious kiss in the Bible was an enemy’s: “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48).

Nathan’s faithful wound. Nathan wounded David faithfully: “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7), and it brought him to repentance. Who in your life has wounded you faithfully? Thank them. And is there a friend who needs you to be that faithful, rather than comfortable?

The faithful Friend. Christ’s wounds are always faithful. He told Peter, “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:23), and after his denial restored him with a threefold question (John 21:15–17). “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3:19). When he wounds, it is to heal.

verseByVerse.quote: One who is full loathes honey, but to one who is hungry everything bitter is sweet. Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abundance dulls the appetite and hunger sweetens everything, and a man who wanders from home is a bird away from its nest.

One who is full loathes honey. Appetite changes how everything tastes. The wealthy can lose the ability to enjoy their luxuries, while the person who has little is grateful for a simple meal. Paul had learned “the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need” (Philippians 4:12). It applies spiritually too: people full of themselves find the gospel tasteless, and people who know they are starving find it sweeter than honey.

A bird that strays. A bird away from its nest leaves its young unprotected and is itself exposed; so is a man who wanders from his family, responsibilities and community. Some men stray physically; others stay at home in body while their heart is elsewhere. Where is your nest, and are you in it?

verseByVerse.quote: Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel. Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity. Better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honest counsel from a friend is a delight, so keep old friends, and value a neighbour near at hand over a relative far away.

Oil and perfume. A friend’s advice, given sincerely, is like perfume in a room.

Do not forsake your friend. Keep old friends, including family friends who knew your father. Long friendships are precious and cannot be replaced.

A neighbor who is near. When disaster strikes, a brother far away, in miles or in heart, is less help than a neighbour who is near. The Christian community close at hand can be closer than family in the day of calamity. Invest in those relationships before the calamity comes. And in Christ God came near: “I have called you friends” (John 15:15).

Uncertain wording. The second line of verse 9 is difficult in Hebrew. The ESV notes that it may be read, “and so does the sweetness of a friend that comes from his earnest counsel.” Either way, a friend’s sincere counsel is sweet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: We are shaped, revealed and tested by one another. A wise son is his father’s best answer to critics (v. 11). The prudent take cover, and a man who guarantees a stranger’s debt needs a pledge taken (vv. 12–13). Loud blessings at dawn and a quarrelsome home wear us down (vv. 14–16). Then the heart of the section: iron sharpens iron, and faithful service is rewarded (vv. 17–18). The heart shows the man, human eyes are never satisfied (vv. 19–20), praise tests us as fire tests metal, and folly survives even being ground in a mortar (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: People shape and reveal one another, and how a man handles praise tests him as fire tests silver.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me. The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise son is his father’s best defence, the prudent avoid danger, and a rash guarantor needs security taken.

Make my heart glad. A father’s reputation is partly in his son’s hands, and when people criticise the father, the best answer is a son who turns out wise. “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth” (3 John 4). One Son has made his Father’s heart wholly glad: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

The prudent sees danger. Word for word the same as 22:3, perhaps because it is so easily forgotten: see the danger coming, and take cover.

Take a man’s garment. Nearly identical to 20:16. A man who has guaranteed the debt of a stranger has shown poor judgment, so do not lend to him without security. In Israel a man’s outer cloak, which doubled as his blanket at night, was the usual pledge, and the law told the lender to return a poor man’s cloak before sunset (Exodus 22:26–27).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of verse 13 reads “a foreign woman”, and that a slight change yields “foreigners”, as in 20:16. The point is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing. A continual dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike; to restrain her is to restrain the wind or to grasp oil in one's right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good words at the wrong time irritate, and a quarrelsome spirit cannot be held back from outside, only changed from within.

With a loud voice. Blessings shouted at your window at dawn feel like a curse. Good words at the wrong time, or too loud, irritate, and people suspect a motive behind them.

A continual dripping. The dripping roof of 19:13 returns, with a second picture. Trying to restrain constant quarrelling is like holding back the wind or gripping oil in your fist. The proverb speaks of a wife, but the same is true of a husband, a parent or a colleague. Contentiousness cannot be controlled from outside; it has to change from inside, and that is the Spirit’s work.

verseByVerse.quote: Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People sharpen one another in honest friendship, and faithful service is rewarded in the end.

Iron sharpens iron. A blade is sharpened against another piece of iron, with friction, heat and sparks, and both pieces are changed. The ESV notes the Hebrew is “sharpens the face of another”: face to face, in real encounter, people make each other sharper.

Friendship with friction. Christian friendship is not meant to be only comfortable. There will be disagreement, challenge and correction, and a friend who never disagrees with you is not sharpening you. “Encourage one another and build one another up” (1 Thessalonians 5:11). Do you have a friend who will ask the hard questions about your marriage, your money, your prayer life, your temper? And whom are you sharpening?

Whoever tends a fig tree. A fig tree takes years of patient care before it fruits well; so the servant who faithfully looks after his master’s interests will be honoured, even if slowly. “It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops” (2 Timothy 2:6).

verseByVerse.quote: As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart shows who a person really is, and human desire, like the grave, is never satisfied, until it is filled with God.

Face reflects face. As water gives back a face, so the heart gives back the man: what he truly is, is found in his heart, not in his appearance or reputation. Looking honestly into your heart is like looking into water: you may not like the face you see. “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). Only God can change it.

Never satisfied. Sheol and Abaddon, the grave and destruction, always have room for more, and human eyes are the same: we see, we want, we get, and we see something else. “The eye is not satisfied with seeing” (Ecclesiastes 1:8). John names “the desires of the eyes” among the things that are “not from the Father” (1 John 2:16).

What fills the emptiness. No amount of acquiring brings contentment. The only thing that fills that emptiness is God himself, who gives himself to us in Christ: “whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 19 is very compressed, literally “as water face to face, so the heart of man to man”. The ESV takes it as the heart revealing the man. It can also mean that as you look into another person’s heart you find your own reflected: the temptations, fears and longings you see in others are in you too. Both readings are true.

verseByVerse.quote: The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise. Crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise tests a person as fire tests metal, and suffering alone will not drive folly out of a fool.

Tested by his praise. The first half repeats 17:3, where the LORD tests hearts in the furnace. But here the fire is praise. Success and applause reveal character as surely as hardship. Some people handle criticism well and are ruined by praise: they believe what is said about them, grow proud and stop listening. When the crowds wanted to make Jesus king, he withdrew to the mountain by himself (John 6:15).

Crush a fool in a mortar. Grind a fool as fine as flour, and his folly will still be in there. Suffering alone does not make a fool wise. Only a changed heart does, and that is God’s work (Ezekiel 36:26).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Steady, attentive care of what God has entrusted to you lasts longer than riches. The closing poem tells a herdsman to know well the condition of his flocks and herds, because wealth runs out and even crowns do not pass safely to every generation (vv. 23–24). If he tends them faithfully, the seasons keep giving: new growth, wool for clothing, goats to buy a field, and enough milk for the whole household (vv. 25–27). After a chapter of warnings, it ends on a quiet picture of contentment, and of the shepherd’s care fulfilled in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: Attentive care for what has been entrusted to you outlasts wealth, and it feeds the household.

verseByVerse.quote: Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay close, personal attention to all that is entrusted to you, because wealth and position do not last.

Know well the condition. A small closing poem to a herdsman, and its counsel is attention: know which sheep is limping, which lamb is not feeding, which ewe is ready to lamb. A good shepherd does not leave the flock to others and hope for the best.

Everyone has a flock. Children, employees, finances, a congregation, students, a business, a household. Know them well, personally, not from a distance. Paul told church elders, “Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock” (Acts 20:28), and Peter, “shepherd the flock of God that is among you” (1 Peter 5:2).

The Good Shepherd. Every such shepherd follows the Good Shepherd, who said, “I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14). He knows the condition of every one of his sheep, and where we have neglected our flocks, he has tended his perfectly, and tends us still.

What this looks like. Knowing your flock is mostly paying attention on purpose. Have a regular look. Read the bank statement, not just the balance; walk round the business or the house and see what needs mending before it breaks. Give each one time alone. Take one child at a time for a walk and ask, “What was the best and the hardest part of your week?” Then listen. Know what people are carrying. A manager who knows an employee has a sick mother will lead her differently; an elder who notices someone has missed church three Sundays can ring before the drift becomes a departure. Pray by name. Bring those entrusted to you to God one by one. You are an under-shepherd, not the chief one, and his care for you is the strength and model for your care of them.

Does a crown endure? Money vanishes and dynasties end, but a well-tended flock renews itself year after year.

verseByVerse.quote: When the grass is gone and the new growth appears and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered, the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field. There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithful care is rewarded with enough, season after season.

The new growth appears. If the herdsman has been attentive, the flock keeps providing, season after season: hay, wool for clothing, and goats to sell for the price of a field.

Enough goats’ milk. The chapter ends on “enough”: enough milk for the family and for the young women who work in the household. Not extravagant wealth, but steady sufficiency, the reward of faithful work.

How the chapter ends. After warnings about boasting, flattery, jealousy and restless eyes, the chapter closes on a quiet picture of contentment: a shepherd who knows his flock, a household fed, a life not grasping but tending. That picture is worth living toward, in the strength the Good Shepherd gives by his Spirit.

27.theology:
Human beings do not control tomorrow (v. 1; Jas 4:14). True love tells the truth even when it wounds (vv. 5-6; 2 Sam 12:7). Believers sharpen one another through honest relationship (v. 17; 1 Thess 5:11).

The heart reveals the person and is deeply flawed (v. 19; Jer 17:9); human desire is never satisfied apart from God (v. 20; 1 John 2:16). Praise tests character (v. 21). Faithful, attentive stewardship is rewarded, and it reflects the Good Shepherd who knows his flock (vv. 23-27; John 10:14; Acts 20:28).
27.examples:
The chapter's people are easy to recognise: the one putting off a reconciliation until tomorrow, the self-promoter online, Nathan with his faithful wound and Judas with his false kiss, the starving man to whom bitter food tastes sweet, and the man ruined not by hardship but by praise.

Its hopeful pictures are the near neighbour in the day of calamity, iron striking sparks to make a sharper blade, and the shepherd who knows which lamb is limping.

keyVerse.quote: Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.
keyVerse.note: The chapter is about the people who make us better: the friend whose wounds are faithful, the neighbour who is near, the one who meets us face to face. This verse sums it up. We do not grow wise alone, and the friction of honest friendship is one of God’s ordinary means of making us more like Christ.

27.reflection:
“Do not boast about tomorrow” (v. 1). What plans or postponed conversations are you holding as if tomorrow were certain? How does knowing that tomorrow belongs to God give both humility and peace?

“Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (v. 6). Who has wounded you faithfully, and how did it help you? What makes it hard to be that kind of friend, and what would help you do it in love?

“A man is tested by his praise” (v. 21). Why might success and applause be a harder test than criticism? How do you tend to respond when people praise you?

Verses 23–27 call us to “know well the condition of your flocks.” Who or what has God entrusted to you, and what is one practical way you could pay closer attention to them this week, following the Good Shepherd?

28.title: He Who Confesses and Forsakes Them Will Obtain Mercy
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion.<sup>2</sup>When a land transgresses, it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue.<sup>3</sup>A poor man who oppresses the poor is a beating rain that leaves no food.<sup>4</sup>Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them.<sup>5</sup>Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely.<sup>6</sup>Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways.<sup>7</sup>The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father.<sup>8</sup>Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor.<sup>9</sup>If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination.<sup>10</sup>Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will have a goodly inheritance.<sup>11</sup>A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out.<sup>12</sup>When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves.<sup>13</sup>Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.<sup>14</sup>Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity.<sup>15</sup>Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people.<sup>16</sup>A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.<sup>17</sup>If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him.<sup>18</sup>Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall.<sup>19</sup>Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty.<sup>20</sup>A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.<sup>21</sup>To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong.<sup>22</sup>A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him.<sup>23</sup>Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue.<sup>24</sup>Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "That is no transgression," is a companion to a man who destroys.<sup>25</sup>A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched.<sup>26</sup>Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered.<sup>27</sup>Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse.<sup>28</sup>When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase.
28.overview:
Where we are. We are in the fourth chapter of the proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men (25:1–29:27). After chapter 27’s friends, neighbours and flocks, chapter 28 widens the view to the whole land: rulers and the poor, law and justice, wealth and integrity.

The message. A life and a land stand or fall by their relationship to God and his law. The wicked live afraid, grasp at wealth and crush the poor; the righteous are bold, honest and open-handed. And at the centre stands the door through which any sinner may come: “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (v. 13). The deepest divide is between trusting the LORD and trusting your own mind (vv. 25–26).

Why it was said. Hezekiah’s court had watched the northern kingdom fall to Assyria after a long run of murdered kings and shifting dynasties (see the introduction). These sayings taught Judah’s leaders and households that justice, honesty and care for the poor are not luxuries but the foundations that keep a nation standing.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the bold righteous and the fleeing wicked (vv. 1–11): a guilty conscience runs from nothing, a land’s sin brings unstable rule, and the law shapes whom we admire, how we gain wealth and whether God hears our prayers. Then the centre (vv. 12–18): confess and forsake your sins and find mercy, keep a tender heart, and beware the ruler who preys on the poor; integrity is safe ground, while crookedness suddenly collapses. Last, faithfulness against haste and greed (vv. 19–28): steady work, impartiality, honest rebuke, honour for parents, trust in the LORD, and an open hand to the poor, ending with the righteous increasing when the wicked perish.

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise and by covenant. Verse 13 promises mercy to the one who confesses, and the New Testament shows how God can give it justly: Christ “is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2). The boldness of verse 1 is the confidence of a conscience cleansed by his blood (Hebrews 9:14). The chapter also longs, by pattern, for the righteous ruler of understanding who will not prey on the poor (vv. 2, 15–16), and that King has come: “Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end” (Isaiah 9:7).

For us. Stop running from what no one is chasing, and bring your hidden sins into the light: confess them, forsake them and receive mercy. Ask whom you admire, how you are getting your money, and where you are hiding your eyes from the poor. And trust the LORD, not your own mind.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Righteous Are Bold as a Lion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A person’s standing with God shows in his courage, his admiration and his use of power and money. The guilty flee when no one is chasing, while the righteous are bold as a lion (v. 1). A sinful land has many rulers, and a poor man who oppresses the poor is a flattening rain (vv. 2–3). Forsaking God’s law leads people to praise the wicked and blinds them to justice (vv. 4–5). Integrity is worth more than crooked wealth, and wealth squeezed from the poor ends with the generous (vv. 6–8). The prayer of one who will not hear is an abomination, and the rich man wise in his own eyes is found out (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: A clear conscience makes a person bold, and a heart that refuses God's word cannot pray.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guilty conscience runs from shadows, but those right with God can face anything with courage.

The wicked flee when no one pursues. One line looks inside two kinds of people. A guilty conscience makes every knock at the door sound like the police and every unread email like exposure. The law described that very curse: “you shall flee when none pursues you” (Leviticus 26:17).

Bold as a lion. A lion does not look over its shoulder. A person with a clear conscience before God can face threats, criticism and danger without panic. When the apostles were threatened, they prayed, and “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31).

Fear and guilt. Much fear in life is really guilt. The way to lion-like boldness is not bravado but a conscience cleansed by the blood of Christ (Hebrews 9:14) and kept clean by honesty. In him “we have boldness and access with confidence” before God himself (Ephesians 3:12). Is there something you keep running from that no one is actually chasing?

verseByVerse.quote: When a land transgresses, it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue. A poor man who oppresses the poor is a beating rain that leaves no food.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A land’s sin brings unstable government, and a poor man who gains power and crushes the poor destroys like a flattening storm.

When a land transgresses. National sin brings political instability: coups, rapid changes of government, factions fighting for power. Israel’s northern kingdom saw one dynasty after another overthrown, and Hezekiah’s court, which gathered these sayings (25:1), had watched it fall to Assyria in his own time, perhaps one reason these chapters say so much about rulers. A single wise and understanding leader brings long stability, and the Son of David is that ruler for ever (Isaiah 9:7).

A poor man who oppresses the poor. When a poor man gains a little power and uses it to crush other poor people, as a foreman, a minor official or the landlord of one room, he is like a beating rain that flattens the crops it should have watered. Sometimes the cruellest oppressors are those who have just escaped oppression themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them. Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your relationship to God’s law shows in whom you admire, and those who seek the LORD see justice clearly.

Those who forsake the law. People who have abandoned God’s standards end up praising the wicked: the ruthless businessman, the unfaithful celebrity, the cruel ruler. People who keep God’s law cannot help opposing wickedness. Whom do you find yourself admiring?

Evil men do not understand justice. Evil blinds the mind; people committed to it have found an excuse for everything. But those who seek the LORD “understand it completely”, because justice is part of who God is. The closer a person draws to God, the clearer his moral vision. “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways. The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father. Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Integrity in poverty is better than crooked wealth, and riches squeezed from the poor will end up with someone who gives to them.

Better is a poor man. Almost identical to 19:1, but now the contrast is explicitly with a rich man. Wealth gained or kept crookedly is worth less than poverty with integrity, a hard truth in a culture that measures people by income.

A son with understanding. Keeping God’s law makes a son wise, and running with gluttons shames his father. The prodigal son’s older brother said the younger had “devoured your property with prostitutes” (Luke 15:30). The friends a person keeps show what he is like.

Interest and profit. The ESV notes that this means “profit that comes from charging interest to the poor”. The law forbade exploiting a poor Israelite with interest: “you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him” (Exodus 22:25). The man who grows rich by squeezing the desperate is, without knowing it, collecting money for someone else: God will see that his wealth ends up with a person who gives it back to the poor.

What it does not mean. The target is profit wrung from the poor in their need. Many Christians, following Calvin, have held that fair interest on business loans is not forbidden; but lending that traps the desperate, as some payday lending does, stands under this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination. Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will have a goodly inheritance. A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will not hear the prayers of someone who refuses to hear his word, and those who lead good people astray will fall into their own pit.

Even his prayer is an abomination. If a person refuses to listen to God, why should God listen to him? Someone who deliberately closes his ears to God’s word while asking God for favours is not really praying. Isaiah said God would hide his eyes from those who prayed with bloody hands (Isaiah 1:15), and the psalmist: “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened” (Psalm 66:18).

What it does not mean. This is not a threat against struggling believers who pray while fighting sin. It warns the person who wants God’s help while refusing God’s word. God hears those who come humbly to him.

Whoever misleads the upright. There is a special judgment for the false teacher, the corrupt mentor, the friend who talks a believer into sin. They dig a pit and fall into it. Jesus spoke of the millstone for “whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin” (Matthew 18:6).

Wise in his own eyes. Wealth tends to make people think they are wise; look how successful they are. But a poor man with real understanding sees what the rich man is really like.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the heart of the chapter stands the way to mercy: confess and forsake your sins. When the righteous triumph people celebrate, and when the wicked rise they hide (v. 12). The one who conceals his sins will not prosper, but the one who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (v. 13). Blessed is the tender heart that always fears; the hardened heart falls (v. 14). A wicked ruler is a roaring lion to the poor, while the ruler who hates unjust gain lasts (vv. 15–16). The murderer is a fugitive until death, and integrity is safe ground while crookedness suddenly falls (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Hidden sin rots; confessed and forsaken sin is met with mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves. Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hidden sin festers, but whoever confesses and forsakes his sins will certainly find mercy.

When the righteous triumph. Good rulers bring freedom and something like a public celebration; under the wicked, people keep their heads down. The saying returns at verse 28.

Whoever conceals his transgressions. One of the great gospel verses of the Old Testament. Everyone has sins; the question is what we do with them. We can conceal them: hide, deny, excuse, blame others. And we “will not prosper”, for hidden sin festers. David described what it did to him: “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3).

He who confesses and forsakes them. Both verbs matter. Admitting a sin while intending to keep doing it is not enough; quietly changing without acknowledging the wrong to God is not enough. And the promise is certain: he “will obtain mercy”. David again: “I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5).

Will obtain mercy. The New Testament gives the same promise: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The tax collector who prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” “went down to his house justified” (Luke 18:13–14). Why can God be called just in forgiving? Because the sins confessed have been paid for: Christ “is the propitiation for our sins”, the sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath (1 John 2:2). Mercy for the confessing sinner is not God overlooking sin; it is God honouring the cross.

Why is it so hard to say “I was wrong”? We have become fluent in confessions that confess nothing: “mistakes were made”, “I’m sorry if anyone was offended”. Our culture offers two places to stand. One is denial, where guilt is an unhealthy feeling to be talked away. The other is exposure without mercy, where once the wrong comes out it follows a person for ever. Who would confess into a world with no forgiveness? Proverbs opens a third door, and only the gospel holds it open. We can tell the whole truth about ourselves, because the verdict we dread has already fallen on someone else. Confession is safe where there is a cross, so Christians, of all people, should be able to say plainly, “I was wrong, and I am sorry.”

In everyday life. Is there something you have been concealing? The way out is not to hide it better but to bring it into the light, to God and, where appropriate, to those you have wronged, and to turn from it. Mercy is waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity. Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people. A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the tender conscience, but a hardened heart, like a ruler who preys on the poor, comes to ruin.

Fears the LORD always. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the words “the LORD”: literally, blessed is the one who fears always. It describes a tender, careful conscience that always takes sin seriously. The opposite is the one who “hardens his heart”, who stops feeling guilt, listening and caring. Hebrews warns, “that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13).

A roaring lion. A wicked ruler over a poor people is as dangerous as a wild beast: tyranny preys on the weak, who have nowhere to hide and nothing to fight with. How different is the King who is both the Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:5–6), whose strength is spent for the weak.

A ruler who lacks understanding. A foolish ruler soon becomes a cruel one, while the ruler who hates unjust gain lasts. Honest leadership is not only right; it also endures.

verseByVerse.quote: If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him. Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A murderer carries his guilt to the grave and should not be shielded from justice, while integrity is safe ground and crookedness suddenly gives way.
