The blood of another. A murderer carries the weight of blood. He will be a fugitive “until death”; the ESV notes the Hebrew is “until the pit”. The proverb tells others not to shield him from justice, however sympathetic they feel.

Not beyond mercy. This is about justice in human society, not a statement that a murderer is beyond God’s mercy. Moses and David both had blood on their hands, and Paul had helped kill Christians, and all found mercy. But the gospel’s mercy does not remove the rightful demands of human justice.

Whoever walks in integrity. Integrity is safe ground. Crookedness looks solid until, suddenly, it gives way. Many collapses that looked sudden to outsiders had been building for years on a crooked foundation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–28 — Whoever Trusts in the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Steady faithfulness and trust in the LORD enrich, while haste and greed impoverish. Hard work brings bread, and haste to be rich brings punishment (vv. 19–20). Justice is sold for a crust, and the stingy man’s grasping brings poverty (vv. 21–22). Honest rebuke wins more favour in the end than flattery, and robbing your parents is destruction (vv. 23–24). The deepest divide follows: greed stirs up strife, but trusting the LORD enriches, and trusting your own mind is folly (vv. 25–26). The open hand will not lack, and the chapter ends where verse 12 began: when the wicked perish, the righteous increase (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: The deepest divide is between trusting yourself and trusting the LORD, and it shows in how you handle money and the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty. A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Steady, faithful work brings plenty, but chasing quick riches leads to poverty and judgment.

Whoever works his land. Nearly the same as 12:11, with a sharp twist. The diligent man has “plenty of bread”; the dreamer chasing worthless schemes has “plenty of poverty”.

A faithful man. Faithfulness is steady and honest over the long haul. Haste to be rich, whether through get-rich schemes, gambling or cutting corners at work, almost always leads sooner or later to doing wrong, and it “will not go unpunished”.

verseByVerse.quote: To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong. A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Justice is often sold for almost nothing, and the grasping man is blind to the poverty his grasping brings.

For a piece of bread. To show partiality is to favour one person unfairly, and the second line shows how cheaply fairness is sold. For a crust, a tiny bribe or a small advantage, a person will abandon justice. Most corruption is not for fortunes but for crumbs. Judas sold the innocent Son of God for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). What is the smallest price at which you would bend the truth?

A stingy man. The ESV notes the Hebrew is “A man whose eye is evil”, the opposite of the good eye of the generous (22:9). He rushes after money, and his grasping leads to poverty, in his wallet or in his soul, and he does not see it coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue. Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "That is no transgression," is a companion to a man who destroys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honest rebuke is valued more in the end than flattery, and stealing from your parents is destruction, whatever excuse you give.

Whoever rebukes a man. Flattery wins favour now; honest rebuke loses it. But “afterward”, when the flattered man’s folly catches up with him, or the rebuked man comes to his senses, the one who told the truth is valued more (compare 27:5–6).

“That is no transgression.” The son who helps himself to his parents’ money, telling himself “It will be mine anyway”, is fooling himself: the proverb sets him beside “a man who destroys”, for he is tearing down his own family. Jesus condemned religious leaders who found clever ways to avoid supporting their parents, “thus making void the word of God by your tradition” (Mark 7:13). Taking advantage of elderly parents, financially or otherwise, is not a small thing.

verseByVerse.quote: A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched. Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real opposite of greed is trust in the LORD, and the real mark of a fool is trusting his own mind.

The one who trusts in the LORD. Greed produces conflict: in families over inheritances, in businesses over profits, between nations over resources. The opposite of the greedy man is not, as we might expect, the generous man, but the one who trusts in the LORD, because the root of greed is lack of trust. The person who trusts God to provide does not need to grab, and he is truly enriched. “The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped” (Psalm 28:7).

Whoever trusts in his own mind. That is the definition of a fool: not low intelligence, but self-reliance. “The heart is deceitful above all things” (Jeremiah 17:9), and “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jeremiah 17:5). The wise walk in a wisdom that comes from outside themselves, and in the end that wisdom is a person: “Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

Two verses together. Put these verses together and you have the whole book of Proverbs: trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding (3:5).

Does trusting the LORD bring wealth? “Enriched” is a general pattern of God’s blessing, not a guarantee of money; the same chapter says, “Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked” (v. 6).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse. When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God cares for the generous, but those who deliberately look away from the poor bring curses on themselves; and the rule of the wicked does not last.

Whoever gives to the poor. God looks after the generous. The one who “hides his eyes”, who looks away from the beggar, crosses the street, changes the channel, will be cursed. The law said, “you shall not harden your heart or shut your hand against your poor brother, but you shall open your hand to him” (Deuteronomy 15:7–8). Looking away is a choice. Christ did not look away from us: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Where have you been hiding your eyes?

When the wicked rise. The chapter ends by repeating verse 12, and 29:2 takes it up again. God’s people may have to hide for a season, but the season ends, and the righteous increase.

Is “will not want” a promise? It is a principle of God’s care for the generous (2 Corinthians 9:8–10; Philippians 4:19), not a formula; and giving in order to get is not generosity.

28.theology:
A guilty conscience breeds fear, and a cleansed one boldness (v. 1). Seeking the LORD makes right and wrong clear (v. 5), while refusing his word makes prayer unacceptable (v. 9). At the chapter's centre, concealed sin brings ruin, but confessed and forsaken sin receives mercy (v. 13), and a tender conscience is blessed (v. 14).

The fundamental choice is between trusting the LORD and trusting oneself (vv. 25-26; 3:5; Jer 17:5, 9). God opposes the exploitation of the poor and rewards generosity (vv. 8, 27; Exod 22:25; Deut 15:7-8).
28.examples:
The guilty hear every knock at the door as the police; the poor foreman crushes the poor; integrity is sold for a piece of bread; and the beggar is avoided by crossing the street. Each is a picture of a heart trusting itself.

Against them stands David, whose bones wasted away while he kept silent, until he confessed and was forgiven. Both verbs matter: confess and forsake, and mercy is waiting.

keyVerse.quote: Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.
keyVerse.note: This is the chapter’s centre and one of the great gospel verses of the Old Testament. Everyone has sins; the only question is whether we hide them or bring them to God. The promise of mercy is certain because Christ has paid for every sin confessed to him.

28.reflection:
“The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion” (v. 1). How does a guilty conscience show itself in fear or defensiveness? What does it look like for a forgiven Christian to live boldly?

Verse 13 says we must both confess and forsake our sins. Why are both needed? Why is it so hard to say “I was wrong” without excuses, and how does the cross make honest confession safe?

Several verses deal with wealth: interest taken from the poor (v. 8), haste to be rich (vv. 20, 22) and the one who “hides his eyes” from the poor (v. 27). Where might you be hiding your eyes, and what would an open hand look like for you or your church?

“Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool” (v. 26). In what decisions are you most tempted to trust your own judgment rather than God’s word, and how could you seek wisdom from outside yourself?

29.title: The Fear of Man Lays a Snare
29.text: <sup>1</sup>He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing.<sup>2</sup>When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.<sup>3</sup>He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.<sup>4</sup>By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down.<sup>5</sup>A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.<sup>6</sup>An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices.<sup>7</sup>A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge.<sup>8</sup>Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath.<sup>9</sup>If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet.<sup>10</sup>Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright.<sup>11</sup>A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back.<sup>12</sup>If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked.<sup>13</sup>The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both.<sup>14</sup>If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever.<sup>15</sup>The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother.<sup>16</sup>When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look upon their downfall.<sup>17</sup>Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart.<sup>18</sup>Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law.<sup>19</sup>By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond.<sup>20</sup>Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.<sup>21</sup>Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir.<sup>22</sup>A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression.<sup>23</sup>One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor.<sup>24</sup>The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing.<sup>25</sup>The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.<sup>26</sup>Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice.<sup>27</sup>An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked.
29.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 29 is the last of the proverbs of Solomon “which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied” (25:1), closing the collection that began in chapter 25. Many of its sayings concern rulers and the people under them.

The message. A heart, a home or a nation stands or falls by whether it will bend to God’s correction and whom it fears. Just rulers lift a people, corrected children bring rest, and a people without God’s word runs wild. Beneath it all lies one choice: “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (v. 25).

Why it was said. Hezekiah’s men gathered these sayings for a court and a nation that had watched kings rise and fall (see the introduction). In Hezekiah’s own reign Samaria fell to Assyria, because the northern kingdom “would not listen, but were stubborn” (2 Kings 17:14; 18:9–12): a people that stiffened its neck and was broken (v. 1).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with the stiff neck that breaks and traces how character spreads outward, through rulers, flatterers, scoffers and the wise man who holds back his spirit (vv. 1–11). Then rulers, children and the word: a lying court, the king who judges the poor faithfully, the rod that gives wisdom, and the summit, that without God’s revelation a people casts off restraint (vv. 12–18). Last, the hasty, the angry and the proud, and the root of much compromise, the fear of man, answered by trust in the LORD, from whom alone justice comes (vv. 19–27).

Where it leads. Chiefly by promise and pattern. “If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever” (v. 14): no king of Judah fully met that test, but God had promised David a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:13), and Isaiah foresaw a King of whom it is said, “with righteousness he shall judge the poor” (Isaiah 11:4). Jesus is that King. The chapter also exposes our need: we all stiffen our necks, and words alone do not change a will (v. 19). And in v. 25 we see Christ himself, the one man never ruled by the fear of man, who “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), so that all who trust in him are safe.

For us. Bend when God corrects you, today rather than later. Use whatever authority you have for those who cannot pay you back. And when other people’s opinions tighten around you like a snare, remember that the verdict that matters has already been given in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stiff Necks and Quiet Restraint
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heart that will not bend to correction breaks, and a wise heart holds itself back. The section opens with its sharpest warning: the one who stiffens his neck against repeated reproof will suddenly be broken (v. 1). Then it traces how character spreads outward: righteous rulers make a people glad, a son’s loves decide his father’s joy, and a king’s justice builds up a land (vv. 2–4). Flattery and sin set traps, while the righteous sing and know the rights of the poor (vv. 5–7). Scoffers inflame a city, the fool rages without end and violent men hate the upright, but “a wise man quietly holds it back” (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology: A heart that will not bend to correction breaks, and a wise heart holds itself back.

verseByVerse.quote: He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing. When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who keeps refusing correction will one day be broken beyond remedy, and a whole people rejoices or groans according to who rules it.

Often reproved. The picture is of an ox that will not bow its neck to the yoke. It is corrected often, and each time it stiffens, until one day the neck does not bend but breaks, suddenly and beyond healing, the same words used of the troublemaker in 6:15.

A pattern many are living in. The warnings come: a friend’s concern, a doctor’s report, a wife’s tears, a sermon that lands, a conscience that speaks, and each time the neck stiffens. Judah’s history ended this way: God “sent persistently to them by his messengers”, “But they kept mocking the messengers of God”, “until there was no remedy” (2 Chronicles 36:15–16).

When the righteous increase. The same truth as 28:12 and 28:28. Pray for leaders, and if you hold any authority, remember how many people your character touches. On leadership in every sphere, from the home to the nation, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Today is the day to bend. Correction is a sign of God’s patience, and it will not continue forever. If you have been warned about the same thing many times, bend today.

Can someone pass the point of no return? This describes the settled hardening of a person who refuses correction again and again. True believers who stumble are kept by Christ (John 10:28), and anyone troubled by this warning shows they are not yet hardened. The call is to respond while it is still “today” (Hebrews 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth. By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What a young man loves decides where his wealth goes, and what a ruler loves decides whether his land is built up or torn down.

He who loves wisdom. The love of wisdom gladdens a father; the love of pleasure empties a purse. The prodigal’s brother said exactly this of the younger son: “this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes” (Luke 15:30). Yet the same parable shows a father running to meet the son who had squandered it all (Luke 15:20).

By justice a king. The one who exacts gifts may be the ruler who “taxes heavily”, as the ESV notes. Corruption and oppressive taxation drain a land of its strength, and in any sphere of leadership justice builds up and taking tears down.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet. An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices. A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flattery traps the one it praises, sin traps the one who commits it, and the righteous, free of both, sing and care for the poor.

A man who flatters. The flatterer spreads a net for his neighbour’s feet, whether he means to or not. Praise beyond the truth gives a person a false picture of himself, and he trips over it.

Ensnared in his transgression. The evil man is caught in his own sin, while the righteous man, free of that trap, sings, with a joy the wicked never know. Paul and Silas, beaten and in the stocks, were singing hymns to God about midnight (Acts 16:25): bound outside, free inside.

The rights of the poor. A righteous person knows the situation of the poor and what is legally owed to them. Job could say, “I was a father to the needy, and I searched out the cause of him whom I did not know” (Job 29:16). The wicked man does not merely ignore such things; he does not understand them, because only someone who cares about right takes the trouble to learn what the poor are owed.

Uncertain wording. In verse 5 the Hebrew does not make clear whose feet are meant. Most take them to be the neighbour’s, some the flatterer’s own; both are true to life (compare 26:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath. If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mockers set a whole community alight while the wise calm it, and arguing with a fool brings no peace.

Scoffers set a city aflame. A few mockers can inflame a whole city; the wise calm it down. In the conflicts around you, are you pouring on fuel or turning away wrath?

An argument with a fool. The wise man brings reasons; the fool rages, then laughs, then rages again. There is no resolution, no quiet. Sometimes the wise thing is to recognise that the argument cannot be won and to step away (compare 26:4).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 9 does not say who rages and laughs. The ESV takes it to be the fool; others, the wise man: whether he grows angry or jokes, there is no quiet. Either way the argument goes nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright. A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Violent men hate the upright because goodness exposes them, and the wise hold back what the fool pours out.

Bloodthirsty men. Violent men do not merely ignore good people; they hate them. The blameless man’s goodness is an accusation against them. The righteous are often persecuted not for what they have done wrong, but because their lives expose what others have done.

The Blameless One. Jesus said the world hated him “because I testify about it that its works are evil” (John 7:7). The one truly blameless man was hunted to death by those his goodness exposed, and died for them.

A fool gives full vent. The fool pours out every feeling and calls it honesty. The wise man feels the same things, but does not let them rule his tongue: “let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20).

Expressing everything you feel. Proverbs does not share the modern idea that expressing every feeling is healthy. Holding back is not unhealthy bottling up; it is wisdom, and the self-control the Spirit grows in believers (Galatians 5:23). What is held back from others can still be poured out to God, as the Psalms do.

Uncertain wording. The second line of verse 10 is compressed. The ESV notes that it may be read, “but the upright seek his soul”: the upright seek to protect the one the violent want to kill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — Rulers, Children and the Word of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nations, families and hearts all come apart without the restraint God’s word provides. A ruler who listens to lies corrupts his whole court, while the king who faithfully judges the poor has a lasting throne, under the God who gives light to oppressor and oppressed alike (vv. 12–14). At home, loving correction gives a child wisdom and his parents rest, and though wickedness spreads, it will not last (vv. 15–17). Then the summit of the section: “Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law” (v. 18). What loving correction is to a child, God’s word is to a people.
verseByVerse.theology: Nations, families and hearts all come apart without the restraint God's word provides.

verseByVerse.quote: If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked. The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ruler shapes everyone around him, one God gives light to oppressor and oppressed alike, and a throne lasts when it does justice for the poor.

A ruler listens to falsehood. A leader sets the tone. If he rewards flattery and lies, those around him learn that lying is how to get ahead.

The poor man and the oppressor. Nearly the same as 22:2: the LORD gives both sight, life and breath. He is generous even to oppressors; the Father “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45). But every morning the oppressor opens his eyes, it is by the gift of the God who made his victim too.

Faithfully judges the poor. What establishes a throne is not military strength but faithful justice for those who cannot pay for it, a test for every government and leader.

The throne established forever. No king of Judah fully met the test, but God’s promise to David reached beyond them all: “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). Isaiah saw the King who would meet it: “with righteousness he shall judge the poor” (Isaiah 11:4). Jesus came preaching “good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18), and of his kingdom “there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

verseByVerse.quote: The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look upon their downfall. Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Loving correction forms wisdom in a child and brings his parents rest, while a child left to himself brings shame; and though wickedness spreads, it will not last.

The rod and reproof. A child left to himself does not grow into wisdom naturally, for folly is bound up in his heart (22:15). Without correction he brings shame, and the proverb notes that it lands especially on his mother. Loving discipline and verbal correction together, the rod and reproof, are how wisdom is formed.

When the wicked increase. Wickedness spreads, but it does not last; the righteous will see its end. That is a word of patience where sin seems to be winning.

Discipline your son. The discipline that feels exhausting now brings rest later. The parent who does the hard work of correcting a young child will one day find peace, and even delight, in a grown son or daughter.

The Father who disciplines. Behind every faithful parent stands the heavenly Father, who corrects his children not to vent his anger but “for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). His discipline is the pattern for ours.

The rod. Here, as at 13:24, the rod is a real rod. Loving, consistent correction is required; whether to use measured physical correction with young children is left to wise parents, and where it is used it comes with reproof, never in anger or to injure (Ephesians 6:4). Anything that frightens or harms a child is abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where God’s word is not heard, a people runs wild; the one who keeps it is blessed.

A misused verse. This verse is often quoted in an older translation, “Where there is no vision, the people perish”, and applied to leadership strategy: a church or company needs a vision statement, a clear plan for the future.

Prophetic vision. The word refers to revelation from God, the word of the LORD given through his prophets. When God’s word is absent, or ignored, people cast off restraint; the same verb describes Israel running wild around the golden calf (Exodus 32:25). The ESV notes it may also mean “the people are discouraged”. The second line confirms the meaning: blessed is he who keeps the law. The contrast is not between having a plan and having none, but between having God’s word and not having it.

When God’s word is rare. In the days of Eli, “the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision” (1 Samuel 3:1), and Israel was in chaos. Amos warned of a famine “not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amos 8:11). We are not left so: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2).

Blessed is he who keeps the law. So this verse argues for faithful preaching and personal Bible reading. A society, church, family or heart that neglects God’s word loses its restraint, and the blessing belongs to those who keep it: “The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul” (Psalm 19:7).

What it does not mean. Planning is not wrong; Proverbs commends it elsewhere (16:3; 21:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — The Snare and the Safe Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fearing people traps us; trusting the LORD sets us on high. The section first shows hearts that resist good order: the servant who understands but will not respond, the hasty talker, the pampered servant who takes over, the angry man who spreads sin and the proud man brought low, while the lowly are honoured (vv. 19–23). Then it names the root of much silence and compromise, in the accomplice who will not speak and in the great saying, “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (vv. 24–25). It ends with where justice truly comes from, the LORD rather than the ruler, and with the lasting divide between the just and the unjust (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology: Fearing people traps us; trusting the LORD sets us in a safe place.

verseByVerse.quote: By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond. Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him. Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Words alone do not move a stubborn will, hasty speech is more hopeless than folly, and what is pampered will in the end take over.

By mere words. A servant may understand exactly what is required and still not do it. So with stubborn hearts: understanding is not the same as obedience.

Hasty in his words? The second line is word for word from 26:12, where it was said of the man wise in his own eyes. Now it is said of the man who speaks too quickly. A fool might learn; the hasty talker is too busy talking to listen.

Whoever pampers his servant. A spoiled servant ends up expecting everything as his right. So with children, and with our own appetites: what we pamper will eventually try to rule.

More than words. If words cannot change a will, we need not more information but a new heart, which God promised (Ezekiel 36:26) and gives by his Spirit in Christ.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the word rendered his heir (v. 21) is uncertain; it appears nowhere else in the Bible. Whatever the exact word, the point is plain.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression. One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angry man spreads strife and sin wherever he goes, and pride ends low while lowliness ends in honour.

A man of wrath. Anger does not only cause arguments; it causes much transgression. An angry man leaves a trail of sin behind him, his own and other people’s: cruel words, violence, broken relationships, bitterness in others.

One’s pride. Once more the proud are brought low and the lowly lifted up: “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10). It is a law of God’s kingdom, and Christ himself lived it perfectly, going down to the cross and being raised to the highest place (Philippians 2:8–9).

verseByVerse.quote: The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keeping silent to shield wrongdoing destroys the one who keeps it, and fear of what people think is a trap from which only trust in the LORD sets us free.

The partner of a thief. In Israel a public curse was pronounced on anyone who knew of a crime and kept silent (Leviticus 5:1). The thief’s accomplice hears the curse, stays silent, and so brings it on himself. Covering for a wrongdoer, whether the wrong is theft, fraud or abuse in a family, business or church, is sharing in it.

The fear of man. The fear of man is the power other people’s opinions have over us: the need for approval, the dread of criticism, the terror of looking foolish, the desire to fit in. And it lays a snare, trapping people into compromise, silence, people-pleasing and sin.

Loving the glory that comes from man. Many believed in Jesus, “but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it”, “for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God” (John 12:42–43). Paul refused that snare: “If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

Fear God more. The answer is not to stop caring about people but to fear God more: “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28). The one who trusts in the LORD is safe, literally set on high, out of the snare’s reach: “The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?” (Psalm 118:6).

He walked this road ahead of us. Jesus “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). The crowd’s scorn did not rule him; the Father’s will did. United to him, we share his standing, and his freedom.

How do I get free of it? Bring it to the LORD, who has already accepted you in Christ. Catch it in the act. The fear of man shows in small things: the email rewritten five times, the silence when faith comes up over lunch, the yes you meant as no. Ask, “Whose verdict am I waiting for?” Settle the first verdict first. Before the meeting or the family visit, remind yourself what God has already said: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Do the small brave thing. Say one true sentence, decline one request you should decline, and find that you survive it. Serve people instead of needing them. When you no longer need someone’s approval, you are free to love him, even to tell him the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice. An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Justice finally comes from the LORD, not from rulers, and the just and the unjust cannot be at ease with each other’s ways.

Many seek the face of a ruler. To seek his face is to seek an audience or a favour. It is right to appeal to earthly authorities, but foolish to treat them as the last word: justice finally comes from the LORD.

An unjust man. The Hezekiah collection (chapters 25 to 29) ends with a hard fact: the unjust and the upright each detest how the other lives, and cannot finally be at ease together. So do not be surprised when living straight provokes hostility. “What is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God” (Luke 16:15), and the reverse is also true: what God loves, the world often hates.

Not a permanent division. Yet for any one person the division need not be permanent. The gospel gives people who once found righteousness abominable new hearts that love it; Paul, once “a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent”, was one of them (1 Timothy 1:13). The righteous detest unjust ways, not the people caught in them, for Christ died for us “while we were enemies” (Romans 5:10).

29.theology:
Repeated refusal of correction leads to sudden ruin (v. 1; 2 Chr 36:15-16). God's revealed word is essential restraint for a people; without it, they run wild (v. 18; 1 Sam 3:1; Amos 8:11).

Leadership shapes whole societies and is judged by its treatment of the poor (vv. 2, 4, 12, 14). Self-control and humility are wise (vv. 11, 23; Jas 1:19-20; 4:10).

The fear of man is a snare broken only by trust in and fear of God (v. 25; Matt 10:28; John 12:42-43; Gal 1:10; Ps 118:6). Christ broke that snare for us, enduring the cross and despising the shame (Heb 12:2), so that those who trust him need no longer live for the approval of others. Final justice comes from the LORD (v. 26).
29.examples:
An ox that will not bow to the yoke, and believers who kept silent for fear of the Pharisees, show the two traps of this chapter: the stiff neck and the fear of man. Against them stand Paul and Silas singing in prison at midnight, free because they feared God and not their jailers.

And the chapter's most misused verse is a warning for every church: "Where there is no vision" is not about a strategy document but about the famine that comes when God's word is not heard.

keyVerse.quote: The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.
keyVerse.note: Much of the chapter is about people who will not bend, rulers who listen to lies and hearts that give way under pressure, and this verse names the root. Whoever we fear most rules us; fearing people traps us, while trusting the LORD sets us on high, out of the snare’s reach. It is the freedom Christ won for those who are his.

29.reflection:
“He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing” (v. 1). What kinds of correction do you find hardest to receive, and how can you tell the difference between God’s patient warning and mere criticism?

Verse 18 is often used to mean “every organisation needs a vision statement”. What does it actually mean, and what would it look like for your home or church to take it seriously?

Verse 14 says a throne is established by faithful justice for the poor. Where do you have some authority or voice, and how could you use it for people who cannot repay you?

“The fear of man lays a snare” (v. 25). Where has the fear of others’ opinions kept you silent, or made you say yes when you meant no? How does knowing God’s verdict on you in Christ loosen that snare?

30.title: The Words of Agur: What Is His Son's Name?
30.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out.<sup>2</sup>Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man.<sup>3</sup>I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One.<sup>4</sup>Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!<sup>5</sup>Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him.<sup>6</sup>Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar.<sup>7</sup>Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die:<sup>8</sup>Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me,<sup>9</sup>lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God.<sup>10</sup>Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty.<sup>11</sup>There are those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.<sup>12</sup>There are those who are clean in their own eyes but are not washed of their filth.<sup>13</sup>There are those—how lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift!<sup>14</sup>There are those whose teeth are swords, whose fangs are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, the needy from among mankind.<sup>15</sup>The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. Three things are never satisfied; four never say, "Enough":<sup>16</sup>Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, "Enough."<sup>17</sup>The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by the vultures.<sup>18</sup>Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand:<sup>19</sup>the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin.<sup>20</sup>This is the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have done no wrong."<sup>21</sup>Under three things the earth trembles; under four it cannot bear up:<sup>22</sup>a slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food;<sup>23</sup>an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress.<sup>24</sup>Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise:<sup>25</sup>the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer;<sup>26</sup>the rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs;<sup>27</sup>the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank;<sup>28</sup>the lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces.<sup>29</sup>Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride:<sup>30</sup>the lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any;<sup>31</sup>the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him.<sup>32</sup>If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth.<sup>33</sup>For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife.
30.overview:
Where we are. After the proverbs copied by Hezekiah’s men (chapters 25–29) comes a new voice: “The words of Agur son of Jakeh” (v. 1), a man of whom nothing else is known. His chapter is the most personal in the book.

The message. Wisdom begins by admitting how little we know. Agur cannot climb to heaven to learn of the Holy One, so he takes refuge in the word God has spoken, and asks only for honesty and enough bread. Then he looks at the world with humbled eyes, and ends by telling the proud to put a hand over their mouths.

Why it was said. Agur may have come from Massa, an Arabian people descended from Ishmael (see the introduction), a man from outside Israel who had come to trust Israel’s God. His weariness speaks to every age that has searched for God in its own strength and come up empty, and his lists to every generation that is proud, greedy and clean in its own eyes.

How the chapter makes its case. First a weary man’s confession, his riddle about the one who ascended and came down, his trust in God’s tested word and his prayer for neither poverty nor riches (vv. 1–9). Then a generation never satisfied: contempt for parents, self-righteousness, pride and cruelty, and the leech, the grave and the fire that never say “Enough” (vv. 10–17). Then four ways too wonderful to understand and four upheavals too heavy to bear (vv. 18–23). Last, four small wise creatures, four stately ones, and a final word to the proud: stop pressing (vv. 24–33).

Where it leads. Above all by the need it exposes and the question it leaves open. “Who has ascended to heaven and come down? … What is his name, and what is his son’s name?” (v. 4). We cannot climb up to God; our only hope is that he comes down. The New Testament answers in Agur’s own terms: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13). Christ also answers the generation “not washed of their filth” (v. 12), for he washes sinners clean, and he taught his disciples to pray Agur’s prayer: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).

For us. Be honest about what you do not know, and run to what God has said. Pray for truth and for enough, and watch for the appetite in you that never says “Enough”. And when you are tempted to strut, remember the Son who came down, and put your hand on your mouth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Weary Man, a Riddle and a Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom begins where Agur begins: admitting what he does not know, trusting God’s word and asking only for what he needs. He opens not with credentials but with exhaustion, confessing he has no knowledge of the Holy One (vv. 1–3). He asks who has gone up to heaven and come down, and what the name of God’s son is, a question the Old Testament leaves open (v. 4). Unable to climb up, he rests on what God has spoken, tested and true, and warns against adding to it (vv. 5–6). Then he prays for two things: to be kept from lies, and to be given neither poverty nor riches, so that he neither forgets God nor dishonours him (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom begins where Agur begins: admitting what he does not know, trusting God's word, and asking only for what he needs.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man. I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agur begins his words of wisdom not with credentials but with exhaustion: he has searched hard and confesses that he does not know the Holy One.

The words of Agur. A new voice. Massa is the name of one of Ishmael’s sons (Genesis 25:14), probably a tribe in northern Arabia. If Agur came from there, Israel’s book of wisdom has made room for a man from outside Israel who had come to trust the LORD and his word (vv. 5, 9).

Starting with exhaustion. A wise man would usually start with his credentials. Agur starts with exhaustion, and he says it to God twice: I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. Anyone who has searched hard for God and come to the end of his strength will recognise the voice.

Too stupid to be a man. The psalmist said something similar when he saw how little he understood of God’s ways: “I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you” (Psalm 73:22).

Not false modesty. This is the beginning of wisdom. Agur has seen how far beyond him God is, and he admits he has no knowledge of the Holy One, the very phrase of 9:10. The fool in Proverbs is always sure of himself; the wise man, having looked honestly at God, knows how much he does not know.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes two uncertainties in verse 1. The word rendered The oracle (massa) may be a place name instead, “the man of Massa”. And I am weary, O God follows a revocalization, a different choice of vowels for the same Hebrew letters; the traditional Hebrew text reads the end of the verse as names, “to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal”, which the KJV keeps.
verseByVerse.note: Nothing is known of Agur except what is in this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has climbed to heaven and brought back the knowledge of God, so if we are to know him, he must come down; and Agur asks the name of the one who rules all things, and of his son.

Who has ascended to heaven? Agur asks a series of questions, like those God asked Job: “Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?” (Job 38:4). Isaiah asks the same: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand” (Isaiah 40:12)? Who holds the wind in his fist, wraps the oceans like a cloak, and fixed the boundaries of the world?

Only God. The answer is: no human being, only God. We cannot climb up to heaven to get wisdom; if we are to know God, he must come down.

What is his son’s name? Agur may be speaking with irony, as God did to Job: if you know so much, tell me who he is. In the Old Testament God’s “son” can be Israel (Exodus 4:22) or David’s royal heir (Psalm 2:7), and Agur may mean no more than that. But the question stands open, waiting for an answer.

The New Testament answer. Without quoting Agur, the New Testament answers his question in his own language. Jesus said, “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13). Paul says, “He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens” (Ephesians 4:10). And Jesus said, “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27). The one who came down to bring the knowledge of the Holy One that Agur longed for has a name, and it is Jesus.

Agur the honest agnostic. The word agnostic was coined in the nineteenth century by the biologist T. H. Huxley, but the stance is far older, and Agur stands close to it. Many today stop where he begins and call it humility: if God cannot be reached by reason, the modest thing is to leave the question open. Agur agrees that no one has climbed to heaven and come back with a report. But he draws the opposite conclusion: if we cannot go up, our only hope is that the one above comes down and speaks, which is why the next verse turns at once to the word of God. So the real choice is not between proud believers and humble doubters. It is between a humility that stops at the edge of the question and a humility willing to listen if God has spoken. The Christian claim is that he has, and not only in words, but in a Son who came down.

verseByVerse.quote: Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where our searching fails, God’s word never does: he shields all who run to him, and no one may add to what he has said.

Every word of God proves true. Agur cannot climb to heaven, but he has God’s word, tested like metal in the fire and found pure (Psalm 12:6). David said almost the same: “the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him” (Psalm 18:30). The weary seeker finds rest not in his own understanding but in God’s word, every word, and in God himself.

What it means to take refuge. We usually think of refuge as a feeling of safety. In Scripture it is more like an action: you run to God and shelter behind what he has said. Ruth did it, a foreign widow with nothing, and Boaz blessed the LORD “under whose wings you have come to take refuge” (Ruth 2:12). Feelings rise and fall in the night; a promise does not.

A refuge in Christ. Hebrews makes the same link: God bound himself by his word and his oath, so that “we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18), a hope anchored where Jesus has already gone ahead of us. So taking refuge often looks very ordinary: when fear or guilt is shouting, you find one thing God has actually promised, and say it back to him.

Do not add to his words. Because God’s word is perfectly true, it must not be tampered with. Moses said, “You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2), and the last chapter of the Bible repeats the warning (Revelation 22:18–19). Treating human rules as God’s, or claiming God said what he did not, makes a person a liar. That is a sober word for every preacher and teacher, and for anyone who says “God told me”.

verseByVerse.quote: Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agur asks for two things before he dies: to be kept from lies, and to be given neither too much nor too little, so that he neither forgets God in plenty nor dishonours him in want.

Two things I ask. Proverbs seldom speaks to God directly; here a man does, and the prayer is short, honest and wise. He asks to be kept from lies, told or believed, and to be given enough.

Lest I be full. The reason is the wisest part. Agur does not think wealth evil or poverty holy; he knows himself. If he is rich, he may grow comfortable and forget God, as Moses warned: “when you have eaten and are full”, “then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 8:12, 14). The full man’s question, Who is the LORD?, is Pharaoh’s (Exodus 5:2). And if Agur is poor, he may be tempted to steal and bring shame on God’s name. So he asks God not to put him in either place, an earlier form of the prayer “lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13).

The prayer Jesus taught. Jesus taught his disciples to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11), and he lived what Agur prayed. Hungry in the wilderness, he would not snatch bread on his own terms: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

Could you pray this? Most of us would quite like to be rich, but Paul learned to say, “if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content” (1 Timothy 6:8). Would more money draw you closer to God, or further from him? Could you pray Agur’s prayer honestly today?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Generations That Are Never Satisfied
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride and greed are bottomless; they never say “Enough”. After a warning not to slander the powerless (v. 10), Agur sketches a whole generation by four marks: it curses its parents, thinks itself clean while unwashed, looks down on everyone, and devours the poor (vv. 11–14). Then come his first numbered sayings. The leech with its two daughters, the grave, the barren womb, dry ground and fire all cry for more (vv. 15–16), pictures of a greed that is never satisfied. The section closes as it began, with contempt for parents, and its shameful end (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride and greed are bottomless; they never say enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty. There are those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers. There are those who are clean in their own eyes but are not washed of their filth. There are those—how lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift! There are those whose teeth are swords, whose fangs are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, the needy from among mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not wrong the powerless; and beware the kind of people who despise their parents, think themselves clean, look down on everyone and devour the poor.

Do not slander a servant. A servant is vulnerable; a word against him to his master could ruin him. The powerless have a defender, and whoever wrongs them will be held guilty.

Those who curse their fathers. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is “There is a generation”, in this verse and the next three. Agur describes a kind of people marked by four things, the first being contempt for parents. Paul lists the same among the marks of the last days: “disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:2).

Clean in their own eyes. The second mark is self-righteousness: they see a clean person in the mirror; God sees filth that has never been washed off. The Pharisee in the temple prayed, “God, I thank you that I am not like other men” (Luke 18:11). The most dangerous sin is the one a person cannot see in himself.

How lofty are their eyes. The third mark is pride, and Agur describes it by the face: eyes raised, eyelids lifted, looking down on everyone else.

Teeth are swords. The fourth mark is cruelty: they devour the poor and needy as a beast devours prey. The portrait fits every generation, including our own.

Washed. The filth these people cannot see is exactly what Christ came to wash away. To former thieves, drunkards and swindlers Paul wrote, “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11). The first step to being clean is to stop being clean in your own eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. Three things are never satisfied; four never say, "Enough": Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, "Enough." The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by the vultures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greed is like the leech, the grave and the fire: it never says “Enough”; and whoever scorns his parents comes to a shameful end.

Give and Give. Agur’s numbered sayings begin with a grotesque, memorable image: the leech’s two suckers named as daughters. (Three, then four, is a Hebrew way of building up a list.) Some people are like that: always taking, never satisfied.

Sheol, the barren womb. Sheol, the grave, always has room. A woman longing for a child aches without end. Agur names that ache as real, not as a reproach; the childless are seen by God, who heard Hannah (1 Samuel 1:10–20) and promised the barren woman a joy of her own (Isaiah 54:1). Dry land soaks up rain and is thirsty again; fire consumes whatever it is given and wants more. Set beside the leech, the lesson is plain: greed is like the grave and the fire. Feed it and it grows. Habakkuk said of the greedy man, “His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough” (Habakkuk 2:5).

What can say “Enough”. The only thing that can quiet a bottomless heart is God himself. Jesus said, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35). Contentment is not getting enough at last; it is finding in Christ the one who is enough.

The eye that mocks a father. The eye that scorned a parent is pecked out by ravens: the scorner ends up unburied, food for birds. In the ancient world there was no worse end. God takes the fifth commandment, to honour father and mother (Exodus 20:12), seriously.

Uncertain wording. The word for leech occurs only here in the Bible; most take it as the bloodsucking leech, which fits the picture well. The ESV notes that the rest of the line may read, “‘Give, give,’ they cry”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Too Wonderful and Too Heavy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some things in God’s world are beyond understanding, and some upheavals are more than the earth can bear. Agur marvels at four ways he cannot fathom, an eagle in the sky, a serpent on a rock, a ship at sea and, greatest of all, “the way of a man with a virgin” (vv. 18–19). Against that wonder he sets the adulteress who eats, wipes her mouth and says she has done no wrong (v. 20). Then, with a touch of humour, four people who suddenly gain what they were not ready for, a slave made king, a fool well fed, an unloved woman married and a servant who displaces her mistress, and make the ground shake for everyone (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Some things in God's world are beyond understanding, and some upheavals are more than the earth can bear.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin. This is the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have done no wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agur marvels at four ways beyond his understanding, the greatest the love between a man and a woman, and sets against it the adulteress who treats sin like a snack.

Too wonderful for me. Agur, who confessed that he knew so little, now marvels at things he cannot explain: four mysteries of movement. An eagle soars through the air, a snake glides across bare rock without legs, a ship finds its way on the open sea with no road. And the fourth, the climax, is the way of a man with a virgin: attraction, courtship and the joining of two lives.

The way of a man with a virgin. Agur finds it wonderful, and it is. It is one of the great mysteries of God’s creation, not to be treated casually or cynically. Paul said of marriage, “This mystery is profound”, and that it points to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32).

The way of an adulteress. Straight after the wonder of love comes its opposite. The adulteress treats sex like a snack: she eats, wipes her mouth and says she has done no wrong. The mystery Agur stood in awe of has become as ordinary to her as a meal. The contrast between verse 19 and verse 20 is the contrast between a biblical view of sexuality and a casual one. One stands in wonder; the other wipes its mouth.

No wrong? “I have done no wrong” is the one sentence that shuts out forgiveness. The way back begins with the opposite words: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Uncertain wording. Agur does not say what the four ways have in common. Many think each leaves no trace, which would explain why the adulteress follows; others, that each moves mysteriously through its element. The word rendered virgin means a young woman of marriageable age; it is the word used in Isaiah 7:14.

verseByVerse.quote: Under three things the earth trembles; under four it cannot bear up: a slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food; an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four people who suddenly gain what they were not ready for make life unbearable for everyone around them.

A slave when he becomes king. With a touch of humour, Agur names four upheavals the earth cannot bear. A servant suddenly given supreme power, with no preparation and no character to carry it, often becomes a tyrant. A fool who has eaten well becomes insufferable: comfortable, loud and pleased with himself.

An unloved woman. The Hebrew is “a hated woman”. Once she finally marries, she may lord it over others. A servant girl who takes her mistress’s place can become proud and bitter; when Hagar conceived by Abram, “she looked with contempt on her mistress” (Genesis 16:4). Yet Scripture also shows God’s tenderness to the unloved: “When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb” (Genesis 29:31).

What the lesson is. The lesson is not that people’s positions should never change. Power, comfort and status test people, and those without the character to bear them make the ground shake for everyone. There is one Servant who could bear the throne: he took “the form of a servant” and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:7, 9), and his rule makes the earth glad, not afraid.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s creatures preach wisdom, and the last word to the proud is to stop. Four small creatures show what strength cannot buy: the ant plans ahead, the rock badger shelters in the cliffs, the locusts move in order without a king, and the lizard reaches the palace (vv. 24–28). Four stately ones walk with confidence, the lion, the rooster, the he-goat and a king with his army, though the rooster hints that some confidence is only strutting (vv. 29–31). So if you have exalted yourself or plotted evil, put your hand on your mouth, because pressing anger, like churning milk or squeezing a nose, always produces something: strife (vv. 32–33).
verseByVerse.theology: God's creatures preach wisdom, and the last word to the proud is: stop talking.

verseByVerse.quote: Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer; the rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs; the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank; the lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four small, weak creatures teach a wisdom that strength cannot buy: forethought, refuge, order and persistence.

The ants. God’s world is full of lessons from unlikely teachers. The ant is the one the sluggard was sent to study in 6:6–8: weak, but wise, because she plans ahead.

The rock badgers. The rock badger, a small furry animal also called the rock hyrax, is defenceless, so it lives among the rocks where predators cannot reach it: “the rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers” (Psalm 104:18). Its wisdom is knowing where to hide. That is the believer’s wisdom too: we are not strong, so we shelter in God our Rock, and “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

The locusts have no king. Locusts have no commander, yet a swarm moves together like a disciplined army (compare Joel 2:7–8). Ordinary people working together in order can accomplish what no individual could.

The lizard. A lizard is so small you can catch it in your hand, yet it gets into the king’s palace, climbing walls and slipping through gaps where guards keep others out.

God uses the small. Four small things, each wise in a different way: preparation, refuge, cooperation and persistence. God delights to use the small: “God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

Uncertain wording. The creature in verse 28 is not certainly known. Most modern versions take it as a lizard, probably the gecko that clings to walls and ceilings; the KJV has “spider”. The lesson is the same either way.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride: the lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any; the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four creatures move with confident dignity, from the lion to a king at the head of his army, though one of them is only a strutting rooster.

Stately in their tread. From the small to the stately. The lion retreats from nothing. Beside it walk the rooster strutting in the yard, the he-goat leading the flock, and a king at the head of his army.

The strutting rooster. There is humour in the list: the lion’s majesty sits next to a strutting rooster. Some confidence is real strength; some is just strutting, and the next two verses speak to the strutters.

The Lion who is a Lamb. Scripture’s greatest Lion is “the Lion of the tribe of Judah”, and when John turns to see him, he sees a Lamb that had been slain (Revelation 5:5–6). His majesty is real, and he used it not to strut but to give himself for others.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the word rendered strutting rooster is uncertain; it may be “the magpie” or “the greyhound”, and is literally “girt-of-loins”. It also notes that a king whose army is with him may mean a king “against whom there is no rising up”.

verseByVerse.quote: If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth. For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you have exalted yourself or plotted evil, stop talking, because pressing anger, like churning milk or squeezing a nose, always produces something: strife.

If you have been foolish. If you have been strutting like the rooster, or plotting wrong, stop and say nothing more. When Job finally saw God, he said, “Behold, I am of small account; what shall I answer you? I lay my hand on my mouth” (Job 40:4). The chapter that began with Agur’s confession ends with the same humility.

Pressing milk. The ESV uses the same word three times: pressing. Churn milk and you get curds. Squeeze a nose and you get blood. Keep pressing anger and you get strife. There is a play on words too: in Hebrew the word for nose and the word for anger are closely related, since anger was pictured as a hot, flaring nostril.

The one who did not press. Christ had every right to press his case, and did not: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). He bore our sin without a word of retaliation, and so ended the strife between us and God.

Stop pressing. Let the argument go. Agur, the weary man who knew he was not wise, ends with some of the wisest advice in the book.

30.theology:
No one can climb to heaven to know God; the knowledge of the Holy One must come down, and it has, in the Son who descended and reveals the Father (vv. 2-4; John 3:13; Eph 4:9-10; Matt 11:27).

Every word of God is true and sufficient, and must not be added to (vv. 5-6; Ps 18:30; Deut 4:2; Rev 22:18-19). Wealth and poverty both carry temptations, and contentment with daily bread is wise (vv. 7-9; Matt 6:11, 13; 1 Tim 6:8). Self-righteousness blinds (v. 12; Luke 18:11). Greed is insatiable (vv. 15-16). God uses the small and weak (vv. 24-28; 1 Cor 1:27).
30.examples:
Agur is a wise man who begins by saying he is worn out, and ends with his hand over his mouth. Between those two points he asks who has gone up to heaven and come down, and prays for neither poverty nor riches.

His pictures teach without explaining themselves: a leech with two daughters called Give and Give, an eagle's path through the sky, a woman who wipes her mouth and says she has done no wrong, a rock badger sheltering in the cliffs, and a rooster strutting beside a lion.

keyVerse.quote: Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of Agur’s words. He has confessed that he cannot climb to heaven to know the Holy One (vv. 2–4), and here he finds where a weary seeker can stand: on the tested word God has spoken, and in God himself. That word has now been spoken in full by the Son who came down from heaven.

30.reflection:
Agur begins with “I am weary, O God” and “I have not learned wisdom” (vv. 1–3). Why is admitting what we do not know the beginning of wisdom rather than the end of faith? Where do you need to say this honestly?

Verse 4 asks, “Who has ascended to heaven and come down?” How does Jesus answer that question (John 3:13), and why does it matter that God came down to us rather than waiting for us to climb up?

Agur prays for “neither poverty nor riches” (vv. 7–9). Would more money draw you closer to God or further from him? What would it look like for you to pray this prayer honestly?

The leech, the grave and the fire never say “Enough” (vv. 15–16). Where do you see a bottomless appetite in our culture, or in yourself, and how does Christ, the bread of life, answer it?

31.title: A Woman Who Fears the LORD Is to Be Praised
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him:<sup>2</sup>What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows?<sup>3</sup>Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings.<sup>4</sup>It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink,<sup>5</sup>lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted.<sup>6</sup>Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress;<sup>7</sup>let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more.<sup>8</sup>Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute.<sup>9</sup>Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy.<sup>10</sup>An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels.<sup>11</sup>The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain.<sup>12</sup>She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life.<sup>13</sup>She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands.<sup>14</sup>She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar.<sup>15</sup>She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens.<sup>16</sup>She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard.<sup>17</sup>She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong.<sup>18</sup>She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night.<sup>19</sup>She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle.<sup>20</sup>She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.<sup>21</sup>She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet.<sup>22</sup>She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.<sup>23</sup>Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land.<sup>24</sup>She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant.<sup>25</sup>Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come.<sup>26</sup>She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue.<sup>27</sup>She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.<sup>28</sup>Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her:<sup>29</sup>"Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all."<sup>30</sup>Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.<sup>31</sup>Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
31.overview:
Where we are. The last chapter of Proverbs holds two final pieces: “The words of King Lemuel”, taught him by his mother (vv. 1–9), and the A to Z poem of the excellent wife (vv. 10–31), the book’s closing portrait.

The message. At the end, wisdom has a face. A mother teaches her son that power exists to protect the helpless, so a king must keep clear of what would cloud his judgment and open his mouth for those who have no voice. Then the book shows the fear of the LORD lived out in a home: a woman trustworthy, hard-working, shrewd, generous and kind, whose worth lies not in charm or beauty but in this, that she “fears the LORD” (v. 30).

Why it was said. Lemuel, perhaps a king of Massa (see the introduction), lived where kings could indulge every appetite while the poor had no voice at court. The poem shows that the wisdom of chapters 1–9 was never abstract: it was meant to be lived in kitchens, fields and marketplaces.

How the chapter makes its case. A mother’s heart-cry to her son (vv. 1–2), her warnings against the women and wine that destroy kings (vv. 3–7), and her charge: open your mouth for the mute (vv. 8–9). Then the poem: a wife more precious than jewels and trusted for life (vv. 10–12); her willing work, enterprise and open hand to the poor (vv. 13–22); her strength, dignity and kind tongue (vv. 23–27); and her praise from her children, her husband and the city, because she fears the LORD (vv. 28–31).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the character of God. Lemuel’s mother describes a king who speaks for the voiceless; Israel needed such a King, and Christ is he: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1), and on the cross he refused the wine that would have dulled his pain (Mark 15:23). The poem shows Wisdom, who called in the streets in chapter 1, at last at home in a life; and Christ, “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), “loved the church and gave himself up for her” to present her in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27).

For us. Use whatever voice you have for those who have none. Value character above charm, in choosing a spouse and in judging yourself. Praise the faithful people in your home out loud. And let the fear of the LORD, not the weight of an impossible list, shape your work, your giving and your words.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — What a Mother Taught a King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Power is for protecting the helpless, and a king must keep himself clear-headed and pure to use it well. Lemuel’s mother begins with a cry from the heart, “What are you doing, my son?”, three times over (vv. 1–2). She warns him not to spend his strength on women, the ruin of many kings (v. 3), nor to drink, lest he forget the law and pervert the rights of the afflicted; strong drink belongs to the dying and the desperate (vv. 4–7). Then the purpose behind both warnings: “Open your mouth for the mute”, judge righteously and defend the poor and needy (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Power is for protecting the helpless, and a king must keep himself clear-headed and pure to use it well.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him: What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book’s last instruction comes from a mother to her son the king, spoken with the love of the woman who carried him and prayed for him.

The words of King Lemuel. The last chapter of Proverbs opens with a king, and with his mother. What stands out is who taught him: not a court philosopher or a prophet, but his mother. The book that began with a father saying “forsake not your mother’s teaching” (1:8) ends with a mother’s teaching written down for all time.

What are you doing, my son? The ESV notes that the Hebrew is simply “What, my son?”, three times: the cry of a mother’s heart, almost wordless. My son, the boy she raised. Son of my womb, the child she carried. Son of my vows, the one she prayed for and dedicated to God, as Hannah did with Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11). She is not lecturing a stranger. Everything she is about to say comes out of that love, and correction has the most power when it comes from someone who has plainly loved you first.

A mother’s words. That should encourage every mother who wonders whether her words to her children make any difference. Lemuel’s mother taught a boy, the boy became a king, and her words became Scripture.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that verse 1 may read “Lemuel, king of Massa”, since the word rendered oracle may be a place name, as in 30:1. If so, he ruled the Arabian people Agur may have come from (see the introduction). Nothing else is known of him.
verseByVerse.note: King Lemuel is otherwise unknown; these are his mother’s words.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king must not squander his strength on women, for lust has ruined many rulers.

Do not give your strength to women. Her first warning is about sexual indulgence. The law said of Israel’s king, “he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). David’s adultery brought violence into his house. Solomon’s many wives turned his heart to other gods (1 Kings 11:1–4).

Your strength. It is the energy, attention and vigour a man has, and it is limited. Spend it on lust, and it will not be there for the work God has given. Many gifted leaders have lost everything here.

What it does not mean. Not that women are a danger to men: the same chapter goes on to praise a woman above jewels. The danger lies in a king’s appetite.

verseByVerse.quote: It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink, lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted. Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress; let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rulers must keep a clear head, because when the powerful drink, the powerless pay; strong drink belongs rather to the dying and the desperate.

It is not for kings. Her second warning is about alcohol. Others might drink; a king must not be drunk, because his responsibility is too great.

Lest they drink and forget. A drunk king forgets the law and makes bad judgments, and those who suffer are the afflicted, the people who most depend on a just ruler. A leader’s self-indulgence is never private; its cost falls on the weakest. So too for a father, a pastor, a surgeon, a pilot: people depend on your clear head. “Do not get drunk with wine” (Ephesians 5:18).

Give strong drink. Wine has a place, she says, with the dying and with those in bitter distress (the ESV notes the Hebrew is “bitter in soul”). In the ancient world strong drink was the commonest pain relief, given to the dying and the desperate to dull their agony. The king must keep his mind clear for justice; the sufferer may be given relief. Scripture recognises a proper medicinal use: Paul told Timothy to “use a little wine for the sake of your stomach” (1 Timothy 5:23).

Jesus refused the wine. At the crucifixion, when Jesus was the one perishing and in bitter distress, “they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it” (Mark 15:23).
