The one person this verse entitled to dull his suffering refused, and went to the cross with his mind clear, bearing the full weight of our sin. He did not forget his misery; he bore it for us.

Does verse 6 permit drink as comfort? It speaks of easing the last hours of the dying and the desperate in an age without painkillers; some read it as ironic, set against the king’s duty to stay sober. It is no licence to drink away sorrow (23:29–35; Ephesians 5:18), and today the grieving need care, counsel and medicine, not drink. Anyone for whom drink has become the comfort should talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor and see a doctor; seeking help is no failure of faith. Nor do these verses forbid wine to everyone: Scripture calls it God’s gift “to gladden the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15) and forbids drunkenness.

verseByVerse.quote: Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reason for the king’s self-control is this: he must speak up and judge rightly for those who cannot defend themselves.

Open your mouth for the mute. Her third instruction is the positive one, and the reason for the other two. A king must keep himself from lust and drunkenness so that he can speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves. The mute are people with no voice: no money, no lawyer, no influence, no platform. The ESV notes that all who are destitute is literally “all who are sons of passing away”, people who could disappear and no one would notice.

Defend the rights of the poor. Open your mouth, twice. Silence in the face of injustice is not neutrality. The one with a voice must use it for those without one. Isaiah said, “seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow’s cause” (Isaiah 1:17), and James calls true religion “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27).

Our Advocate. Behind all of it stands the one who spoke up for us when we had nothing to say for ourselves: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). He did not stay silent about our case; he took it up and paid what it cost. Those who have been defended so freely can afford to spend their voice on someone else.

Whose voice can you be? Few readers are kings, but most have some voice somewhere: at work, in a church, in a community, online, at the ballot box. Speaking up is rarely a speech. Notice who is missing. In the meeting about redundancies, the planning decision or the church budget, ask who will be affected and is not in the room. Find out the facts. Speak for people accurately, not from a headline, and listen to them before you speak for them. Say it to someone who can act. A quiet word to the manager, a letter to the councillor, a vote cast with the poor in mind, does more than a complaint at the dinner table. Keep at it, and keep it kind. Go on “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15), even when it costs you a promotion or a friendship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–22 — An Excellent Wife Who Can Find?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poem works through the Hebrew alphabet to show wisdom lived out: strong, industrious, shrewd, generous and utterly trustworthy. It opens with a question, “An excellent wife who can find?”, and with the first thing to be said of her: her husband trusts her, and she does him good all her life (vv. 10–12). Then her hands: she works willingly, ranges like a merchant ship for food, rises before dawn, buys a field and plants a vineyard, and keeps her lamp burning (vv. 13–19). The same hands open to the poor (v. 20), and her foresight clothes her household against the snow and herself in fine linen and purple (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The poem works through the Hebrew alphabet to show wisdom lived out: strong, industrious, shrewd, generous and utterly trustworthy.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wife of strong character is rare and worth more than jewels, and the first thing said of her is that her husband can trust her completely, for life.

An excellent wife who can find? Here begins one of the most famous poems in the Bible. Its acrostic form (see the note) makes it an A to Z of a woman of wisdom.

An excellent wife. She is a woman of strength and worth; the Hebrew phrase is often rendered “a woman of valour”. The same description was used at 12:4, “An excellent wife is the crown of her husband”. Ruth is called “a worthy woman” by Boaz (Ruth 3:11), and she is a living picture of this poem: loyal, hard-working, generous and faithful to God. The question who can find? says such a woman is rare, and far more precious than jewels is the very comparison the book used for wisdom herself (3:15; 8:11). The book began with Wisdom portrayed as a woman calling in the streets; it ends with a flesh-and-blood woman who lives that wisdom out in a home.

The heart of her husband. The first thing said of her is not what she does but that she can be trusted. He does not worry about what she does when he is away, or whether she will waste what they have.

She does him good. Not only in the early years of romance, but in sickness, hard times and old age, all the days of her life. That is the kind of faithfulness every husband and wife can aim at.

Where Christians differ. Many read the poem as the portrait of an ideal wife, held up to young men choosing a wife and to women growing in wisdom. Others read it chiefly as a picture of Wisdom herself, the woman of chapters 1–9, now keeping house. Many in the early and medieval church read it as an allegory of the church, the bride of Christ.

This commentary’s view. The poem portrays a real woman in a real home, in whom the Wisdom of chapters 1–9 is lived out. It may remind us of the bride Christ is preparing (see the note on vv. 21–22), but turning it into an allegory would lose the dignity it gives to ordinary faithful work.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 10–31 are an acrostic poem, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands. She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar. She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She works gladly and early, goes out of her way to provide the best for her household, and cares for those who work for her.

Willing hands. She works gladly, not grudgingly. Wool for warm clothing, flax for linen: she provides for her family through skill and effort.

Like the ships of the merchant. Merchant ships sailed to far ports and returned with goods that could not be found locally. She goes out of her way to find the best for her household, looking beyond the nearest and easiest option.

She rises while it is yet night. She is up before dawn to feed her family, and she also looks after the women who work for her, giving them their portions. Her care reaches beyond her own children to those under her authority.

Not a checklist. This poem is not a checklist that every woman must match in every detail to be acceptable to God, and it was never meant to crush tired mothers. It is a portrait of wisdom lived out, a picture to admire and grow toward, not a standard of performance. Its heart is in verse 30.

verseByVerse.quote: She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard. She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong. She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She is a capable woman of enterprise: she weighs a purchase, invests for the long term, makes herself strong for work and knows the worth of what she makes.

She considers a field. She is a businesswoman: she weighs a purchase carefully, and plants a vineyard, an investment that takes years to return. The Bible’s portrait of the ideal wife is not of a woman confined to insignificance, but of a woman of real ability and enterprise.

She dresses herself with strength. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is “She girds her loins”, the picture of someone tucking up her robe to work hard or to run. She is strong, physically and in character.

Her lamp does not go out. She knows the value of what she produces; she is not naive about business. And her lamp does not go out at night: she may work late, or her household may be so well provided that its lamp never runs out of oil. Either way, her house is never dark. Compare the lamp of the wicked, which “will be put out” (13:9; 24:20).

May a wife work outside the home? This woman buys land, plants a vineyard and trades (vv. 16, 24), and her husband trusts her (v. 11). Nothing here forbids a wife’s enterprise or paid work. What the poem assumes is a household ordered in love, in which she looks well to the ways of her household (v. 27), and in which, as the New Testament teaches, her husband leads in love (Ephesians 5:22–33) and the care of the home is honoured (Titus 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle. She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same hands that spin her thread open wide to the poor: she works hard so that she has something to give.

The distaff. The distaff and spindle were tools for spinning thread: the most ordinary daily work.

She opens her hand to the poor. The same hands open wide to the poor and reach out to the needy. She works hard so that she has something to give, as Paul told believers to work honestly “so that he may have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28).

Tabitha. The early church had a woman like this. In Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, or Dorcas, “was full of good works and acts of charity” (Acts 9:36). When she died, the widows stood weeping, showing the garments she had made for them (Acts 9:39).

Open hands. Her open hand reflects the God who opens his hand to satisfy every living thing (Psalm 145:16), and the Lord who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Uncertain wording. The word rendered distaff appears only here in the Bible, and some think it means part of the spindle instead. Either way, it is a tool for spinning.

verseByVerse.quote: She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet. She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because she has prepared, she does not fear winter for her family, and her household and she herself are well and finely clothed.

Not afraid of snow. Winter does not frighten her, because she has prepared. Her household is dressed warmly in good clothes. She has looked ahead to the cold season and made ready: the wisdom of the ant (6:6–8), applied to a whole family.

Fine linen and purple. Fine linen and purple were expensive, royal fabrics. The Bible does not despise beauty or quality, and her appearance reflects dignity.

The Bride’s fine linen. There is a lovely echo at the end of the Bible. The church, the Bride of Christ, is given “fine linen, bright and pure”, “for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints” (Revelation 19:8). Many Christians have seen in the excellent wife a small picture of the Bride that Christ is preparing for himself, though the poem’s own subject is a real woman in a real home.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that scarlet may instead be read “in double thickness”; the two readings differ only in the vowels. Either way, her household is warmly clothed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Her Children Call Her Blessed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends where it began, with the fear of the LORD, now lived out in a home and honoured in the city. Her husband sits among the elders, her trade reaches the merchants, and she is clothed with strength and dignity, laughing at the time to come (vv. 23–25). Her tongue carries wisdom and kindness, and she watches over her household without idleness (vv. 26–27). Then the praise: her children and her husband rise to bless her (vv. 28–29). And the heart of it all: “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (v. 30), so let her works praise her in the gates (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends where it began, with the fear of the LORD, now lived out in a home and honoured in the city.

verseByVerse.quote: Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land. She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant. Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her husband is honoured among the city’s leaders, her trade reaches the market, and, clothed in strength and dignity, she faces the future without fear.

Known in the gates. Her husband is a respected leader, sitting with the elders at the city gate, where decisions were made. This verse about him stands in the middle of her portrait, which suggests that his standing owes much to her. A wise and capable wife frees her husband for public responsibility and adds to his good name; as 12:4 says, she is his crown.

Linen garments. She makes garments and sells them to the merchants, so her influence reaches beyond her household into the economy of her town.

Strength and dignity. Verse 22 described her clothes; this is her real clothing. Then one of the most beautiful phrases in the poem: she laughs at the time to come. She has prepared, but more deeply, she trusts. The simple who refused wisdom in chapter 1 meet calamity with terror (1:26–27); this woman faces the unknown future with laughter.

She laughs at the time to come. That is a gift worth praying for, for any reader: not a carefree ignorance of what might go wrong, but a settled confidence in the God who holds tomorrow. Jesus told his anxious disciples that “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32).

verseByVerse.quote: She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her words are both wise and kind, and she watches over her household with diligent care.

The teaching of kindness. After her hands, her mouth: she teaches, and she teaches kindly, a rare combination. The word for kindness is hesed, the steadfast, loyal love God shows his people. Some people are wise but harsh; some are kind but have nothing to say. Her words are both true and gracious, an echo of the Word made flesh, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

Older women teaching. Paul tells older women “to teach what is good, and so train the young women” (Titus 2:3–4). This is the kind of woman whose teaching younger women seek out.

The ways of her household. She pays attention to what is happening in her home, knowing its ways, as the good herdsman of 27:23 knew the condition of his flock. And she is never idle. The sluggard who filled so many chapters of this book is her opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: "Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who know her best, her children and her husband, rise up to praise her.

Her children rise up. Here is the reward, and it comes from the people who know her best. Her children, who have seen her at her worst and most tired, rise up and call her blessed. Her husband, who has lived with her for years, praises her. Public praise is easy to get; praise from your own family is earned over a lifetime.

You surpass them all. Her husband has not measured her against every other woman; it is the language of love and gratitude, the way every husband should see the wife God gave him.

Praise out loud. A husband reading this should ask whether he praises his wife, out loud, often. Children should ask whether they have ever risen up and called their mother blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Charm deceives and beauty fades, but the fear of the LORD lasts, and the woman who fears him is to be praised, at home and in public.

A woman who fears the LORD. Here is the heart of the poem, and the key to the whole book. After all the praise of her skill, strength and generosity, the poet names what made her who she is.

Beauty is breath. The word rendered vain is hebel, the breath of Ecclesiastes. Beauty is real, as breath on a cold morning is real, and it does not stay. Our culture fights this with filters, procedures and a whole industry promising to hold back the years. The pressure falls hardest on women, and not only preachers have said so; in The Beauty Myth the feminist writer Naomi Wolf argued that impossible standards of beauty keep women anxious and exhausted. Proverbs is more radical than both the advertisers and their critics. It does not despise beauty, and it does not place a woman’s worth in her face; her glory lies in something that grows while the face fades.

Where the book began. Proverbs began with its motto, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7), and it ends here, with a woman who fears the LORD. Everything in between has unfolded what that fear looks like in real life, and this woman shows it, in the kitchen before dawn, in the marketplace and with her hands open to the poor. Her hard work and generosity grew out of her fear of the LORD, as fruit grows from a root.

Good news, not a burden. That is why the poem is good news. Its standard is not an impossible list of accomplishments but the fear of the LORD, which the Spirit grows in every woman who belongs to Christ, single or married, rich or poor, gifted or ordinary. Peter says the lasting adornment is “the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious” (1 Peter 3:4), and Paul speaks of women adorned “with good works” (1 Timothy 2:10).

Give her of the fruit. Let her enjoy the fruit of her work, and let it speak for her. She is to be honoured publicly, in the gates, where the elders sat and where Wisdom first called out in chapter 1.

Well done. Her Lord will say the same on the last day: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master” (Matthew 25:21). And the gospel adds what Proverbs could only point toward: the bodies of those who belong to Christ will be “raised in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:43). No surgeon can promise that, and no wrinkle can take it away.

How Proverbs closes. The book began with a father teaching his son to fear the LORD, and it ends with a woman who did. Behind both stands the one who is himself the wisdom of God, who “loved the church and gave himself up for her”, “so that he might present the church to himself in splendor” (Ephesians 5:25, 27). The fear of the LORD begins wisdom; Christ completes it; and every life that fears him will be praised in the gates.

What if I look nothing like her? First, the poem may well continue a mother’s counsel to her son about what to prize in a wife (31:1), and it gathers the fruit of a whole lifetime into one portrait; no woman lives every line at once, in every season. Second, many faithful women are single, widowed, childless, unwell, or married to a husband who never praises them, and none of them is shut out of verse 30. Third, a woman’s standing before God never rested on her output. It rests on Christ, whose perfect life and death are counted to all who trust him, and his Well done is spoken to the faithful, not to the impressive.

31.theology:
Power is given to protect the powerless, and leaders must keep themselves free of indulgence for the sake of those who depend on them (vv. 1-9; Deut 17:17; Isa 1:17).

The book closes as it opened, with the fear of the LORD (v. 30; 1:7). Wisdom, pictured as a woman in chapters 1-9, is now seen in a real woman whose industry, generosity, strength, speech and faithfulness are the fruit of reverence for God. True beauty is inward (1 Pet 3:3-5). Many Christians have also heard in it an echo of the Bride Christ prepares for himself (Eph 5:25-27; Rev 19:7-8).
31.examples:
A mother's anxious "What, my son?" becomes Scripture, and her charge to keep a clear head for the sake of the afflicted is met most fully in Jesus, who refused the wine mixed with myrrh. Every reader with any voice is asked to lend it to those who have none.

Then the poem shows the same hands at the spindle and open to the poor, a woman laughing at the time to come, and children rising to call their mother blessed. Charm and beauty fade; the fear of the LORD remains.

keyVerse.quote: Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
keyVerse.note: After all the praise of her skill, strength and generosity, the poem names the root of it all, and the whole book closes where it began: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). What fades is set against what lasts, and the standard is not an impossible list of achievements but a heart that reveres God, which the Spirit grows in every believer.

31.reflection:
Lemuel’s mother tells her son that a ruler must keep a clear head so that he can “open your mouth for the mute” (vv. 4–9). Who in your world has no voice, and what would it look like for you to speak up for them, wisely and kindly?

The excellent wife is trustworthy, hard-working, enterprising and generous (vv. 10–27). Which of these qualities do you most admire, and how can a church honour such faithfulness in both women and men without turning the poem into a checklist?

“Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain” (v. 30). How does our culture’s pressure about appearance affect you or people you love, and how does the fear of the LORD, and the hope of being raised in glory, set us free from it?

“Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her” (v. 28). Whom in your home or church do you need to thank or praise out loud this week?
